cited.name: Adaptive Sampling (Sparse Grid)
ctx: Adaptive Sampling (Sparse Grid) is a rendering optimization that exploits coherence in projections—often introduced by sensing device blurring—to reduce computational overhead by casting a sparse grid of rays (less than one per pixel) and adaptively increasing ray density in regions of high image complexity.
It differs from uniform sampling by prioritizing high-frequency details and from pure brute-force methods by achieving savings of more than two orders of magnitude for many datasets.
It is particularly well-suited for scan-conversion methods where polygons are filtered prior to ray tracing.

cited.name: Hybrid Ray Tracing
ctx: Hybrid Ray Tracing is a method for mixing geometric and volumetric data by casting rays through the ensemble of both, drawing samples of each, and compositing them in depth-sorted order.

Unlike pure volume rendering methods that ignore geometry or pure rasterization methods that ignore volume attenuation, Hybrid Ray Tracing explicitly handles the occlusion and attenuation interactions between the two data types.

title: Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction via Orthogonal Neural Plane
abstract: Intraoperative imaging techniques for reconstructing deformable tissues in vivo are pivotal for advanced surgical systems. Existing methods either compromise on rendering quality or are excessively computationally intensive, often demanding dozens of hours to perform, which significantly hinders their practical application. In this paper, we introduce Fast Orthogonal Plane (Forplane), a novel, efficient framework based on neural radiance fields (NeRF) for the reconstruction of deformable tissues. We conceptualize surgical procedures as 4D volumes, and break them down into static and dynamic fields comprised of orthogonal neural planes. This factorization discretizes the four-dimensional space, leading to a decreased memory usage and faster optimization. A spatiotemporal importance sampling scheme is introduced to improve performance in regions with tool occlusion as well as large motions and accelerate training. An efficient ray marching method is applied to skip sampling among empty regions, significantly improving inference speed. Forplane accommodates both binocular and monocular endoscopy videos, demonstrating its extensive applicability and flexibility. Our experiments, carried out on two in vivo datasets, the EndoNeRF and Hamlyn datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. In all cases, Forplane substantially accelerates both the optimization process (by over 100 times) and the inference process (by over 15 times) while maintaining or even improving the quality across a variety of non-rigid deformations. This significant performance improvement promises to be a valuable asset for future intraoperative surgical applications. The code of our project is now available at https://github.com/Loping151/ForPlane.

cited.name: Exponential Depth Cueing
ctx: An efficient ray marching algorithm designed to accurately generate spatial-temporal points for deformable tissue reconstruction, balancing rendering speed and reconstruction quality.
It outperforms the Depth-Cueing method in PSNR (33.374 vs 31.325) and SSIM (0.907 vs 0.897) on the EndoNeRF dataset, while maintaining competitive inference speed (1.73 fps vs 1.95 fps).

The Depth-Cueing method suffers from suboptimal performance due to reliance on noisy and incomplete stereo depth data and is inapplicable for temporal interpolation due to the absence of stereo depth in certain contexts.

cited.name: Monocular Depth Consistency Loss
ctx: Monocular Depth Consistency Loss enforces geometric consistency between the depth rendered from a neural radiance field (NeRF) and depth predicted by a pre-trained monocular depth estimator.

It solves the problem of scale and shift ambiguity inherent in monocular depth priors by introducing learnable scale (\eta) and shift (\epsilon) parameters that align the rendered depth with the predicted depth.
Unlike standard L2 depth losses that assume metric alignment, this method treats monocular depth as a relative cue, allowing the NeRF to optimize its geometry without requiring metric ground truth.

cited.name: Forplane Optimization Losses
ctx: Forplane Optimization Losses are a set of regularization terms designed to stabilize the training of neural radiance fields that utilize orthogonal neural planes (Forplanes) for spatiotemporal volume representation.
They solve the problem of entanglement between static and dynamic scene components in dynamic volume rendering, where the model may incorrectly assign dynamic motion to static geometry or vice versa.

Unlike standard Total Variation regularization which smooths spatial features, Forplane losses specifically target the structural integrity of the orthogonal plane representations by enforcing spatial smoothness, temporal consistency, and static-field isolation.

cited.name: Spatiotemporal Importance Sampling
ctx: Spatiotemporal importance sampling is a strategy that assigns higher sampling probabilities to tissue pixels occluded by tools or exhibiting extensive motion ranges, and lower probabilities to stationary tissues, to improve convergence and efficiency.
It addresses the challenge of tool occlusion and stationary tissue redundancy, which exacerbate learning complexity and reduce efficiency compared to uniform sampling.

ctx: Surface Point Sampling for SDFs generates a set of 3D points distributed around the implicit surface defined by a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to serve as input for neural rendering or geometric reconstruction pipelines.

Unlike standard sphere tracing which terminates at a single hit point, this method samples multiple points along rays or within the volume to capture surface geometry and local features for subsequent processing.

It differs from its sibling Sphere Tracing with SDFs by focusing on generating a dense, structured point cloud for neural field training or rendering, rather than just determining visibility or shading for a single pixel.

cited.name: Forplane
ctx: Forplane is a method for reconstructing deformable 4D scenes (3D space + time) from monocular or binocular video by factorizing the volume into a static 3D field and a dynamic 3D field, both represented by 2D neural planes.
It solves the problem of efficient reconstruction of deformable tissues in surgical scenes, where tool occlusion and complex deformations make standard 3D NeRF approaches slow and inaccurate.

Unlike sibling methods that treat time as an independent static volume per step or use displacement fields, Forplane uses orthogonal space-time planes to reduce computational complexity from O(N^4) to O(N^2) while maintaining high reconstruction quality.

title: Fast Voxelization and Level of Detail for Microgeometry Rendering
abstract: Many materials show anisotropic light scattering patterns due to the shape and local alignment of their underlying micro structures: surfaces with small elements such as fibers, or the ridges of a brushed metal, are very sparse and require a high spatial resolution to be properly represented as a volume. The acquisition of voxel data from such objects is a time and memory-intensive task, and most rendering approaches require an additional Level-of-Detail (LoD) data structure to aggregate the visual appearance, as observed from multiple distances, in order to reduce the number of samples computed per pixel (E.g.: MIP mapping). In this work we introduce first, an efficient parallel voxelization method designed to facilitate fast data aggregation at multiple resolution levels, and second, a novel representation based on hierarchical SGGX clustering that provides better accuracy than baseline methods. We validate our approach with a CUDA-based implementation of the voxelizer, tested both on triangle meshes and volumetric fabrics modeled with explicit fibers. Finally, we show the results generated with a path tracer based on the proposed LoD rendering model.

ctx: Unidirectional Path Tracing is a Monte Carlo method for simulating light transport in participating media by extending classical path tracing to allow rays to enter volumetric regions, sample scattering events, and continue random walks.

ctx: Voxel Grid Indexing maps 3D voxel coordinates (i, j, k) to a 1D linear memory index and vice versa, enabling efficient random access to dense volumetric data stored in contiguous arrays.

cited.name: Sparse Voxel Tree (SVO Tree)
ctx: A Sparse Voxel Tree (SVO) is a hierarchical data structure for sparse voxel grids where the 3D domain is recursively subdivided, and each internal node has up to 8 children (one for each octant).
It builds on the concept of octrees, where dividing all 3 dimensions results in 8 leaves per node.
The structure has been widely adopted in neural rendering, such as in Neural Sparse Voxel Fields and PlenOctrees, to accelerate geometry queries and store view-dependent color representations.

cited.name: Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF)
ctx: Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF) is a hybrid neural scene representation that accelerates free-viewpoint rendering by combining the high-quality implicit modeling of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with an explicit sparse voxel grid structure.

Unlike NeRF, which uses a monolithic MLP for the entire volume, NSVF decomposes the scene into local voxel-bounded implicit functions, allowing parameter growth to be additive rather than multiplicative.
Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of non-empty voxels, which is significantly less than dense voxel grids or the parameter count of a monolithic MLP for large scenes.

cited.name: KiloNeRF
ctx: KiloNeRF is a sparse and efficient representation that accelerates Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering by decomposing a large, deep neural network into thousands of small, shallow MLPs arranged in a 3D grid.

It sets itself apart from siblings like Mega-NeRF by focusing on extreme model thinning (tiny MLPs) rather than just spatial partitioning for caching, and from SRF by using learned MLPs per cell rather than fixed feature vectors.
These networks are significantly smaller and shallower than the original NeRF MLP because they only need to capture local scene information. 3.

title: Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization
abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have focused on accelerating optimization while preserving reconstruction quality. However, many proposed methods entangle implementation-level improvements with fundamental algorithmic modifications or trade performance for fidelity, leading to a fragmented research landscape that complicates fair comparison. In this work, we consolidate and evaluate the most effective and broadly applicable strategies from prior 3DGS research and augment them with several novel optimizations. We further investigate underexplored aspects of the framework, including numerical stability, Gaussian truncation, and gradient approximation. The resulting system, Faster-GS, provides a rigorously optimized algorithm that we evaluate across a comprehensive suite of benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that Faster-GS achieves up to 5$\times$ faster training while maintaining visual quality, establishing a new cost-effective and resource efficient baseline for 3DGS optimization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that optimizations can be applied to 4D Gaussian reconstruction, leading to efficient non-rigid scene optimization.

title: Gaussian Splashing: Unified Particles for Versatile Motion Synthesis and Rendering
abstract: We demonstrate the feasibility of integrating physics-based animations of solids and fluids with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to create novel effects in virtual scenes reconstructed using 3DGS. Leveraging the coherence of the Gaussian Splatting and Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) in the underlying representation, we manage rendering, view synthesis, and the dynamics of solids and fluids in a cohesive manner. Similar to GaussianShader, we enhance each Gaussian kernel with an added normal, aligning the kernel's orientation with the surface normal to refine the PBD simulation. This approach effectively eliminates spiky noises that arise from rotational deformation in solids. It also allows us to integrate physically based rendering to augment the dynamic surface reflections on fluids. Consequently, our framework is capable of realistically reproducing surface highlights on dynamic fluids and facilitating interactions between scene objects and fluids from new views. For more information, please visit our project page at \url{https://gaussiansplashing.github.io/}.

title: iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting.
abstract: In volume visualization, users can interactively explore the three-dimensional data by specifying color and opacity mappings in the transfer function (TF) or adjusting lighting parameters, facilitating meaningful interpretation of the underlying structure. However, rendering large-scale volumes demands powerful GPUs and high-speed memory access for real-time performance. While existing novel view synthesis (NVS) methods offer faster rendering speeds with lower hardware requirements, the visible parts of a reconstructed scene are fixed and constrained by preset TF settings, significantly limiting user exploration. This article introduces inverse volume rendering via Gaussian splatting (iVR-GS), an innovative NVS method that reduces the rendering cost while enabling scene editing for interactive volume exploration. Specifically, we compose multiple iVR-GS models associated with basic TFs covering disjoint visible parts to make the entire volumetric scene visible. Each basic model contains a collection of 3D editable Gaussians, where each Gaussian is a 3D spatial point that supports real-time scene rendering and editing. We demonstrate the superior reconstruction quality and composability of iVR-GS against other NVS solutions (Plenoxels, CCNeRF, and base 3DGS) on various volume datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/TouKaienn/iVR-GS.

title: Memory-Efficient On-The-Fly Voxelization of Particle Data
abstract: In this paper we present a novel GPU-friendly real-time voxelization technique for rendering homogeneous media that is defined by particles, e.g. fluids obtained from particle-based simulations such as Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH). Our method computes view-adaptive binary voxelizations with on-the-fly compression of a tiled perspective voxel grid, achieving higher resolutions than previous approaches. It allows for interactive generation of realistic images, enabling advanced rendering techniques such as ray casting-based refraction and reflection, light scattering and absorption, and ambient occlusion. In contrast to previous methods, it does not rely on preprocessing such as expensive, and often coarse, scalar field conversion or mesh generation steps. Our method directly takes unsorted particle data as input. It can be further accelerated by identifying fully populated simulation cells during simulation. The extracted surface can be filtered to achieve smooth surface appearance.

title: NeRF in detail: Learning to sample for view synthesis
abstract: Neural radiance fields (NeRF) methods have demonstrated impressive novel view synthesis performance. The core approach is to render individual rays by querying a neural network at points sampled along the ray to obtain the density and colour of the sampled points, and integrating this information using the rendering equation. Since dense sampling is computationally prohibitive, a common solution is to perform coarse-to-fine sampling. In this work we address a clear limitation of the vanilla coarse-to-fine approach -- that it is based on a heuristic and not trained end-to-end for the task at hand. We introduce a differentiable module that learns to propose samples and their importance for the fine network, and consider and compare multiple alternatives for its neural architecture. Training the proposal module from scratch can be unstable due to lack of supervision, so an effective pre-training strategy is also put forward. The approach, named `NeRF in detail' (NeRF-ID), achieves superior view synthesis quality over NeRF and the state-of-the-art on the synthetic Blender benchmark and on par or better performance on the real LLFF-NeRF scenes. Furthermore, by leveraging the predicted sample importance, a 25% saving in computation can be achieved without significantly sacrificing the rendering quality.

title: NeUDF: Leaning Neural Unsigned Distance Fields with Volume Rendering
abstract: Multi-view shape reconstruction has achieved impressive progresses thanks to the latest advances in neural implicit surface rendering. However, existing methods based on signed distance function (SDF) are limited to closed surfaces, failing to reconstruct a wide range of real-world objects that contain open-surface structures. In this work, we introduce a new neural rendering framework, coded NeUDF11Visit our project page at http://geometrylearning.com/neudf/, that can reconstruct surfaces with arbitrary topologies solely from multi-view supervision. To gain the flexibility of representing arbitrary surfaces, NeUDF leverages the unsigned distance function (UDF) as surface representation. While a naive extension of an SDF-based neural renderer cannot scale to UDF, we propose two new formulations of weight function specially tailored for UDF-based volume rendering. Furthermore, to cope with open surface rendering, where the in/out test is no longer valid, we present a dedicated normal regularization strategy to resolve the surface orientation ambiguity. We extensively evaluate our method over a number of challenging datasets, including DTU [21], MGN [5], and Deep Fashion 3D [61]. Experimental results demonstrate that NeUDF can significantly outperform the state-of-the-art method in the task of multi-view surface reconstruction, especially for complex shapes with open boundaries.

cited.name: U-density Function
ctx: The U-density function is a rendering weight function designed for Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF) to ensure globally unbiased volume rendering.

Unlike the NeuS weight function, which violates the unbiased property for UDFs by allowing weight leakage to invisible surfaces, the U-density function concentrates rendering weight near the first surface intersection, ensuring the final color is derived solely from the visible surface geometry.

ctx: NeUDF is a neural rendering framework that reconstructs surfaces with arbitrary topologies, including open surfaces, from multi-view 2D image supervision by leveraging the Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) as the implicit surface representation.

Unlike its sibling Volume SDF Rendering, which is limited to closed (watertight) surfaces, NeUDF resolves the ambiguity of surface orientation in open structures by introducing a specialized "Udensity" probability density function and a normal regularization strategy.
It differs from naive extensions of SDF-based rendering by avoiding spurious surfaces in void regions through an unbiased, occlusion-aware weighting paradigm tailored for UDFs.

title: Parallel Isosurface Extraction for 3D Data Analysis Workflows in Distributed Environments
abstract: Abstract In this paper we discuss the issues related to the development of efficient parallel implementations of the Marching Cubes algorithm, one of the most used methods for isosurface extraction, which is a fundamental operation for 3D data analysis and visualization. We present three possible parallelization strategies and we outline the pros and cons of each of them, considering isosurface extraction as stand‐alone operation or as part of a dynamic workflow. Our analysis shows that none of these implementations represents the most efficient solution for arbitrary situations. This is a major issue, because in many cases the quality of the service provided by a workflow depends on the possibility of selecting dynamically the operations to perform and, consequently, the more efficient basic building block for each stage. In this paper we present a set of guidelines that permits to achieve the highest performance for the extraction of isosurface in the most common situations, considering the characteristics of the data to process and of the workflow. These guidelines represent a suitable example to support the efficient configurations of workflows for 3D data processing in a dynamic and complex computing environment. title: Physics-Based Differentiable Rendering for Efficient and Plausible Fluid Modeling from Monocular Video
abstract: Realistic fluid models play an important role in computer graphics applications. However, efficiently reconstructing volumetric fluid flows from monocular videos remains challenging. In this work, we present a novel approach for reconstructing 3D flows from monocular inputs through a physics-based differentiable renderer coupled with joint density and velocity estimation. Our primary contributions include the proposed efficient differentiable rendering framework and improved coupled density and velocity estimation strategy. Rather than relying on automatic differentiation, we derive the differential form of the radiance transfer equation under single scattering. This allows the direct computation of the radiance gradient with respect to density, yielding higher efficiency compared to prior works. To improve temporal coherence in the reconstructed flows, subsequent fluid densities are estimated via a coupled strategy that enables smooth and realistic fluid motions suitable for applications that require high efficiency. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrated our method's capacity to reconstruct plausible volumetric flows with smooth dynamics efficiently. Comparisons to prior work on fluid motion reconstruction from monocular video revealed over 50-170x speedups across multiple resolutions.

title: Rendering piecewise approximations of SDFs through analytic intersections
abstract: Signed distance fields (SDFs) have emerged as an alternative shape representation for real-time collision detection and lighting effects. Computing these for complex models can be expensive, so one popular approach is to prepare an approximation via sampling and interpolation. Then, these may be rendered using sphere marching, which gets close to the surface quickly, but needs several iterations to converge to it. In this paper, we propose an alternative that computes the intersection of a given ray and the surface analytically at a narrow band. This may be combined with other enhancements like having variable error for the approximation depending on the distance to the surface and skipping regions that do not contain the surface to accelerate the outer band ray traversal while reducing the required memory. To achieve smoother representations with minimal computational cost, we propose a method for computing surface intersections and normals from separate interpolants. We evaluate all these to find the optimal combination improving the rendering performance and memory consumption of these SDF approximations.

title: Representing Volumetric Videos as Dynamic MLP Maps
abstract: This paper introduces a novel representation of volumetric videos for real-time view synthesis of dynamic scenes. Recent advances in neural scene representations demonstrate their remarkable capability to model and render complex static scenes, but extending them to represent dynamic scenes is not straightforward due to their slow rendering speed or high storage cost. To solve this problem, our key idea is to represent the radiance field of each frame as a set of shallow MLP networks whose parameters are stored in 2D grids, called MLP maps, and dynamically predicted by a 2D CNN decoder shared by all frames. Representing 3D scenes with shallow MLPs significantly improves the rendering speed, while dynamically predicting MLP parameters with a shared 2D CNN instead of explicitly storing them leads to low storage cost. Experiments show that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality on the NHR and ZJU-MoCap datasets, while being efficient for real-time rendering with a speed of 41.7 fps for $512 \times 512$ images on an RTX 3090 GPU. The code is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/mlp_maps/.

It guarantees that the ray never penetrates or overshoots the surface by computing the maximum safe step size using a global Lipschitz constant \lambda.

Unlike adaptive methods that estimate local gradients, this method relies on a pre-computed global bound, making it simple to implement and numerically stable, though potentially less efficient for complex scenes with varying feature scales.

title: Self-Supervised Dual Contouring
abstract: Learning-based isosurface extraction methods have recently emerged as a robust and efficient alternative to axiomatic techniques. However, the vast majority of such approaches rely on supervised training with axiomatically computed ground truths, thus potentially inheriting biases and data artefacts of the corresponding axiomatic methods. Steering away from such dependencies, we propose a self-supervised training scheme to the Neural Dual Contouring meshing framework, resulting in our method: SelfSupervised Dual Contouring (SDC). Instead of optimizing predicted mesh vertices with supervised training, we use two novel self-supervised loss functions that encourage the consistency between distances to the generated mesh up to the first order. Meshes reconstructed by SDC surpass existing data-driven methods in capturing intricate details while being more robust to possible irregularities in the input. Furthermore, we use the same self-supervised training objective linking inferred mesh and input SDF, to regularize the training process of Deep Implicit Networks (DINs). We demonstrate that the resulting DINs produce higher-quality implicit functions, ultimately leading to more accurate and detail-preserving surfaces compared to prior baselines for different input modalities. Finally, we demonstrate that our self-supervised losses improve meshing performance in the single-view reconstruction task by enabling joint training of predicted SDF and resulting output mesh. We open-source our code at https://github.com/Sentient07/SDC.

title: Show HN: Msplat – 3D Gaussian Splatting training in ~90s on M4 Max, native Metal
abstract: Hey HN, I built msplat because I wanted to train 3DGS scenes on my Mac without pulling in torch. Most ports I came across go through autograd and hence come with ~2GB of framework overhead, which felt overkill for a pipeline that's just a few dozen GPU kernels + an optimizer. So I wrote the whole training pipeline from scratch as Metal shaders: projection, tile-based rasterization, SSIM loss, backward pass, Adam, and densification. Everything runs on the GPU msplat trains 7k iterations of full-resolution Mip-NeRF 360 scenes in ~90s on my M4 Max. In the README I compare against gsplat's published numbers, which were measured on a TITAN RTX. Ofc these are different hardware classes, so take the wall-time comparisons with a grain of salt Python bindings are on PyPI (pip install msplat), and there are Swift bindings if you want to embed this in a native app. Happy to answer questions about any of the internals Repo: https://github.com/rayanht/msplat (Apache 2.0)

title: Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) show impressive performance in photo-realistic free-view rendering of scenes. Recent improvements on the NeRF such as TensoRF and ZipNeRF employ explicit models for faster optimization and rendering, as compared to the NeRF that employs an implicit representation. However, both implicit and explicit radiance fields require dense sampling of images in the given scene. Their performance degrades significantly when only a sparse set of views is available. Researchers find that supervising the depth estimated by a radiance field helps train it effectively with fewer views. The depth supervision is obtained either using classical approaches or neural networks pre-trained on a large dataset. While the former may provide only sparse supervision, the latter may suffer from generalization issues. As opposed to the earlier approaches, we seek to learn the depth supervision by designing augmented models and training them along with the main radiance field. Further, we aim to design a framework of regularizations that can work across different implicit and explicit radiance fields. We observe that certain features of these radiance field models overfit to the observed images in the sparse-input scenario. Our key finding is that reducing the capability of the radiance fields with respect to positional encoding, the number of decomposed tensor components or the size of the hash table, constrains the model to learn simpler solutions, which estimate better depth in certain regions. By designing augmented models based on such reduced capabilities, we obtain better depth supervision for the main radiance field. We achieve state-of-the-art view-synthesis performance with sparse input views on popular datasets containing forward-facing and 360$^\circ$ scenes by employing the above regularizations.Comment: The source code for our model can be found on our project page: https://nagabhushansn95.github.io/publications/2024/Simple-RF.html. arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2309.0395

title: Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering
abstract: We propose an efficient radiance field rendering algorithm that incorporates a rasterization process on adaptive sparse voxels without neural networks or 3D Gaussians. There are two key contributions coupled with the proposed system. The first is to adaptively and explicitly allocate sparse voxels to different levels of detail within scenes, faithfully reproducing scene details with 655363 grid resolution while achieving high rendering frame rates. Second, we customize a rasterizer for efficient adaptive sparse voxels rendering. We render voxels in the correct depth order by using ray direction-dependent Morton ordering, which avoids the well-known popping artifact found in Gaussian splat- ting. Our method improves the previous neural-free voxel model by over 4db PSNR and more than 10x FPS speedup, achieving state-of-the-art comparable novel-view synthesis results. Additionally, our voxel representation is seamlessly compatible with grid-based 3D processing techniques such as Volume Fusion, Voxel Pooling, and Marching Cubes, enabling a wide range of future extensions and applications. Code: github.com/NVlabs/svraster

title: Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has transformed novel-view synthesis with its fast, interpretable, and high-fidelity rendering. However, its resource requirements limit its usability. Especially on constrained devices, training performance degrades quickly and often cannot complete due to excessive memory consumption of the model. The method converges with an indefinite number of Gaussians -- many of them redundant -- making rendering unnecessarily slow and preventing its usage in downstream tasks that expect fixed-size inputs. To address these issues, we tackle the challenges of training and rendering 3DGS models on a budget. We use a guided, purely constructive densification process that steers densification toward Gaussians that raise the reconstruction quality. Model size continuously increases in a controlled manner towards an exact budget, using score-based densification of Gaussians with training-time priors that measure their contribution. We further address training speed obstacles: following a careful analysis of 3DGS\u27 original pipeline, we derive faster, numerically equivalent solutions for gradient computation and attribute updates, including an alternative parallelization for efficient backpropagation. We also propose quality-preserving approximations where suitable to reduce training time even further. Taken together, these enhancements yield a robust, scalable solution with reduced training times, lower compute and memory requirements, and high quality. Our evaluation shows that in a budgeted setting, we obtain competitive quality metrics with 3DGS while achieving a 4--5x reduction in both model size and training time. With more generous budgets, our measured quality surpasses theirs. These advances open the door for novel-view synthesis in constrained environments, e.g., mobile devices

cited.name: k*-Buffer Analysis
ctx: k-Buffer Analysis is a software-based diagnostic method that determines the optimal fixed buffer size k for the k-buffer visibility sorting algorithm in hardware-assisted volume rendering.
It measures the required k by recording insertion depths into an ideal A-buffer, avoiding the unbounded memory of a true A-buffer while offering a less conservative sorting scheme than ZSWEEP.
The method consists of two phases: the operational logic of the k-buffer itself and the analytical procedure to derive the required k.

cited.name: Hardware Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS)
ctx: Hardware Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS) is a hybrid volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids that combines object-space sorting on the CPU with image-space fragment sorting on the GPU.
It solves the visibility problem for arbitrary non-convex meshes without requiring topological connectivity or preprocessing.

Unlike sorting-free methods like Projected Tetrahedra (SPT) which avoid artifacts but may be slower, or pure ray-casting which is memory-bound by texture units, HAVS uses a k-buffer to incrementally sort fragments, offering a compromise between implementation complexity, robustness, and image quality.

cited.name: HAVS with Dynamic LOD
ctx: An algorithm for dynamic Level of Detail (LOD) that builds on Hardware Assisted Visibility Sorting (HAVS), separating boundary and internal faces, sorting internal faces by importance, and dynamically adjusting the number of faces drawn based on frame rate.
It solves the problem of maintaining interactive frame rates on large tetrahedral datasets by progressively streaming approximations that increase in quality during idle frames.
Unlike Optimized HAVS (Sorted k-buffer), which focuses on sorting optimization, this method focuses on adaptive primitive reduction to balance interactivity and visual fidelity.

cited.name: K-Buffer Isosurface Extraction
ctx: K-Buffer Isosurface Extraction is a framework for extracting flat-shaded isosurfaces from volumetric data by adapting the K-Buffer rasterization technique.
It replaces the 3D pre-integrated volume integral table used in standard volume rendering with a 2D lookup table.

This method distinguishes itself from its parent, Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces, by explicitly utilizing a 2D texture-based lookup table for boolean isosurface detection between front and back scalar values, enabling a simple and fast extraction process.

cited.name: CPU Radix Sort for Face Centroids

It converts IEEE 754 floating-point numbers to 32-bit unsigned integers and performs a Least Significant Digit (LSD) radix sort using counting sort on 8-bit blocks.

It is chosen over general-purpose sorts or re-sorting-optimized algorithms like mergesort because viewing direction changes significantly alter the ordering, making frequent full re-sorting more efficient than adaptive re-sorting overhead.

cited.name: Level-of-detail (LOD) methods
ctx: Level-of-detail (LOD) methods are techniques for interactive visualization of large scalar fields that maintain responsive frame rates by generating reduced-resolution approximations of the original data during viewpoint interaction.

cited.name: k-buffer
ctx: The k-buffer is a fixed-depth fragment sorting structure used in image-space volume rendering to manage visibility for non-convex grids.
The fragments are assumed to be partially sorted in object space by the CPU.
Strengths: Reduces memory requirement compared to unbounded A-buffer; simple enough to implement on existing graphics architectures; shifts sorting burden to GPU.

cited.name: Face Subsampling
ctx: Face Subsampling is a Level-of-Detail (LOD) technique for tetrahedral volume rendering that dynamically selects a subset of mesh faces to render, balancing visual fidelity against frame rate constraints.
It solves the problem of interactive rendering on large tetrahedral meshes by reducing the number of rasterized primitives without pre-aggregating data into voxels or bricks.

It differs from sibling methods like Hierarchical Culling & Multi-resolution Approximation by operating directly on the unstructured mesh topology rather than a hierarchical grid, and from Focus Point Based Brick LOD Selection by being primarily face-centric rather than brick-centric.

cited.name: Nearly-Sorted Object-Space Visibility Ordering
ctx: Nearly-Sorted Object-Space Visibility Ordering (k-NSS) is a relaxation of exact visibility sorting where primitives are ordered such that rasterized fragments are at most k positions out of order in the sorted sequence.

This allows for the use of faster, approximate object-space sorting algorithms (such as centroid sorting or coarse BSP traversal) while deferring the guarantee of correct compositing to an exact sorting step during fragment processing.

It differs from its parent Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant) by performing the initial ordering in object space rather than per-pixel, and from siblings like Mammen's Technique by explicitly bounding the displacement error k to enable linear-time correction.

title: Three-dimensional encoding/two-dimensional decoding of medical data
abstract: We propose a fully three-dimensional (3-D) wavelet-based coding system featuring 3-D encoding/two-dimensional (2-D) decoding functionalities. A fully 3-D transform is combined with context adaptive arithmetic coding; 2-D decoding is enabled by encoding every 2-D subband image independently. The system allows a finely graded up to lossless quality scalability on any 2-D image of the dataset. Fast access to 2-D images is obtained by decoding only the corresponding information thus avoiding the reconstruction of the entire volume. The performance has been evaluated on a set of volumetric data and compared to that provided by other 3-D as well as 2-D coding systems. Results show a substantial improvement in coding efficiency (up to 33%) on volumes featuring good correlation properties along the z axis. Even though we did not address the complexity issue, we expect a decoding time of the order of one second/image after optimization. In summary, the proposed 3-D/2-D multidimensional layered zero coding system provides the improvement in compression efficiency attainable with 3-D systems without sacrificing the effectiveness in accessing the single images characteristic of 2-D ones.

It solves the problem of identifying which coefficients at a coarser level contribute to a specific sample at a finer level during synthesis, exploiting the recursive nature of the lifting scheme.
Unlike methods that decode entire subbands, this approach calculates the exact Generalized Projection of a sample into the transformed domain, minimizing the number of subband images to decode.

cited.name: Plane Composing Algorithms
ctx: Plane Composing Algorithms are a category of direct volume rendering methods that operate by compositing several slices which comprise a volumetric model.

This approach differs from ray casting by leveraging spatial coherence through slicing, often enhanced by texture-based rendering techniques.

cited.name: Supersampling
ctx: Supersampling is a technique to minimize aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel and averaging the results, effectively sampling the scene at a higher spatial frequency than the displayed resolution.

It addresses the coarse granularity of per-pixel sampling, which causes visible artifacts such as jagged edges (staircase artifacts) and moiré patterns, particularly along object silhouettes where intensity changes abruptly.
Unlike standard single-sampling, supersampling provides a more accurate color representation for each pixel by integrating the signal over the pixel area.

title: Volumetric Multi‐View Rendering
abstract: International audienceRendering photo-realistic images using Monte Carlo path tracing often requires sampling a large number of paths to reach acceptable levels of noise. This is particularly the case when rendering participating media, that complexify light paths with multiple scattering events. Our goal is to accelerate the rendering of heterogeneous participating media by exploiting redundancy across views, for instance when rendering animated camera paths, motion blur in consecutive frames or multi-view images such as lenticular or light-field images. This poses a challenge as existing methods for sharing light paths across views cannot handle heterogeneous participating media and classical estimators are not optimal in this context. We address these issues by proposing three key ideas. First, we propose new volume shift mappings to transform light paths from one view to another within the recently introduced null-scattering framework, taking into account changes in density along the transformed path. Second, we generate a shared path suffix that best contributes to a subset of views, thus effectively reducing variance. Third, we introduce the multiple weighted importance sampling estimator that benefits from multiple importance sampling for combining sampling strategies, and from weighted importance sampling for reducing the variance due to non contributing strategies. We observed significant reuse when views largely overlap, with no visible bias and reduced variance compared to regular path tracing at equal time. Our method further readily integrates into existing volumetric path tracing pipelines

cited.name: Octree Building Pass
ctx: This method builds a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a queue of voxel fragments, resolving collisions where multiple fragments map to the same leaf by averaging their attributes.

It distinguishes itself by using InterlockedMax() for dynamic geometry updates to improve performance at the cost of lighting quality, while preserving atomic averaging for static geometry, and integrates tightly with a 3D texture brick for storing reflected radiance and alpha.

cited.name: Multiple Importance Sampling without Selection (mismvpt)
ctx: Multiple Importance Sampling without Selection (mismvpt) is a multi-view rendering estimator that combines base paths and shifted paths (reused from other cameras) using standard MIS weights.
It solves the problem of integrating light transport contributions across multiple viewpoints by reusing geometric prefixes, avoiding the bias and complexity of prefix selection mechanisms.

Unlike its sibling Multi-View Path Tracing with MWIS, which uses a self-normalized estimator to reweight samples toward a target pdf, mismvpt uses a standard unbiased MIS estimator, resulting in higher variance when the distribution of shifted prefixes does not follow ideal importance sampling.

cited.name: Fraboni et al. Prefix Selection
ctx: Prefix Selection is a stochastic filtering mechanism for multi-view path tracing that rejects shifted path prefixes when their scattering distributions at the pivot point significantly mismatch the base prefix.
It addresses the variance explosion caused by large Jacobian variations and scattering function differences when reusing paths across different camera views.

Unlike methods that reuse all prefixes regardless of scattering properties, this method ensures that only prefixes with similar scattering behavior are included in the Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) estimator, thereby reducing noise and preventing the bias artifacts associated with naive reuse.

cited.name: Majorant optical depth shift
ctx: The majorant optical depth shift maps a medium interaction depth t sampled on a base viewing segment to a corresponding depth t' on a target viewing segment.
This enables path reuse in multi-view rendering by accounting for differences in volume geometry and extinction coefficients between views.
The method relies on the piecewise constant approximation of the majorant optical depth along a ray.

cited.name: Null Interactions Shift
ctx: Null Interactions Shift is a bijective transformation method used in volumetric multi-view rendering to map medium interaction depths sampled on a base viewing segment to valid, corresponding depths on a target viewing segment.

It solves the problem of reusing Monte Carlo samples across different camera viewpoints by ensuring that shifted interactions remain within the medium, thereby maintaining a well-defined probability density function (pdf).
Unlike simpler random number replay techniques which may place interactions outside the medium, this method uses the majorant optical depth to guarantee validity.

cited.name: Lens Shift
ctx: Lens shift is a path construction technique in volumetric multi-view rendering that transforms a point sampled on one camera's lens aperture to match a different camera's aperture geometry.
It reuses the random numbers that sampled the base lens interaction to adapt to different aperture radii.
Input: Base lens interaction point x{\text{lens}} (2D coordinates on the base aperture), base aperture radius r, target aperture radius r'.

cited.name: Multi-View Path Tracing with MWIS
ctx: Multi-View Path Tracing with MWIS (MVPT) accelerates the rendering of heterogeneous participating media by exploiting redundancy across multiple camera views, such as in animated sequences or light fields.
It jointly renders a sequence by reusing computation during simulation, specifically by transforming light paths from a base view to other views and generating a shared path suffix.

Unlike standard multi-view methods that use unbiased Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) or discard shifted paths based on strict selection criteria, MVPT uses a self-normalized Multiple Weighted Importance Sampling (MWIS) estimator.

cited.name: Weighted Importance Sampling
ctx: Weighted Importance Sampling (WIS) is a biased but consistent technique used to simulate the use of a known target probability density function (PDF) p with samples drawn from an arbitrary source PDF q.

It addresses the problem of evaluating integrals where the ideal sampling distribution is known but difficult or impossible to sample from directly, such as when shifted paths in volumetric rendering do not follow the base PDF of sampling the path from the pixel.
It sets itself apart from Resampled Importance Sampling (RIS) by avoiding the intractable resampling of path prefixes required for unbounded paths, accepting bias in exchange for feasibility.

ctx: Delta tracking is a Monte Carlo method for sampling the distance to the next interaction (scattering or absorption) in a heterogeneous participating medium where the extinction coefficient varies spatially.

It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a constant "majorant" upper bound on extinction to propose interaction distances, then probabilistically accepting or rejecting these proposals based on the local density, effectively treating the medium as homogeneous with "fake" particles.

cited.name: Ratio Tracking with Null Scattering
ctx: Ratio tracking with null scattering is a Monte Carlo method for estimating transmittance in participating media that avoids the high variance of binary visibility tests by accumulating a continuous product of null-scattering ratios.
Variance: Significantly lower than binary delta tracking for transmittance estimation, as it avoids the high variance of Russian roulette termination on absorption.
Limitations: Can be slower than delta tracking if the number of scattering events increases significantly due to non-termination on absorption.

cited.name: Russian Roulette
ctx: Russian Roulette is an unbiased alternative to deterministic threshold-based early ray termination, used to probabilistically terminate volumetric paths or ray-marching steps with low contribution weights.

It solves the bias introduced by simply breaking a loop when transmittance or opacity exceeds a fixed threshold, ensuring that the expected value of the rendered pixel remains correct while significantly reducing computation time in dense or deep volumes.
Unlike deterministic early stop methods, it maintains statistical unbiasedness by scaling up the weight of surviving paths.

cited.name: Biased Sampling for Path Depth
ctx: Biased Sampling for Path Depth is a variance reduction technique for volumetric path tracing in dense, highly anisotropic participating media (such as clouds) that exponentially decays the medium's extinction coefficient and anisotropy parameter as the ray depth increases.

By reducing the frequency of scattering events and the directionality of scattering at deeper bounces, the method significantly shortens path lengths and accelerates convergence, trading a slight, visually negligible bias for massive performance gains.

title: Wavelet-based Multiresolution Isosurface Rendering
abstract: We present an interactive rendering method for isosurfaces in a voxel grid. The underlying trivariate function is represented as a spline wavelet hierarchy, which allows for adaptive (view-dependent) selection of the desired level-of-detail by superimposing appropriately weighted basis functions. Different root finding techniques are compared with respect to their precision and efficiency. Both wavelet reconstruction and root finding are implemented in CUDA to utilize the high computational performance of Nvidia's hardware and to obtain high quality results. We tested our methods with datasets of up to 5123 voxels and demonstrate interactive frame rates for a viewport size of up to 1024x768 pixels.

title: A Generative Model for Volume Rendering
abstract: We present a technique to synthesize and analyze volume-rendered images using generative models. We use the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework to compute a model from a large collection of volume renderings, conditioned on (1) viewpoint and (2) transfer functions for opacity and color. Our approach facilitates tasks for volume analysis that are challenging to achieve using existing rendering techniques such as ray casting or texture-based methods. We show how to guide the user in transfer function editing by quantifying expected change in the output image. Additionally, the generative model transforms transfer functions into a view-invariant latent space specifically designed to synthesize volume-rendered images. We use this space directly for rendering, enabling the user to explore the space of volume-rendered images. As our model is independent of the choice of volume rendering process, we show how to analyze volume-rendered images produced by direct and global illumination lighting, for a variety of volume datasets.

title: A hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithm for single scattering
abstract: Volumetric effects such as beams of light through participating media are an important component in the appearance of the natural world. Many such effects can be faithfully modeled by a single scattering medium. In the presence of shadows, rendering these effects can be prohibitively expensive: current algorithms are based on ray marching, i.e., integrating the illumination scattered towards the camera along each view ray, modulated by visibility to the light source at each sample. Visibility must be determined for each sample using shadow rays or shadow-map lookups. We observe that in a suitably chosen coordinate system, the visibility function has a regular structure that we can exploit for significant acceleration compared to brute force sampling. We propose an efficient algorithm based on partial sum trees for computing the scattering integrals in a single-scattering homogeneous medium. On a CPU, we achieve speedups of 17--120x over ray marching.Intel Corporation (PhD Fellowship)Singapore-MIT GAMBIT Game La

title: Adaptive surface extraction from anisotropic volumetric data: contouring on generalized octrees
abstract: In this article, we present an algorithm to extract adaptive surfaces from anisotropic volumetric data. For example, this kind of data can be obtained from a set of segmented images, from the sampling of an implicit function or it can be built by using depth images produced by time-of-flight cameras. However, for many applications as geometry modelling, rendering or finite elements, it is better to use an explicit surface representation. This surface must fit to the geometrical and topological features of the object in order to obtain a good approximation and to avoid topological artefacts. Our algorithm is able to extract adaptive sur- faces that accurately approximate the geometry of the original object while minimizing aliasing effects. In addition, our solution is suitable to handle the anisotropy of volumetric representations. In comparison with relevant methods in the state of the art, ours offers a good compromise between mesh quality and precision in the geometrical approximation

title: Differentiable Rendering with Reparameterized Volume Sampling
abstract: In view synthesis, a neural radiance field approximates underlying density and radiance fields based on a sparse set of scene pictures. To generate a pixel of a novel view, it marches a ray through the pixel and computes a weighted sum of radiance emitted from a dense set of ray points. This rendering algorithm is fully differentiable and facilitates gradient-based optimization of the fields. However, in practice, only a tiny opaque portion of the ray contributes most of the radiance to the sum. We propose a simple end-to-end differentiable sampling algorithm based on inverse transform sampling. It generates samples according to the probability distribution induced by the density field and picks non-transparent points on the ray. We utilize the algorithm in two ways. First, we propose a novel rendering approach based on Monte Carlo estimates. This approach allows for evaluating and optimizing a neural radiance field with just a few radiance field calls per ray. Second, we use the sampling algorithm to modify the hierarchical scheme proposed in the original NeRF work. We show that our modification improves reconstruction quality of hierarchical models, at the same time simplifying the training procedure by removing the need for auxiliary proposal network losses.Comment: Accepted at AISTATS 2024. Short version of this paper appeared in ICLR 2023 Neural Fields worksho

title: feat(niivue): streamed multi-LOD rendering fixes, LOD compensation, budget plans, and block inspection
abstract: Stacked on #110. Base is `feat/multichannel-microscopy-formats`, so the diff here is just this branch's 39 commits. Draft, opened to exercise CI. The through-line: make a streamed multi-LOD volume look right. That started as the swap flicker and grew to cover every reason a brick could read wrong (geometry, brightness, opacity, reconstruction), then the controls and demos needed to see those defects at all. ## The flicker Every refocus swaps the chunk plan, synchronously destroying unmatched bricks, and a brick with no resident texture draws nothing, so the scene background showed through until the re-stream landed. `NVChunkedVolume` now fetches the coarsest pyramid level once and installs it as a whole-volume floor behind the octree (`coarseFloor: false` opts out; skipped when that level is too big for one texture upload). Adds `chunkFadeMs` (default 120 ms, 0 disables) on both backends so fine detail dissolves in over the floor instead of popping. The OME-Zarr demo builds its plans by hand, so the automatic floor never reached it; it now builds one from the coarse data it already keeps resident. Also in this group: picking tissue exposed by a clip plane in chunked volumes (installs `NVImage.pickSampler` in the `NVChunkedVolume` constructor, teaches `clipRaySegment` cutaway mode to return a skip slab, and makes both views march before falling back). ## Brick misregistration (the real seam) A multi-LOD brick's fetch box is snapped out to whole voxels of its own pyramid level, so it covers up to one level voxel more than the brick owns on each face. Both backends' `chunkUniformsFor` and `chunkSampleTransform` treated that fetched box as the owned box, so the shader mapped the brick's common-grid edges onto the fetched region's edges. Content inside every coarse brick was shifted and stretched, and because neighbouring bricks snap independently, two neighbours disagreed about the level coordinate at their shared face. That disagreement is a geometric seam, which no brightness knob can remove. `chunkOwnedTexBox` is now the single source for the remap in all three call sites. On the real hoa_heart pyramid this moves brick content by up to 3.4 / 6.3 / 8.7 common voxels at L2 / L3 / L4 and corrects a stretch of up to 5.9 / 12.4 / 23.7, about 61 um of displacement on an L4 brick. A single-level plan takes an exact path and is bit-identical to before. ## Ray-march ringing and slab tiling - Oversampled the 3D ray march. - Each fine sample now owns the slab it is the midpoint of, clipped to the brick's segment, so slab thicknesses tile `[0, len]` exactly at LOD interfaces. - The empty-space skip now probes one stride past each cube's exit face. It restarted at every chunk / coarse-floor cube face and strode 1.9 level voxels, so material in the last sub-stride was never probed, the cube contributed zero, and its exit face showed as a discontinuity. CPU replica: worst-case two-cube split error -3.99% to +0.68%. Browser A/B (HOA heart, pinned L4, 64 chunks, WebGPU): whole-image TV -2.7% x / -2.2% y. - The coarse floor renders as volume rather than a dark shell. ## Gamma and LOD compensation `scene.gamma` was declared, settable, and persisted in NVD, but no renderer ever read it, so the property was dead while FEATURE_PARITY claimed it worked. It is now wired into both backends' ray-march and the 2D slice tiles. Semantics follow the old package (classified RGB raised to 1/gamma, alpha untouched, 1.0 an exact no-op). Measured headless on both backends, mean canvas luminance: 13.59 at 0.7, 17.85 at 1.0, 29.56 at 2.0, 36.91 at 3.0, the two backends agreeing to within 0.003. Downsampling averages voxels, which destroys the correlation between a sample's colour and its opacity, so a coarse brick integrates darker than the fine data it stands in for. `volumeLodBrightnessCompensation` applies a per-chunk exponent that multiplies the gamma exponent, so a level-0 brick or any single-level plan is an exact no-op. The coarse floor draws through its own uniform block and initially got no correction at all, which put the scene's largest brightness step exactly at the edge of the resident fine region; its downsample now comes from its own dims. **The law was wrong, and that was the seam.** The lift grew with `downsample - 1`, which assumes a level-4 brick loses eight times what a level-1 brick loses. Averaging does not work that way: every level reduces the same 2x2x2 neighbourhood, so it is one comparable step per level. It is now `log2(downsample)`. Under the old form a level-6 brick asked for exponent -0.386 on a seven-level pyramid, the 0.25 clamp caught it, and the correction became the artifact: measured across the strongest seam on hoa_heart, +35.7% at the default against -34.0% with compensation off, having overshot the null by about 6x. The floor sat pinned at the clamp, which was the pale flash on zoom. Default refit to 0.08 per level; seam response is now monotonic across the whole slider (-33.0% at 0, -10.1% at 0.08). `volumeLodOpacityCompensation` is the matching alpha knob, ray-march only, and defaults to **0** as a measured choice: over four probe regions, raising c from 0 to 0.5 cut mean alpha error from 6.7% to 5.1% while driving colour error from 15.3% to 25.7%. Sparse thin material has a genuine deficit that no global scale recovers; fixing it needs a coverage-preserving pyramid, not a renderer knob. Both coefficients are exact no-ops on a non-multi-LOD volume and nothing on screen said so, so `nv.lodCompensation()` reports `isActive` plus an `inactiveReason`, then per level the downsample factor, bricks drawn, and the exact exponent and scale handed to the shader (floor reported separately, via a new `ViewBackend.coarseFloorDims()` in both views). Setting a non-zero coefficient with no multi-LOD volume loaded now warns at the moment of the set. Covered by `e2e/lod-compensation-report.spec.ts`. ## Opt-in tricubic B-spline reconstruction `volumeIsCubicInterpolation`, both backends, default off. It fixes the texel staircase; it does not remove the ringing (see above). Cubic needs a 2-voxel halo, so `chunking.ts` gained `LINEAR_MIN_HALO` / `CUBIC_MIN_HALO` / `planSupportsHalo` / `planSupportsCubic`, and `NVChunkedVolume.raiseHaloTo()` re-plans a loaded volume when the setter fires. Both views gate cubic per draw on halo >= 2 and on not-a-label-volume, including the coarse-floor cube. Public default halo stays `[1,1,1]`. New unit test `src/volume/chunkHalo.test.ts` carries a CPU replica of `sampleTricubic`. New example `vox.interp.html` (linear vs cubic, A/B split or flip); the range demo gained an interp selector, a draggable A/B divider, and a samples-per-voxel control. ## Named budget plans A chunked volume had exactly one policy: an octree focused on the crosshair. That is right for exploring and wrong for a whole-volume figure or for holding a frame rate while rotating. `budgetPlans.ts` owns the `BudgetPlan` type, three presets (`focus` / `uniform` / `interactive`) and `resolveBudgetPlan`. Precedence lowest first: focus baseline, named preset, explicit plan object, individual options, so every existing call keeps its behavior. `radius: 'volume'` is all `uniform` needs, since the detail shrink pass only bites beyond the radius and the budget pass converges on the finest uniform level that fits. `setBudgetPlan` switches mid-session and re-folds over the load options so an app-pinned knob still wins; `minLevel` and halo come from current state so a switch cannot undo `setMaxDetail` or undercut a wider kernel already streamed for. `targetFrameMs` is resolved and readable but nothing acts on it yet. Design doc: `docs/budget-plans.md`. Remaining streaming work is tracked in `docs/streaming-todos.md` (off-thread chunk decode is the next item). ## Chunk 0 eviction blanked the volume (WebGL2) Reported as "stopped loading chunks when I moved the crosshairs to the opposite surface of the clipped volume". `draw()` early-returned on a null `volumeTexture` / `volumeGradientTexture`. For a chunked volume those are only a best-effort alias of chunk 0 (the real textures bind per chunk, and the coarse-floor cubes bind the floor textures), so a refocus that evicted chunk 0 silently killed the whole volume. WebGPU already branched on the chunked entry before its equivalent guard, which is why this was WebGL2-only. Two dangling-pointer paths fixed alongside it: `swapChunkedVolumePlan` never refreshed the aliases after `manager.remap()` destroyed unmatched chunks, and switching from a chunked volume to a single one let the single-volume path delete textures the chunked cache entry still owned. ## GPU context recovery A lost context was permanent: `NVViewGL` latched `_contextLost` and stopped rendering, and its `webglcontextlost` listener was `{ once: true }` so a second loss was not even reported. Both views now expose an `onContextLost` hook, wired by the controller inside its RAF callback so it survives view recreation (the same treatment `overlayDraw` gets). WebGL2 calls `preventDefault()` (which is what makes the browser promise a replacement) and fires on `webglcontextrestored`; WebGPU has no restored event so it fires straight from `device.lost`, with a `_destroyed` latch so deliberate teardown does not ask for a rebuild. The controller rebuilds via `recreateView`, capped at two attempts, with a canvas overlay while rebuilding and a "GPU most likely ran out of memory" message on giving up. The range demo asked for an 8 GB GPU residency budget against a 2 GB plan budget, so the LRU never evicted and each refocus piled bricks on top of the old ones: 1.67 GB across 177 bricks measured on hoa_heart L0. WebGL2 now gets 1.25 GB, deliberately below the plan budget. WebGPU unchanged. ## Block inspection (how the above gets seen) A registration or reconstruction error inside one brick is nearly invisible in the full render and obvious with the brick beside its own fine data. Two demos, in two halves. `examples/vox.block.pick.html`, CPU-resident NIfTI. `pickExplodedBlock(clientX, clientY)` resolves a pointer onto one visible brick, CPU-side: it slab-tests each brick's EXPLODED mm AABB and inverts the exploded `matRAS`, because GPU depth picking cannot see the render-time per-brick translation. `extractSubVolume` / `extractChunkBlock` (`src/volume/ChunkExtract.ts`) copy a voxel box out as a complete NIfTI whose affine is the parent's with its origin walked to the box, so an oblique parent stays oblique and the child reports true anatomical mm. The brick's DATA region is used rather than its halo region, so adjacent blocks tile the parent without overlap. `examples/vox.block.pick.zarr.html`, streamed multi-LOD hoa_heart, which is the part that actually tests `chunkOwnedTexBox`. A streamed volume has no CPU `img`, so `extractSubVolume` returns null and the right pane cannot be built by copying. It opens a SECOND streamed volume over the same store, cropped to the picked brick's common-grid box, and lets that volume's octree pull the crop toward level 0 near its crosshair. A brick is already one texture's worth at its own level, so re-fetching it there buys nothing; the detail comes from the crop source's finest levels. Picking needed a core fix: `pickExplodedDraw` sampled the parent's CPU `img`, so on a streamed volume every pick landed on the brick's box face. It now falls back to `vol.pickSampler` (mm-space, backed by the coarse floor), in `control/` so both backends get it. The lattice you pick out of also needs a block COUNT you choose, and the planner could not express one. `chunkVolumeMultiLOD` sized bricks from a scalar `cellEdge`, so the count fell out of the pyramid: on hoa_heart L5 (181x186x246, not a cube) the reachable counts step 2, 8, 12, 16, 27, and 4 or 9 are unreachable at any edge length. `maxBricks` only coarsens by raising the level floor, which fights the demo's own level control. A new `gridDims` option replaces the octree with an exact lattice, `gridDims[a]` bricks per axis all drawn from `minLevel`, and sets real `gridDims` / `stride` on the plan so `chunkAtVoxel` indexes it (multi-LOD plans previously returned a degenerate `[1,1,1]`). An axis grows when a brick would exceed `deviceLimit`, since `emitBrick` clamps an oversize texture and that squashes the sampling, so callers read the built plan's own `gridDims` back. The zarr demo gets a Blocks control (4 / 9 / 16) on top of it, choosing the factorization whose blocks come out closest to cubic, and reports what was built plus the asked-for count when an axis had to grow. Its lattice budget option is dropped as inert: the plan budget only shapes the octree, and GPU residency is capped separately by the renderer. Per-pane block-loading badges in both the zarr block demo and the range demo. `pending` is the GPU upload QUEUE, not a finite work list (the octree re-requests its working set every frame), so the badge keys on the resident count moving, counts against what the stream actually asked for rather than the plan total (absent and empty bricks are never fetched and the LRU evicts), and holds a per-episode high-water mark so the bar only moves forward. Verified against a fake clock in isolation, then live on both backends. ## DANDI app: one store, two viewers `VolumeSliceSource` adapts a chunked volume store to the NVSlide tile source interface, so one OME-Zarr drives both the volumetric view and the deep-zoom pane without opening the store twice. `apps/dandi-demo` puts them side by side over a single zarrita byte cache: a plane the deep-zoom viewer already pulled costs the volumetric stream nothing. The panes link both ways (crosshair moves the slide plane, debounced; clicking the slide refocuses the multi-LOD budget). It lives in `apps/` rather than `packages/niivue/examples` because its measuring ruler comes from `@niivue/uikit`, which builds against niivue's dist, and importing it from examples would close a cycle in the task graph. The ruler holds endpoints in slide base pixels and scales each leg by its own axis spacing, so it stays pinned to tissue through pan, zoom and level swaps on anisotropic planes. Three verified stores: a 106 MB OCT block, the 4.5 GB OCT volume it comes from, and a 17.7 GB light-sheet SPIM. On the 30 GB NeuN slab, the ruler reads 2.96 mm on WebGPU and 550 um on WebGL2, both matching the level's um-per-pixel by hand. ## Known remaining Residual LOD seams. At the refitted default the measured step across a level boundary is about -10% on hoa_heart, down from +36%. No single coefficient nulls every dataset (sparse thin material wants ~0.11, dense structure ~0.05), so closing the rest is structural: cross-LOD blending at brick faces, or publishing a coverage-preserving pyramid. The max/mean blend prototype landed every measured region within 4% at every level and is the stronger lead. Tracked in `docs/streaming-todos.md`. OME-NGFF `translation` still never reaches a streamed volume's affine. Measured on hoa_heart, every level's translation is exactly half its own scale, which is the voxel-centre convention rather than a world origin, so for this store the gap is a uniform half-voxel shift with no inter-level misregistration. It still matters for any store declaring a real world origin. Shape of the fix is written up in the TODO; `vox.block.pick.zarr.html` prints the numbers so the convention is visible. ## Verification `nx affected -t format lint typecheck test build`, `check-boundaries`, and codespell all green. 1191 unit tests pass. Rendering changes verified manually in the browser on both backends via each demo's `?backend=webgl2|webgpu` switch. Not verified by a live test: the context-recovery path. I could not get a context loss to reproduce on demand (five rapid refocuses across all six faces held), so that path is verified by construction and typecheck only. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Hardware Accelerated Point Rendering of Isosurfaces
abstract: Interactive volume sculpting and volume editing often employ surface based visualization techniques, and interactive applications require fast generation and rendering of surface primitives. In this paper, we revisit point primitives as an alternative to triangle primitives. We propose an approximate technique for point scaling using distance attenuation which makes it possible to render points stored in display lists or vertex arrays. This enables us to render points quickly using OpenGL. Our comparisons show that point generation is significantly faster than triangle generation and that the advantage of rendering points as opposed to triangles increases with the size and complexity of the volumes. title: Interactive volume isosurface rendering using BT volumes
abstract: This paper presents a volume representation format called BT Volumes, along with a technique to interactively render them and two methods to create useful data in BT Volume format, including high quality reconstruction filtering. Medical applications rely heavily on isosurface data to visualize anatomy, but current real-time iso-surface rendering techniques such as Marching Cubes are limited in flexibility and provide only low-order linear reconstruction filtering. As an alternative to creating triangular geometry to represent the surface, we ray trace an exact isosurface directly inside a pixel shader. We construct a set of Bézier Tetrahedra to approximate any reconstruction filter with arbitrary footprint. We then precompute the volume convolved with this filter as a tetrahedral grid with Bézier weights that can be ray traced in graphics hardware. Our technique is fast, renders any isosurface level without additional work, and performs high quality reconstruction filtering with arbitrary footprints and reconstruction kernels.

title: LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering
abstract: Volumetric rendering has become central to modern novel view synthesis methods, which use differentiable rendering to optimize 3D scene representations directly from observed views. While many recent works build on NeRF or 3D Gaussians, we explore an alternative volumetric scene representation. More specifically, we introduce two new scene representations based on linear primitives - octahedra and tetrahedra - both of which define homogeneous volumes bounded by triangular faces. To optimize these primitives, we present a differentiable rasterizer that runs efficiently on GPUs, allowing end-to-end gradient-based optimization while maintaining real-time rendering capabilities. Through experiments on real-world datasets, we demonstrate comparable performance to state-of-the-art volumetric methods while requiring fewer primitives to achieve similar reconstruction fidelity. Our findings deepen the understanding of 3D representations by providing insights into the fidelity and performance characteristics of transparent polyhedra and suggest that adopting novel primitives can expand the available design space.

title: Mathematical models for volume rendering and neutron transport
abstract: This paper reviews several different models for light interaction with volume densities of absorbing, glowing, reflecting, or scattering material. They include absorption only, glow only, glow and absorption combined, single scattering of external illumination, and multiple scattering. The models are derived from differential equations, and illustrated on a data set representing a cloud. They are related to corresponding models in neutron transport. The multiple scattering model uses an efficient method to propagate the radiation which does not suffer from the ray effect.

cited.name: P-N Method (Spherical Harmonics)
ctx: The P-N method solves the multiple scattering integral equation by expanding the directional intensity I(X, \omega) into spherical harmonics over the unit sphere direction \omega, converting the integral equation into a coupled system of partial differential equations for the harmonic coefficients.

It is mathematically equivalent to the discrete ordinates method with M properly placed directions, which specify the directional intensity distribution to the same detail as M spherical harmonic coefficients.
Input: The scattering source term Z(z, s) (or Z(X, \omega)), representing emission and single-scattering contributions.

cited.name: Discrete Ordinates Method
ctx: The Discrete Ordinates Method (DOM) solves the Radiative Transfer Equation by approximating the continuous angular dependence of radiance with a finite set of M discrete directions chosen to provide optimal Gaussian quadrature over the solid angle.

It differs from the P-N method by working directly with directional intensities rather than spherical harmonic coefficients, and from ray-tracing methods by discretizing the angular domain into bins to mitigate ray effects.
It is primarily used for computing multiple scattering in participating media, such as clouds, where it provides a global illumination solution via iterative flux propagation.

cited.name: Emission-only Model
ctx: The Emission-only Model renders a participating medium that adds light to the view ray via emission but neglects absorption and scattering.
It solves for the accumulated glow intensity of a luminous medium, such as a hot tenuous gas or fluorescent stains, where the material is effectively transparent to its own light.
In many implementations, g is proportional to f. 3.

cited.name: Binary Volume Rendering (Opacity Thresholding)
ctx: Binary volume rendering is a technique where voxels are classified as either completely opaque or completely transparent based on whether their scalar density exceeds a specific threshold.

This reduces the rendering problem to projecting opaque geometric primitives (cubes or their front faces) onto the image plane, effectively visualizing the iso-surface corresponding to the threshold interface.

Unlike direct volume rendering methods that integrate optical properties along rays, this approach treats the volume as a collection of discrete opaque objects, relying on standard rasterization visibility techniques such as the z-buffer or a back-to-front painter's algorithm.

cited.name: Single Scattering Model
ctx: The Single Scattering Model approximates light transport in participating media by accounting only for light that undergoes zero or exactly one scattering event, ignoring multiple scattering and emitted radiance.

It is distinguished from the Absorption-only model by including scattering phase functions and from the Emission-Absorption Volume Rendering by explicitly modeling the redirection of light via a phase function and scattering albedo.
Phase function p(\omega, \omega') depending on the angle between viewing direction \omega and light direction \omega'.

cited.name: Multiple Scattering Model (Integral Equation)
ctx: The Multiple Scattering Model (Integral Equation) is a deterministic method for solving the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) by explicitly accounting for multiple scattering events in participating media.

It formulates the radiance at a point as a path integral that includes in-scattering from all directions along the ray, creating a self-referential equation where the unknown intensity appears on both sides.

Unlike single-scattering approximations, this model captures the complex light transport in dense or high-albedo media, distinguishing it from its siblings by providing the exact integral formulation that other methods (like Monte Carlo or P-N) approximate.

title: Methods and Strategies for Improving the Novel View Synthesis Quality of Neural Radiation Field
abstract: Neural Radiation Field (NeRF) technology can learn a 3D implicit model of a scene from 2D images and synthesize realistic novel view images. This technology has received widespread attention from the industry and has good application prospects. In response to the problem that the rendering quality of NeRF images needs to be improved, many researchers have proposed various methods to improve the rendering quality in the past three years. The latest relevant papers are classified and reviewed, the technical principles behind quality improvement are analyzed, and the future evolution direction of quality improvement methods is discussed. This study can help researchers quickly understand the current state and evolutionary context of technology in this field, which is helpful in inspiring the development of more efficient algorithms and promoting the application of NeRF technology in related fields.
