title: feat(#40): Find the voxel at the screen center with a voxel ray
abstract: ## What and why The app had no way to find the voxel at the center of the screen. The legacy project used `Physics.Raycast` on the mesh colliders. The app has no colliders. This pull request adds a voxel ray that reads the voxel data directly, and draws a box around the voxel at the screen center. Fixes #40 ### Changes - **Voxel data** (`VoxelWorld`): the world builder now keeps the block types of each chunk. A position outside all the chunks is empty. `Min` and `Max` give the world limits. The sample scene uses 32 MiB for the voxels. #45 changes this storage in M2. - **Voxel ray** (`VoxelRay.TryCast`): the voxel traversal of Amanatides and Woo. The result (`VoxelRayHit`) gives: - the solid voxel and its block type, - the face that the ray crosses (`Normal` and `Face`), - the empty voxel before the hit (`EmptyVoxel`), - the distance. The ray stops at the maximum distance (default: 64 voxels) or at the world limits. At an edge or a corner, the ray crosses X first, then Y, then Z. - **Selection box**: a new pipeline draws the 12 edges of the voxel as black lines. The vertex shader makes the vertices, thus there is no vertex buffer. The depth test hides the edges behind voxels. The shader moves the lines a little nearer to the camera. Without this offset, the faces hid parts of the lines. - **Debug overlay**: a new line "Target" gives the voxel, the block type, the face and the distance. - **Shader compiler**: the two pipelines use one compiler. A second compiler added approximately 60 ms to the start of the app. ### Tests - 31 tests for the ray, and 12 tests for the voxel world: - rays along each axis in the two directions, - diagonal rays and the order at a corner, - rays across chunk borders, - negative coordinates, - origins on a voxel boundary, - the maximum distance and the world limits, - an origin in a solid voxel, - incorrect arguments. - 300 random rays are compared with a ray that is sampled every 0.0001 voxels. A ray that goes near an edge or a corner is skipped. More than 200 rays must be checked. - Mutations that the tests find: the tie order, the sign of the normal, `Floor` changed to a truncation, `>` changed to `>=` at the maximum distance, an incorrect first boundary, a world box one voxel too small. ### Manual test (Xvfb and lavapipe, Linux) - The box follows the voxel at the screen center, on the top faces and on the walls. - Debug build with the synchronization validation (`VK_LAYER_ENABLES=VK_VALIDATION_FEATURE_ENABLE_SYNCHRONIZATION_VALIDATION_EXT`): 0 error and 0 warning messages. - Start of the pipelines: approximately 100 ms, as before. An independent review found no blocking defect. The last commit corrects the defect and the text problems that it found. The defect: an origin exactly on a voxel boundary, with a ray in the negative direction, hit the voxel behind the origin. ### To check on Windows 1. Start the app, then press M to go to fly mode. 2. Look at a voxel. The black box must be on the voxel at the screen center. 3. Look at the "Target" line in the overlay (F3). ### Notes for #41 - The ray also runs in menu mode. In menu mode, the cursor is free. Thus #41 must use the clicks only in fly mode. - `EmptyVoxel` can be outside the world, for example above the highest chunk layer. #41 must not place a block there, or in the voxel of the camera. - `VoxelWorld` has no `SetVoxel` method yet. #41 adds it. ## Checklist - [x] The pull request links one issue (`Fixes #n`). - [x] The pull request targets `develop`. Only `release/` and `hotfix/` branches target `main`. - [x] The pull request does one change. - [x] The CI passes. - [x] A `port` or `refactor` pull request does not change behavior, except the changes that its issue lists. - [x] A `perf` pull request gives the benchmark results before and after the change. - [x] The text follows STE100 (docs/STYLE.md). https://claude.ai/code/session_01JygSjeYRV2itjLUrfC7nis --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)_

title: feat(terrain): DDA voxel raycast + editing brushes with undo/redo
abstract: Closes #728. Click a voxel surface in the editor and place, carve, fill or paint it. A drag is one undo step. ## Picking — `VoxelRaycast` Amanatides–Woo traversal over the sparse grid, entered through a slab test against the volume's world AABB. **Chunks are not a second traversal level.** A cell in a missing chunk is simply empty, so a ray crosses a chunk edge without the marcher knowing one is there — no chunk marcher, no special case at the boundary, and the negative-coordinate side works for the same reason. The hit carries the exact grid cell, the **entered face normal** (what a placement brush needs — zero only when the ray starts inside solid, where there is no entered face), the distance, and the world point. ## Editing — `VoxelEdit` Four operations (Place / Carve / Fill / Paint) over a world-space radius, addressed on the **unbounded grid** rather than chunk-local indices, so behaviour does not change at a 32-cell boundary. **A stroke snapshots whole chunks, not cell deltas.** That is what makes undo lossless on a *sparse* volume: undoing an edit that created a chunk removes the chunk again rather than leaving an empty allocation behind. Only chunks whose cells actually changed are kept, so the snapshot stays proportional to the edit. ## Remesh `VoxelOverride` grows unbounded-grid accessors that mark the owning chunk — and any *existing* neighbour across a shared face — dirty, so an edit rebuilds a ring around itself instead of the volume. Both meshers now prune meshes for chunks that no longer exist. This is the non-obvious half: **an undo that deletes a chunk leaves no dirty flag to drive a rebuild from.** The chunk simply stops existing, nothing in the dirty-chunk path can mention it again, and without the prune its quads keep drawing forever — the undone stroke stays on screen while every CPU assertion still passes. ## Editor New **Voxel** mode in the Terrain Editor panel (operation, radius, material). `EditorLayer` transforms the mouse ray into each voxel terrain's local space before traversal, so a moved or scaled terrain picks correctly. The stroke accumulates across frames and pushes one `VoxelEditCommand` on release. ## Verification - **5 CPU contracts** — chunk-boundary hit and entered face, negative grid coordinates mapping to the right chunk, exact multi-chunk undo/redo, dirty-region scope, material serialization round-trip. - **1 GL-attached integration test** driving the real `VoxelGreedyMeshBuilder` across an edit/undo cycle. **Verified to fail when the prune is removed** (`undo deleted chunk (1,0,0) but its mesh is still being drawn`) rather than merely passing alongside it. Skips cleanly with no GL 4.6 context. - **Full suite: 6741 run, 6715 passed, 26 skipped, 0 failed.** - Editor boots clean — all shaders compile, scene deserializes 18/18 entities, no errors in `OloEngine.log`. The brush *gesture* itself is not machine-verifiable here (there is no way to drive a viewport click-drag headlessly), so the editor check is a boot/render smoke test; the picking and editing logic underneath it is covered by the contracts above. ## Also in this branch One unrelated commit: the `PreToolUse` build-lock hook resolved its guard script by a bare relative path, so any `cd` into a subdirectory made it unresolvable — and since it gates every shell call, it then blocked the `cd` back out, wedging the shell for the rest of the session. Now resolved against `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` with the old path as fallback. Happy to split it out if you'd rather. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Added voxel terrain editing with Place, Carve, Fill, and Paint brush operations. - Added voxel editing mode with configurable brush radius and material selection. - Added ray-based voxel selection and editing across terrain chunk boundaries. - Added undo and redo support for complete voxel brush strokes. - Voxel material data is now preserved when terrain is saved and loaded. - **Bug Fixes** - Improved mesh cleanup when voxel chunks are removed or restored, including during undo operations. - Fixed terrain editing guard behavior when launched from different project locations.

title: Gaussian in the Wild: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unconstrained Image Collections
abstract: Novel view synthesis from unconstrained in-the-wild images remains a meaningful but challenging task. The photometric variation and transient occluders in those unconstrained images make it difficult to reconstruct the original scene accurately. Previous approaches tackle the problem by introducing a global appearance feature in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). However, in the real world, the unique appearance of each tiny point in a scene is determined by its independent intrinsic material attributes and the varying environmental impacts it receives. Inspired by this fact, we propose Gaussian in the wild (GS-W), a method that uses 3D Gaussian points to reconstruct the scene and introduces separated intrinsic and dynamic appearance feature for each point, capturing the unchanged scene appearance along with dynamic variation like illumination and weather. Additionally, an adaptive sampling strategy is presented to allow each Gaussian point to focus on the local and detailed information more effectively. We also reduce the impact of transient occluders using a 2D visibility map. More experiments have demonstrated better reconstruction quality and details of GS-W compared to NeRF-based methods, with a faster rendering speed. Video results and code are available at https://eastbeanzhang.github.io/GS-W/.

By extracting dynamic appearance features from a reference image and allowing each Gaussian point to sample from multiple feature maps, the method captures local details such as highlights and shadows that global embeddings miss.
It sets itself apart from methods like NeRF-W and Ha-NeRF, which use global scene embeddings, and CR-NeRF, which integrates features at the 2D level without dynamic 3D environmental information.

It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a U-Net encoder-decoder structure and a fusion network to map image features to Gaussian attributes, rather than using direct MLPs or spherical harmonics.

title: GES: Generalized Exponential Splatting for Efficient Radiance Field Rendering
abstract: Advancements in 3D Gaussian Splatting have significantly accelerated 3D reconstruction and generation. However, it may require a large number of Gaussians, which creates a substantial memory footprint. This paper introduces GES (Generalized Exponential Splatting), a novel representation that employs Generalized Exponential Function (GEF) to model 3D scenes, requiring far fewer particles to represent a scene and thus significantly outperforming Gaussian Splatting methods in efficiency with a plug-and-play replacement ability for Gaussian-based utilities. GES is validated theoretically and empirically in both principled 1D setup and realistic 3D scenes. It is shown to represent signals with sharp edges more accurately, which are typically challenging for Gaussians due to their inherent low-pass characteristics. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that GEF outperforms Gaussians in fitting natural-occurring signals (e.g. squares, triangles, and parabolic signals), thereby reducing the need for extensive splitting operations that increase the memory footprint of Gaussian Splatting. With the aid of a frequency-modulated loss, GES achieves competitive performance in novel-view synthesis benchmarks while requiring less than half the memory storage of Gaussian Splatting and increasing the rendering speed by up to 39%. The code is available on the project website https://abdullahamdi.com/ges .Comment: CVPR 2024 paper. project website https://abdullahamdi.com/ge

It builds on Frequency-aware Mask Generation by spatially weighting the error based on the spectral content of the ground truth image, allowing the model to prioritize low-frequency structures early in training and high-frequency details later.
The method computes a frequency-specific binary mask from the ground truth image and applies an L1 loss weighted by this mask.

title: GPU Volume Rendering with Hierarchical Compression Using VDB
abstract: We propose a compression-based approach to GPU rendering of large volumetric data using OpenVDB and NanoVDB. We use OpenVDB to create a lossy, fixed-rate compressed representation of the volume on the host, and use NanoVDB to perform fast, low-overhead, and on-the-fly decompression during rendering. We show that this approach is fast, works well even in a (incoherent) Monte Carlo path tracing context, can significantly reduce the memory requirements of volume rendering, and can be used as an almost drop-in replacement into existing 3D texture-based renderers.

title: Gradient‐based Interpolation and Sampling for Real‐time Rendering of Inhomogeneous, Single‐scattering Media
abstract: Abstract We present a real‐time rendering algorithm for inhomogeneous, single scattering media, where all‐frequency shading effects such as glows, light shafts, and volumetric shadows can all be captured. The algorithm first computes source radiance at a small number of sample points in the medium, then interpolates these values at other points in the volume using a gradient‐based scheme that is efficiently applied by sample splatting. The sample points are dynamically determined based on a recursive sample splitting procedure that adapts the number and locations of sample points for accurate and efficient reproduction of shading variations in the medium. The entire pipeline can be easily implemented on the GPU to achieve real‐time performance for dynamic lighting and scenes. Rendering results of our method are shown to be comparable to those from ray tracing.

title: Implicit Surface Compression -- with Good Old Discrete Cosine Transform and Motion Compensation
abstract: The rapid adoption of volumetric capture technologies has created a pressing need for efficient storage and streaming of dynamic 3D content. Unfortunately, current compression standards often treat dynamic sequences as independent frames or rely on computationally expensive non-rigid registration, making them unsuitable for real-time applications or large-scale environments. In this paper, we present a novel end-to-end compression framework for dynamic Truncated Signed Distance Field volumes derived from captured 3D content, leveraging a representation that is temporally stable, easily parallelizable, and already widely used in scene reconstruction and volumetric fusion pipelines. We then adapt classic 2D video coding paradigms such as spatial coding via Discrete Cosine Transform and temporal coding using a real-time motion compensation pipeline to provide robust, real-time, and training-free encoding and decoding for 3D content. Extensive evaluations on human performance captures demonstrate that our codec achieves ~35% bitrate savings at equal distortion while operating in real time at 30 FPS, while stronger temporal coherence in large-scale synthetic environments yields up to 12× bitrate reduction at equal distortion.

It solves the problem of efficiently encoding sparse, locally smooth TSDF data by decomposing the volume into fixed-size voxel blocks, applying a 3D Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to concentrate energy in low frequencies, and entropy coding the retained coefficients.

It is distinguished from its siblings by its use of a fixed, data-independent 3D DCT (avoiding the overhead of learned transforms like KLT) and its specific strategy of grouping coefficients by DCT index across all active blocks to optimize probability models for range coding.

title: Improving Robustness for Joint Optimization of Camera Poses and Decomposed Low-Rank Tensorial Radiance Fields
abstract: In this paper, we propose an algorithm that allows joint refinement of camera pose and scene geometry represented by decomposed low-rank tensor, using only 2D images as supervision. First, we conduct a pilot study based on a 1D signal and relate our findings to 3D scenarios, where the naive joint pose optimization on voxel-based NeRFs can easily lead to sub-optimal solutions. Moreover, based on the analysis of the frequency spectrum, we propose to apply convolutional Gaussian filters on 2D and 3D radiance fields for a coarse-to-fine training schedule that enables joint camera pose optimization. Leveraging the decomposition property in decomposed low-rank tensor, our method achieves an equivalent effect to brute-force 3D convolution with only incurring little computational overhead. To further improve the robustness and stability of joint optimization, we also propose techniques of smoothed 2D supervision, randomly scaled kernel parameters, and edge-guided loss mask. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves superior performance in novel view synthesis as well as rapid convergence for optimization.Comment: AAAI 2024. title: Interactive Global Light Propagation in Direct Volume Rendering using Local Piecewise Integration
abstract: A novel technique for efficient computation of global light propagation in interactive DVR is presented in this paper. The approach is based on a combination of local shadows from the vicinity of each voxel with global shadows calculated at high resolution but stored in a sparser grid. The resulting intensities are then used as the initial illumination for an additional pass that computes first order scattering effects. The method captures global shadowing effects with enhanced shadows of near structures. title: Interactive volume illustration
abstract: In this paper we describe non-photorealistic rendering techniques for volumetric data sets. First, we outline an automatic approach that generates line drawings to illustrate such data sets and to augment traditional volume rendering techniques. For a number of seed points that are placed appropriately to represent selected volume structures curvature lines are traced and encoded by a sparse set of control points. These curves are finally drawn as hatching strokes modulated by anisotropic lighting and transparency. Second, in addition to line-art drawings we present efficient implementations of volume toon-shading and silhouette rendering using fragment shader hardware. All techniques together allow us to interactively illustrate volumetric data sets and to enhance important features using nonphotorealistic rendering techniques.

title: Isosurface extraction and interpretation on very large datasets in geophysics
abstract: International audienceIn order to deal with the heavy trend in size increase of volumetric datasets, research in isosurface extraction has focused in the past few years on related aspects such as surface simplification and load balanced parallel algorithms. We present in this paper a parallel, bloc-wise extension of the tandem algorithm [Attali et al. 2005], which simplifies on the fly an isosurface being extracted. Our approach minimizes the overall memory consumption using an adequate bloc splitting and merging strategy and with the introduction of a component dumping mechanism that drastically reduces the amount of memory needed for particular datasets such as those encountered in geophysics. As soon as detected, surface components are migrated to the disk along with a meta-data index (oriented bounding box, volume, etc) that will allow further improved exploration scenarios (small components removal or particularly oriented components selection for instance). For ease of implementation, we carefully describe a master and slave algorithm architecture that clearly separates the four required basic tasks. We show several results of our parallel algorithm applied on a 7000×1600×2000 geophysics dataset

title: Joint importance sampling of low-order volumetric scattering
abstract: Central to all Monte Carlo-based rendering algorithms is the construction of light transport paths from the light sources to the eye. Existing rendering approaches sample path vertices incrementally when constructing these light transport paths. The resulting probability density is thus a product of the conditional densities of each local sampling step, constructed without explicit control over the form of the final joint distribution of the complete path. We analyze why current incremental construction schemes often lead to high variance in the presence of participating media, and reveal that such approaches are an unnecessary legacy inherited from traditional surface-based rendering algorithms. We devise joint importance sampling of path vertices in participating media to construct paths that explicitly account for the product of all scattering and geometry terms along a sequence of vertices instead of just locally at a single vertex. This leads to a number of practical importance sampling routines to explicitly construct single-and double-scattering subpaths in anisotropically-scattering media. We demonstrate the benefit of our new sampling techniques, integrating them into several path-based rendering algorithms such as path tracing, bidirectional path tracing, and many-light methods. We also use our sampling routines to generalize deterministic shadow connections to connection subpaths consisting of two or three random decisions, to efficiently simulate higher-order multiple scattering. Our algorithms significantly reduce noise and increase performance in renderings with both isotropic and highly anisotropic, low-order scattering.

ctx: Soft Rasterizer is a differentiable rendering method that replaces the deterministic, z-buffer-based triangle selection of traditional rasterization with a probabilistic aggregation approach.
It computes pixel color as a weighted sum of contributions from all mesh triangles, including occluded ones, by modeling each triangle as a probabilistic cloud with a blur radius.

This allows gradients to flow to blocked and distant triangle vertices, making it particularly suitable for geometry optimization tasks where other methods fail to propagate gradients through occlusions.

title: K-Planes: Explicit Radiance Fields in Space, Time, and Appearance
abstract: We introduce k-planes, a white-box model for radiance fields in arbitrary dimensions. Our model uses d choose 2 planes to represent a d-dimensional scene, providing a seamless way to go from static (d=3) to dynamic (d=4) scenes. This planar factorization makes adding dimension-specific priors easy, e.g. temporal smoothness and multi-resolution spatial structure, and induces a natural decomposition of static and dynamic components of a scene. We use a linear feature decoder with a learned color basis that yields similar performance as a nonlinear black-box MLP decoder. Across a range of synthetic and real, static and dynamic, fixed and varying appearance scenes, k-planes yields competitive and often state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity with low memory usage, achieving 1000x compression over a full 4D grid, and fast optimization with a pure PyTorch implementation. For video results and code, please see https://sarafridov.github.io/K-Planes.

title: Low-Cost Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis, but their long training times and reliance on dense input views limit accessibility. We present a comparative study of three accelerated NeRF variants - DS-NeRF, TensoRF, and HashNeRF and explore extensions targeted at the low-compute, low-data regime. First, we add a depth-supervision loss derived from COLMAP keypoints to TensoRF (TensoRF-DS) and evaluate it on the LLFF dataset under reduced view counts. Second, we ablate the feature-decoding MLP of TensoRF and study the effect of input downsampling on PSNR and runtime on the synthetic Lego scene. Third, we propose four architectural variants of the HashNeRF color and density networks, including residual and convolutional designs, and report PSNR/training-time tradeoffs under matched iteration budgets. Under iso-time evaluation, none of our extensions conclusively outperform the published baselines, but the experiments characterize which extensions transfer to constrained settings and surface design questions for future work.

title: NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) 19970021689: Direct Volume Rendering with Shading via Three-Dimensional Textures
abstract: A new and easy-to-implement method for direct volume rendering that uses 3D texture maps for acceleration, and incorporates directional lighting, is described. The implementation, called Voltx, produces high-quality images at nearly interactive speeds on workstations with hardware support for three-dimensional texture maps. Previously reported methods did not incorporate a light model, and did not address issues of multiple texture maps for large volumes. Our research shows that these extensions impact performance by about a factor of ten. Voltx supports orthographic, perspective, and stereo views. This paper describes the theory and implementation of this technique, and compares it to the shear-warp factorization approach. A rectilinear data set is converted into a three-dimensional texture map containing color and opacity information. Quantized normal vectors and a lookup table provide efficiency. A new tesselation of the sphere is described, which serves as the basis for normal-vector quantization. A new gradient-based shading criterion is described, in which the gradient magnitude is interpreted in the context of the field-data value and the material classification parameters, and not in isolation. In the rendering phase, the texture map is applied to a stack of parallel planes, which effectively cut the texture into many slabs. The slabs are composited to form an image.

cited.name: Manifold Vertex Clustering

While standard adaptive contouring reduces polygon count by clustering vertices based on Quadratic Error Function (QEF) thresholds, it may produce non-manifold artifacts such as edges shared by four polygons or vertices with non-disk-like neighborhoods.

This method adds a topological criterion to the collapse decision, guaranteeing that every edge is shared by exactly two polygons and every vertex is surrounded by a disk-like neighborhood, thereby preserving the genus of the original surface.

This approach departs from earlier methods [Lev90a, LL94] by using a linear approximation of the field function to estimate the distance to the material boundary, allowing for a probabilistic classification that handles noise and nonlinearity.

title: NeRF-SDP: Efficient Generalizable Neural Radiance Field with Scene Depth Perception
abstract: In recent years, neural radiance fields have exhibited impressive performance in novel view synthesis. However, exploiting complex network structures to achieve generalizable NeRF usually results in inefficient rendering. Existing methods for accelerating rendering directly employ simpler inference networks or fewer sampling points, leading to unsatisfactory synthesis quality. To address the challenge of balancing rendering speed and quality in generalizable NeRF, we propose a novel framework, NeRF-SDP, which achieves both efficiency and high fidelity by introducing scene depth perception. We incorporate more scene information into the radiance field by using our proposed geometry feature extraction and depth-encoded ray transformer to improve the model’s inference capabilities with sparse points. With the aid of scene depth perception, NeRF-SDP can better understand the scene’s structure, thus better reconstructing the objects’ edges with significantly fewer artifacts. Experimental results demonstrate that NeRF-SDP achieves comparable synthesis quality to state-of-the-art methods while significantly improving rendering efficiency. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that the depth-encoded ray transformer enhances the model’s robustness to varying numbers of sampling points.

title: NeRFusion: Fusing Radiance Fields for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction
abstract: While NeRF [28] has shown great success for neural reconstruction and rendering, its limited MLP capacity and long per-scene optimization times make it challenging to model large-scale indoor scenes. In contrast, classical 3D reconstruction methods can handle large-scale scenes but do not produce realistic renderings. We propose NeRFusion, a method that combines the advantages of NeRF and TSDF-based fusion techniques to achieve efficient large-scale reconstruction and photo-realistic rendering. We process the input image sequence to predict per-frame local radiance fields via direct network inference. These are then fused using a novel recurrent neural network that incrementally reconstructs a global, sparse scene representation in real-time at 22 fps. This global volume can be further fine-tuned to boost rendering quality. We demonstrate that NeR-Fusionachieves state-of-the-art quality on both large-scale indoor and small-scale object scenes, with substantially faster reconstruction than NeRF and other recent methods.11https://jetd1.github.io/NeRFusion-Web/

title: Neuralangelo: High-Fidelity Neural Surface Reconstruction
abstract: Neural surface reconstruction has been shown to be powerful for recovering dense 3D surfaces via image-based neural rendering. However, current methods struggle to recover detailed structures of real-world scenes. To address the issue, we present Neuralangelo, which combines the representation power of multiresolution 3D hash grids with neural surface rendering. Two key ingredients enable our approach: (1) numerical gradients for computing higher-order derivatives as a smoothing operation and (2) coarse-to-fine optimization on the hash grids controlling different levels of details. Even without auxiliary inputs such as depth, Neuralangelo can effectively recover dense 3D surface structures from multiview images with fidelity significantly surpassing previous methods, enabling detailed large-scale scene reconstruction from RGB video captures.

ctx: The Total Loss Function is the composite objective used to optimize radiance field parameters (such as density, color, geometry, or Gaussian attributes) by aggregating multiple distinct error metrics and regularization terms into a single scalar value.
The general form is a linear combination: \mathcal{L} = \sumk wk \mathcal{L}k where wk are scalar weights and \mathcal{L}k are individual loss terms.
Eikonal Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{eik}}): Enforces the eikonal equation \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|2 = 1 for Signed Distance Functions (SDFs).

cited.name: Numerical Gradient Eikonal Loss
ctx: Numerical Gradient Eikonal Loss is a regularization technique used in differentiable volume rendering with hash-encoded Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) to enforce the eikonal equation \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|2 = 1.

It addresses the "locality problem" inherent in analytical gradients of hash encodings, where non-differentiable rounding operations restrict back-propagation updates to only the local hash grid cells involved in trilinear interpolation.

By computing surface normals via numerical finite differences, the method distributes optimization updates beyond the immediate local grid cell, acting as a smoothed gradient that ensures non-local smoothness and consistent surface reconstruction without requiring auxiliary networks.

title: Non-line-of-Sight Imaging via Neural Transient Fields
abstract: We present a neural modeling framework for non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging. Previous solutions have sought to explicitly recover the 3D geometry (e.g., as point clouds) or voxel density (e.g., within a pre-defined volume) of the hidden scene. In contrast, inspired by the recent Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) approach, we use a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to represent the neural transient field or NeTF. However, NeTF measures the transient over spherical wavefronts rather than the radiance along lines. We therefore formulate a spherical volume NeTF reconstruction pipeline, applicable to both confocal and non-confocal setups. Compared with NeRF, NeTF samples a much sparser set of viewpoints (scanning spots) and the sampling is highly uneven. We thus introduce a Monte Carlo technique to improve the robustness in the reconstruction. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate NeTF achieves state-of-the-art performance and can provide reliable reconstructions even under semi-occlusions and on non-Lambertian materials.

title: On-the-fly decompression and rendering of multiresolution terrain
abstract: We present a streaming geometry compression codec for multiresolution, uniformly-gridded, triangular terrain patches that supports very fast decompression. Our method is based on linear prediction and residual coding for lossless compression of the full-resolution data. As simplified patches on coarser levels in the hierarchy already incur some data loss, we optionally allow further quantization for more lossy compression. The quantization levels are adaptive on a per-patch basis, while still permitting seamless, adaptive tessellations of the terrain. Our geometry compression on such a hierarchy achieves compression ratios of 3:1 to 12:1. Our scheme is not only suitable for fast decompression on the CPU, but also for parallel decoding on the GPU with peak throughput over 2 billion triangles per second. Each terrain patch is independently decompressed on the fly from a variable-rate bitstream by a GPU geometry program with no branches or conditionals. Thus we can store the geometry compressed on the GPU, reducing storage and bandwidth requirements throughout the system. In our rendering approach, only compressed bitstreams and the decoded height values in the view-dependent 'cut' are explicitly stored on the GPU. Normal vectors are computed in a streaming fashion, and remaining geometry and texture coordinates, as well as mesh connectivity, are shared and re-used for all patches. We demonstrate and evaluate our algorithms on a small prototype system in which all compressed geometry fits in the GPU memory and decompression occurs on the fly every rendering frame without any cache maintenance.

cited.name: Hierarchical Data Distribution with Error-Guided Bucketization
ctx: Hierarchical Data Distribution with Error-Guided Bucketization is a data distribution scheme for parallel volume rendering that partitions a wavelet-based volume hierarchy among processors to minimize inter-processor communication dependencies and ensure balanced rendering workloads.

It solves the problem of parent-child node dependencies in wavelet reconstruction, which typically force processors to communicate during rendering, by pre-reconstructing data at specific intervals and grouping independent data into "distribution units".

Unlike standard space-filling curve distributions that only consider spatial locality, this method incorporates error-guided bucketization to ensure that nodes with similar reconstruction errors (and thus similar rendering costs) are distributed across different processors, preventing contention and load imbalance.

It builds on Parallel Multiresolution Volume Rendering with Error-Guided Load Balancing by introducing a selection algorithm that prioritizes nodes for reconstruction based on a benefit function, thereby reducing the runtime reconstruction overhead.
The method operates on a wavelet tree distributed across P processors using a hierarchical space-filling curve (specifically the Hilbert curve) and error-guided bucketization.

title: Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations
abstract: In modern computer vision, the optimal representation of 3D shape remains task-dependent. One fundamental operation applied to such representations is differentiable rendering, which enables learning-based inverse graphics approaches. Standard explicit representations are often easily rendered, but can suffer from limited geometric fidelity, among other issues. On the other hand, implicit representations generally preserve greater fidelity, but suffer from difficulties with rendering, limiting scalability. In this work, we devise Directed Distance Fields (DDFs), which map a ray or oriented point (position and direction) to surface visibility and depth. This enables efficient differentiable rendering, obtaining depth with a single forward pass per pixel, as well as higher-order geometry with only additional backward passes. Using probabilistic DDFs (PDDFs), we can model the inherent discontinuities in the underlying field. We then apply DDFs to single-shape fitting, generative modelling, and 3D reconstruction, showcasing strong performance with simple architectural components via the versatility of our representation. Finally, since the dimensionality of DDFs permits view-dependent geometric artifacts, we conduct a theoretical investigation of the constraints necessary for view consistency. We find a small set of field properties that are sufficient to guarantee a DDF is consistent, without knowing which shape the field is expressing.

title: R$^2$-Gaussian: Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction
abstract: 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) has shown promising results in image rendering and surface reconstruction. However, its potential in volumetric reconstruction tasks, such as X-ray computed tomography, remains under-explored. This paper introduces R$^2$-Gaussian, the first 3DGS-based framework for sparse-view tomographic reconstruction. By carefully deriving X-ray rasterization functions, we discover a previously unknown integration bias in the standard 3DGS formulation, which hampers accurate volume retrieval. To address this issue, we propose a novel rectification technique via refactoring the projection from 3D to 2D Gaussians. Our new method presents three key innovations: (1) introducing tailored Gaussian kernels, (2) extending rasterization to X-ray imaging, and (3) developing a CUDA-based differentiable voxelizer. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in accuracy and efficiency. Crucially, it delivers high-quality results in 4 minutes, which is 12$\times$ faster than NeRF-based methods and on par with traditional algorithms. Code and models are available on the project page https://github.com/Ruyi-Zha/r2_gaussian.Accepted to NeurIPS 2024. Project page: https://github.com/Ruyi-Zha/r2_gaussia

cited.name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (Cone-Beam/Scanner Space)

It solves the problem of simulating X-ray CT projections from learned 3D Gaussian fields by adapting the rasterization pipeline to a pinhole camera model, enabling analytical integration of radiative density.

Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which composites opacities, this method sums projected 2D densities, fundamentally addressing integration bias issues where learning integrated density in 2D leads to inconsistencies in 3D density retrieval.

Unlike siblings that use 3DGS only for data augmentation or replace rasterization with simulators, R2-Gaussian maintains efficient differentiable rasterization while enabling direct 3D density volume extraction.

title: Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Efficient X-Ray Novel View Synthesis
abstract: X-ray is widely applied for transmission imaging due to its stronger penetration than natural light. When rendering novel view X-ray projections, existing methods mainly based on NeRF suffer from long training time and slow inference speed. In this paper, we propose a 3D Gaussian splatting-based framework, namely X-Gaussian, for X-ray novel view synthesis. Firstly, we redesign a radiative Gaussian point cloud model inspired by the isotropic nature of X-ray imaging. Our model excludes the influence of view direction when learning to predict the radiation intensity of 3D points. Based on this model, we develop a Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR) with CUDA implementation. Secondly, we customize an Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) strategy that directly uses the parameters of the X-ray scanner to compute the camera information and then uniformly samples point positions within a cuboid enclosing the scanned object. Experiments show that our X-Gaussian outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 6.5 dB while enjoying less than 15% training time and over 73x inference speed. The application on sparse-view CT reconstruction also reveals the practical values of our method. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/caiyuanhao1998/X-Gaussian . A video demo of the training process visualization is at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gDVf_Ngeghg .ECCV 2024; The first 3D Gaussian Splatting-based method for X-ray 3D reconstructio

ctx: Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR) is a GPU-friendly rasterization process implemented in CUDA that renders novel X-ray projections from radiative Gaussian point clouds.

It solves the problem of differentiable rendering for X-ray imaging by projecting 3D Gaussians to a 2D detector plane and accumulating radiation intensity per pixel, allowing gradients to flow back to Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, and radiation intensity).

Unlike standard optical Gaussian Splatting which uses alpha compositing for color, DRR sums the radiation intensities of intersection points weighted by the Gaussian probability density, tailored for the physics of X-ray attenuation.

title: Real-time Deblocked GPU Rendering of Compressed Volumes
abstract: The wide majority of current state-of-the-art compressed GPU volume renderers are based on block-transform coding, which is susceptible to blocking artifacts, particularly at low bit-rates. In this paper we address the problem for the first time, by introducing a specialized deferred filtering architecture working on block-compressed data and including a novel deblocking algorithm. The architecture efficiently performs high quality shading of massive datasets by closely coordinating visibility- and resolution-aware adaptive data loading with GPU-accelerated per-frame data decompression, deblocking, and rendering. A thorough evaluation including quantitative and qualitative measures demonstrates the performance of our approach on large static and dynamic datasets including a massive 5124 turbulence simulation (256GB), which is aggressively compressed to less than 2 GB, so as to fully upload it on graphics board and to explore it in real-time during animation.Vision, Modeling & Visualizatio

cited.name: Deferred Filtering Architecture for Compressed Volumes
ctx: Deferred Filtering Architecture is a specialized rendering pipeline that performs high-quality shading of massive volumetric datasets by coordinating visibility- and resolution-aware adaptive data loading with GPU-accelerated per-frame decompression, deblocking, and rendering.

It solves the problem of blocking artifacts inherent in block-compressed data and the memory bandwidth limitations of full-volume decompression by keeping data in compressed format until the final rendering stages.

Unlike Stripe-based On-the-fly Decoding, which processes sequential blocks in a single pass, or CPU-Based Block Decompression, which offloads decoding to the host, this architecture integrates deblocking as a post-loop filtering stage on the GPU, allowing pluggable compression methods without modifying the encoder.

title: Real-time spectral scattering in large-scale natural participating media
abstract: Real-time rendering of participating media in nature presents a difficult problem. The reason is that realistic reproduction of such media requires a proper physical simulation in all cases. In our work we focus on real-time rendering of planetary atmospheres and large areas of water. We first formulate a physically-based model for simulation of light transport in these environments. This model accounts for all necessary light contributions --- direct illumination, indirect illumination caused by the scattered light and interreflections between the planetary surface and the atmospheric volume, as well as reflections from the seabed. We adopt the precomputation scheme presented in the previous works to precompute the colours of the arbitrarily dense atmosphere and large-scale water surfaces into a set of lookup tables. All these computations are fully spectral, which increases the realism. Finally we utilize these tables in a GPU-based algorithm that is capable of rendering a whole planet with its atmosphere from all viewpoints above the planetary surface. This approach is capable to achieve hundreds of frames per second on today's graphics hardware.

cited.name: One-pass Spectral Rendering Integral
ctx: Spectral Precomputation is a variant that uses full spectral computation instead of RGB to simulate light scattering, resulting in smoother, less saturated, and more natural colors.

Constants must be spectral (sampled at more than three wavelengths), and incident light intensity is calculated as blackbody radiation at 5778K according to Planck's law.

This variant treats Mie scattering intensity I{SM} as monochromatic, occupying only one channel in the scattering texture, and shades it during rendering by multiplying by the attenuated direct illumination I0^I.

title: Rendering Large Volume Datasets in Unreal Engine 5: A Survey
abstract: In this technical report, we discuss several approaches to in-core rendering of large volumetric datasets in Unreal Engine 5 (UE5). We explore the following methods: the TBRayMarcher Plugin, the Niagara Fluids Plugin , and various approaches using Sparse Volume Textures (SVT), with a particular focus on Heterogeneous Volumes (HV). We found the HV approach to be the most promising. The biggest challenge we encountered with other approaches was the need to chunk datasets so that each fits into volume textures smaller than one gigavoxel. While this enables display of the entire dataset at reasonable frame rates, it introduces noticeable artifacts at chunk borders due to incorrect lighting, as each chunk lacks information about its neighbors. After addressing some (signed) int32 overflows in the Engine's SVT-related source code by converting them to to (unsigned) uint32 or int64, the SVT-based HV system allows us to render sparse datasets up to 32k x 32k x 16k voxels, provided the compressed tile data (including MIP data and padding for correct interpolation) does not exceed 4 gigavoxels. In the future, we intend to extend the existing SVT streaming functionality to support out-of-core rendering, in order to eventually overcome VRAM limitations, graphics API constraints, and the performance issues associated with 64-bit arithmetic in GPU shaders.

Unlike dense grids, SVT circumvents API limits by mapping a large logical coordinate space onto a smaller physical texture containing only active tiles, though it incurs overhead from padding and mipmap hierarchies.

cited.name: Niagara Fluids Volume Rendering
ctx: Niagara Fluids Volume Rendering is a technique that repurposes Unreal Engine’s grid-based fluid simulation system for volume rendering by ignoring the simulation step and utilizing only the rendering pipeline.

It differs from dedicated volume renderers by leveraging the engine’s native Niagara particle system and material domain, allowing for the use of existing volume materials and interactive transfer function authoring within the Editor.

Unlike Gaussian Splashing or Position Based Fluids, which generate geometry or particles, this method treats the simulation grid as a static volumetric texture container, albeit with significant memory overhead due to the underlying simulation data structures.

title: RGB-D Mapping and Tracking in a Plenoxel Radiance Field
abstract: The widespread adoption of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) have ensured significant advances in the domain of novel view synthesis in recent years. These models capture a volumetric radiance field of a scene, creating highly convincing, dense, photorealistic models through the use of simple, differentiable rendering equations. Despite their popularity, these algorithms suffer from severe ambiguities in visual data inherent to the RGB sensor, which means that although images generated with view synthesis can visually appear very believable, the underlying 3D model will often be wrong. This considerably limits the usefulness of these models in practical applications like Robotics and Extended Reality (XR), where an accurate dense 3D reconstruction otherwise would be of significant value. In this paper, we present the vital differences between view synthesis models and 3D reconstruction models. We also comment on why a depth sensor is essential for modeling accurate geometry in general outward-facing scenes using the current paradigm of novel view synthesis methods. Focusing on the structure-from-motion task, we practically demonstrate this need by extending the Plenoxel radiance field model: Presenting an analytical differential approach for dense mapping and tracking with radiance fields based on RGB-D data without a neural network. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results in both mapping and tracking tasks, while also being faster than competing neural network-based approaches. The code is available at: https://github.com/ysus33/RGB-D_Plenoxel_Mapping_Tracking.git.

title: Segmentation Assisted Object Distinction for Direct Volume Rendering
abstract: Ray casting is a direct volume rendering technique for visualizing 3D arrays of sampled data. It has vital applications in medical and biological imaging. Nevertheless, it is inherently open to cluttered classification results. It suffers from overlapping transfer function values and lacks a sufficiently powerful voxel parsing mechanism for object distinction. In this research work, we are proposing an image processing based approach towards enhancing ray casting technique’s object distinction process. The ray casting architecture is modified to accommodate object membership information generated by a K-means based hybrid segmentation algorithm. Object membership information is assigned to cubical vertices in the form of ID tags. An intra-object buffer is devised and coordinated with inter-object buffer, allowing the otherwise global rendering module to embed multiple local (secondary) rendering processes. A local rendering process adds two advantageous aspects to global rendering module. First, depth oriented manipulation of interpolation and composition operations that lead to freedom of interpolation method choice based on the number of available objects in various volumetric depths, improvement of LOD (level of details) for desired objects and reduced number of required mathematical computations. Second, localization of transfer function design that enables the utilization of binary (non-overlapping) transfer functions for color and opacity assignment. A set of image processing techniques are creatively employed in the design of K-means based hybrid segmentation algorithm

title: Single-Pass High-Quality Splatting
abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel real-time splat rendering pipeline that relies on components of state-of-the-art splat and mesh rendering methods to enable high-quality shader effects such as reflection and refraction for splats. Our pipeline consists of one single rendering pass and aggressively utilizes the most practical components of both techniques. The entire pipeline is compactly implemented in the vertex and fragment stage on current GPUs. Our renderer simplifies current splatting techniques, accelerates rendering, and, moreover, achieves excellent visual quality.

cited.name: Mesh-to-Octree Volumetric Spot Noise Generation
ctx: Volumetric Spot Noise is a technique for representing three-dimensional textures algorithmically using small kernels (impulses), treating textures as sparse volumetric data by storing only the set of impulses rather than explicitly storing the texture.
It generates these impulses on a mesh surface using an octree subdivision to ensure uniform distribution, then renders them via EWA splatting with order-independent transparency.

It is distinct from its parent Mesh-to-Octree Voxelization via BVH Ray Casting by focusing on procedural texture synthesis (e.g., hair, grass) rather than solid geometry classification, and from standard ray-traced volume rendering by using a single-pass splatting approximation that is significantly faster.

cited.name: DirectXSplat Renderer Integration
ctx: DirectXSplat is a D3D12-based renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates directly into an application's graphics pipeline.
It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of 3D Gaussians with minimal CPU overhead by managing GPU memory residency, Level-of-Detail culling, and chunk-based scene mutations.
Unlike convenience wrappers that own the entire frame loop, this integration method allows the host application to retain control over the D3D12 command queue and resource lifecycle.

cited.name: Single-Pass Splat Rendering Pipeline
ctx: A real-time splat rendering pipeline that combines splat and mesh rendering components to enable high-quality shader effects (reflection, refraction) in a single rendering pass.
It avoids multi-pass blending artifacts and reduces memory/workload compared to dense point sets by interpolating attributes in object space rather than screen space.
Each patch is parameterized as an elevation map over a planar domain and resampled on a regular grid.

cited.name: Continuous Attribute Interpolation
ctx: Continuous Attribute Interpolation is a method for obtaining continuous reconstruction of UV coordinates for attribute interpolation on splats, specifically designed to avoid visual artifacts at splat boundaries.
It solves the problem of discontinuous attribute sampling that arises when intersecting view rays with flat splat planes, which can cause large UV coordinate jumps for neighboring fragments.

It sets itself apart from naive direct interpolation by using a "correct interpolation" variant that projects intersections onto a plane defined by elevated neighboring points, ensuring smooth attribute transitions.

cited.name: Splat Radius Adjustment Based on Normal Angle
ctx: This method adjusts the radius of individual splats to prevent visual holes that occur when surface samples are elevated in the normal direction of a base plane.
It scales the splat radius based on the angle between the splat's normal vector and the base plane's normal vector.
Unlike fixed-radius splatting, which assumes a flat distribution, this approach increases radii in areas with high local elevation variance, ensuring continuous coverage.

title: Size-based Transfer Functions: A New Volume Exploration Technique
abstract: Size-based Transfer Functions: A New Volume Exploration Technique Through a number of examples, we show that size-based transfer functions can improve classification and enhance volume rendering techniques, such as maximum intensity projection.

cited.name: GPU Laplacian Scale-Space Maxima Detection
ctx: This method detects local maxima of the Laplacian \nabla^2 f across a scale space to identify blob-like structures in volumetric data, encoding the results as a scale abstraction.
This approach solves the memory bottleneck associated with storing full-resolution scale fields for large volumes.
Input: A 3D volume texture representing the current iteration's scalar field.

cited.name: Laplacian Grid Computation
ctx: Limitations: Sensitive to noise; linear diffusion can cause nearby objects to merge into a single blob before detection, leading to inaccurate scale maxima localization.
Non-linear conductivity filters can mitigate this but add complexity.

The concept of using the Laplacian for blob detection and scale-space analysis was formalized in the context of computer vision and scientific visualization, particularly in the work on Size-based Transfer Functions.

cited.name: GPU Backprojection
ctx: GPU Backprojection is a rendering pass that visualizes detected scale-space blobs by generating small slices for each blob, computing weighted contributions, and blending them to form the final image, followed by normalization.

It is distinct from standard ray-casting as it operates on a sparse abstraction of the volume (scale maxima) rather than the full voxel grid, decoupling the expensive scale-space computation from the frequent backprojection step.
In a separate pass, normalize the accumulated result by dividing by the sum of weights, which is stored in a separate channel.

cited.name: Nonlinear Conductivity Filter
ctx: The Nonlinear Conductivity Filter is a variation of nonlinear diffusion used in scale-space computation for volume rendering to improve scale detection.

Unlike the standard Perona-Malik filter which stops diffusion at edges (causing false maxima), this method controls diffusion direction to favor movement towards the medial axis and prevent edge crossing.
It achieves this by using signed forward differences instead of gradient magnitude to compute conductivity.

cited.name: Size-Based Transfer Functions
ctx: Size-Based Transfer Functions (SBTF) map the local scale (relative size) of volumetric features to color and opacity, allowing the classification and segmentation of data based on spatial extent rather than scalar intensity alone.
S is a 3D scalar field where each voxel represents the local scale or size of the feature containing that voxel.
Scale Space Computation (Preprocessing): Compute the scale field S from the input data F using continuous scale-space analysis.

Limitations: Can create non-manifold vertices, which may be a problem for some applications.

cited.name: Marching Tetrahedrons
ctx: It sets itself apart from its parent Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra by operating on a fixed tetrahedral decomposition of the standard cubic grid rather than a general unstructured subgrid, and from its sibling Optimal Extraction via Partition Index by using a deterministic lookup table of edge intersections rather than…
The primary advantage is that it produces a manifold surface without the topological ambiguities inherent in Marching Cubes, at the cost of generating approximately 4x more geometry.
Performance: The algorithm generates approximately 4x more geometry than Marching Cubes, making it slower in both computation and rendering.

cited.name: Dual Methods
ctx: Dual methods are a class of isosurface extraction algorithms that generate surface topology by creating an (n-1)-cell for every edge crossing the boundary in 3D, resulting in a mesh where topology is completely determined by the sample complex.

Unlike primal methods such as Marching Cubes, which suffer from topological ambiguity in non-simplicial cells, dual methods resolve ambiguities by construction, though they may produce non-manifold vertices.
The position of this vertex is assigned based on a specific rule (e.g., the cell center for Surface Nets). 3.

cited.name: Bounding Spheres Optimization
ctx: Bounding Spheres Optimization reduces the computational cost of sphere tracing by grouping scene objects into larger enclosing spheres, thereby eliminating unnecessary distance calculations during ray traversal.

It differs from its parent, Bounding Volume Culling, which typically discards rays entirely based on geometric bounds, by deferring the evaluation of individual object distances until the ray actually penetrates the enclosing volume.

Unlike Orthogonal Culling Optimization, which pre-computes object visibility via orthogonal projection to reduce per-step evaluations, Bounding Spheres Optimization dynamically manages the active set of distance fields based on ray proximity.

cited.name: Orthogonal Culling Optimization
ctx: Orthogonal Culling is a pre-computation optimization for sphere tracing that reduces the number of signed distance function (SDF) evaluations per ray by determining which scene objects lie within the ray's path before the marching loop begins.

It differs from its parent, Bounding Spheres Optimization, which minimizes distance calculations during traversal, and its sibling, Frustum Culling (Sphere vs Frustum), which typically relies on CPU-side broad-phase culling; Orthogonal Culling performs a geometric intersection test between the ray and object bounding…
Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, and a list of scene objects, each defined by a bounding sphere with center \mathbf{c} and radius r.

cited.name: Beam Optimization
ctx: Beam Optimization is an acceleration technique for primary rays in distance-field ray marching that groups adjacent rays into beams to reduce redundant scene queries.

By marching a group of rays together along a central path, the method exploits spatial coherence to advance multiple rays simultaneously when the distance to the nearest geometry exceeds the group's spatial extent.
This reduces the total number of SDF evaluations, at the cost of splitting overhead when rays diverge near surfaces.

Standard Constant Step Ray Marching
ctx: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching is an iterative technique for finding the intersection of a ray with implicit surfaces or volumetric media by advancing the ray along its direction by a fixed distance \Delta t at each iteration.
It solves the problem of rendering implicit surfaces or volumes without explicit polygonal meshes by discretizing the ray path into uniform intervals.
Typical values range from 0.001 to 0.1 depending on scene scale and desired accuracy.

ctx: It serves as a fundamental implicit primitive for distance-field ray marching and volume rendering, providing an analytically exact distance estimator that enables safe, large step sizes along rays.

ctx: What sets it apart from standard ray marching is its use of the SDF value as a guaranteed lower bound on the distance to the nearest surface, allowing the ray to "leap" forward by exactly that distance.
Since f is an SDF (\lambda=1), d is the exact distance to the nearest surface, so stepping by d is safe.

cited.name: Object Space Ray Setup
ctx: Object Space Ray Setup constructs ray origins and directions in the local coordinate system of the rendered mesh rather than world space.
This ensures that the raytraced object moves, scales, and rotates rigidly with the mesh transform, treating the object as a self-contained volume.
Unlike world-space methods where the object acts as a static window into a larger world, this approach simplifies scene graph transformations for isolated volume rendering.

title: Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi‐Phase SPH Data
abstract: In this paper, we present a novel method for the direct volume rendering of large smoothed‐particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation data without transforming the unstructured data to an intermediate representation. By directly visualizing the unstructured particle data, we avoid long preprocessing times and large storage requirements. This enables the visualization of large, time‐dependent, and multivariate data both as a post‐process and in situ. To address the computational complexity, we introduce stochastic volume rendering that considers only a subset of particles at each step during ray marching. The sample probabilities for selecting this subset at each step are thereby determined both in a view‐dependent manner and based on the spatial complexity of the data. Our stochastic volume rendering enables us to scale continuously from a fast, interactive preview to a more accurate volume rendering at higher cost. Lastly, we discuss the visualization of free‐surface and multi‐phase flows by including a multi‐material model with volumetric and surface shading into the stochastic volume rendering.Computer Graphics ForumArticles40

cited.name: Gradual Opacity Decay and Residual Regularization
ctx: Gradual Opacity Decay and Residual Regularization is a training configuration strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that replaces hard opacity resets with a smoother decay mechanism to facilitate primitive pruning without disrupting the optimization trajectory.

It addresses the problem of misleading error statistics and unstable densification decisions caused by sudden opacity drops, while introducing a regularization term to prevent the model from exploiting the background to hide scene holes.

Residual Transmittance: For each pixel p, the residual transmittance T{res, p} is the product of transmittances of all splats behind the last contributing splat, or effectively the unaccounted light transmission through the scene.

cited.name: Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling
ctx: Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling reduces overall sampling error in SPH rendering by selecting well-distributed particle subsets within an acceleration structure's cells.

It differs from naive random discarding by enforcing a structured selection process based on cell and position importance, ensuring that the statistical properties of the particle neighborhood are preserved more accurately during ray marching.
Particle set \mathcal{P} organized in a uniform grid acceleration structure.

cited.name: SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling
ctx: SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling is a precomputation technique that assigns sampling probabilities to SPH particles based on the local information complexity of their attributes and the presence of phase interfaces.

It solves the problem of high-frequency shading errors and subsampling artifacts at phase boundaries by ensuring that regions with high attribute variation or discontinuous phase transitions are sampled more densely.

The method operates in two phases: a precomputation phase that builds an importance grid from the particle data, and a runtime phase that queries this grid during ray marching to determine particle sampling probabilities.

cited.name: Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data
ctx: A direct volume rendering technique for large, unstructured smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) data that avoids intermediate grid representations by stochastically sampling a subset of particles during ray marching.
It differs from standard DVR by using view-dependent and spatial-complexity-based probabilities to select particles, enabling continuous scaling from interactive previews to high-quality renders.
It specifically addresses multi-phase flows by reconstructing interfaces between different fluid types using a combined volumetric and surface shading model.

cited.name: Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering
ctx: Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering is a technique to increase rendering performance by reducing the number of particles used during rendering, using a non-uniform sampling strategy based on data importance and view-dependent criteria.

It solves the problem of high computational cost when rendering large, unstructured Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) datasets by ensuring that particles in complex regions (e.g., phase interfaces, vortices) are sampled more densely than those in homogeneous areas.
It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by avoiding equal-time high-error trade-offs.

cited.name: Volume Resampling
ctx: Volume resampling converts unstructured particle data (such as SPH particles) into a structured 3D grid representation to enable efficient direct volume rendering.
It solves the problem of rendering point clouds by discretizing data onto a voxel grid, allowing standard hardware-accelerated volume rendering pipelines to be used.
It differs from direct particle rendering by shifting computational cost to a long preprocessing phase, resulting in significantly faster per-frame rendering times.

title: Towards Fully Dynamic Omnitrees: Moment-Conserving Anisotropic Compression With Wavelets
abstract: Recently, omnitrees were introduced as a flexible space partitioning tree that improves upon the benefits of both octrees and k-d trees: Omnitrees' efficient encoding of anisotropic refinements holds particular interest for applications with anisotropic features and high dimensionality. These include, but are not limited to, computer graphics, databases, machine learning, and physics simulations. The present paper defines new operations on the omnitree encoding that extend its capabilities from the existing refinement to also include coarsening and therefore fully adaptive compression. It demonstrates natural integration of omnitrees with wavelets, which conserves moments of the stored function by design. For omnitrees, the wavelet coefficients can be interpreted as local refinement priorities, which can be used to guide the adaptation process. We derive algorithms for coarsening and downsplit that are guided by wavelet coefficients, and show their application to a large dataset of 3D shapes, as well as the continuous-valued density field of a cloud. The comparison to OpenVDB, a widely-used data structure for sparse volumetric data in computer graphics, enables a demonstration of the practical benefits of omnitrees even for moderately anisotropic three-dimensional data. Compared to OpenVDB, objects can be stored using up to 28x less space, and asymptotically show savings that exceed theoretical expectations. Using lossy compression, the cloud dataset can be compressed by $\approx5\times$ compared to OpenVDB, with negligible loss of visual quality. This demonstrates the potential of omnitrees for efficient storage and processing, and motivates further research into their applications in various domains.

cited.name: Hierarchical Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees
ctx: Hierarchical Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees is a compression strategy that transforms nodal omnitree data into wavelet coefficients to enable lossless or lossy compression via pruning and tree restructuring (downsplit).

It solves the problem of minimizing storage size for 3D volumetric data by exploiting anisotropic refinement, setting itself apart from isotropic siblings like Wavelet-based Multiresolution Rendering by explicitly defining mathematical basis functions over the omnitree structure to achieve superior approximation rates.
Input: A volumetric function f represented on a grid of resolution level l (subdividing the unit cube into 2^l voxels per dimension) or a continuous density distribution.

cited.name: Omnitree Coarsening
ctx: Omnitree coarsening reverses omnitree refinement by fusing child nodes along specified dimensions to reduce tree resolution.
It simplifies a previously refined sparse voxel representation while preserving the set of leaf boxes.
Unlike general tree restructuring, it restricts requests to last-level refinements, ensuring deterministic fusion without validating subtree symmetry across arbitrary depths.

cited.name: Omnitree Refinement
ctx: Omnitree refinement transforms an initial hierarchical dyadic partition of a d-dimensional Cartesian domain into a target partition with higher resolution in specific dimensions.
It solves the problem of anisotropically increasing the granularity of a sparse voxel representation by attaching refinement markers to nodes and propagating them through the tree structure.
The method explicitly supports per-dimension refinement levels (\vec{m} \in \mathbb{N}^d), allowing for non-cubic, rectangular subdomains.

cited.name: Downsplit
ctx: Downsplit is a tree restructuring operation in hierarchical wavelet-based volume compression that factors a multi-dimensional split into a cascade of lower-dimensional splits.
It restructures an omnitree without modifying the set of leaf boxes, serving as the inverse to normalization.
By moving parent refinements down to children, it exposes new coarsening opportunities that multi-dimensional splits would otherwise obscure, enabling more efficient pruning of wavelet coefficients.

cited.name: Coarsening Compression
ctx: Coarsening compression is a lossy compression step that prunes small wavelet detail coefficients to reduce the number of leaf nodes in a hierarchical omnitree, while preserving the integral of the represented function.
It differs from sibling methods like Downsplit by operating directly on coefficient magnitudes to merge nodes, whereas downsplit restructures the tree topology to expose new coarsening opportunities.
Input: A hierarchized omnitree with wavelet coefficients w\tau^v associated with each node v and dimension subset \tau \subseteq \sigma(v), and an error density threshold \varepsilon \ge 0.

cited.name: Haar Wavelet Transform on Omnitrees
ctx: This method transforms piecewise constant volume data stored in an omnitree structure from its nodal representation into a hierarchical wavelet coefficient representation using the tensor-product Haar basis.

The nodal representation stores f as a sum over leaf nodes v with b(v)=\vec{0}: f = \sum{v: \vec{b}(v)=\vec{0}} s^v \phi^v where \phi^v is the indicator function for the hyper-rectangular region rect(v) (1 if x \in rect(v), 0 otherwise).
If bj(v)=1 and mj(v)=-1, then bj(v')=0, removing the split in that dimension.

title: Unifying points, beams, and paths in volumetric light transport simulation
abstract: Efficiently computing light transport in participating media in a manner that is robust to variations in media density, scattering albedo, and anisotropy is a difficult and important problem in realistic image synthesis. While many specialized rendering techniques can efficiently resolve subsets of transport in specific media, no single approach can robustly handle all types of effects. To address this problem we unify volumetric density estimation, using point and beam estimators, and Monte Carlo solutions to the path integral formulation of the rendering and radiative transport equations. We extend multiple importance sampling to correctly handle combinations of these fundamentally different classes of estimators. This, in turn, allows us to develop a single rendering algorithm that correctly combines the benefits and mediates the limitations of these powerful volume rendering techniques.

cited.name: YZ-Plane Fill Voxelization
ctx: YZ-Plane Fill Voxelization is a voxelization step that fills voxels along the YZ plane for a fixed X coordinate by scanning from the lower bound to the upper bound and back, marking empty space between surface voxels as solid in a buffer.
It distinguishes itself from the enhanced variant FillYZ2 by omitting connectivity checks, which makes it faster but less robust for complex geometries.
It iterates through the bounding box of the mesh, fixing the X coordinate and scanning the Y and Z dimensions.

cited.name: Extended Multiple Importance Sampling
ctx: Extended Multiple Importance Sampling (Extended MIS) is a framework for combining estimators of integrals defined on spaces of different dimensions, such as standard path sampling and extended-space density estimators (e.g., photon mapping or beam tracing).
It solves the problem of variance reduction in volumetric path tracing when mixing unbiased path contributions with biased density estimates that operate on higher-dimensional spaces.

Unlike standard MIS, which requires all strategies to sample from the same domain, Extended MIS derives a balance heuristic that accounts for the additional integration over the kernel support inherent in extended-space techniques.

cited.name: Volumetric Radiance Estimators
ctx: [2011a] that estimate equilibrium radiance in participating media by reconstructing values from discrete samples (photon points or photon beams) using spatial blurring.

They differ from unbiased path integral estimators by lacking a general path contribution function and pdf, instead relying on specific radiometric quantities and kernel dimensions to approximate the radiance field.
The naming convention for estimators (e.g., B-P3D) indicates radiance data (Photon Points or Photon Beams), query type (Point or Beam), and kernel dimension (1D, 2D, 3D) in that order.

cited.name: Path Integral Framework
ctx: The Path Integral Framework formulates light transport simulation as a Monte Carlo integration problem over the space of light transport paths, serving as the basis for combining photon density estimation and Monte Carlo path integration.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Volumetric Radiance Estimators by providing the rigorous mathematical measure and domain definition required to apply variance reduction techniques such as Multiple Importance Sampling.
The path has N segments and N+1 vertices.

cited.name: Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP)
ctx: Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP) is a combined rendering algorithm that fuses volumetric radiance estimators (Point-Point, Point-Beam, Beam-Beam) with unbiased bidirectional path tracing (BPT) techniques.

It solves the problem of efficiently simulating light transport in participating media by leveraging the strengths of both biased photon-based methods (for dense, complex scattering) and unbiased path tracing (for long-distance connections).
Unlike its siblings, UPBP subsumes earlier methods like Volumetric Connection Mapping (VCM) by unifying surface and medium photon mapping with beam-based estimators in a single framework.

cited.name: Extended Balance Heuristic
ctx: The Extended Balance Heuristic is a variance reduction technique used to combine estimates from a mixture of sampling techniques, specifically balancing unbiased path sampling with extended-space volumetric estimators (such as photon mapping).

It differs from the standard balance heuristic by incorporating the kernel support size of the volumetric estimators into the weighting function, ensuring that the weights correspond exactly to the vertex merging pdfs used in prior work.
It solves the problem of optimally combining disparate estimators (e.g., path tracing and photon mapping) to reduce variance in volumetric light transport simulation.
