abstract: Adds a complete 3D inverse-distance weighting (IDW) interpolation pipeline that generates a scalar field from drill-hole sample data and renders it as a shader-driven voxel volume inside the existing Three.js scene. ## New modules ### Pure-JS interpolation kernel (no Three.js dependency) - **`SpatialHash3D`** — uniform 3D hash grid; `queryRadius()` and `queryKNearest()`; O(1) cell lookup, predictable performance for static datasets - **`IDWSampler`** — `getValueAt(x,y,z)` with configurable `power`, `searchRadius`, `maxNeighbors`, `minNeighbors`, `epsilon`; exact-hit short-circuit; designed for reuse by future slice/section/probe tools - **`computeVolumeBounds`** — AABB with configurable padding from any `{x,y,z}` point array - **`buildVoxelGrid`** — evaluates sampler onto a `Float32Array` voxel grid; async with event-loop yielding, `onProgress` callback, and cancellation token - **`buildInterpSamplesFromAssays`** — extracts midpoint support points from desurveyed assay rows; falls back to straight-line-vertical when desurvey coords are absent ### Three.js rendering - **`IDWVolumeRenderer`** — uploads grid as `Data3DTexture` (one float/voxel), raymarches through a unit-cube `ShaderMaterial`; supports **block mode** (snap to voxel centres → crisp block-model look) and smooth compositing; display `min/max`, `opacity`, `threshold`, and colour gradient are uniform-only updates (no texture re-upload) - Inline GLSL (`idwVolume.vert/frag.glsl`) — front-to-back compositing, nodata sentinel skip (` Original prompt ---- *This section details on the original issue you should resolve* 3d idw # Baselode Feature Specification: 3D IDW Interpolation Volume and Voxel Visualisation ## Purpose Add a new Baselode feature that generates a continuous 3D scalar field from drill-hole sample data using inverse distance weighting (IDW), then visualises that field inside a bounded 3D volume as voxels in the existing Three.js scene. This feature is intended for exploration-style inspection of interpolated values such as `Au_ppb`, `Cu_pct`, or any other numeric downhole/sample attribute. It should work on a selected set of drill holes and support later extension to section and slice tools. --- ## Goals 1. Compute a 3D bounding volume from a set of selected drill holes or sample points. 2. Build a spatial lookup structure for efficient nearest-sample queries. 3. Implement IDW interpolation for any point in 3D space. 4. Voxelise the interpolation volume and render it efficiently in the scene. 5. Expose controls for attribute selection, IDW exponent, search radius, voxel resolution, and display thresholds. 6. Design the implementation so it can later support section/slice inspection along X/Y/Z planes. --- ## Non-goals for first implementation 1. No kriging, RBF, or advanced geostatistics. 2. No anisotropy or variogram modelling. 3. No hard geological domain constraints. 4. No implicit meshing / iso-surface extraction in v1. 5. No production-grade resource estimation claims. This is a visual analytic tool only. --- ## User story As a user viewing drill holes in a 3D Baselode scene, I want to select a numeric sample attribute and generate an interpolated 3D voxel volume around those holes so that I can visually inspect spatial patterns and potential trends between samples. --- ## Scope ### Inputs - A Three.js scene already containing drill-hole geometry and/or drill-hole sample data. - A selected subset of drill holes, or all currently visible drill holes. - A numeric sample attribute name, e.g. `Au_ppb`. - Sample intervals with 3D locations. - Optional interval lengths, downhole traces, and desurveyed positions. ### Outputs - A computed 3D interpolation volume over a bounded box. - A rendered voxel/block-style representation in the scene. - A reusable scalar-field evaluation API for arbitrary 3D points. - Parameters exposed to the application/UI. --- ## Data assumptions The interpolation should operate on sample support points in 3D. Preferred input form per sample: ```ts type InterpSamplePoint = { id: string holeId: string x: number y: number z: number value: number from?: number to?: number length?: number metadata?: Record } ``` ### How sample points are derived For interval data, create a representative point for each interval. Default approach: - Use the midpoint of the sample interval along the drill trace. - Use desurveyed coordinates if available. - If desurvey is unavailable, allow a fallback assumption such as vertical or straight-line collar-to-end-of-hole. This feature must not assume only collar positions. It should interpolate from interval/sample support points distributed downhole. --- ## Functional requirements ## 1. Bounding box generation Create a 3D axis-aligned bounding box that encloses the selected drill holes or selected sample points. ### Requirements - Compute bounds from all participating sample points. - Allow optional padding in world units on all sides. - Store: - `minX`, `minY`, `minZ` - `maxX`, `maxY`, `maxZ` - dimensions - center - Support user override of padding and resolution. ### API shape ```ts type VolumeBounds = { min: [number, number, number] max: [number, number, number] size: [number, number, number] center: [number, number, number] } ``` --- ## 2. Spatial lookup / neighbour search IDW should not scan all samples for every voxel if the sample count is large. ### Requirement Implement a reusable spatial index for 3D nearest-neighbour or radius-based queries. ### Acceptable implementations - Uniform 3D grid / hash grid - KD-tree in 3D - Octree ### Recommended v1 Use a simple spatial hash grid because: - data are static for each interpolation run - implementation is straightforward - radius queries are easy - performance is predictable ### Required capabilities - insert sample points - query points within a search radius - optionally cap to max nearest neighbours - handle empty-neighbour cases ### API shape ```ts interface SpatialIndex3D { build(points: T[]): void queryRadius(x: number, y: number, z: number, radius: number): T[] queryKNearest?(x: number, y: number, z: number, k: number): T[] } ``` --- ## 3. IDW interpolation Implement inverse distance weighting for any point in 3D. ### Formula For a query point `p`, using nearby samples `i`: - weight: `w_i = 1 / d_i^power` - interpolated value: `v = sum(w_i * value_i) / sum(w_i)` Wher... - Fixes darkmine-oss/baselode#14 --- 📱 Kick off Copilot coding agent tasks wherever you are with [GitHub Mobile](https://gh.io/cca-mobile-docs), available on iOS and Android.

title: GRay: Ray Tracing 3D Gaussians Near the Speed of Splats
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a popular representation for radiance field reconstruction, distinguished by the rendering speed of its rasterization-based renderer. While 3D Gaussians can also be ray traced, this approach has so far been slower, with 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (3DGRT) [Moenne-Loccoz et al. 2024 ] taking nearly one order of magnitude longer to optimize. To address this, we present GRay, a fast ray tracer for 3D Gaussians designed to close this performance gap and match 3DGS’s speed. Our method leverages the algorithmic difference between both approaches: unlike rasterization, ray tracing evaluates only Gaussians that are actually intersected by a ray, leading to potentially logarithmic—rather than linear—scaling in the number of primitives. This property allows ray tracing to better exploit dense scenes composed of numerous tiny Gaussians, a configuration which has largely been overlooked. Notably, we show that dense initialization—which creates many small Gaussians—slows down rasterization, but instead speeds up ray tracing. Designed to leverage this effect, GRay renders nearly 4 × faster and optimizes nearly 10 × faster than 3DGRT while maintaining similar quality, and has competitive speed with 3DGS albeit at somewhat lower quality. Code will be released upon publication.

title: Hearthlight: sun/moon shadows, voxel local lights, hand fixed
abstract: Hearthlight: real sun/moon shadow map + voxel ray-traced local lights for Minecraft 26.2 + Iris. ## How it works | Stage | What it does | |---|---| | `shadow.vsh/gsh/fsh` | One shadow pass, two jobs: a distorted sun/moon shadow map (terrain, translucents, entities, players, block entities, alpha-tested) and a geometry stage that voxelises terrain into a 128³ volume of half-block octants. | | `prepare_a/b/c.csh` | Count voxelised blocks, collect emitters into an SSBO light list, bin them into 8³-block cells. | | `gbuffers_*` | Albedo, normal, vanilla sky/block light, emissive flag. The hand writes a zero mask. | | `deferred.fsh` | Ambient sky + sun/moon PCF shadow map + tinted vanilla fill + ranked ray-traced local lights + fog and horizon haze. Hand pixels are identified through `depthtex2` and left alone. | | `final.fsh` | Hue-preserving highlight normalisation and exposure. | ## This round **The hand, properly this time.** Relying on the G-buffer mask only works while the hand's own program runs; if it falls back or writes nothing, the terrain's mask is still underneath and deferred re-lights the hand away. `depthtex2` is the world depth Iris copies immediately before the hand is drawn, so `depth < depthtex2` identifies hand pixels directly, whatever program drew them. They now return before any lighting, with `HAND_BRIGHTNESS` applied. The hand also no longer goes pure black in unlit rooms (the hand pass floors the vanilla lightmap at 0.10), and **Debug View 7** paints hand pixels red so it is unambiguous whether the hand is drawn at all. **Local-light shadows removed**, as agreed. The depth-buffer ray was the source of the phantom wedges: 16% of traceable pixels were wrongly shadowed because the depth buffer only stores the nearest surface. Sun and moon shadows are unaffected. **More settings**, on five screens: sun and moon strength, sun warmth, shadow quality and softness, sun path tilt; daytime and night ambient, sunrise/sunset tint, rain darkening, horizon haze; light intensity, range, colour strength, vanilla fill, daylight suppression; shadow resolution and distance, lights per pixel, ray steps; hand brightness, fog distance, exposure. Debug View now reaches 7. ## Verification Minecraft cannot be run here. Three offline harnesses run against the shipped zip: - `tools/validate.py` — expands every `#include`, injects Iris' own defines, compiles and links all 24 stages with glslang. - `tools/iris_compat.py` — preprocesses each program exactly as Iris does; no identifier collides with an Iris define. - `tools/simulate.py` — volume/SSBO layout, id tables, packed light byte, octant bit layout, shadow distortion, the sun/moon direction convention, the octant DDA, and checks that the hand is identified through `depthtex2` and that the removed ray stays removed. ## Known limitations - Entities cast sun/moon shadows but do not block local (torch) light. - Local-light occlusion is half-block resolution. - In first person your own body is not rendered, so it casts no sun shadow; use third person. - The hand item is vanilla-lit (plus Hand Brightness). Download: `tools/Hearthlight.zip`.

title: High Performance GPU-Based Fourier Volume Rendering
abstract: Fourier volume rendering (FVR) is a significant visualization technique that has been used widely in digital radiography. As a result of its 𝒪(N (2)log⁡N) time complexity, it provides a faster alternative to spatial domain volume rendering algorithms that are 𝒪(N (3)) computationally complex. Relying on the Fourier projection-slice theorem, this technique operates on the spectral representation of a 3D volume instead of processing its spatial representation to generate attenuation-only projections that look like X-ray radiographs. Due to the rapid evolution of its underlying architecture, the graphics processing unit (GPU) became an attractive competent platform that can deliver giant computational raw power compared to the central processing unit (CPU) on a per-dollar-basis. The introduction of the compute unified device architecture (CUDA) technology enables embarrassingly-parallel algorithms to run efficiently on CUDA-capable GPU architectures. In this work, a high performance GPU-accelerated implementation of the FVR pipeline on CUDA-enabled GPUs is presented. This proposed implementation can achieve a speed-up of 117x compared to a single-threaded hybrid implementation that uses the CPU and GPU together by taking advantage of executing the rendering pipeline entirely on recent GPU architectures.

ctx: Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) is a visualization technique that generates attenuation-only projections resembling X-ray radiographs by operating on the spectral representation of a 3D volume rather than its spatial representation.
It exploits the Fourier projection-slice theorem to compute these projections in O(N^2 \log N) time per view, avoiding the O(N^3) cost of spatial domain methods like ray casting.

Unlike its sibling Fourier Projection-Slice Volume Rendering, which focuses on the theoretical basis of generating projections, FVR describes the complete algorithmic pipeline including preprocessing, resampling, and inverse transformation to produce the final image.

For 100% zero-padding, the new dimensions are doubled in each axis: D'x = 2Dx, D'y = 2Dy, D'z = 2Dz. 2.

title: High-Quality Extraction of Isosurfaces from Regular and Irregular Grids
abstract: Isosurfaces are ubiquitous in many fields, including visualization, graphics, and vision. They are often the main computational component of important processing pipelines (e.g. , surface reconstruction), and are heavily used in practice. The classical approach to compute isosurfaces is to apply the Marching Cubes algorithm, which although robust and simple to implement, generates surfaces that require additional processing steps to improve triangle quality and mesh size. An important issue is that in some cases, the surfaces generated by Marching Cubes are irreparably damaged, and important details are lost which can not be recovered by subsequent processing. The main motivation of this work is to develop a technique capable of constructing high-quality and high-fidelity isosurfaces. We propose a new advancing front technique that is capable of creating high-quality isosurfaces from regular and irregular volumetric datasets. Our work extends the guidance field framework of Schreiner et al. to implicit surfaces, and improves it in significant ways. In particular, we describe a set of sampling conditions that guarantee that surface features will be captured by the algorithm. We also describe an efficient technique to compute a minimal guidance field, which greatly improves performance. Our experimental results show that our technique can generate high-quality meshes from complex datasets.

cited.name: Multi-threaded Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction

Compared to Marching Cubes Marching Cubes or Marching Tetrahedra Marching Tetrahedra, the algorithm is slower but generates meshes requiring negligible or no downstream processing, unlike MC/MT results.

cited.name: Advancing Front Isosurface Extraction with Guidance Field
ctx: This method extracts isosurfaces from implicit functions using an advancing front algorithm guided by a scalar field g(\mathbf{x}) that constrains edge lengths based on surface curvature and user parameters.

It builds on the Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces by replacing heuristic edge sizing with a theoretically grounded guidance field that ensures robust front interference detection and well-shaped triangles.

The algorithm constructs a guidance field from initial surface samples to determine ideal edge lengths, culls redundant samples for efficiency, seeds the front, and iteratively advances the front by adding triangles or merging/splitting fronts based on interference checks.

title: Improved Neural Radiance Fields Using Pseudo-depth and Fusion
abstract: Since the advent of Neural Radiance Fields, novel view synthesis has received tremendous attention. The existing approach for the generalization of radiance field reconstruction primarily constructs an encoding volume from nearby source images as additional inputs. However, these approaches cannot efficiently encode the geometric information of real scenes with various scale objects/structures. In this work, we propose constructing multi-scale encoding volumes and providing multi-scale geometry information to NeRF models. To make the constructed volumes as close as possible to the surfaces of objects in the scene and the rendered depth more accurate, we propose to perform depth prediction and radiance field reconstruction simultaneously. The predicted depth map will be used to supervise the rendered depth, narrow the depth range, and guide points sampling. Finally, the geometric information contained in point volume features may be inaccurate due to occlusion, lighting, etc. To this end, we propose enhancing the point volume feature from depth-guided neighbor feature fusion. Experiments demonstrate the superior performance of our method in both novel view synthesis and dense geometry modeling without per-scene optimization

title: Integrating Dynamic Deformations into Interactive Volume Visualization
abstract: Non-linear geometric deformation (or warping) is a useful tool for working with volumes. Unfortunately, the computational expense of performing the resampling needed to implement volume deformation has precluded its use in interactive applications. In this paper, we show how non-linear deformations can be integrated into interactive volume visualization allowing for dynamic deformations to be used along with interactive viewing, exploration, and manipulation tools. We describe how hardware assisted volume rendering can be adapted to resample volume deformations, leveraging programmable shaders to compute deformations and the local coordinate transformations required for shading effects. We describe how volume interaction techniques, such as ray picking and plane slicing, can be used in concert with our deformation methods. Our methods extend to simultaneous display of multiple volumes enabling comparisons. We demonstrate dynamic volume deformation at interactive rates on commodity hardware for interactive deformation control, animated deformations, and volume widgets.EUROVIS - Eurographics /IEEE VGTC Symposium on Visualizatio

title: Interaction with volumetric displays
abstract: For almost 50 years, researchers have been exploring the use of stereoscopic displays for visualizing and interacting with three-dimensional (3D) data. Unfortunately, a number of unfavorable qualitative properties have impeded the wide-spread adoption of traditional 3D displays. The volumetric display, a more recent class of 3D display to emerge, possesses unique features which potentially makes it more suitable for integration into workplace, classroom, and even home environments. In this dissertation we investigate volumetric displays as an interactive platform for 3D applications. We identify the inherent affordances unique to volumetric displays, such as their true 3D display volume, 360° viewing angle, and enclosing surface. Identifying these properties exposes human factor issues which we investigate and interaction issues which we address. First, we evaluate the user’s ability perceive imagery displayed by a volumetric display. In a formal experiment, we show that depth perception can be improved, in comparison to more traditional platforms. We then perform an experiment which evaluates users’ ability to read text under 3D rotations, and present a new algorithm which optimizes text rotation when viewed my multiple users. Next, we investigate the user’s ability to select 3D imagery within the display. Results show that the dimension defining the depth of the object can constrain user performance as much as or more than the other two dimensions of the target. This leads us to explore alternative methods of selection which are less constraining to the user. We define a suite of new selection techniques, of which several are found to have significant benefits in comparison to techniques traditionally used in 3D user interfaces. Next, we describe our development of the first working interactive application, where a volumetric display is the sole device for input and display. The application presents a first glance at what the equivalent of today’s graphical user interface might be on a volumetric display. We then develop a prototype application which allows multiple users to simultaneously interact with the volumetric display. We discuss and address the core issues related to providing such a collaborative user interface, and report feedback obtained from usage sessions and expert interviews.

title: Interaction‐Dependent Semantics for Illustrative Volume Rendering
abstract: In traditional illustration the choice of appropriate styles and rendering techniques is guided by the intention of the artist. For illustrative volume visualizations it is difficult to specify the mapping between the 3D data and the visual representation that preserves the intention of the user. The semantic layers concept establishes this mapping with a linguistic formulation of rules that directly map data features to rendering styles. With semantic layers fuzzy logic is used to evaluate the user defined illustration rules in a preprocessing step. In this paper we introduce interaction-dependent rules that are evaluated for each frame and are therefore computationally more expensive. Enabling interaction-dependent rules, however, allows the use of a new class of semantics, resulting in more expressive interactive illustrations. We show that the evaluation of the fuzzy logic can be done on the graphics hardware enabling the efficient use of interaction-dependent semantics. Further we introduce the flat rendering mode and discuss how different rendering parameters are influenced by the rule base. Our approach provides high quality illustrative volume renderings at interactive frame rates, guided by the specification of illustration rules.Computer Graphics Forum27

title: Interactive three-dimensional holographic displays
abstract: Computer graphics is confined chiefly to flat images. Images may look three-dimensional (3D), and sometimes create the illusion of 3D when displayed, for example, on a stereoscopic display [16, 13, 12]. Nevertheless, when viewing an image on most display systems, the human visual system (HVS) sees a flat plane of pixels. Volumetric displays can create a 3D computer graphics image, but fail to provide many visual depth cues (e.g. shading texture gradients) and cannot provide the powerful depth cue of overlap (occlusion). Discrete parallax displays (such as lenticular displays) promise to create 3D images with all of the depth cues, but are limited by achievable resolution. Only a real-time electronic holographic ("holovideo") display [11, 6, 8, 7, 9, 21, 22, 20, 2] can create a truly 3D computer graphics image with all of the depth cues (motion parallax, ocular accommodation, occlusion, etc.) and resolution sufficient to provide extreme realism [13]. Holovideo displays promise to enhance numerous applications in the creation and manipulation of information, including telepresence, education, medical imaging, interactive design and scientific visualization.The technology of electronic interactive three-dimensional holographic displays is in its first decade. Though fancied in popular science fiction, only recently have researchers created the first real holovideo systems by confronting the two basic requirements of electronic holography: computational speed and high-bandwidth modulation of visible light. This article describes the approaches used to address these problems, as well as emerging technologies and techniques that provide firm footing for the development of practical holovideo.

cited.name: Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) Calculation
ctx: Definition: A time-multiplexed holographic display technique that uses a fast Acousto-Optic Modulator (AOM) to phase-modulate a small number of samples (~1000) at any instant, scanning the modulated light beam rapidly to create a larger apparent holographic fringe integrated by the human visual system.
The eye time-integrates the displayed fringe during this interval.
AOM instantaneous capacity: phase modulates about 1000 samples at any one instant in time.

cited.name: Liquid-Crystal and Related SLMs
ctx: Liquid-Crystal and Related SLMs are electro-optic or micromechanical devices used to modulate light with computed holographic fringes for volumetric display and holography.
They solve the challenge of generating high-resolution fringe patterns by leveraging parallel spatial modulation rather than time-multiplexed scanning.

Unlike scanned-AOM systems which require high-speed analog conversion and complex scanning mirrors, LCDs and DMDs are more readily interfaced to digital electronics, requiring only demagnification and optical concatenation.

cited.name: Diffraction-Specific Approach
ctx: Instead of summing complex wavefronts from object elements against a reference wavefront for every pixel, it treats the holographic fringe as being subsampled spatially into functional holographic elements called "hogels" and spectrally into an array of "hogel vectors".

This approach builds on Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) Calculation by leveraging standard 3D computer graphics rendering (orthographic projections) to generate the data, significantly increasing computation speed and achieving bandwidth compression compared to the Interference-Based Approach.
It trades off image sharpness for speed, introducing a blur that can be matched to the acuity of the human visual system (HVS).

title: IRCasTRF: Inverse Rendering by Optimizing Cascaded Tensorial Radiance Fields, Lighting, and Materials From Multi-view Images
abstract: We propose an inverse rendering pipeline that simultaneously reconstructs scene geometry, lighting, and spatially-varying material from a set of multi-view images. Specifically, the proposed pipeline involves volume and physics-based rendering, which are performed separately in two steps: exploration and exploitation. During the exploration step, our method utilizes the compactness of neural radiance fields and a flexible differentiable volume rendering technique to learn an initial volumetric field. Here, we introduce a novel cascaded tensorial radiance field method on top of the Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition to boost model compactness beyond conventional methods. In the exploitation step, a shading pass that incorporates a differentiable physics-based shading method is applied to jointly optimize the scene's geometry, spatially-varying materials, and lighting, using image reconstruction loss. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed inverse rendering pipeline, IRCasTRF, outperforms prior works in inverse rendering quality. The final output is highly compatible with downstream applications like scene editing and advanced simulations. Further details are available on the project page: https://ircasrf.github.io/.

title: IRIS: Intersection-aware Ray-based Implicit Editable Scenes
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields achieve high-fidelity scene representation but suffer from costly training and rendering, while 3D Gaussian splatting offers real-time performance with strong empirical results. Recently, solutions that harness the best of both worlds by using Gaussians as proxies to guide neural field evaluations, still suffer from significant computational inefficiencies. They typically rely on stochastic volumetric sampling to aggregate features, which severely limits rendering performance. To address this issue, a novel framework named IRIS (Intersection-aware Ray-based Implicit Editable Scenes) is introduced as a method designed for efficient and interactive scene editing. To overcome the limitations of standard ray marching, an analytical sampling strategy is employed that precisely identifies interaction points between rays and scene primitives, effectively eliminating empty space processing. Furthermore, to address the computational bottleneck of spatial neighbor lookups, a continuous feature aggregation mechanism is introduced that operates directly along the ray. By interpolating latent attributes from sorted intersections, costly 3D searches are bypassed, ensuring geometric consistency, enabling high-fidelity, real-time rendering, and flexible shape editing. title: Loss-Guided Density Control and Efficient Backward Optimisation for Compact Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Abstract Novel view synthesis based on explicit Gaussian primitives has achieved an effective balance between rendering quality and real-time visualisation, but its training process can remain computationally expensive because adaptive density control may introduce many redundant primitives. This paper proposes an efficient training framework for compact Gaussian Splatting through loss-guided densification, opacity-gradient pruning, and backward-pass optimisation. First, a loss accumulation guided density-control strategy is introduced. Instead of relying only on image-plane gradient magnitude, the method reuses the loss map generated during standard backpropagation to identify persistently under-reconstructed image regions. A binary high-loss mask is accumulated across multiple iterations, and each Gaussian primitive receives a densification score according to its coverage of these regions. Only primitives that consistently contribute to high-error areas are allowed to split or clone, thereby reducing unnecessary growth in well-reconstructed regions. Second, an opacity-gradient-based pruning criterion is designed to remove unstable or low-contribution primitives after densification. By combining opacity, opacity gradients, and training loss over multiple views, the proposed pruning strategy aims to preserve useful primitives while suppressing redundant ones. Third, the CUDA backward pass is optimised through warp-level parallelism and vectorised memory access to reduce redundant global memory transactions. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Deep Blending, and Tanks \& Temples indicate that the proposed framework substantially reduces training time and the final number of Gaussian primitives while maintaining competitive PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS performance compared with representative efficient Gaussian-splatting baselines. The results suggest that loss-aware density control can provide a practical route towards faster and more compact Gaussian Splatting. Our project page is available at https://github.com/Allen-key-20/Loss-Guided-Density-Control-and-Efficient-Backward-Optimisation.git

title: Lossy-to-lossless compression of medical volumetric data using three-dimensional integer wavelet transforms
abstract: We study lossy-to-lossless compression of medical volumetric data using three-dimensional (3-D) integer wavelet transforms. To achieve good lossy coding performance, it is important to have transforms that are unitary. In addition to the lifting approach, we first introduce a general 3-D integer wavelet packet transform structure that allows implicit bit shifting of wavelet coefficients to approximate a 3-D unitary transformation. We then focus on context modeling for efficient arithmetic coding of wavelet coefficients. Two state-of-the-art 3-D wavelet video coding techniques, namely, 3-D set partitioning in hierarchical trees (Kim et al., 2000) and 3-D embedded subband coding with optimal truncation (Xu et al., 2001), are modified and applied to compression of medical volumetric data, achieving the best performance published so far in the literature-both in terms of lossy and lossless compression.

title: MERF: Memory-Efficient Radiance Fields for Real-time View Synthesis in Unbounded Scenes
abstract: Neural radiance fields enable state-of-the-art photorealistic view synthesis. However, existing radiance field representations are either too compute-intensive for real-time rendering or require too much memory to scale to large scenes. We present a Memory-Efficient Radiance Field (MERF) representation that achieves real-time rendering of large-scale scenes in a browser. MERF reduces the memory consumption of prior sparse volumetric radiance fields using a combination of a sparse feature grid and high-resolution 2D feature planes. To support large-scale unbounded scenes, we introduce a novel contraction function that maps scene coordinates into a bounded volume while still allowing for efficient ray-box intersection. We design a lossless procedure for baking the parameterization used during training into a model that achieves real-time rendering while still preserving the photorealistic view synthesis quality of a volumetric radiance field.Comment: Video and interactive web demo available at https://merf42.github.i

title: Mobile-GS: Real-time Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Devices
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful representation for high-quality rendering across a wide range of applications.However, its high computational demands and large storage costs pose significant challenges for deployment on mobile devices. In this work, we propose a mobile-tailored real-time Gaussian Splatting method, dubbed Mobile-GS, enabling efficient inference of Gaussian Splatting on edge devices. Specifically, we first identify alpha blending as the primary computational bottleneck, since it relies on the time-consuming Gaussian depth sorting process. To solve this issue, we propose a depth-aware order-independent rendering scheme that eliminates the need for sorting, thereby substantially accelerating rendering. Although this order-independent rendering improves rendering speed, it may introduce transparency artifacts in regions with overlapping geometry due to the scarcity of rendering order. To address this problem, we propose a neural view-dependent enhancement strategy, enabling more accurate modeling of view-dependent effects conditioned on viewing direction, 3D Gaussian geometry, and appearance attributes. In this way, Mobile-GS can achieve both high-quality and real-time rendering. Furthermore, to facilitate deployment on memory-constrained mobile platforms, we also introduce first-order spherical harmonics distillation, a neural vector quantization technique, and a contribution-based pruning strategy to reduce the number of Gaussian primitives and compress the 3D Gaussian representation with the assistance of neural networks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed Mobile-GS achieves real-time rendering and compact model size while preserving high visual quality, making it well-suited for mobile applications.

title: Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting on GPU
abstract: We present multi-layer volume ray casting that integrates various volume rendering enhancements into a unified framework, including empty-space skipping, volume clipping, embedding opaque and semi-transparent objects, volume editing through constructional solid geometry (CSG) operations, etc. The central idea is to consider all these objects as volume-of-interests(VOIs). Each VOI is assigned a priority number to determine how the overlapped regions are handled. All the information of the VOIs are encoded into a ray-layer buffer through depth peeling combined with layer simplification. Each pixel of a ray-layer buffer contains the information of a set of ray segments, including the starting locations and the material IDs. The multi-layer ray caster then renders (or skips) each ray segment with the proper viewing parameters depending on the material IDs. The ray-layer buffer is also used to estimate the gradients of surfaces between the layers to improve shading.IEEE/ EG Symposium on Volume Graphic

ctx: Multi-layer volume ray casting is a GPU-accelerated rendering method that handles complex volume-of-interest (VOI) interactions, including clipping, embedding, and CSG operations, by encoding spatial overlaps into a pre-generated ray-layer buffer.

Unlike standard ray casting which processes a single continuous segment or requires multiple passes for layered objects, this method iterates through non-overlapping ray segments stored in the buffer, applying material-specific transfer functions and priorities per segment within a single rendering pass.

It sets itself apart from polygon-assisted ray casting by storing only the Z-coordinate of layer starts rather than full 3D texture coordinates, reducing memory usage and ensuring bricking compatibility.

title: NeAT: Neural Adaptive Tomography
abstract: In this paper, we present Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT), the first adaptive, hierarchical neural rendering pipeline for multi-view inverse rendering. Through a combination of neural features with an adaptive explicit representation, we achieve reconstruction times far superior to existing neural inverse rendering methods. The adaptive explicit representation improves efficiency by facilitating empty space culling and concentrating samples in complex regions, while the neural features act as a neural regularizer for the 3D reconstruction. The NeAT framework is designed specifically for the tomographic setting, which consists only of semi-transparent volumetric scenes instead of opaque objects. In this setting, NeAT outperforms the quality of existing optimization-based tomography solvers while being substantially faster.

title: NerfAcc: A General NeRF Acceleration Toolbox

title: Neural Harmonic Textures for High-Quality Primitive Based Neural Reconstruction
abstract: Primitive-based methods such as 3D Gaussian Splatting have recently become the state-of-the-art for novel-view synthesis and related reconstruction tasks. Compared to neural fields, these representations are more flexible, adaptive, and scale better to large scenes. However, the limited expressivity of individual primitives makes modeling high-frequency detail challenging. We introduce Neural Harmonic Textures, a neural representation approach that anchors latent feature vectors on a virtual scaffold surrounding each primitive. These features are interpolated within the primitive at ray intersection points. Inspired by Fourier analysis, we apply periodic activations to the interpolated features, turning alpha blending into a weighted sum of harmonic components. The resulting signal is then decoded in a single deferred pass using a small neural network, significantly reducing computational cost. Neural Harmonic Textures yield state-of-the-art results in real-time novel view synthesis while bridging the gap between primitive- and neural-field-based reconstruction. Our method integrates seamlessly into existing primitive-based pipelines such as 3DGUT, Triangle Splatting, and 2DGS. We further demonstrate its generality with applications to 2D image fitting and semantic reconstruction.

title: Neural Radiance Fields-Comprehensive Survey
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) is a machine learning model that can generate high-resolution, photorealistic 3D models of scenes or objects from a set of 2D images. It does this by learning a continuous 3D function that maps positions in 3D space to the radiance (intensity and color) of the light that would be observed at that position in the scene. To create a NeRF model, the model is trained on a dataset of 2D images of the scene or object, along with their corresponding 3D positions and orientations. The model learns to predict the radiance at each 3D position in the scene by using a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and a differentiable renderer.

title: NeuS: Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces by Volume Rendering for Multi-view Reconstruction
abstract: We present a novel neural surface reconstruction method, called NeuS, for reconstructing objects and scenes with high fidelity from 2D image inputs. Existing neural surface reconstruction approaches, such as DVR [Niemeyer et al., 2020] and IDR [Yariv et al., 2020], require foreground mask as supervision, easily get trapped in local minima, and therefore struggle with the reconstruction of objects with severe self-occlusion or thin structures. Meanwhile, recent neural methods for novel view synthesis, such as NeRF [Mildenhall et al., 2020] and its variants, use volume rendering to produce a neural scene representation with robustness of optimization, even for highly complex objects. However, extracting high-quality surfaces from this learned implicit representation is difficult because there are not sufficient surface constraints in the representation. In NeuS, we propose to represent a surface as the zero-level set of a signed distance function (SDF) and develop a new volume rendering method to train a neural SDF representation. We observe that the conventional volume rendering method causes inherent geometric errors (i.e. bias) for surface reconstruction, and therefore propose a new formulation that is free of bias in the first order of approximation, thus leading to more accurate surface reconstruction even without the mask supervision. Experiments on the DTU dataset and the BlendedMVS dataset show that NeuS outperforms the state-of-the-arts in high-quality surface reconstruction, especially for objects and scenes with complex structures and self-occlusion.</p

title: Non-linear sphere tracing for rendering deformed signed distance fields
abstract: Signed distance fields (SDFs) are a powerful implicit representation for modeling solids, volumes and surfaces. Their infinite resolution, controllable continuity and robust constructive solid geometry operations, coupled with smooth blending, enable powerful and intuitive sculpting tools for creating complex SDF models. SDF metric properties also admit efficient surface rendering with sphere tracing. Unfortunately, SDFs remain incompatible with many popular direct deformation techniques which re-position a surface via its explicit representation. Linear blend skinning used in character articulation, for example, directly displaces each vertex of a triangle mesh. To overcome this limitation, we propose a variant of sphere tracing for directly rendering deformed SDFs. We show that this problem reduces to integrating a non-linear ordinary differential equation. We propose an efficient numerical solution, with controllable error, which first automatically computes an initial value along each cast ray before walking conservatively along a curved ray in the undeformed space according to the signed distance. Importantly, our approach does not require knowledge, computation or even global existence of the inverse deformation, which allows us to readily apply many existing forward deformations. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness for interactive rendering of a variety of popular deformation techniques that were, to date, limited to explicit surfaces.

Unlike Sphere Tracing, which assumes a static metric space, NLST formulates the ray traversal as an initial value problem (IVP) solved via numerical integration of an ordinary differential equation (ODE), allowing it to follow the curved ray trajectory in undeformed space while maintaining large step sizes.

title: OD-NeRF: Efficient Training of On-the-Fly Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: Dynamic neural radiance fields (dynamic NeRFs) have achieved remarkable successes in synthesizing novel views for 3D dynamic scenes. Traditional approaches typically necessitate full video sequences for the training phase prior to the synthesis of new views, akin to replaying a recording of a dynamic 3D event. In contrast, on-the-fly training allows for the immediate processing and rendering of dynamic scenes without the need for pre-training on full sequences, offering a more flexible and time-efficient solution for dynamic scene rendering tasks. In this paper, we propose a highly efficient on-the-fly training algorithm for dynamic NeRFs, named OD-NeRF. To accelerate the training process, our method minimizes the training required for the model at each frame by using: 1) a NeRF model conditioned on multi-view projected colors, which exhibits superior generalization across multiple frames with minimal training, and 2) a transition and update algorithm that leverages the occupancy grid from the last frame to sample efficiently at the current frame. Our algorithm can achieve an interactive training speed of 10FPS on synthetic dynamic scenes on-the-fly, and a 3×-9× training speed-up compared to the state-of-the-art on-the-fly NeRF on real-world dynamic scenes.

Unlike standard dynamic NeRFs that optimize over full video sequences to reconstruct 4D space-time, this approach treats the radiance field as a hidden state updated incrementally, requiring minimum optimization iterations per frame to achieve interactive speeds.
It is specifically designed for dynamic scenes captured by multi-view forward-facing cameras.

This implicit correspondence allows the model to effectively utilize radiance fields from previous frames, requiring the minimum number of optimization iterations for each new frame while maintaining interactive training and rendering speeds.

title: Opt-in exact AMR rendering, new pynbody.imaging package, and SPH perspective fixes
abstract: AMR gas (currently Ramses) can now be rendered as what it is: piecewise-constant cubic cells, rather than SPH particles. This covers slices, projections, perspective images and healpix maps. It is opt-in, through a config option or a per-call argument; the default is still SPH rendering. Rendering moves from `pynbody.sph` to a new `pynbody.imaging` package, with the old names kept working. Two bugs in SPH perspective rendering are also fixed. ## Before / after **Synthetic 6-level AMR grid**, rotated, zoom on the disc centre. Slices now show the actual cells; SPH smears them. The projection is noise-free. ```` **Slice values along one row of the synthetic grid**, compared with the true cell values. The exact renderer reproduces the cell values; SPH (denoised) is biased and smooth. `````` **Ramses test output `output_00080`, face-on.** Seen face-on, the cells are at an arbitrary rotation to the image. ```````` **Perspective projection** of the same output, camera at $z=25$ kpc. The SPH panel already includes the $\sec\theta$ fix below. The remaining differences are the faces of large cells near the camera, which SPH smooths over. `````````` **Healpix projection** (nside 64) from the densest cell, out to 200 kpc. The disc appears as a ring. Mass is conserved to $2\times10^{-8}$, against $5\times10^{-3}$ for SPH. ```````````` ## AMR rendering Each cell is a cube of side `smooth`, volume `mass/rho`, with edges along the original simulation axes. A snapshot declares its AMR families through `SimSnap._amr_cell_families`, which `RamsesSnap` sets to gas. **Opting in.** AMR rendering is off by default, and can be switched on at two levels: - **Config file:** `use-true-amr` in `[sph]`, `False` by default. If it is set to `True`, `make_render_pipeline` (and so `plot.image` etc.) uses an AMR renderer whenever the snapshot consists only of AMR cells, unless a `kernel` is given or the target is `'volume'`. - **Per call:** `use_true_amr` on `make_render_pipeline`, `plot.image`, `velocity_image` and `render_spherical_image`. - `None` (the default) follows the config file. - `False` always uses SPH. - `True` forces AMR rendering. It raises `ValueError` if the snapshot's format does not declare AMR cells, if the snapshot mixes families, or if a `kernel` or `target='volume'` is given. **Images** (`AMRImageRenderer`): - **Slices** give the exact pixel-averaged cross-section. Aligned cells use separable overlaps; rotated cells use polygon clipping. A slice lying exactly along cell faces consistently takes the +z cells. - **Aligned projections** (including after 90° rotations) are exact separable overlaps. - **Rotated projections, by default (`approximate_fast=True`):** cells up to 16 px across interpolate a tabulated corner function $F(X,Y)$, the volume of the cell with $x\le X$, $y\le Y$. This is mass-exact, with pixel errors of typically 1e-5 and at most 1e-3. - **Rotated projections, exact:** larger cells, cells cut by the depth limits, or all cells with `approximate_fast=False` use an exact row-difference method, whose cost scales with the cell's perimeter. The exact corner volumes come from the divergence theorem. - **Perspective projections** give $\int q\,dl$ along each ray from the camera. - Under the perspective map each face stays planar, so the depth where a ray crosses it is $K/L(X,Y)$ with $L$ affine. A pixel's integral is a sum of $\int 1/L$ over convex polygons. These use series from polygon moments where they converge, otherwise exact Hermite–Genocchi formulas on triangles. - The $\sec\theta$ path-length factor is integrated to second order per pixel. - Shared faces cancel, so cells tile exactly. - With `approximate_fast=True`, cells whose perspective image differs from their scaled orthographic image by less than `perspective_tolerance` (0.1 px) at every corner use the orthographic tables, with exact totals. In images of small cells this is several times faster, with r.m.s. errors around 1e-4 of the peak. - **Perspective slices** are orthographic slices of the plane, rescaled. - **Orientation** follows rotations applied to the snapshot, via the new `Transformable.net_rotation_matrix`. Copy-on-access snapshots inherit their base's rotation and AMR families. There is an explicit `orientation=` / `set_orientation` override for positions rotated outside pynbody's transformations. - **No kernel or SPH approximation is used:** `set_kernel` accepts only `None`, and denoising is off unless `smooth_floor` makes cells overlap. **Healpix maps** (`AMRHealpixRenderer`): - **Projections:** each pixel gets $qV(\text{cell}\cap\text{cone}_p)/\Omega_p$, from exact clipping of each cube to the pixel's cone. The curved sides of healpix pixels are corrected separately. Mass is conserved to round-off: $2\times10^{-8}$ on the Ramses test data, against $5\times10^{-3}$ for SPH. - **Thin shells** (`shell_distance`) sample sub-pixels, with exact tangent-plane fractions for sub-pixels at cell edges. **Pipeline:** - `approximate_fast` now means "approximations are allowed for speed", interpreted per renderer: multi-resolution rendering for SPH, tables for AMR, and none for healpix. - `with_approximate()` raises for renderers that can't approximate. - `velocity_image` renders its vectors the same way as its image. ## Timings Wall-clock seconds for `make_render_pipeline(...).render()` with the default settings (4 threads, and `approximate_fast` from the default config, i.e. True). Each is the better of two runs on a shared cloud machine, so expect variations of about ±30%. - The Ramses rows use the test output `output_00080` (1.75M cells), centred on its densest cell and rotated 30° about $x$ and 20° about $y$. - The uniform-grid rows use $96^3$ cells, rotated in the same way, in a 1.6 kpc field. - The AMR columns use `use_true_amr=True`; the last also forces `approximate_fast=False`. | case | SPH | AMR | AMR, `approximate_fast=False` | |---|---|---|---| | Ramses, slice, 60 kpc, 500² | 0.58 | 0.13 | — | | Ramses, projection, 60 kpc, 500² | 0.30 | 0.45 | 0.63 | | Ramses, projection, 1 Mpc, 1000² | 0.62 | 2.50 | 3.18 | | Ramses, perspective projection, 60 kpc, 500², camera at 120 kpc | 5.90 | 4.31 | 3.72 | | Ramses, healpix projection, nside 64, within 200 kpc | 3.59 | 4.55 | — | | uniform 96³ grid, projection, 150² (cells ≈ 1 px) | 0.07 | 0.06 | 0.71 | | uniform 96³ grid, perspective projection, 150² (cells ≈ 1 px) | 0.09 | 0.30 | 1.53 | | uniform 96³ grid, projection, 500² (cells ≈ 3.3 px) | 0.64 | 0.19 | 3.96 | | uniform 96³ grid, perspective projection, 500² (cells ≈ 3.3 px) | 0.68 | 4.44 | 4.94 | - **Orthographic images:** comparable to SPH, and faster for slices. The exception is views dominated by cells hundreds of pixels across, such as the 1 Mpc view above, where the exact large-cell path costs a few times more. - **Perspective projections:** usually slower than SPH, because every face/pixel overlap of a cell is a separate exact integral. The approximate mode helps mainly when cells are about a pixel or smaller; for larger cells it falls back to the exact path. - **Healpix:** subagent measurements found AMR as fast as SPH or faster at nside ≥ 64, up to 4× faster at nside 256, and 4–7× slower at nside 4–8. ## `pynbody.imaging` package - **Moves:** `renderers`, `render_image`, `render_3d_grid` and `render_spherical_image` move from `pynbody.sph` to `pynbody.imaging`, along with the Cython cores. - **Deprecated forwarding:** the old names still work through module `__getattr__` forwarding, with a `DeprecationWarning`. - **Plotting alias:** `pynbody.plot.sph` becomes `pynbody.plot.imaging`; the old name is kept as a silent alias. - **What stays in `pynbody.sph`:** kernels and the `smooth`/`rho` derived arrays. ## Bug fixes (SPH perspective, `z_camera`) - **Projections:** the kernel was integrated along $z$ rather than along the oblique ray, so off-axis particles were too faint by $\cos\theta$ and not elongated radially. It is now evaluated at the impact parameter perpendicular to the ray. - **Slices:** pixels were placed at each particle's depth rather than the depth of the slice plane. ## Docs and tests - **Docs:** `versionadded`/`versionchanged` 2.9.0 notes on the affected functions, an overhaul note in the `pynbody.imaging` docstring, and an AMR note in the images tutorial explaining how to opt in. The release notes should repeat the SPH perspective fixes and the new opt-in AMR rendering. - **New tests:** `tests/amr_image_test.py`, `tests/amr_healpix_test.py`, `tests/sph_perspective_test.py` and `tests/imaging_compatibility_test.py`. They cover brute-force ray-sampling references, mass conservation, tiling of subdivided cells, orthographic limits, renderer selection (including SPH remaining the default) and the Ramses test data. The AMR test modules switch `use-true-amr` on with an autouse fixture. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01NpDSCZg7LTrfc2UXLDPuTU

cited.name: X-cube loop connection criteria
ctx: X-cube loop connection criteria determine how to resolve topological ambiguities within X-cubes after X-faces have been processed, specifically by deciding whether to connect remaining free loops.
Unlike X-face slashing criteria, which merge loops across cube faces, these criteria operate on loops contained entirely within an X-cube.

The choice of criterion directly influences the topological invariants of the resulting mesh, specifically the number of shells (S) and handles (H), allowing the algorithm to prioritize either mesh simplicity (fewer shells) or feature preservation (more shells).

cited.name: X-face slashing criteria
ctx: X-face slashing criteria are a set of four decision rules used in the Cubical Marching Squares Algorithm to decide how to slash an X-face, which merges two loops in an isosurface extraction algorithm.

An X-face slash alters the loop count of the incident cubes, and the criteria determine whether to merge or split loops based on global topological objectives, such as maximizing or minimizing the total loop count L or the number of equivalence classes (shells) S.
They build on Cubical Marching Squares Algorithm by providing the specific logic for handling X-face ambiguities.

Unlike standard Marching Cubes, which uses local lookup tables to resolve ambiguous configurations, this method identifies "X-faces" and "X-cubes" and uses auxiliary data structures (X-face graph, Merge Tree) to make consistent decisions that minimize global complexity.

title: Out-of-Core Construction of Sparse Voxel Octrees
abstract: Out-of-Core Construction of Sparse Voxel Octrees - KU Leuven The main problem with converting massively large and highly detailed triangle-based scenes into sparse voxel octrees is the size of the intermediate high-resolution voxel data, which typically exceeds the available memory. In this paper, we present an out-of-core algorithm for constructing a sparse voxel octree from a triangle mesh.

cited.name: Sparse Voxel Octree Construction (Optimized Version)
ctx: This method constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a stream of non-empty voxel Morton codes by optimizing the handling of empty space.

Unlike the basic version, which inserts empty child nodes individually, this approach calculates the number of empty nodes between consecutive input leaves and directly inserts empty parent nodes into higher-level queues.
This reduces the number of queue operations significantly, as pushing back 2^d empty nodes is equivalent to pushing back a single node at the level above.

cited.name: Sparse Voxel Octree Construction (Basic Version)
ctx: Sparse Voxel Octree Construction (Basic Version) builds a hierarchical Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a stream of voxelized data, typically Morton codes, by maintaining a set of queues per depth level and merging nodes when queues fill up.

It differs from its siblings, such as Brute Force SVO Construction, by processing the input in a streaming, bottom-up manner that avoids storing the full octree in memory, and from Sparse Voxel Octree Construction via Morton Code Sorting by not requiring a global sort of all points before construction.
Trade-offs include higher memory usage compared to optimized variants due to processing empty nodes, but it offers a straightforward implementation for out-of-core construction.

cited.name: Morton Code Encoding/Decoding
ctx: Morton Code Encoding/Decoding is a method to rearrange pixels or voxels from an N-dimensional regular grid into a linear 1D form using the Morton Space Filling Curve (MSFC), also known as the Z-order curve.

This method sets itself apart from simple row-major linearization by using bit-interleaving rather than arithmetic strides, which minimizes the distance between indices of spatially neighboring voxels more effectively.
Strengths: Preserves spatial locality better than row-major ordering; hierarchical nature allows efficient octree construction; simple bitwise operations are hardware-friendly.

cited.name: Out-of-Core Sparse Voxel Octree Construction
ctx: This method constructs a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) from a triangle mesh while ensuring that memory usage remains logarithmic relative to the size of the SVO, allowing the processing of scenes larger than available RAM.

It achieves this by streaming an intermediate high-resolution 3D voxel grid in Morton order, which enables the SVO construction phase to operate in a bottom-up, queue-based manner without storing the full hierarchy in memory.

Unlike top-down methods such as Laine and Karras 2010a, which may require arbitrarily large initial build data for the root node, this approach guarantees out-of-core operation by consuming input and producing output in a streaming fashion.

cited.name: Hierarchical Data Distribution with Error-Guided Bucketization
ctx: Hierarchical Data Distribution with Error-Guided Bucketization is a data distribution scheme for parallel volume rendering that partitions a wavelet-based volume hierarchy among processors to minimize inter-processor communication dependencies and ensure balanced rendering workloads.

Unlike standard space-filling curve distributions that only consider spatial locality, this method incorporates error-guided bucketization to ensure that nodes with similar reconstruction errors (and thus similar rendering costs) are distributed across different processors, preventing contention and load imbalance.
By default, the root is a representative node, and all leaf nodes are associated nodes.

cited.name: Parallel Multiresolution Volume Rendering with Error-Guided Load Balancing
ctx: A two-stage parallel algorithm for visualizing large 3D datasets that uses a wavelet tree, error-guided bucketization, and on-the-fly reconstruction to enable interactive multiresolution rendering with minimal inter-processor communication and balanced workload.

It builds on Hierarchical Data Distribution with Error-Guided Bucketization by adding a run-time traversal and rendering pipeline that selects nodes based on a user-specified error tolerance, reconstructs data blocks on the fly, and composites partial images via screen-space tiling.
Inputs: Raw 3D dataset (single byte per voxel), user-specified error tolerance E{tol}, number of processors P, caching limits (memory M{cache}, disk D{cache}).

cited.name: Hierarchical Error Metric Calculation
ctx: This method calculates an error metric for each node in an adaptive octree (specifically a wavelet tree) by comparing a parent node's low-resolution data block against its eight immediate child nodes' data blocks, while incorporating the maximum error of those children.
It solves the problem of high computational cost and I/O overhead associated with standard Mean Square Error (MSE) calculations that require comparing data against the original raw volume.

Unlike standard MSE, which becomes increasingly expensive as one traverses toward the root due to growing volume sizes, this hierarchical approach operates on fixed-size child blocks and guarantees that a parent's error is always greater than or equal to its children's errors.

cited.name: Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS
ctx: Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS is a method to estimate the gradient of a loss function with respect to scene parameters by importance sampling an intermediate path vertex as the "differential vertex".

It solves the problem of high variance in gradient estimation, particularly for specular materials, by combining differential vertex sampling with standard BRDF sampling using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS).

Unlike standard BRDF sampling, which treats all vertices identically, this method explicitly biases the sampling distribution to capture the boundary component of the gradient integral, significantly reducing variance for microfacet and mixture BRDFs.

cited.name: Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE
ctx: This method computes the gradient of the rendered image with respect to scene parameters \theta by integrating differential measurement contributions over path space.

The method distinguishes itself by combining Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) with Next Event Estimation (NEE) to allow the differential vertex to be located at any intermediate vertex or at the emitter connection, rather than being restricted to the final vertex as in standard NEE.

The estimator computes \partial\theta I by generating standard paths and NEE paths, calculating differential contributions for all possible differential vertices, and weighting them by a mixture probability that accounts for both BRDF sampling and emitter sampling strategies.

cited.name: Multiple Importance Sampling for Boundary Paths
ctx: This method combines the unidirectional and bidirectional volume boundary estimators using path-level Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) with the balanced heuristic to reduce variance in differentiable volume rendering.

It addresses the limitation of single-estimator approaches by allowing independent sampling of boundary paths from both strategies, weighting their contributions based on their respective sampling probabilities.

Unlike the unidirectional estimator which traces from the detector, or the bidirectional estimator which connects a sampled boundary vertex to both light and detector, this method treats the boundary path as a complete entity sampled by either strategy and blends them.

cited.name: Boundary Path Integral Formulation
ctx: Unlike its siblings Reparameterized Volume Sampling and Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering, which typically rely on differentiable sampling within the volume or standard CDF inversion, this method converts interior volume integrals into boundary area integrals using the divergence theorem.
This eliminates the need to evaluate the deformation mapping inside the volume, avoiding expensive tetrahedralizations.

The method reparameterizes the rendering integral using a reference configuration independent of the shape parameter \theta, then applies the divergence theorem to move derivative terms from the volume interior to the material boundary.

cited.name: Tensor Approximation
ctx: Tensor Approximation (TA) is a compression and feature extraction method for volume data that interprets the dataset (or blocks thereof) as a multi-dimensional tensor and factorizes it into a core tensor and a set of factor matrices (the Tucker model).

Unlike standard Level-of-Detail (LOD) reduction which typically results in blurring, lower-rank TA removes small-scale features while highlighting specific structural features at different spatial scales, such as non-axis aligned patterns.
Input: A third-order tensor A \in \mathbb{R}^{I1 \times I2 \times I3} representing a volume block (e.g., a brick in a multiresolution hierarchy).

cited.name: Tensor-Specific Quantization
ctx: Tensor-Specific Quantization is a fixed bit-length encoding strategy used to compactly represent Tucker decomposition coefficients, thereby reducing disk-to-host-to-device bandwidth during volume rendering.

It distinguishes itself from generic floating-point storage by applying uniform linear quantization to factor matrices and logarithmic quantization to the core tensor, a design choice that simplifies parallel decoding on the GPU.
Input: The three factor matrices U^{(1)}, U^{(2)}, U^{(3)} and the core tensor B from a Tucker decomposition.

cited.name: Tensor Times Matrix (TTM) Reconstruction
ctx: It reconstructs a volume brick from a core tensor and factor matrices by sequentially applying three n-mode products, thereby reducing the computational complexity per voxel from cubic to linear with respect to the rank R.

Unlike naive reconstruction that loads the entire core tensor into each thread, this approach stores intermediate tensors in global memory, optimizing for shared memory constraints and enabling interactive frame rates on large datasets.
Factor matrices U^{(1)}, U^{(2)}, U^{(3)}, each of size B \times R, where B is the brick dimension (typically 32) and R is the Tucker rank (typically 16).

cited.name: Bricked Multiresolution Tensor Approximation
ctx: Bricked Multiresolution Tensor Approximation is a data management and rendering technique for interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets.

It solves the problem of limited working memory by dividing the volume into small cubical bricks, approximating each brick using rank-reduced Tucker decomposition, and organizing them into an out-of-core octree structure.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods by combining offline tensor-based compression with an adaptive, view-dependent loader that maintains a GPU cache of reconstructed bricks, enabling stack-less ray-casting with on-demand reconstruction only upon cache misses.

cited.name: Range Mapping
ctx: Range mapping is a technique that redistributes scalar values non-linearly to spread regions of interest evenly across a fixed-size lookup table, addressing the resolution limitations of hardware lookup tables for high dynamic range (HDR) data.

Unlike its sibling method, Histogram Equalization, which automatically redistributes values and breaks continuity, range mapping uses piecewise linear functions to provide user control while maintaining the continuity and order of the scalar range.

It exploits the non-linear shape of the histogram to magnify specific data clusters, allowing users to focus on narrow clusters of scalar values without the resolution artifacts inherent in fixed-size textures.

cited.name: Histogram Equalization
ctx: Histogram Equalization is an automatic technique that redistributes scalar values in volume rendering data to spread out clustered regions, thereby enhancing features hidden within high-density areas of the data distribution.
It differs from its sibling method, Range Mapping, by being fully automatic and lacking user control, which often results in breaking the continuity of the scalar range.
Lookup Table (LUT): A precomputed array mapping input indices to output values, used for speed.

cited.name: Multi-Space Transfer Function Blending (Hardware Limitation Approach)
ctx: Multi-Space Transfer Function Blending is a method for combining transfer functions defined in different data spaces (e.g., scalar value and gradient magnitude) by limiting the combination to at most three unique dimensions that do not share a common space.
It solves the problem of specifying complex, multi-dimensional classification mappings within the constraints of standard graphics hardware texture units.
Unlike Style Aggregation, which aggregates styles, this method blends the underlying RGBA lookup tables directly, restricted by the hardware limit of 3D textures.

It sets itself apart from Multi-Space Transfer Function Blending by operating on transfer functions that share the same data space (typically scalar value) rather than blending across different dimensions like gradient magnitude, and from Style Aggregation by using boolean-like arithmetic operations on RGBA values…

cited.name: Empirical Volume Shading with Indirect Light Approximation
ctx: Empirical Volume Shading with Indirect Light Approximation is a real-time shading model for participating media that approximates global illumination by blurring direct light within a local neighborhood cone and applying a separate indirect attenuation term.

It solves the computational intractability of full light transport in participating media by decoupling indirect lighting from high-resolution volume data, allowing for interactive frame rates without pre-computed global illumination caches.

It differs from traditional volume rendering by adding indirect attenuation and local light diffusion, and from full global illumination by restricting scattering to a local blur rather than computing transport from all directions.

cited.name: Half-angle slicing
ctx: It solves the problem of efficiently calculating light attenuation through a volume without pre-computing or storing large 3D shadow maps.
Half-angle slicing relies on hardware rasterization of proxy geometry, which is generally faster for large volumes but less accurate for complex internal structures.
Performance: Achieves high-resolution shadow effects without pre-computation.

cited.name: Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation
ctx: Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation enhances coarse, low-resolution volumetric data by superimposing high-frequency details using procedural noise, creating wispy, cloud-like filaments suitable for real-time clouds, smoke, and fire.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Implicit Surface Primitives or Distance to Hypertextures by avoiding the computational cost of increasing voxel resolution or recomputing geometric gradients; instead, it warps the sampling domain or modulates optical properties at render time.
Output: A rendered image with high-frequency detail that appears equivalent to a much higher resolution dataset.

cited.name: Empirical Translucent Volume Shading
ctx: Empirical Translucent Volume Shading is an interactive optical model that approximates the qualitative appearance of translucency and volumetric shadows by adding a blurred indirect light contribution to the direct light term.

Unlike physically accurate multiple scattering simulations, which are computationally prohibitive for interactive rates, this method focuses on visual fidelity—specifically color bleeding and diffusion of light across boundaries—rather than quantitative physical accuracy.

It distinguishes itself from analytical approximations (such as the diffusion approximation) by imposing no restrictions on external illumination or optical properties, allowing it to work with arbitrary volumes and scanned data.

title: PDF Light Weight Space Leaping using Ray Coherence
abstract: Light Weight Space Leaping using Ray Coherence We present a space leaping technique for accelerating volume ren-dering with very low space and run-time complexity. Our technique exploits the ray coherence during ray casting by using the distance a ray traverses in empty space to leap its neighboring rays.

cited.name: Backtracking Space Leap Rays
ctx: Backtracking Space Leap Rays is a correction mechanism applied to space leap rays in volume rendering to ensure that no non-transparent sample points are missed during the leap phase.
It solves the problem where a space leap ray, accelerated by a detector ray, might jump past the boundary of a non-empty cell group, thereby skipping valid data.

It is distinguished from standard space leaping by the explicit verification of the first sample's location relative to empty space and the subsequent backward movement of the ray origin if it lands inside a non-empty cell.

cited.name: PDF Light Weight Space Leaping
ctx: PDF Light Weight Space Leaping (LWSL) is a space-leaping acceleration technique for volume rendering that exploits ray coherence to skip empty space without requiring pre-processing or 3D data structures.

It divides image-plane rays into two groups: detector rays, which perform full ray casting to determine the distance to the first non-empty cell, and space leap rays, which are accelerated by skipping empty space based on information propagated from detector rays.

Unlike data-structure-based methods (e.g., DFB) or temporal coherence techniques, LWSL is an image-space method with memory and run-time complexity proportional only to the image size, making it independent of dataset complexity and transfer function changes.

cited.name: Boundary Pixel Detector Ray Casting
ctx: Boundary Pixel Detector Ray Casting is a safety mechanism within Space Leaping [5863-space-leaping.md] that ensures objects projecting only on boundary pixels are not missed by considering all boundary pixels as detector pixels.

It distinguishes itself from standard space leaping by treating all image boundary pixels as mandatory detector pixels, preventing the algorithm from leaping over objects located at the periphery of the view frustum.
Input: Image buffer dimensions (width W, height H) and the leap buffer state.

cited.name: Space Leaping
ctx: Space Leaping is a ray-coherence-based acceleration technique for volume rendering that skips empty regions by leveraging the spatial correlation between adjacent rays.

Unlike hierarchical data structures (e.g., octrees) that require complex traversal logic and significant memory overhead, this method uses a lightweight image-plane leap buffer to record the sample count to the first non-empty voxel for each pixel, allowing neighboring rays to skip empty space based on that…
It cannot achieve as much empty space skipping as techniques using data structures for empty/non-empty voxel info because it only leaps one out of every 4 rays, getting 75% of possible acceleration.

title: PDF Ray Tracing Animated Scenes using Coherent Grid Traversal
abstract: Ray Tracing Animated Scenes using Coherent Grid Traversal Abstract We present a new approach to interactive ray tracing of moderatesized animated scenes based on traversing frustum-bounded packets of coherent rays through uniform grids. By incrementally computing the overlap of the frustum with a slice of grid cells, we accelerate grid traversal by more than a factor of 10, and achieve ray tracing performance competitive with the fastest known packet ...

cited.name: Macrocell Grid Traversal
ctx: Macrocell Grid Traversal is a hierarchical acceleration technique for ray tracing uniform voxel grids, designed to skip empty regions of the volume by superimposing a coarser grid over the fine data structure.

It differs from flat grid traversal by introducing a two-level hierarchy where the coarse level acts as a boolean occupancy map for blocks of fine cells, allowing the ray to bypass entire M \times M \times M sections of the volume in a single step.

This method is specifically optimized for animated scenes with medium-sized grids where the acceleration structure is rebuilt every frame, prioritizing low build overhead over complex hierarchical balancing.

cited.name: Coherent Grid Traversal
ctx: Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) is a ray tracing acceleration technique that traverses packets of coherent rays through uniform grids by incrementally computing the overlap of a bounding frustum with grid slices along a dominant axis.

It solves the state invalidation problem of standard Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal when rays in a packet diverge into different cells, by abandoning cell-by-cell stepping in favor of slice-by-slice processing.
Unlike DDA which fails when rays demand different next cells, CGT keeps the packet coherent by processing entire slices, allowing it to amortize voxel look-ups and avoid expensive packet splitting.

cited.name: Coarse Grid for Large Models

It differs from the standard Grid Resolution Selection via Lambda approach, which targets moderate scenes with \lambda \approx 5, by prioritizing build speed over traversal efficiency for models exceeding several million triangles.
The method modifies the grid resolution parameter \lambda based on the triangle count of the scene.
