title: Clustered Grid Cell Data Structure for Isosurface Rendering
abstract: Active grid cells in scalar volume data are typically identified by many isosurface rendering methods when extracting another representation of the data for rendering. However, the use of grid cells themselves as rendering primitives is not extensively explored in the literature. In this paper, we propose a cluster-based data structure for storing the data of active grid cells for fast cell rasterisation via billboard splatting. Compared to previous cell rasterisation approaches, eight corner scalar values are stored with each active grid cell, so that the full volume data is not required during rendering. The grid cells can be quickly extracted and use about 37 percent memory compared to a typical efficient mesh-based representation, while supporting large grid sizes. We present further improvements such as a visibility buffer for cluster culling and EWA-based interpolation of attributes such as normals. We also show that our data structure can be used for hybrid ray tracing or path tracing to compute global illumination

cited.name: Enhanced Sphere Tracing
ctx: Enhanced Sphere Tracing is a family of ray-marching optimizations that accelerate convergence toward implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by taking steps larger than the strict Lipschitz bound or by predicting optimal step sizes based on local surface geometry.

Unlike standard sphere tracing, which uses the queried distance value as the step size, enhanced variants either over-relax the step size by a constant factor or infer the next step size from the previous two distance queries to approximate the surface as locally flat.

The term "Enhanced Sphere Tracing" refers to two distinct but related algorithmic strategies: Aggressive/Over-relaxed Marching (accelerating convergence via scalar multiplication) and Geometric Enhancement (predicting step size via historical data).

cited.name: Relaxed Sphere Tracing

A typical value cited is 0.6, resulting in a step size multiplier of 1.6.

title: Cube-4 Implementations on the Teramac Custom Computing Machine
abstract: We present two implementations of the Cube-4 volume rendering architecture on the Teramac custom computing machine. Cube-4 uses a slice­ parallel ray-casting algorithm that allows for a paral­ lel and pipelined implementation of ray-casting with tri-linear interpolation and surface normal estimation from interpolated samples. Shading, classification and compositing are part of rendering pipeline. With the partitioning schemes introduced in this paper, Cube-4 is capable of rendering large datasets with a limited number of pipelines. The Teramac hardware simulator at the Hewlett-Packard research laboratories, Palo Alto, CA, on which Cube-4 was implemented, belongs to the new class of custom computing machines. Teramac combines the speed of special-purpose hardware with the flexibility of general-purpose computel's. With Teramac as a development tool we were able to implement in just five weeks working Cube-4 prototypes, capable of rendering for example datasets of 1283 voxels in 0.65 seconds at 0,96 MHz processing frequency. The performance results from these implementations indicate real-time performance for high-resolution data-sets.

title: Cubical Marching Squares: Adaptive Feature Preserving Surface Extraction from Volume Data
abstract: In this paper, we present a new method for surface extraction from volume data which preserves sharp features, maintains consistent topology and generates surface adaptively without crack patching. Our approach is based on the marching cubes algorithm, a popular method to convert volumetric data to polygonal meshes. The original marching cubes algorithm suffers from problems of topological inconsistency, cracks in adaptive resolution and inability to preserve sharp features. Most of marching cubes variants only focus on one or some of these problems. Although these techniques could be combined to solve these problems altogether, such a combination might not be straightforward. Moreover, some feature-preserving variants introduce an additional problem, inter-cell dependency. Our method provides a relatively simple and easy-to-implement solution to all these problems by converting 3D marching cubes into 2D cubical marching squares, resolving topology ambiguity with sharp features and eliminating inter-cell dependency by sampling face sharp features. We compare our algorithm with other marching cubes variants and demonstrate its effectiveness on various applications.

title: DASNeRF: depth consistency optimization, adaptive sampling, and hierarchical structural fusion for sparse view neural radiance fields.
abstract: To address the challenges of significant detail loss in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) under sparse-view input conditions, this paper proposes the DASNeRF framework. DASNeRF aims to generate high-detail novel views from a limited number of input viewpoints. To address the limitations of few-shot NeRF, including insufficient depth information and detail loss, DASNeRF introduces accurate depth priors and employs a depth constraint strategy combining relative depth ordering fidelity regularization and depth structural consistency regularization. These methods ensure reconstruction accuracy even with sparse input views. The depth priors provide high-quality depth data through a more accurate monocular depth estimation model, enhancing the reconstruction capability and stability of the model. The depth ordering fidelity regularization guides the network to learn relative relationships using local depth ranking priors, reducing blurring caused by inaccurate depth estimation. Depth structural consistency regularization maintains global depth consistency by enforcing continuity across neighboring depth pixels. These depth constraint strategies enhance DASNeRF's performance in complex scenes, making 3D reconstruction under sparse views more accurate and natural. In addition, we utilize a three-layer optimal sampling strategy, consisting of coarse sampling, optimized sampling, and fine sampling during the three-layer sampling process to better capture details in key regions. In the optimized sampling phase, the sampling point density in key regions is adaptively increased while reducing sampling in low-priority regions, enhancing detail capture accuracy. To alleviate overfitting, we proposed an MLP structure with per-layer input fusion. This design preserves the model's detail perception ability while effectively avoids overfitting. Specifically, each layer's input includes the output features from the previous layer and incorporates processed five-dimensional information, further enhancing fine detail reconstruction. Experimental results show that DASNeRF outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the LLFF and DTU dataset, achieving better performance in metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. The reconstructed details and visual quality are significantly improved, demonstrating DASNeRF's potential in 3D reconstruction under sparse-view conditions.

It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling by replacing uniform or fixed-density refinement with a priority-driven allocation mechanism that uses dilation to expand coverage in high-density areas, thereby improving sampling efficiency and rendering quality in sparse reconstruction scenarios.

title: DBARF: Deep Bundle-Adjusting Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: Recent works such as BARF and GARF can bundle adjust camera poses with neural radiance fields (NeRF) which is based on coordinate-MLPs. Despite the impressive results, these methods cannot be applied to Generalizable NeRFs (GeNeRFs) which require image feature extractions that are often based on more complicated 3D CNN or transformer architectures. In this work, we first analyze the difficulties of jointly optimizing camera poses with GeNeRFs, and then further propose our DBARF to tackle these issues. Our DBARF which bundle adjusts camera poses by taking a cost feature map as an implicit cost function can be jointly trained with GeNeRFs in a self-supervised manner. Unlike BARF and its follow-up works, which can only be applied to per-scene optimized NeRFs and need accurate initial camera poses with the exception of forward-facing scenes, our method can generalize across scenes and does not require any good initialization. Experiments show the effectiveness and generalization ability of our DBARF when evaluated on real-world datasets. Our code is available at https://aibluefisher.github.io/DBARF.

title: Depth-supervised NeRF: Fewer Views and Faster Training for Free
abstract: A commonly observed failure mode of Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) is fitting incorrect geometries when given an insufficient number of input views. One potential reason is that standard volumetric rendering does not enforce the constraint that most of a scene\u27s geometry consist of empty space and opaque surfaces. We formalize the above assumption through DS-NeRF (Depth-supervised Neural Radiance Fields), a loss for learning radiance fields that takes advantage of readily-available depth supervision. We leverage the fact that current NeRF pipelines require images with known camera poses that are typically estimated by running structure-from-motion (SFM). Crucially, SFM also produces sparse 3D points that can be used as free depth supervision during training: we add a loss to encourage the distribution of a ray\u27s terminating depth matches a given 3D keypoint, incorporating depth uncertainty. DS-NeRF can render better images given fewer training views while training 2-3x faster. Further, we show that our loss is compatible with other recently proposed NeRF methods, demonstrating that depth is a cheap and easily digestible supervisory signal. And finally, we find that DS-NeRF can support other types of depth supervision such as scanned depth sensors and RGB-D reconstruction outputs.Project page: http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~dsnerf/ GitHub: https://github.com/dunbar12138/DSNeR

Unlike methods relying on data-driven priors from other scenes or semantic consistency, DS-NeRF imposes a loss that forces the rendered ray termination distribution to match the surface priors defined by these keypoints, thereby reducing overfitting to empty space and speeding up convergence.

title: DEV-015: 3-D voxel grid with ray/voxel DDA traversal (Stage 3)
abstract: ## Summary Adds a true 3-D voxel geometry so the scattering path transports through a patient-like `Nx×Ny×Nz` grid at arbitrary incidence — the remaining Stage-3 **Voxelized geometries** capability (beyond the slab/layered phantoms the V3 gates used), and a Stage-4 prerequisite (decision `0020`). ### Approach - **`VoxelGrid3D`** — lab-axis-aligned, per-voxel mass density, single material (density-only first cut); flat index `(i·Ny+j)·Nz+k`; a `from_voxel_slab` reduction constructor and a `uniform` factory. - **Amanatides-Woo voxel DDA**, per-step recompute, phrased as a strict generalization of the beam-frame 1-D limiter: the material coordinate `u = n̂·p` and its step limit become three lab-axis coordinates `u_k = p0[k] + mᵏ·q` (`mᵏ` = rows of the beam-frame `R`) with a per-axis distance to the next voxel face; the step is clipped to the nearest face. Axis-parallel rays → infinite face distance; on-face ties → direction-aware `s_tie = 1e-4 mm` nudge. Geometry state is recomputed each step, so no float state drifts between backends. The grid is not rotated (an oblique beam already exercises full 3-D traversal). - **Parallel drivers** (`_run_scattering_reference_grid3d`, `csda_scattering_grid3d_kernel` + `ScatteringGrid3DKernel`), dispatched on geometry type — the 1-D `VoxelSlab` path is untouched and stays bit-exact. ### Files - `src/ionmc/transport/geometry.py` (`VoxelGrid3D`), `src/ionmc/transport/engine.py` (constructor branch + grid reference driver + dispatch), `src/ionmc/backend/warp_transport.py` (grid kernel + launcher), `src/ionmc/transport/__init__.py` - `decisions/0020-voxelized-3d-grid-dda.md`, `validation/v3_voxel_grid_3d.py`, `tests/ionmc/test_voxel_grid_3d.py` - docs: physics, validation, roadmap (DEV-014 → completed at `f9e3c90`, **V3 closed**; DEV-015 added) ## Validation Host GPU (RTX A6000, CUDA, Warp 1.17.0), SHA `45f3ee2`, run `RUN-20260911T001659Z-0c7182e2` — **all 7 gates pass**: | gate | result | |---|---| | single-column grid reduces to VoxelSlab | **bit-exact** (cum 0.0) | | homogeneous box vs WaterSlab | energy 0.0, R80 0.0 | | oblique beam vs independent Siddon WET oracle | rel diff **1.7e-5** | | energy conservation (contained) | balance -1e-14 | | reference vs Warp CPU (grid, scattering) | depth-dose 1.0e-3 (DDA face-flip budget 3e-3), σ_x tight | | CUDA σ_x vs Fermi-Eyges / CUDA vs CPU depth dose | < 1 % / **6.1e-5** | **Note on the cross-backend tolerance:** the reference(float64)-vs-Warp(float32) depth-dose cumulative is ~1e-3 (looser than the 1-D path's ~1e-4) because the DDA clips at *every* voxel face (~160 z-crossings + lateral crossings per history), so float32-vs-float64 near-corner face-decision flips decorrelate proportionally more histories. This is a genuine, understood property of the accelerated DDA, not a bug: the **same-precision CUDA-vs-CPU** depth dose is tight (6.1e-5), a deterministic (scattering-off) grid run stays tight (~3e-6), and σ_x (the physics metric) agrees. Documented in decision 0020. Local full pytest suite green (reference + Warp CPU). Recorded as `VAL-20260911-001833-C6FCC3`. ## Deferred Per-voxel material map (a pure data extension of the flat arrays), grid rotation, a 3-D lab-frame scoring volume, non-uniform spacing, and CT/Hounsfield ingestion. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: dhoby-ghaut: GPU rendering for the 3D and 2D views (sphere impostors for pebbles; GPU or accelerated CSG ray tracing)
abstract: Part of #561. Maintainer, 2026-10-05: "why is the 2D and 3D rendering slow, are there not shaders available?" Measured: a full-resolution HTR-10 half-section ray trace takes 5-7 s (16-core machine, Xvfb). Cause: both views use outram-blender's CPU port of OpenMC's ray tracer / slice plotter; every pixel walks the CSG through nested lattices (core lattice -> pebble -> TRISO) with no BVH. outram-blender has no GPU rendering (its only wgpu code is a vertex-transform compute kernel) and no CSG tessellator, so there is nothing for a rasteriser to draw. Proposed, in order: 1. **Pebble views (DEM pour, bed overview):** instanced sphere impostors in an egui wgpu paint callback (one quad per pebble, sphere shading + depth in the fragment shader). 27 000 pebbles at interactive rates. This draws DEM centres, not solver geometry, and must be labelled so. 2. **Solver-geometry views and the review gate** (must stay a trace of the assembled geometry, drawing HARD RULE): either a WGSL ray-marcher over the CSG primitives (quadrics, planes, rect/hex lattices, translations) with a CPU parity test against the OpenMC-parity plotter, or a BVH / lattice-aware acceleration of the CPU tracer. Pixel parity with the existing tracer is the acceptance gate.

title: diffct: Differentiable CT Operators from Circular Orbits to Arbitrary Trajectories
abstract: diffct implements computed-tomography projection and reconstruction in PyTorch using Numba CUDA kernels. Its native forward model integrates a cell-constant attenuation field along rays defined by per-view acquisition geometry; the backprojector is the matched discrete adjoint. The same model supports parallel, fan and cone beams, non-circular trajectories, and parameterized detector surfaces. This report describes the implementation through release 2.2.1: the geometry and sampling conventions, Siddon traversal, data and first-order geometry derivatives, differentiable analytical FBP/FDK, and execution on one or several GPUs. We derive the ownership and reduction rules for distributed view and spatial partitions and explain how spatial, view and detector blocks extend native operations to CPU-backed and disk-backed data. Experiments include measured walnut cone-beam data, synthetic reconstruction and calibration, and a recorded 512³ scaling benchmark. On A100-SXM-64GB GPUs, eight GPUs on two nodes reduce forward projection from 493.05 to 73.18 ms and the amortized cost of a ten-step CGLS solve from 2054.36 to 373.38 ms per iteration. Analytical gathers have their own discrete transposes; differentiability does not make FDK an exact inverse. We distinguish numerical correctness, reconstruction quality and execution cost, and state the limits of each experiment.

title: Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) Algorithm for 3D Grid/Voxels
abstract: This is an implementation of the DDA algorithm for a 3D Grid, aka voxels, using glam for ze math. It's not optimally fast, but thats okay; this is simply a working impl for anyone to copy-paste. ```rust use glam::{BVec3, BVec3A, IVec3, Vec3A, Vec3Swizzles, Vec4}; /// The Digital-Differential-Analyzer (DDA) Algorithm for a 3D Grid / Voxels. /// /// ```rust /// use glam::Vec3A; /// const MAX_STEPS: usize = 128; /// let ro = Vec3A::new(0.0, 1.8, 0.0); // origin /// let rd = Vec3A::new(0.0, 0.0, 1.0); // direction /// let mut dda = DDAState::from_pos_and_dir(ro, rd); /// /// for _ in 0..MAX_STEPS { /// // check if dda.next_voxelpos is 'inside' a voxel /// // use the dda.hit_* functions here /// if false { break; } /// // no hit? step the ray /// dda.step_mut(); /// } /// ``` #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)] pub struct DDAState { /// The initial position of the ray. pub ray_origin: Vec3A, /// The direction the ray is going. pub ray_direction: Vec3A, /// The current largest component of/to the next boundary. pub max_boundary_mask: BVec3A, /// Per-component signum to the next voxel position. pub diff_voxelpos: IVec3, // = signum(dir) /// The next voxel position to be visited. pub next_voxelpos: IVec3, /// Per-component distance to next boundary plane. pub diff_boundary: Vec3A, /// The distances to the next voxel boundary on the X/Y/Z axes. pub next_boundary: Vec3A, } // This exists so DDAState can be directly used as Iterator. impl Iterator for DDAState { type Item = DDAState; fn next(&mut self) -> Option { self.step_mut(); Some(*self) } } impl DDAState { #[inline(always)] pub fn from_pos_to_pos( ray_origin: glam::Vec3A, ray_target: glam::Vec3A ) -> Self { let ray_direction = (ray_target - ray_origin).normalize_or_zero(); Self::from_pos_and_dir(ray_origin, ray_direction) } #[inline(always)] pub fn from_pos_and_dir( ray_origin: glam::Vec3A, ray_direction: glam::Vec3A ) -> Self { let ray_origin_grid = ray_origin.floor(); let ray_origin_grid_i = ray_origin_grid.as_ivec3(); let mut ray_direction = ray_direction; if ray_direction.x == 0.0 { ray_direction.x = 0.00001; } if ray_direction.y == 0.0 { ray_direction.y = 0.00001; } if ray_direction.z == 0.0 { ray_direction.z = 0.00001; } let ray_direction = ray_direction.normalize(); let ray_sign = ray_direction.signum(); // Step let ray_dir_inv = Vec3A::ONE / ray_direction; // invDir // vec3 sideDist = (sign(rayDir) * (vec3(mapPos) - rayPos) + (sign(rayDir) * 0.5) + 0.5) * deltaDist; let ray_dist = ray_dir_inv.abs(); let next_dist = (ray_sign * (ray_origin_grid - ray_origin) + (ray_sign * 0.5) + 0.5) * ray_dist; Self { ray_origin, ray_direction, // Values that stay fixed. diff_boundary: ray_dist, diff_voxelpos: ray_sign.as_ivec3(), max_boundary_mask: BVec3A::FALSE, next_boundary: next_dist, next_voxelpos: ray_origin_grid_i, } } #[inline(always)] pub fn step_mut(&mut self) { // Find the longest component of `next_boundary` and store it. self.max_boundary_mask = self.next_boundary.xyz().cmple(self.next_boundary.yzx().min(self.next_boundary.zxy())); self.next_voxelpos += self.diff_voxelpos * IVec3::from(self.max_boundary_mask); self.next_boundary += self.diff_boundary * Vec3A::from(self.max_boundary_mask); } #[inline(always)] pub fn step_new(&self) -> Self { let mut next = *self; next.step_mut(); next } #[inline(always)] pub fn hit_distance(&self) -> f32 { ( (self.next_boundary - self.diff_boundary) * Vec3A::from(self.max_boundary_mask) ).element_sum() } /// Global position of the hit, but at a different distance. #[inline(always)] pub fn hit_position_at_distance(&self, ray_distance: f32) -> Vec3A { self.ray_origin + (self.ray_direction * ray_distance) } /// Global position of the hit on the next voxels boundary. #[inline(always)] pub fn hit_position(&self) -> Vec3A { self.hit_position_at_distance(self.hit_distance()) } /// Global position and distance of/to the hit on the next voxels boundary. #[inline(always)] pub fn hit_position_and_distance(&self) -> glam::Vec4 { let ray_distance = self.hit_distance(); ( self.hit_position_at_distance(ray_distance), ray_distance ).into() } /// Local position of the hit on the next voxels boundary. #[inline(always)] pub fn hit_boundary(&self) -> Vec3A { self.hit_position() - self.next_voxelpos.as_vec3a() } /// Normal of the hit on the next voxels boundary. #[inline(always)] pub fn hit_normal(&self) -> Vec3A { -self.diff_voxelpos.as_vec3a() * Vec3A::from(self.max_boundary_mask) } } ```

title: DINER: Depth-aware Image-based NEural Radiance fields
abstract: We present Depth-aware Image-based NEural Radiance fields (DINER). Given a sparse set of RGB input views, we predict depth and feature maps to guide the reconstruction of a volumetric scene representation that allows us to render 3D objects under novel views. Specifically, we propose novel techniques to incorporate depth information into feature fusion and efficient scene sampling. In comparison to the previous state of the art, DINER achieves higher synthesis quality and can process input views with greater disparity. This allows us to capture scenes more completely without changing capturing hardware requirements and ultimately enables larger viewpoint changes during novel view synthesis. We evaluate our method by synthesizing novel views, both for human heads and for general objects, and observe significantly improved qualitative results and increased perceptual metrics compared to the previous state of the art. The code is publicly available through the Project Webpage.

ctx: Hierarchical DDA converts ray parameters when entering a finer resolution sub-grid from a coarser voxel, preserving inverse slopes to avoid recalculation.

cited.name: Two-Step Discrete Ray Tracing
ctx: Two-Step Discrete Ray Tracing is a ray traversal optimization for huge voxel spaces that replaces a single deep octree traversal with a two-level hierarchy of coarser and finer grids.

It solves the performance penalty of traversing empty space at high resolution by first stepping through a coarse grid, then transitioning ray parameters into a finer sub-grid only when an occupied coarse voxel is hit.
It differs from single-step discrete ray-tracing by using an octree to represent the scene at several resolutions, bypassing memory limits and optimizing traversal time.

cited.name: Piecewise Linear Spectrum Model
ctx: The Piecewise Linear Spectrum Model is a continuous spectral representation method for volume rendering that replaces discrete binning with exact positions and intensities, ensuring energy conservation and accurate Doppler shift representation.

Unlike the Point-Sampled Spectrum Model, which suffers from information loss and accuracy issues due to fixed bands, this model represents spectral lines as trapezoidal bands with linearly varying intensity, allowing for precise handling of non-uniform spectral intervals.

cited.name: Point-Sampled Spectrum Model
ctx: The Point-Sampled Spectrum Model is a discrete spectral representation method for volume rendering that approximates spectral distribution functions by dividing the spectrum into N uniform bands via point-sampling at uniform intervals.
It solves the problem of integrating emission and absorption along viewing rays in participating media with spectral variation, specifically supporting the Doppler effect.

Unlike the Piecewise Linear Spectrum Model, which replaces discrete binning with exact positions and intensities to tackle energy conservation and accuracy issues, this model suffers from information loss and accuracy degradation due to its fixed-band discretization.

cited.name: Doppler Volume Rendering
ctx: Doppler Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that simulates the relativistic Doppler effect on light emitted or absorbed by volumetric matter moving according to a 3D velocity field.

Unlike standard volume rendering which maps scalar values to static RGB colors, this method computes spectral radiance at each sample, shifting wavelengths based on the relative velocity between the emitter and the observer to produce physically accurate color shifts.

It distinguishes itself from traditional spectral volume rendering by employing a dynamic piecewise linear spectral representation, which avoids the energy conservation errors and spectral broadening artifacts inherent in point-sampled (bin-based) spectral discretization when velocities vary along the ray.

title: DTIC ADA302573: Runtime Volume Visualization for Parallel CFD.
abstract: This paper discusses some aspects of the design of a data distributed, massively parallel volume rendering library for runtime visualization of parallel computational fluid dynamics simulations in a message-passing environment. Unlike the traditional scheme in which visualization is a postprocessing step, the rendering is done in place on each node processor. Computational scientists who run large-scale simulations on a massively parallel computer can thus perform interactive monitoring of their simulations. The current library provides an interface to handle volume data on rectilinear grids. The same design principles can be generalized to handle other types of grids. For demonstration, we run a parallel Navier- Stokes solver making use of this rendering library on the Intel Paragon XP/S. The interactive visual response achieved is found to be very useful. Performance studies show that the parallel rendering process is scalable with the size of the simulation as well as with the parallel computer.

Unlike sibling methods that may rely on binary-swap compositing or require regular data partitioning, this interface selects direct compositing to remain independent of the specific data partitioning scheme, prioritizing generic applicability over peak compositing performance.

title: Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction of Deforming Volumes
abstract: The motion of a sample while being scanned in a tomograph prevents its proper volume reconstruction. In the present study, a procedure is proposed that aims at estimating both the kinematics of the sample and its standard 3D imaging from a standard acquisition protocol (no more projection than for a rigid specimen). The proposed procedure is a staggered two-step algorithm where the volume is first reconstructed using a "Dynamic Reconstruction" technique, a variant of Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART) compensating for a "frozen" determination of the motion, followed by a Projection-based Digital Volume Correlation (P-DVC) algorithm that estimates the space/time displacement field, with a "frozen" microstructure and shape of the sample. Additionally, this procedure is combined with a multi-scale approach that is essential for a proper separation between motion and microstructure. A proof-of-concept of the validity and performance of this approach is proposed based on two virtual examples. The studied cases involve a small number of projections, large strains, up to 25%, and noise.

cited.name: Motion-Compensated Algebraic Reconstruction Technique
ctx: Motion-Compensated Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (DynART) is an iterative algebraic reconstruction method designed to reconstruct deforming volumes from tomographic projections acquired during motion.
It extends the standard Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART) by jointly minimizing the discrepancy between acquired projections and the projections of a volume warped by a displacement field.

Unlike standard ART, which assumes a static object, DynART warps the reconstructed volume according to a motion field before projection and unwarp the correction term before updating the static reference volume, allowing for the reconstruction of high-quality volumes from single scans of moving or deforming objects.

cited.name: Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART)
ctx: The Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART) is an iterative algebraic method for tomographic reconstruction that minimizes the quadratic norm of the difference between acquired projections and the projected reconstructed volume, avoiding the explicit storage of the large linear system matrix.

It differs from simultaneous methods like SIRT by updating the volume estimate sequentially for each projection angle, and from analytical methods like FBP by solving the inverse problem via iterative optimization rather than direct inversion.

Formulas: The functional to minimize is: \Gamma{ART}[\psi] = \sum{r,\theta} \| \rho(r, \theta) \|^2 where \rho(r, \theta) = p(r, \theta) - R\theta[\psi(x)] is the residual between the acquired projection p and the forward projection R\theta of the current volume estimate \psi.

cited.name: Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction with Motion Identification (DynTomo)
ctx: DynTomo is a staggered iterative method for reconstructing deforming 3D volumes from 2D projection data acquired over time, simultaneously identifying the full 2D space-time displacement field.

It solves the problem of motion artifacts in tomography by alternating between algebraic volume reconstruction (DynART) and projection-based digital volume correlation (PDVC) for motion identification.

Unlike standard Algebraic Reconstruction Techniques (ART) which produce blurry or split reconstructions under large displacements, DynTomo corrects for motion to yield sharp edges and accurate gray levels.

title: Efficient Encoding of Graphics Primitives with Simplex-based Structures
abstract: Grid-based structures are commonly used to encode explicit features for graphics primitives such as images, signed distance functions (SDF), and neural radiance fields (NeRF) due to their simple implementation. However, in $n$-dimensional space, calculating the value of a sampled point requires interpolating the values of its $2^n$ neighboring vertices. The exponential scaling with dimension leads to significant computational overheads. To address this issue, we propose a simplex-based approach for encoding graphics primitives. The number of vertices in a simplex-based structure increases linearly with dimension, making it a more efficient and generalizable alternative to grid-based representations. Using the non-axis-aligned simplicial structure property, we derive and prove a coordinate transformation, simplicial subdivision, and barycentric interpolation scheme for efficient sampling, which resembles transformation procedures in the simplex noise algorithm. Finally, we use hash tables to store multiresolution features of all interest points in the simplicial grid, which are passed into a tiny fully connected neural network to parameterize graphics primitives. We implemented a detailed simplex-based structure encoding algorithm in C++ and CUDA using the methods outlined in our approach. In the 2D image fitting task, the proposed method is capable of fitting a giga-pixel image with 9.4% less time compared to the baseline method proposed by instant-ngp, while maintaining the same quality and compression rate. In the volumetric rendering setup, we observe a maximum 41.2% speedup when the samples are dense enough.Comment: 10 pages, 8 figure

cited.name: Snap Marching Cubes
ctx: Snap Marching Cubes (SnapMC) is an isosurface extraction algorithm that improves mesh quality by reducing the number of triangles and eliminating small angles, which are common artifacts in standard Marching Cubes.
It achieves this by modifying the scalar field to "snap" isosurface vertices that are geometrically close to grid vertices onto those grid vertices, causing nearby geometric elements to merge.

Unlike adaptive methods such as Advancing Front Framework for Implicit Surfaces or DelIso, SnapMC is non-adaptive and operates on a uniform grid, offering a significant speedup over adaptive counterparts at the cost of potential topological errors and non-manifold surfaces.

title: Fast CSG voxelization by frame buffer pixel mapping
abstract: This paper describes a fast algorithm for the volume conversion and rendering of CSG models constructed from both geometric and volumetric primitives. Using 3D texture mapping and frame buffer pixel operations, the algorithm can interactively generate a binary volume of the CSG model. The result can be used for volume rendering and other applications. Boolean operations are implicitly computed by a Point-Classification Map, and implemented by a hardware assisted frame buffer pixel map. The algorithm can be applied to any regions of interest of the model, thus provides a multi-resolution rendering solution through dynamic voxelization of the viewing regions. Since no pre-processing is required for any change of the CSG tree, it can be used as an effective rendering tool in a volumetric CSG modeling environment.

title: Fast Learning Radiance Fields by Shooting Much Fewer Rays
abstract: Learning radiance fields has shown remarkable results for novel view synthesis. The learning procedure usually costs lots of time, which motivates the latest methods to speed up the learning procedure by learning without neural networks or using more efficient data structures. However, these specially designed approaches do not work for most of radiance fields based methods. To resolve this issue, we introduce a general strategy to speed up the learning procedure for almost all radiance fields based methods. Our key idea is to reduce the redundancy by shooting much fewer rays in the multi-view volume rendering procedure which is the base for almost all radiance fields based methods. We find that shooting rays at pixels with dramatic color change not only significantly reduces the training burden but also barely affects the accuracy of the learned radiance fields. In addition, we also adaptively subdivide each view into a quadtree according to the average rendering error in each node in the tree, which makes us dynamically shoot more rays in more complex regions with larger rendering error. We evaluate our method with different radiance fields based methods under the widely used benchmarks. Experimental results show that our method achieves comparable accuracy to the state-of-the-art with much faster training.

title: feat(raytrace): parallel-beam voxel ray tracer for transmission imaging
abstract: Part of the Bragg edge epic (#451). ## What New `crates/nereids-raytrace/` crate implementing parallel-beam ray tracing through a 3D voxel grid for neutron transmission imaging. ## Core algorithm Amanatides-Woo DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer): - Given a ray origin and direction, step through voxels one at a time - At each step, advance to the next voxel boundary along the axis with the smallest t_max value - Record (voxel_index, path_length) for each traversed voxel - O(N) where N is the number of traversed voxels (typically ≈ grid_size) Reference: Amanatides & Woo, "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing" (Eurographics 1987). ## Types ```rust pub struct VoxelGrid { pub dims: [usize; 3], // (Nx, Ny, Nz) pub size: [f64; 3], // physical size in meters pub origin: [f64; 3], // physical origin } pub struct RaySegment { pub voxel_index: usize, // flat index into dims[0]*dims[1]*dims[2] pub path_length: f64, // meters } ``` ## Functions ### Single ray ```rust pub fn trace_ray( grid: &VoxelGrid, origin: [f64; 3], direction: [f64; 3], ) -> Vec ``` ### Parallel beam projection (single value per voxel) ```rust pub fn parallel_projection( grid: &VoxelGrid, values: &[f64], // flat array, one value per voxel beam_direction: [f64; 3], ) -> Array2 // (det_rows, det_cols) line integrals ``` Detector pixel grid: for beam along z, detector is in the xy-plane with the same pixel pitch as the voxel grid. For arbitrary beam directions, the detector grid is perpendicular to the beam. Parallelized with rayon: each detector pixel (ray) is independent. ### Wavelength-resolved projection ```rust pub fn spectral_projection( grid: &VoxelGrid, cross_sections: &Array4 , // (Nx, Ny, Nz, N_lambda) in cm^-1 beam_direction: [f64; 3], ) -> Array3 // (det_rows, det_cols, N_lambda) transmission ``` Optimization: compute ray path once per pixel, then accumulate −ln(T_λ) = Σ_k Σ_k(λ) × δ_k for all wavelength bins simultaneously. The inner loop is a dot product (path_lengths · cross_sections per voxel), which is SIMD-friendly. Returns transmission T = exp(−line_integral) for each pixel and wavelength. ## Tests 1. **Uniform block**: all voxels same value σ. Line integral along z-axis through center equals σ × Nz × voxel_size_z. 2. **Single voxel**: 1×1×1 grid, T = exp(−σ × size_z). 3. **Off-axis ray**: beam at 45° through a 2D grid, path lengths equal voxel_size × √2 for diagonal traversal. 4. **Empty voxels**: zero cross-section voxels contribute nothing. 5. **Symmetry**: rotating beam direction 90° and transposing the grid gives the same result. 6. **Spectral consistency**: spectral_projection with identical cross-sections at all wavelengths gives uniform transmission across wavelength axis. ## Dependencies - nereids-core (constants) - ndarray (Array2, Array3, Array4) - rayon (parallel iteration)

title: feat(renderer): draw FogVolume and FogMaterial into the volumetric fog
abstract: ## What changes Before: a FogVolume drew nothing, so its local fog, and the fog a negative density carves out, were missing from the volumetric fog. A texture saved as its own `.tres`, and an ImageTexture or ImageTexture3D with its pixels saved inline, drew nothing either. After: each FogVolume adds its FogMaterial's density, albedo and emission to the froxels its shape covers, as Godot 4.6.3's volume pass does (`volumetric_fog.glsl:165-278`, `fog_material.cpp:149-163`). Every shape works: box, ellipsoid, cone, cylinder and world. Height falloff, edge fade, negative density and Godot's default fog shader for a volume without a material work too. A FogMaterial `density_texture` shapes the density. It can be a NoiseTexture3D or an ImageTexture3D, inline or saved as its own `.tres`, or an image its import sidecar imports as a 3D texture. How: - `godot/fogVolume.ts` ports the froxel range of a volume's pass (`fog.cpp:551-718`). `r3f/fog/fogVolumeRows.ts` packs each visible, unculled volume into a row texture, and `fogVolumeShader.ts` adds the volumes' fixed-point sums in the light pass, with Godot's packed-colour overflow. - `nodes/3d/fogvolume/` gains a parser and a Component, and `resources/materials/fogmaterial/` decodes FogMaterial. - The new `resources/textures/noisetexture3d/` slice builds the texture as a worker job. Its texels and seamless blend match Godot byte for byte. `r3f/fog/fogDensityAtlas.ts` stacks every density texture in depth into one 3D texture, because a WebGL2 shader cannot index a sampler array in a loop. The stack holds floats once a density texture does. - An imported 3D texture is cut into slices as Godot's layered importer cuts it (`resource_importer_layered_texture.cpp:370-386`). - The new `resources/textures/imagetexture3d/` slice and `resources/textures/image/decode.ts` read an `Image` sub-resource in every uncompressed format: 8-bit, 16-bit, half, float, RGBA4444, RGB565 and RGBE9995, unpacked as `Image::_get_color_at_ofs` does (`image.cpp:3382-3406`, `:3451-3525`). A float texel uploads raw as a half float, because Godot gives a float format no sRGB view and WebGL2 always filters a half float. An atlas crop of a half-float sheet stays half float, and a canvas read of one converts it to bytes. - `useTextResourceSlot` reads a slot that names a `.tres` as that file's `[resource]` in the file's own tables. Every Texture2D and Texture3D slot uses it, so a `.tres` AtlasTexture now takes the inline route. - Found on the way: - The colour ramp shared with NoiseTexture2D reads the luminance in float and truncates each channel, as Godot does (`color.h:106-108`, `image.cpp:3577-3580`). - The Gradient sampler and `channelToByte` run in float, as `Gradient::get_color_at_offset` and `Color::get_r8` do (`gradient.h:151-235`, `color.h:228`). Godot-measured ramp bytes off by one drop from 1212 to 0 of 2244. - A GradientTexture2D with `use_hdr` keeps a channel above 1 (`gradient_texture.cpp:239-270`). - The ArrayMesh byte reader now narrows a listed -1 to 255, as Godot does (`variant_parser.cpp:650`). - NoiseTexture2D and NoiseTexture3D apply the FastNoiseLite domain warp, as `get_noise_2d` and `get_noise_3d` do (`fastnoise_lite.cpp:318-338`). `patches/fastnoise-lite@1.1.1.patch` exports the port's `Vector2` and `Vector3`, which its `DomainWrap` requires. - `fogVolumePass.ts` and `fogVolumeShaders.ts` are now `volumetricFogPass.ts` and `volumetricFogShaders.ts`, because the glossary keeps "fog volume" for the node. - FogMaterial, NoiseTexture3D, ImageTexture3D and CompressedTexture3D declare validators. Texture3D joins the undeclared-resource list as a record: it is an abstract tier with no properties of its own. ### Goldens - `fog-volume` (new): the issue's 3×3×3 box at (0, 1, −5). Against converged Godot 4.6.3, the mean error drops from 3.476/255 (no volume) to 0.205/255. - `fog-volume-density-image`, `fog-volume-density-volume-tres` and `fog-volume-density-half-tres` (new): an imported 3D texture, an 8-bit ImageTexture3D `.tres` and a half-float one whose density passes 1. - `sprite2d-imagetexture-tres` and `sprite2d-imagetexture-half-tres` (new): an RGB8 and an RGBAHalf ImageTexture `.tres`. - `noisetexture2d-domain-warp` (new): a progressive, reduced-simplex domain warp. - Moved, all closer to Godot: - `noisetexture2d`: max 1/255 from the ramp fix, mean 0.776/255 → 0.735/255. - `sprite3d-gradienttexture`: mean 1.887/255 → 1.882/255. - `texturerect-gradienttexture`: 682816 → 682496 pixels off Godot. - `isometric-dungeon`: 2 px at 1/255 from the point light's gradient. Pixel (367, 584) goes from 5 to 4 in red, and Godot draws 4. The other pixel sits on an edge where the frame's mean error against Godot is unchanged. - Every other fog, gradient, noise and atlas golden is unchanged. ### Value check `pnpm ref:diff`, mean error over the pixels the volume changes in Godot, before → after: | Scene | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | box | 13.05 | 0.40 | | ellipsoid | 10.66 | 0.22 | | cone | 8.90 | 0.40 | | cylinder | 15.67 | 0.41 | | world shape | 14.07 | 0.25 | | negative density | 3.65 | 0.26 | | height falloff 2 | 9.58 | 0.24 | | edge fade 0 | 14.21 | 0.40 | | edge fade 4 | 2.55 | 0.08 | | no material (default fog) | 13.21 | 0.35 | | albedo and emission | 32.91 | 1.13 | | density 8 | 23.92 | 0.45 | | rotated and scaled | 13.73 | 0.30 | | spot and sun lights | 24.70 | 0.60 | | NoiseTexture3D box | 6.54 | 0.81 | | NoiseTexture3D world | 7.90 | 0.26 | | NoiseTexture3D colour ramp | 6.67 | 0.82 | | NoiseTexture3D seamless ellipsoid | 5.13 | 0.13 | | NoiseTexture3D inverted, unnormalised | 6.58 | 0.80 | `pnpm ref:diff`, mean error over the whole frame, before → after: | Scene | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | imported 3D texture | 3.554 | 0.209 | | ImageTexture3D `.tres`, Lum8 | 4.459 | 0.206 | | NoiseTexture3D `.tres` | 5.418 | 0.196 | | ImageTexture3D `.tres`, RHalf | 2.227 | 0.215 | | ImageTexture3D `.tres`, RFloat | 2.229 | 0.216 | | ImageTexture3D `.tres`, R16 | 1.153 | 0.184 | | ImageTexture3D `.tres`, RGBE9995 | 2.229 | 0.215 | | NoiseTexture3D warp, simplex | 0.714 | 0.194 | | NoiseTexture3D warp, reduced simplex, progressive | 0.683 | 0.199 | | NoiseTexture3D warp, basic grid, independent | 0.496 | 0.196 | | ImageTexture `.tres` sprite, RGB8 | 0.596 | 0.000 | | NoiseTexture2D `.tres` sprite | 7.455 | 0.019 | | ImageTexture sprite, RGBAHalf | 0.581 | 0.002 | | ImageTexture sprite, RGBAFloat | 0.581 | 0.002 | | ImageTexture sprite, RGBA4444 | 0.595 | 0.002 | | ImageTexture sprite, RGB565 | 0.845 | 0.000 | | ImageTexture sprite, RGBA16 | 0.621 | 0.002 | | GradientTexture2D `use_hdr` sprite | 6.880 | 0.007 | Each sprite scene modulates by 0.4, so a channel above 1 shows. With the Environment's fog off, a volume adds nothing, in both engines. A NoiseTexture2D sprite with each warp drops from a maximum error of 143 to 187/255 to 1 to 3/255. Its whole-frame mean stays at 0.72/255, because `main` clears the 2D background to grey 77 where Godot clears to 76. A separate thread fixes that. ### Known limitations These are in the comparison sheets: - A fog ShaderMaterial runs no fog shader. That needs a shading-language runtime: #734. - An Image in a block-compressed format draws nothing: #736. An Image in an integer format draws nothing too, since a float sampler cannot read it. - A NoiseTexture3D shows even density until its build lands. - Past 2048 stacked density slices, further textures leave the density even. A 3D colour slot still decodes every texture as sRGB. Godot reads a format without an sRGB view raw, so a Lum8 or grey-noise albedo draws too dark. This predates this pull request and touches every 3D material path: #737. ## How you checked it - `pnpm check` passes. - `pnpm test:unit` passes, run by directory. - `pnpm test:visual` passes on every fog, gradient, noise, atlas and sprite scene, and on `isometric-dungeon`. - `pnpm docs:lint-sections`, `pnpm docs:index` and `pnpm docs:gallery` pass with `--check`. Closes #665

cited.name: Fog Volume Grid Rendering
ctx: Fog Volume Grid Rendering is a technique for integrating FogVolume and FogMaterial nodes into a froxel-based volumetric fog system by adding their density, albedo, and emission properties to the froxels (volumetric grid cells) that the volume's shape covers.
It solves the problem of missing local fog contributions and negative density carving in real-time approximations, matching the behavior of Godot 4.6.3.

Unlike sibling methods that focus on temporal stability or depth distribution, this method specifically handles the geometric mapping of arbitrary volume shapes (box, ellipsoid, cone, cylinder, world) and the texture-based density modulation required for static and dynamic fog volumes.

title: Feature-Guided Diffusion for Non-Differentiable Inverse Rendering
abstract: Inverse rendering is traditionally solved via differentiable renderers and gradient descent, which requires substantial problem-specific engineering and is prone to getting stuck in local minima due to ambiguities. Derivative-free approaches alleviate engineering requirements, but often heavily depend on a good problem initialization. In this work, we propose Feature-Informed Diffusion Evolution (FIDE), a fully black-box framework that requires no gradients or specific initialization: the renderer is treated as an opaque function whose only requirement is to produce images. Our key insight is feature guiding: rather than reducing each candidate rendering to a scalar loss value, we use a Vision Transformer (ViT) to extract dense visual features from it. We subsequently use these features to train a diffusion-based candidate proposal model, allowing the network to use visual cues to predict parameters that would match the target image. The candidate solutions proposed by this diffusion model are then refined in a closed loop with a CMA evolution strategy, continuously narrowing the proposal region as optimization progresses. We validate across diverse inverse problems from path tracing, vector splines, Voronoi shaders, and robotics, and demonstrate that feature-guiding substantially improves convergence over scalar-loss baselines and reliably escapes local minima where gradient-based methods stall.

cited.name: Optimization Baselines
ctx: Unlike gradient-based siblings that rely on automatic differentiation or adjoint methods, these methods treat the renderer as an opaque function, minimizing a photometric loss \mathcal{L} by iteratively sampling and evaluating parameter candidates.

The family is distinguished by its reliance on population-based search distributions (typically Gaussian) that adapt to the local loss landscape without explicit gradient information, offering robustness against local minima and Monte Carlo noise.

The core mechanism involves maintaining a search distribution \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) over the parameter space \mathbb{R}^d, where \boldsymbol{\mu} is the mean and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is the anisotropic covariance matrix capturing correlations between parameters.

cited.name: Feature-Guided Diffusion for Inverse Rendering
ctx: Feature-Guided Diffusion for Inverse Rendering (FIDE) is a fully black-box framework for solving non-differentiable inverse rendering problems by combining a diffusion-based inverse prediction model with Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES).

Unlike scalar-loss baselines like DiBO or DiffBBO, FIDE conditions the proposal distribution on dense visual features extracted from the target image, avoiding the information bottleneck of scalar loss values and mitigating mode averaging in ill-posed inverse problems.

The core mechanism involves maintaining a search distribution \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) over the parameter space \mathbb{R}^d, where \boldsymbol{\mu} is the mean and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is the anisotropic covariance matrix capturing correlations between parameters.

cited.name: Scan Offset Computation
ctx: Scan Offset Computation recomputes the scanoffsets array for a classified volume, where each ScanOffset entry stores the first length offset and first data offset for a specific scanline (j, k) plane.

Unlike ComputeIndex, which maps every voxel coordinate to a specific run position, this method only stores the starting offsets for each scanline (j, k), requiring the renderer to traverse the RLE runs sequentially along the i-axis to locate voxels.
The method iterates through the volume dimensions in the order k, then j, accumulating the lengths of RLE headers and data payloads to compute cumulative offsets.

cited.name: Volpack Run-Length Encoded Volume Classification and Storage
ctx: Volpack Run-Length Encoded Volume Classification and Storage is a pre-processing method that converts a dense voxel grid into three axis-aligned Run-Length Encoded (RLE) structures (one for X, Y, and Z viewing axes) to optimize ray casting by skipping transparent regions.

It differs from standard RLE by classifying voxel data into opacity/material categories during construction and storing shading fields alongside quantized opacity, enabling the renderer to bypass empty space efficiently.

Unlike Scan Offset Computation, which only provides lookup tables for ray entry points, this method fully constructs the compressed data streams for all three orthogonal axes, allowing the renderer to traverse runs sequentially along the viewing axis.

title: Generalizing Spatial Transformers to Projective Geometry with Applications to 2D/3D Registration
abstract: Differentiable rendering is a technique to connect 3D scenes with corresponding 2D images. Since it is differentiable, processes during image formation can be learned. Previous approaches to differentiable rendering focus on mesh-based representations of 3D scenes, which is inappropriate for medical applications where volumetric, voxelized models are used to represent anatomy. We propose a novel Projective Spatial Transformer module that generalizes spatial transformers to projective geometry, thus enabling differentiable volume rendering. We demonstrate the usefulness of this architecture on the example of 2D/3D registration between radiographs and CT scans. Specifically, we show that our transformer enables end-to-end learning of an image processing and projection model that approximates an image similarity function that is convex with respect to the pose parameters, and can thus be optimized effectively using conventional gradient descent. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to describe the spatial transformers in the context of projective transmission imaging, including rendering and pose estimation. We hope that our developments will benefit related 3D research applications. The source code is available at https://github.com/gaocong13/Projective-Spatial-Transformers.

cited.name: Projective Spatial Transformer (ProST)
ctx: ProST is a differentiable volume rendering module that generalizes spatial transformers to projective geometry, enabling volumetric rendering of transmission images that are differentiable with respect to both the input volume and the pose parameters.

It solves the problem of performing end-to-end differentiable projection of voxelized data onto 2D planes, which is essential for tasks like 2D/3D registration where gradients must flow from a 2D similarity metric back through the projection to the 3D pose.
Unlike mesh-based differentiable renderers, ProST operates directly on voxel grids using a cone-beam ray casting approach, making it suitable for medical imaging applications.

cited.name: Geodesic Loss Approximation for 2D/3D Registration
ctx: This method trains a deep neural network to approximate the geodesic gradient in SE(3), enabling end-to-end learning of a convex similarity metric for 2D/3D registration.

It differs from standard supervised registration by optimizing the network parameters \phi such that the gradient of the learned loss LN with respect to pose \theta aligns directionally with the true geodesic gradient \partial LG / \partial \theta, rather than minimizing pixel-wise error directly.
This approach extends the capture range of initialization compared to traditional image-based methods like Grad-NCC.

cited.name: Hybrid 2D/3D Registration Optimization Pipeline
ctx: This method is a two-stage optimization pipeline for 2D/3D registration that minimizes a differentiable network similarity loss (LN) for global convergence, then switches to a traditional Gradient-based Normalized Cross-Correlation (Grad-NCC) loss (L{GNNC}) for local refinement.

It addresses the sensitivity of joint optimization to initialization by leveraging the robust global convergence of neural similarity metrics and the precise local convexity of correlation-based metrics.
In the source implementation, rotation is optimized directly, and translation is optimized directly.

title: Image-space sheet-buffered splatting on the GPU
abstract: Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting is a popular high quality volume-rendering technique specially suitable for zoomed views of the data. However, the bottleneck of the method is the computation of the buckets, i.e the structure handling the voxels to be rendered in each slab. This stage of the method is done on the CPU. title: Improve surface rendering
abstract: CAMotics currently uses Marching Cubes (MC) to extract the cut surface. MC has problems detecting sharp features. This is particularly noticeable when simulating a conical tool. You can simulate at higher resolution but you will always get [jaggies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaggies) in the sharp corners. They just get smaller at the cost of exponentially increasing simulation time. [Dual Contouring](http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html) does a better job of detecting sharp features but requires "[Hermite data](http://math.stackexchange.com/questions/48245/what-is-hermite-data)" which means we need not only edge intersection points but also the surface normal at those points. Surface normals are not easy to calculate because we don't have a closed form depth function for tool sweeps. Surface normals can however be estimated to arbitrary precision with a binary search for the surface plane about the point of interest. Note, the typical method of estimating a surface normal by numerical integration of a depth function but again we don't have such a function. [Cubical Marching Squares](http://graphics.csie.ntu.edu.tw/CMS/) is also an interesting option. It too requires Hermite data and is significantly more complicated to implement but has several advantages over DC.

title: Interactive Volume Illustration Using Intensity Filtering
abstract: We propose a simple and interactive technique for volume illustration by using the difference between the original intensity values and a low-pass filtered copy. This difference, known as unsharped mask, provides us with a spatial importance map that captures salient and separability information about regions in the volume. We integrate this map in the visualization pipeline and use it to modulate the color and the opacity assigned by the transfer function to produce different illustrative effects. We also apply stipple rendering modulating the density of the dots with the spatial importance map. The core of our approach is the computation of a 3D Gaussian filter, which is equivalent to three consecutive 1D filters. This separability feature allows us to obtain interactive rates with a CUDA implementation. We show results of our approach for different data sets.

title: Isosurface Extraction Using Fixed-Sized Buckets
abstract: We present a simple and output optimal algorithm for accelerated isosurface extraction from volumetric data sets. Output optimal extraction algorithms perform an amount of work dominated by the size of the (output) isosurface rather than the size of the (input) data set. While several optimal methods have been proposed to accelerate isosurface extraction, these algorithms are relatively complicated to implement or require quantized values as input. Our method is based on a straightforward array data structure that only requires an auxiliary sorting routine for construction. The method works equally well for floating point data as it does for quantized data sets. We demonstrate how the data structure can exploit coherence between isosurfaces by performing searches incrementally. We show results for real application data validating the method's optimality.EUROVIS 2005: Eurographics / IEEE VGTC Symposium on Visualizatio

It builds on Fixed-Sized Buckets for Isosurface Extraction by maintaining boundary markers that allow the algorithm to skip over cells whose active status is known to be unchanged, rather than re-evaluating every cell in the active range.

cited.name: Fixed-Sized Buckets for Isosurface Extraction
ctx: Fixed-Sized Buckets is an output-optimal algorithm for accelerated isosurface extraction from volumetric data sets.

It sets itself apart from its parent Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction by using a simpler array-based structure that avoids tree traversal overhead, and from siblings like Interval Table for Isosurface Extraction by relying on two-pass sorting rather than interval merging.

title: kit: ray traversal, graph analysis, bin packing, hex A* — round 7
abstract: ## Summary External-survey round 7 — the algorithm-layer gaps (taxonomy leftovers are all intentionally out-of-scope: derive macro, hot reload, socket transport). Four additions, all integer-exact, all verified against independent oracles: - **`gridcast`** — Amanatides–Woo DDA ray traversal (`grid_ray`, `ray_blocked_at`, `clear_los`). Unlike `geometry`'s Bresenham (one cell per column), this walks *every cell a segment enters* in entry order — needed for ballistic/LOS sweeps. All coordinates doubled (endpoints are cell centres, boundaries even), the `tMaxX ` = canonical lexicographic order, `None` on cycle), and `UnionFind` (path-halving + union-by-rank, smaller-index root on ties so representatives are pure functions of the union sequence — the structure `voronoi::mst_edges` used internally, now public). Edge case nailed down: the tree-edge skip tracks a *per-frame* `par_skipped` flag, so a parallel edge to the parent still lowers `low` — parallel edges are correctly never reported as bridges. - **`pack`** — skyline (bottom-left) rectangle bin packing (Jylänki, *A Thousand Ways to Pack the Bin*, 2010). `pack_skyline(rects, bin_w, bin_h)` drops each rect onto the lowest fitting skyline segment — input order is placement order, so output is a pure function of the slice. Texture atlases / inventory grids / dialog tiling. - **`hexgrid::hex_astar`** — hex-grid A* (redblobgames): the exact hex `distance` is a consistent heuristic, so nodes expand at most once and results are true shortest paths; `(f, h, q, r)` heap tie-break + ordered-map bookkeeping; `max_steps` bounds the search since the hex lattice is unbounded. ## Verification Every addition is oracle-tested rather than hand-verified: - `grid_ray` vs an independent slab-test (segment ∩ open cell box has positive length) over 500 random rays — plus symmetry, no-dup, 8-connected checks. - `strongly_connected` vs mutual-BFS-reachability; `articulation_points`/`bridges` vs remove-and-recount; `topo_sort` vs linear-extension validity + cycle rejection; `UnionFind` vs a reference set model. - `pack_skyline` invariants (no overlap, inside bin) over 200 random rect sets. - `hex_astar` vs BFS shortest-path length on random obstacle fields. `bash tools/gate.sh` — all green: fmt, workspace tests, clippy 0 warnings, rustdoc clean, pinned determinism hashes unchanged (`0xd1a9236e96a2c802` / `0x5286d1420200fe66` / kit_bridge `353498ec4fbcd160`), all 30 examples reproduce byte-identically, both crates package. title: L0-Sampler: An L0Model Guided Volume Sampling for NeRF
abstract: Since its proposal, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) has achieved great success in related tasks, mainly adopting the hierarchical volume sampling (HVS) strategy for volume rendering. However, the HVS of NeRF approximates distributions using piecewise constant functions, which provides a relatively rough estimation. Based on the obser-vation that a well-trained weight function$w(t)$and the$L_{0}$distance between points and the surface have very high sim-ilarity, we propose$L_{0}$-Sampler by incorporating the$L_{0}$model into$w(t)$to guide the sampling process. Specif-ically, we propose using piecewise exponential functions rather than piecewise constant functions for interpolation, which can not only approximate quasi-$L_{0}$weight distri-butions along rays quite well but can be easily imple-mented with a few lines of code change without additional computational burden. Stable performance improvements can be achieved by applying$L_{0}$-Sampler to NeRF and re-lated tasks like 3D reconstruction. Code is available at https://ustc3dv.github.io/L0-Sampler/.

title: Light Propagation Maps on Parallel Graphics Architectures
abstract: Light going through a participating medium like smoke can be scattered or absorbed by every point in the medium. To accurately render such a medium we must compute the radiance resulting at every point inside the medium because of these physical effects, which have been modeled by the radiative transfer equation. Computing the radiance at any point inside a participating medium amounts to numerically solving this radiative transport equation. Discrete Ordinate Method (DOM) is a widely used solution method. DOM is computationally intensive. Fattal [Fat09] proposed Light Propagation Maps (LPM) to expedite DOM computation. In this paper we propose a streaming based parallelization of LPM to run on SIMD graphics hardware. Our method is fast and scalable. We report more than 20x speed improvement by using our method as compared to Fattal's original method. Using our approach we are able to render 64x64x64 dynamic volumes with multiple scattering of light at interactive speed on complex lighting, and are able to render volumes of any size independent of the GPU memory capability.Eurographics Symposium on Parallel Graphics and Visualizatio

title: MaskGaussian: Adaptive 3D Gaussian Representation from Probabilistic Masks
abstract: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has demonstrated remarkable performance in novel view synthesis and real-time rendering, the high memory consumption due to the use of millions of Gaussians limits its practicality. To mitigate this issue, improvements have been made by pruning unnecessary Gaussians, either through a hand-crafted criterion or by using learned masks. However, these methods deterministically remove Gaussians based on a snapshot of the pruning moment, leading to sub-optimized reconstruction performance from a long-term perspective. To address this issue, we introduce MaskGaussian, which models Gaussians as probabilistic entities rather than permanently removing them, and utilize them according to their probability of existence. To achieve this, we propose a masked-rasterization technique that enables unused yet probabilistically existing Gaussians to receive gradients, allowing for dynamic assessment of their contribution to the evolving scene and adjustment of their probability of existence. Hence, the importance of Gaussians iteratively changes and the pruned Gaussians are selected diversely. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in achieving better rendering quality with fewer Gaussians than previous pruning methods, pruning over 60% of Gaussians on average with only a 0.02 PSNR decline. Our code can be found at: https://github.com/kaikai23/MaskGaussian

cited.name: Masked-Rasterization

It differs from sibling methods like Analytic-Splatting by applying masks during the blending stage rather than modifying Gaussian attributes (opacity/scale) prior to rasterization, which prevents the loss of gradient flow.

title: MeshGS: Adaptive Mesh-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for High-Quality Rendering
abstract: Recently, 3D Gaussian splatting has gained attention for its capability to generate high-fidelity rendering results. At the same time, most applications such as games, animation, and AR/VR use mesh-based representations to represent and render 3D scenes. We propose a novel approach that integrates mesh representation with 3D Gaussian splats to perform high-quality rendering of reconstructed real-world scenes. In particular, we introduce a distance-based Gaussian splatting technique to align the Gaussian splats with the mesh surface and remove redundant Gaussian splats that do not contribute to the rendering. We consider the distance between each Gaussian splat and the mesh surface to distinguish between tightly-bound and loosely-bound Gaussian splats. The tightly-bound splats are flattened and aligned well with the mesh geometry. The loosely-bound Gaussian splats are used to account for the artifacts in reconstructed 3D meshes in terms of rendering. We present a training strategy of binding Gaussian splats to the mesh geometry, and take into account both types of splats. In this context, we introduce several regularization techniques aimed at precisely aligning tightly-bound Gaussian splats with the mesh surface during the training process. We validate the effectiveness of our method on large and unbounded scene from mip-NeRF 360 and Deep Blending datasets. Our method surpasses recent mesh-based neural rendering techniques by achieving a 2dB higher PSNR, and outperforms mesh-based Gaussian splatting methods by 1.3 dB PSNR, particularly on the outdoor mip-NeRF 360 dataset, demonstrating better rendering quality. We provide analyses for each type of Gaussian splat and achieve a reduction in the number of Gaussian splats by 30% compared to the original 3D Gaussian splatting.ACCV (Asian Conference on Computer Vision) 202

title: Modelado de geometría mediante "Signed Distance Functions" y desarrollo de algoritmos para su intersección
abstract: Aunque la representación más común de la geometría en entornos de ray tracing sean las mallas de triángulos, existen otras formas de representar geometrías complejas. Una de estas representaciones alternativas son las SDFs (Signed Distance Functions). Estas funciones devuelven la distancia con signo a la superficie desde cualquier punto en el espacio (para cada punto p, f(p)=0 en la superficie, f(p)0 en el exterior). Su naturaleza geométrica permite una manipulación de la geometría mucho más directa que la basada en polígonos: se modifica directamente la ecuación implícita de los volúmenes, en lugar de modificar individualmente los vértices de los polígonos. En este trabajo, presentamos una librería para la definición y manipulación de geometría mediante SDFs. Mostramos distintos ejemplos de estas funciones y sus capacidades, así como algunas aplicaciones al margen de la representación de geometría. El código implementado se ha integrado con el renderer Mitsuba2 para sintetizar escenas avanzadas con estas geometrías.Pese a todas las ventajas que ofrecen las SDFs para representar geometría, estas complican en cierta medida la intersección con las superficies. Durante los años, se han desarrollado diversos métodos para abordar este problema. En este trabajo, se han implementado tanto algunos de los algoritmos más populares de este tipo (Sphere Tracing y Enhanced Sphere Tracing), como otros métodos nuevos diseñados para este proyecto (Newton Marching y Forward Newton Marching), basados en el método de Newton para intersectar más rápidamente superficies planas. Se han comparado todos los métodos experimentalmente, y se han analizado las capacidades y limitaciones de los nuevos algoritmos. Se muestra también la posibilidad que ofrecen los nuevos algoritmos de intersectar geometría definida por otro tipo de funciones derivables (no necesariamente SDFs).<br /

title: n-Dimensional Sparse Voxel Trees for Compact Representation of Dimensionally Upscaled Voxelized Three-Dimensional Scenes
abstract: This paper addresses the issue of how to represent the geometry of voxelized threedimensional scenes using domain-specific hierarchical data structures.It provides a comprehensive overview of these data structures, delving into the specifics of sparse voxel octrees in greater depth.Then, it discusses the proposed use of dimensionality upscaling, i.e. the transformation of a three-dimensional voxelized scene into a higher number of dimensions, to enable the representation of the geometry of this scene via an n-dimensional sparse voxel tree hierarchical data structure.This approach allows a smaller size of binary representation of the 3D scene geometry -compared to its representation using a sparse voxel octree.This is documented in the next section of the paper, where we summarize the results of tests encoding the geometries of the respective scenes (based on voxelization of polygonal surface models), into sparse voxel trees of different levels of dimensionality.We achieved the highest compactness of the binary representation of the resulting data structure, compared to the traditional sparse voxel octree (increase in compactness ranged from 2.02 to 4.44 times), using upscaling to 6D and 7D, respectively.

It maps N-dimensional coordinates (x, y, z) into a single integer index such that points close in Euclidean distance have close indices, thereby preserving spatial locality in linear memory.

This method sets itself apart from simple row-major linearization by using bit-interleaving rather than arithmetic strides, which minimizes the distance between indices of spatially neighboring voxels more effectively.

It solves the problem of storage efficiency in 3D volume rendering by upscaling the dimensionality of the scene from 3D to mD (m > 3), reducing the total number of nodes and pointers required to represent the geometry.

Unlike its sibling Morton-coded Sparse Voxel Tree which remains strictly 3D, or Hashed-Octree which uses hashing for flat storage, the nD SVT trades increased per-node complexity (larger child masks) for a significantly reduced tree depth and node count.

title: NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) 19940009248: A data distributed parallel algorithm for ray-traced volume rendering
abstract: This paper presents a divide-and-conquer ray-traced volume rendering algorithm and a parallel image compositing method, along with their implementation and performance on the Connection Machine CM-5, and networked workstations. This algorithm distributes both the data and the computations to individual processing units to achieve fast, high-quality rendering of high-resolution data. The volume data, once distributed, is left intact. The processing nodes perform local ray tracing of their subvolume concurrently. No communication between processing units is needed during this locally ray-tracing process. A subimage is generated by each processing unit and the final image is obtained by compositing subimages in the proper order, which can be determined a priori. Test results on both the CM-5 and a group of networked workstations demonstrate the practicality of our rendering algorithm and compositing method.

title: NeRF--: Neural Radiance Fields Without Known Camera Parameters
abstract: Considering the problem of novel view synthesis (NVS) from only a set of 2D images, we simplify the training process of Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) on forward-facing scenes by removing the requirement of known or pre-computed camera parameters, including both intrinsics and 6DoF poses. To this end, we propose NeRF$--$, with three contributions: First, we show that the camera parameters can be jointly optimised as learnable parameters with NeRF training, through a photometric reconstruction; Second, to benchmark the camera parameter estimation and the quality of novel view renderings, we introduce a new dataset of path-traced synthetic scenes, termed as Blender Forward-Facing Dataset (BLEFF); Third, we conduct extensive analyses to understand the training behaviours under various camera motions, and show that in most scenarios, the joint optimisation pipeline can recover accurate camera parameters and achieve comparable novel view synthesis quality as those trained with COLMAP pre-computed camera parameters. Our code and data are available at https://nerfmm.active.vision.

title: NeuManifold: Neural Watertight Manifold Reconstruction with Efficient and High-Quality Rendering Support
abstract: While existing volumetric rendering approaches provide photorealistic results, extracting high-quality meshes from optimized neural field representations is challenging. Conversely, existing differentiable rasterization-based methods are typically sensitive to initialization and suffer from poor mesh rendering quality. In this paper, we introduce Neu-Manifold, a novel method for reconstructing watertight manifold meshes with high-quality textures from multi-view input images. NeuManifold overcomes the limitations of existing approaches by first learning a neural volumetric field and then refining it through differentiable mesh extraction and surface rendering. To eliminate artifacts and preserve mesh properties during iso-surface extraction, we introduce a novel differentiable marching cubes method. Instead of traditional textures, we use neural textures to enhance rendering quality. To integrate with modern graphics rendering pipelines, we also provide customized GLSL shader support for neural textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeuManifold outperforms existing mesh-based reconstruction methods in both mesh quality and rendering metrics, achieving comparable or superior rendering quality to prior volume-rendering-based methods. The generated results enable real-time, high-quality rendering and seamlessly support numerous graphics pipelines and applications requiring high-quality meshes, such as 3D printing and physical simulation. https://sarahweiii.github.io/neumanifold/.

title: Neural Dual Contouring
abstract: We introduce neural dual contouring (NDC), a new data-driven approach to mesh reconstruction based on dual contouring (DC). Like traditional DC, it produces exactly one vertex per grid cell and one quad for each grid edge intersection, a natural and efficient structure for reproducing sharp features. However, rather than computing vertex locations and edge crossings with hand-crafted functions that depend directly on difficult-to-obtain surface gradients, NDC uses a neural network to predict them. As a result, NDC can be trained to produce meshes from signed or unsigned distance fields, binary voxel grids, or point clouds (with or without normals); and it can produce open surfaces in cases where the input represents a sheet or partial surface. During experiments with five prominent datasets, we find that NDC, when trained on one of the datasets, generalizes well to the others. Furthermore, NDC provides better surface reconstruction accuracy, feature preservation, output complexity, triangle quality, and inference time in comparison to previous learned (e.g., neural marching cubes, convolutional occupancy networks) and traditional (e.g., Poisson) methods. Code and data are available at https://github.com/czq142857/NDC.

cited.name: Neural Dual Contouring
ctx: Neural Dual Contouring (NDC) is a data-driven mesh reconstruction method that replaces the hand-crafted Quadratic Error Function (QEF) minimization of classical Dual Contouring with a neural network that directly predicts vertex positions and edge crossings.

It solves the problem of reconstructing high-fidelity meshes from implicit inputs (SDFs, point clouds, or voxels) without requiring explicit surface gradients or suffering from the ill-defined QEF scenarios that plague classical methods.

Unlike its sibling Dual Contouring, which relies on precise normals and QEF optimization, NDC produces meshes with better tessellation quality and can generate open surfaces with boundaries directly, avoiding the watertight constraint of methods like Marching Cubes.

title: Neural Rendering Techniques
abstract: Neural rendering has transformed 3D scene representation and novel view synthesis by replacing explicit geometricprimitives with implicit neural representations that encode scene appearance and geometry directly in neural networkweights. This study presents a systematic evaluation of five neural rendering approaches -- Neural Radiance Fields(NeRF), Instant-NGP (hash-encoded radiance fields), 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), Mip-NeRF 360 (unboundedscenes), and NeuS (surface reconstruction) -- across four rendering tasks: bounded object synthesis (NeRF Synthetic /Blender dataset, 8 objects), unbounded forward-facing scenes (LLFF, 8 scenes), unbounded 360-degree scenes(Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, 9 scenes), and surface reconstruction (DTU dataset, 15 objects). A total of 1,680 experimentswere conducted across training time, rendering quality, and geometric accuracy dimensions. 3D Gaussian Splattingachieved real-time rendering at 68.4 +- 4.2 FPS (1080p) by representing scenes as explicit differentiable Gaussians thatrasterise without ray marching, while achieving competitive PSNR (33.2 +- 0.4 dB on Blender vs. NeRF's 31.0 +- 0.6 dB).Instant-NGP reduced NeRF training from hours to 2.4 +- 0.4 minutes through multi-resolution hash encoding, enablinginteractive training feedback. Mip-NeRF 360 achieved the highest unbounded scene quality (PSNR = 29.4 +- 0.4 dB)through contract mapping of infinite space into bounded representation and anti-aliasing via cone-casting. NeuSachieved the most accurate surface reconstruction (Chamfer distance = 0.62 +- 0.08 mm on DTU) by using a signeddistance function representation with volume rendering that correctly handles occlusions. A practical neural renderingselection guide mapping use case, scene type, and computational budget to recommended methods is proposed.
