title: [✨ feature] Emissive Volume Rendering
abstract: ## Description This PR adds emissive event sampling in the null-scattering volpathmis integrator for sampling the VRE and MIS for emission. It supersedes the previous PR https://github.com/mitsuba-renderer/mitsuba3/pull/40. Adds emissive volume support by adding a volume emitter. The interface adds a `volumelight` emitter to a given shape that is then sampled as part of the medium sampling routines in volpath/volpathmis/prbvolpath. The current implementation modifies none of the interfaces of endpoint and thus does not work with MIS as-of-yet. I am unsure of the best way to implement this in terms of modifying the interface. The cleanest solution seems to be that the endpoint sampling methods take an extra float to sample a 3d point, but whether this should be implemented by changing the existing Point2f sample to Point3f or adding an additional argument is unclear to me. The current implementation is feature complete except for NEE for volume emitters, I have added and tested the python interfaces by bringing the prbvolpath implementation to parity with volpath. ## Checklist - [x] My code follows the [style guidelines](https://mitsuba.readthedocs.io/en/latest/src/developer_guide.html#coding-style) of this project - [x] My changes generate no new warnings ~~- generates warnings about unused parameters in `volumelight`, these methods will be implemented and the parameters used.~~ There are no longer any new warnings. - [x] My code also compiles for `cuda_*` and `llvm_*` variants. I have compiled every single variant and run all the tests, and everything passes except for the tutorial notebooks, but these throw an unicode char encoding error so I think it's unrelated. I will check with a fresh master copy if the same error occurs, might be a windows only issue. - [x] I have commented my code - [x] I have made corresponding changes to the documentation - [x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works - ~~this is in-progress, have added emissive volume scenes and tests that I will make a PR for in the [mitsuba-renderer/mitsuba-data](https://github.com/mitsuba-renderer/mitsuba-data) repo.~~ Created the following PR to merge emissive volume tests: mitsuba-renderer/mitsuba-data#17 - [x] I cleaned the commit history and removed any "Merge" commits - [x] I give permission that the Mitsuba 3 project may redistribute my contributions under the terms of its [license](https://github.com/mitsuba-renderer/mitsuba/blob/master/LICENSE) ## Notes * The implementation uses non-analogue probabilities as described in [Monte Carlo Methods for Volumetric Light Transport Simulation](https://cs.dartmouth.edu/wjarosz/publications/novak18monte.pdf). This leads to more consistent results when a given radiance channel is zero and better convergence in all the tests I've done. * Both `volpath` and `prbvolpath` have implementations of the analogue, maximum and mean event probability calculations for testing. The issue of inconsistency only appears with analogue probabilities in non-scalar modes, and only for volpathmis and prbvolpath. * Sorry for the delay in the implementation! The move to Mitsuba 3 meant I had to rewrite a lot of the code, but I managed to be significantly more thorough this time around so everything compiles and all the tests pass. * I've attached an example render as well! ![homogeneous-emissive-cuda](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11709271/232779686-d71ffd12-f9ee-4ba7-8fa3-97f7b8312a48.png)

cited.name: Emissive Volume Rendering
ctx: Emissive Volume Rendering extends path tracing algorithms to support participating media that emit light, enabling the simulation of radiative transfer within volumetric emitters.

It distinguishes itself by integrating volume emission sampling directly into the medium interaction routines, requiring only minimal code changes to existing integrators, while avoiding the performance penalties of direct solid-angle-to-volume PDF conversion for Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS).
Inputs: A scene containing shapes defined as volumetric emitters, with associated emission properties and medium scattering/absorption coefficients.

cited.name: Next Event Estimation for Emissive Volumes
ctx: Next Event Estimation (NEE) for emissive volumes computes the direct lighting contribution from light-emitting media by sampling points directly on the emissive volume geometry rather than relying solely on volumetric scattering along the ray.

This method reduces noise in scenes containing bright emissive regions by ensuring that light sources are explicitly sampled, addressing the high variance inherent in pure path tracing through participating media.

It differs from analytic shading Direct volume rendering with Phong shading by using statistical sampling for direct illumination rather than local gradient approximations, and from illumination caching Illumination caching by computing lighting dynamically per sample rather than pre-integrating it into 3D textures.

title: A Clustering Based Transfer Function for Volume Rendering Using Gray-Gradient Mode Histogram
abstract: Volume rendering is an emerging technique widely used in the medical field to visualize human organs using tomography image slices. In volume rendering, sliced medical images are transformed into attributes, such as color and opacity through transfer function. Thus, the design of the transfer function directly affects the result of medical images visualization. A well-designed transfer function can improve both the image quality and visualization speed. In one of our previous paper, we designed a multi-dimensional transfer function based on region growth to determine the transparency of a voxel, where both gray threshold and gray change threshold are used to calculate the transparency. In this paper, a new approach of the transfer function is proposed based on clustering analysis of gray-gradient mode histogram, where volume data is represented in a two-dimensional histogram. Clustering analysis is carried out based on the spatial information of volume data in the histogram, and the transfer function is automatically generated by means of clustering analysis of the spatial information. The dataset of human thoracic is used in our experiment to evaluate the performance of volume rendering using the proposed transfer function. By comparing with the original transfer function implemented in two popularly used volume rendering systems, visualization toolkit (VTK) and RadiAnt DICOM Viewer, the effectiveness and performance of the proposed transfer function are demonstrated in terms of the rendering efficiency and image quality, where more accurate and clearer features are presented rather than a blur red area. Furthermore, the complex operations on the two-dimensional histogram are avoided in our proposed approach and more detailed information can be seen from our final visualized image.

cited.name: Gray-Gradient Mode Histogram Clustering Transfer Function
ctx: This method automatically generates a volume rendering transfer function (TF) by embedding volume data attributes (gray value and gradient mode) into a two-dimensional histogram, performing hierarchical clustering to identify tissue boundaries, and mapping the results to color, opacity, and gradient-based opacity…
It solves the problem of manual TF specification by distinguishing tissues based on gray ranges and enhancing boundary visibility through clustering analysis of the gray-gradient mode histogram.

Unlike standard piecewise-linear interpolation which may cause blurring at tissue edges, this method assigns constant color and opacity within identified tissue ranges defined by histogram valleys, ensuring uniform appearance for specific tissues.

cited.name: Clustering-Based Gray-Gradient Transfer Function
ctx: This method automatically generates a two-dimensional transfer function for volume rendering by clustering a gray-gradient mode histogram to identify tissue zones, mapping gray values and gradient modes to color and opacity without manual adjustment.

It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like the Gaussian Sum Transfer Function by relying on histogram mode clustering rather than probabilistic density estimation, and from Support Vector Machine (SVM) Classification by using unsupervised clustering of data attributes rather than supervised classification…
It solves the problem of tedious manual transfer function design and the loss of edge details (such as bone-medulla distinction) common in standard 1D opacity mappings.

title: A Comparison of Fundamental Methods for Iso-surface Extraction
abstract: In this paper four fundamental methods for an iso-surface extraction are compared, based on cell decomposition to tetrahedra. The methods are compared both on mathematically generated data sets as well as on real data sets. The comparison using mathematical data is made from different points of view such as area approximation, volume approximation. On the other hand, the Hausdorff distance and root mean square are used to compare methods on real data sets. The presented comparison can be helpful when deciding among tested methods which one to choose, as well as when we need to compare a newly developed method with other existing approaches.

cited.name: Improved Marching Cubes Algorithm
ctx: The Improved Marching Cubes (IMC) algorithm is a variant of the standard Marching Cubes method designed to enhance computational efficiency and topological robustness in 3D reconstruction, particularly for medical CT imaging.

It addresses two primary limitations of the standard approach: the generation of topological voids due to ambiguous saddle points and the high computational cost of linear interpolation and dense voxel traversal.

By expanding the topological configuration set from 15 to 24 cases, employing a tunable interpolation scheme, and utilizing larger voxel representations, IMC reduces reconstruction time while maintaining geometric accuracy.

cited.name: Marching Cubes on Structured Grids
ctx: An improved MC algorithm that increases the side length of voxels to reduce the number of voxels traversed during 3D reconstruction, thereby improving operation efficiency.
Benchmarks show efficiency improvements of 61.09% to 93.54% compared to traditional MC, with minimal impact on visual accuracy for large datasets.
The "Improved Marching Cubes with Voxel Changes" variant demonstrates that reducing the number of voxels (by increasing voxel size) can yield significant speedups (up to 93.5%).

title: A Novel Image-Centric Approach Toward Direct Volume Rendering
abstract: Transfer function (TF) generation is a fundamental problem in direct volume rendering (DVR). A TF maps voxels to color and opacity values to reveal inner structures. Existing TF tools are complex and unintuitive for the users who are more likely to be medical professionals than computer scientists. In this article, we propose a novel image-centric method for TF generation where instead of complex tools, the user directly manipulates volume data to generate DVR. The user’s work is further simplified by presenting only the most informative volume slices for selection. Based on the selected parts, the voxels are classified using our novel sparse nonparametric support vector machine classifier, which combines both local and near-global distributional information of the training data. The voxel classes are mapped to aesthetically pleasing and distinguishable color and opacity values using harmonic colors. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets and a detailed user survey show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

cited.name: Image-Centric Volume Rendering with SN-SVM Classification
ctx: This method enables direct volume rendering by allowing users to interact with raw 2D volume slices to define training data for an SN-SVM classifier, which then automatically classifies all voxels and assigns colors via color harmonization.

It distinguishes itself from siblings like Classified Volume Rendering by avoiding pre-processing steps such as branch decomposition or contour tree computation, thereby preserving raw data granularity and preventing information loss during initial semantic realization.
Select the top three slices (one from each direction) to present to the user.

cited.name: SN-SVM Color and Opacity Assignment
ctx: This method assigns color and opacity to voxel groups identified by SN-SVM classification to enhance visual aesthetics, contrast, and boundary details without ad-hoc user input.

It differs from standard transfer function approaches by deriving opacity and hue variation directly from spatial variance and gradient magnitude, respectively, rather than relying on user-defined scalar-to-RGBA mappings.
Hue Range Width: The difference \xi{hi} - \xi{li} is fixed at 5% of the hue wheel, which corresponds to 18^\circ.

title: A novel interpolation scheme for dual marching cubes on octree volume fraction data

cited.name: Dual Marching Cubes
ctx: It modifies the computation of mesh vertex positions in dual marching cubes to be more appropriate for volume fraction data by approximating octant shapes as spheres rather than cubes.
It computes the dual grid from the input octree grid.
It computes a surface mesh vertex on each dual edge that crosses the object's surface using the novel interpolation scheme.

title: Abstract Feature Space Representation for Volumetric Transfer Function Exploration
abstract: The application of n-dimensional transfer functions for feature segmentation has become increasingly popular in volume rendering. Recent work has focused on the utilization of higher order dimensional transfer functions incorporating spatial dimensions (x,y, and z) along with traditional feature space dimensions (value and value gradient). However, as the dimensionality increases, it becomes exceedingly difficult to abstract the transfer function into an intuitive and interactive workspace. In this work we focus on populating the traditional two-dimensional histogram with a set of derived metrics from the spatial (x, y and z) and feature space (value, value gradient, etc.) domain to create a set of abstract feature space transfer function domains. Current two-dimensional transfer function widgets typically consist of a two-dimensional histogram where each entry in the histogram represents the number of voxels that maps to that entry. In the case of an abstract transfer function design, the amount of spatial variance at that histogram coordinate is mapped instead, thereby relating additional information about the data abstraction in the projected space. Finally, a non-parametric kernel density estimation approach for feature space clustering is applied in the abstracted space, and the resultant transfer functions are discussed with respect to the space abstraction.

cited.name: Non-parametric Transfer Function Generation using Spatial Variance
ctx: This method enhances a 2D histogram-based transfer function by mapping histogram entries to the spatial variance of the voxels that populate them, rather than the voxel count.

It solves the problem of background noise inclusion and incorrect feature segmentation (e.g., including air values with leaves) common in conventional transfer function views by leveraging spatial relationships.
It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using the magnitude of spatial standard deviation as the primary statistical property for clustering and density estimation in the abstract feature space.

cited.name: Non-Parametric Transfer Function Generation
ctx: Non-Parametric Transfer Function Generation is a clustering method for 2D histograms (conventional or abstracted) that groups data based on neighborhood information using variable kernel density estimation.
It differs from discrete histogram-based clustering by operating on continuous density estimates, thereby avoiding spurious peaks and preserving spatial relationships of neighboring data points.

Unlike frequency binning methods that consider only density magnitude, this method incorporates position in feature space via adaptive kernel widths, preventing disjoint segments for the same density value.

title: Accelerating Transfer Function Update for Distance Map based Volume Rendering
abstract: Direct volume rendering using ray-casting is widely used in practice. By using GPUs and applying acceleration techniques as empty space skipping, high frame rates are possible on modern hardware. This enables performance-critical use-cases such as virtual reality volume rendering. The currently fastest known technique uses volumetric distance maps to skip empty sections of the volume during ray-casting but requires the distance map to be updated per transfer function change. In this paper, we demonstrate a technique for subdividing the volume intensity range into partitions and deriving what we call partitioned distance maps. These can be used to accelerate the distance map computation for a newly changed transfer function by a factor up to 30. This allows the currently fastest known empty space skipping approach to be used while maintaining high frame rates even when the transfer function is changed frequently.5 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, presented at IEEE VIS 2024, for associated mp4 file, see https://osf.io/n5k6z ; source code available at https://github.com/CalamityMichL/DVR_ESS_PD

cited.name: Direct Volume Rendering with Partitioned Distance Maps (PDM) based Empty Space Skipping
ctx: Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) with Partitioned Distance Maps (PDM) based Empty Space Skipping (ESS) is an acceleration technique for distance-field ray marching that subdivides the volume's intensity range into n partitions to precompute individual distance maps.
When a transfer function (TF) changes, only the relevant PDMs are merged to form the final distance map D', avoiding a full recomputation of the distance transform.

Unlike the base method Partitioned Distance Map Combination which recomputes the global distance map on every TF change, PDM-based ESS trades higher memory usage and one-time initialization cost for significantly faster TF update times, maintaining high frame rates during frequent TF adjustments.

cited.name: Partitioned Distance Map (PDM) Acceleration
ctx: Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) with Partitioned Distance Maps (PDM) based Empty Space Skipping (ESS) is an acceleration technique for distance-field ray marching that subdivides the volume's intensity range into n partitions to precompute individual distance maps.

Unlike the base method Partitioned Distance Map Combination which recomputes the global distance map on every TF change, PDM-based ESS trades higher memory usage and one-time initialization cost for significantly faster TF update times, maintaining high frame rates during frequent TF adjustments.

title: Accelerating Volume Reconstruction with 3D Texture Hardware
abstract: Accelerating Volume Reconstruction with 3D Texture Hardware We have presented a volume rendering approach that leverages the 3D texturing hardware available on high-performance graphics systems. The texturing hardware accelerates the reconstruction and resampling process inherent in all volume visualization algorithms.

cited.name: Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering via 3D Texturing
ctx: Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering via 3D Texturing is a direct volume rendering technique that leverages 3D texture mapping hardware to perform reconstruction and resampling of volumetric data.

It solves the problem of interactive rendering performance by offloading the computationally intensive trilinear interpolation and resampling steps to the GPU's texture engine, which processes polygons embedded in the volume in parallel.
They must be reoriented to lie in the plane most parallel to the view-plane as the viewpoint changes. 2.

cited.name: PixelFlow Volume Rendering
ctx: PixelFlow Volume Rendering is a polygon resampling method designed for the PixelFlow graphics system that overcomes the lighting and data size limitations of the RealityEngine by allowing pixel processors to manipulate 3D texture values directly.

It differs from its siblings by replacing precomputed shading coefficients with on-the-fly Phong lighting calculations derived from interpolated volume gradients, enabling general image-space lighting.
Each 32-bit value is treated as four 8-bit components: three for the normalized data gradient (gx, gy, gz) and one for the raw data value (d).

title: Adaptive Algorithm for Accelerating Direct Isosurface Rendering on GPU
abstract: Direct isosurface volume rendering is the most prominent modern method for medical data visualization. It is based on finding intersection points between the rays corresponding to pixels on the screen and isosurface. This article describes a two-pass algorithm for accelerating the method on the graphic processing unit (GPU). On the first pass, the intersections with the isosurface are found only for a small number of rays, which is done by rendering into a lower-resolution texture. On the second pass, the obtained information is used to efficiently calculate the intersection points of all the other. The number of rays to use during the first pass is determined by using an adaptive algorithm, which runs on the central processing unit (CPU) in parallel with the second pass of the rendering. The proposed approach allows to significantly speed up isosurface visualization without quality loss. Experiments show acceleration up to 10 times in comparison with a common ray casting method implemented on GPU. To the authors’ knowledge, this is the fastest approach for ray casting which does not require any preprocessing and could be run on common GPUs.

cited.name: Level-of-detail (LOD) methods
ctx: They solve the problem of computational intensity in volume rendering by dynamically adjusting the discretization of the rendering process—such as step size, sample count, or spatial resolution—based on a metric of visual error or performance.
Auxiliary Texture (for GPU isosurface methods): A texture T storing the rendered isosurface, analyzed to determine texel density.

cited.name: Adaptive Auxiliary Texture Resolution for Isosurface Raycasting
ctx: This method accelerates direct isosurface volume rendering on GPUs by decoupling the intersection search from the final pixel shading using a two-pass approach.

It renders ray-isosurface intersections into a low-resolution auxiliary texture in the first pass, then uses this depth information to predict starting points for ray marching in the second pass, effectively skipping empty space for most pixels.
Unlike preprocessing-based acceleration techniques (e.g., octrees or histogram pyramids), it constructs its auxiliary data dynamically every frame, requiring no prior analysis of the volume dataset.

title: Adaptive Spatio‐Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scenes with Oscillatory Motion
abstract: Abstract Our goal is to reconstruct scenes with stochastic, incoherent motion such as leaves moving in the wind, that can be particularly challenging because of small objects with similar appearance that move independently. Previous dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting solutions either represent motion implicitly with neural networks achieving good quality but lower framerate, or explicitly with a function, often with higher training times and lower quality. To overcome these limitations, we propose an explicit method that introduces adaptive space‐time densification and smoother optimization. We introduce a new densification approach based on error moments that are used to guide primitive splitting, and we adaptively refine the number of keyframes used based on the variance of error. We observe that dynamic reconstruction from monocular video is hard for standard optimization pipelines. To counter this, we introduce a weighted Adam approach that improves results based on primitive visibility. Finally, to handle the hard case of independent motion of similar‐looking objects, we introduce an image‐driven as‐rigid‐as‐possible regularization. Our method has higher quality than previous explicit solutions, and has significantly higher framerate for rendering.

cited.name: Gaussian Splitting and Pruning
ctx: Spatial Splitting with Error Moments is a densification technique that splits Gaussians with error above a threshold \tau{space} by placing a splitting plane through the Gaussian's center, oriented based on the error moments rather than the Gaussian's longest axis.

Unlike FCC 24 and DDL 25b which use a plane perpendicular to the Gaussian's longest axis, this method uses the error moments to determine orientation to avoid Gaussians becoming too small too quickly.

cited.name: Temporal Densification
ctx: Temporal densification is a strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that detects and resolves reconstruction errors caused by object or camera motion by splitting Gaussians based on the variance of their normalized image error across time segments.

It addresses the limitation of static spatial densification, which assumes Gaussians are stationary, by identifying Gaussians whose error fluctuates significantly between keyframes, indicating they fail to track motion.
Hyperparameters: temporal threshold \tau{time}, KNN count K=10, minimum segment length l{seg}.

title: Add anisotropic voxel mipmaps and separate diffuse/reflection bias to VoxelGI
abstract: ## What problem(s) does this PR solve? VoxelGI's voxel mipmaps are purely isotropic: each coarser octree level is just the plain average of its 8 children's color+alpha. Cone tracing against this chain has no notion of *which side* of a coarse cell is occluded, so light leaks through thin geometry (walls, floors, thin props) once cones start sampling higher mip levels. Separately, the diffuse (multi-cone) and reflection (single specular cone) cone traces always shared the exact same `bias` value, even though they usually want different tuning (reflections benefit from a smaller bias for sharp contact reflections; diffuse GI benefits from a larger bias to reduce self-occlusion noise). This PR adds: 1. **Anisotropic voxel mipmaps.** During mip generation, each octree cell now also builds 6 directional (+X/-X/+Y/-Y/+Z/-Z) copies of its color+alpha by compositing its 8 children front-to-back along each axis (the technique from Crassin & Green, *Octree-Based Sparse Voxelization*), instead of a single isotropic average. Cone tracing blends the 3 axis-matching directional textures weighted by `direction * direction`, which lets it pick up directional occlusion instead of always sampling an isotropic blur. This is opt-in per probe via a new `VoxelGIData.anisotropic_strength` (`0.0` by default = identical behavior/cost to before; the bake blends the isotropic and anisotropic result by this factor and the run-time cone tracer only samples the anisotropic textures when it's `> 0`). 2. **Separate diffuse/reflection tracing bias.** `VoxelGIData.bias` now only affects the diffuse cones; a new `VoxelGIData.reflection_bias` controls the single specular/reflection cone independently. Both properties are wired end-to-end: `VoxelGIData` (scene) → `RenderingServer` → `RendererGI` → the RD (Forward+/Mobile) backend, which is the only backend that actually implements VoxelGI cone tracing (GLES3/Compatibility and the dummy backend already no-op every VoxelGI method, so they just got matching empty overrides for the new virtuals). The forward-clustered inline GI path (used for transparent/forward-shaded materials) also picks up `reflection_bias`; wiring up anisotropic sampling there as well is left as follow-up since it needs its own texture bindings in that shader's descriptor set. ## Additional information **Use of AI disclosure:** this PR was written by Claude (Anthropic's Claude Code), including the design of the anisotropic compositing algorithm, all C++/GLSL changes, and this description, from a request to add anisotropic voxel mipmaps and separate diffuse/reflection tracing parameters to VoxelGI. It has not been tested against a real engine build (no build environment was available in the session), so please treat it as a from-scratch review candidate rather than a validated patch. Implementation notes for reviewers: - `servers/rendering/renderer_rd/shaders/environment/voxel_gi.glsl`: bake-time compute shader. Adds an `aniso_outputs` storage buffer (6 `vec4`s per octree cell) alongside the existing isotropic `outputs` buffer, a leaf-level init that scales opacity per direction by `dot(normal, dir)` (radiance is view-independent, but a thin surface has near-zero cross-section edge-on/from behind), and the front-to-back compositing pass per internal octree level, gated by `aniso_strength` (a previously-declared-but-unused push constant field). - `servers/rendering/renderer_rd/shaders/environment/gi.glsl`: run-time cone tracer. Adds 6 new `texture3D[MAX_VOXEL_GI_INSTANCES]` bindings and a `sample_aniso_voxel()` helper that blends them; `voxel_cone_trace()`/`voxel_cone_trace_45_degrees()` take a `bool p_anisotropic` and fall back to the original single-texture sampling when it's false. - The `VoxelGIData` uniform struct byte layout is duplicated in 4 places (`gi.h`, `gi.glsl`, `scene_forward_clustered_inc.glsl`, `volumetric_fog_process.glsl`); all 4 were updated in lockstep to keep the std140 layout identical, since a mismatch there would silently corrupt every existing field, not just the new ones. - Descriptor/VRAM cost: the anisotropic textures and buffers are always allocated once a probe has any mipmaps (to keep the uniform set layout simple), costing roughly one extra full copy of the base mip chain's memory (6 directions × mip levels 1..N is smaller than one full level-0-sized copy). The 6 new sampled-image array bindings in `gi.glsl` are also always declared in the shader regardless of whether any probe uses them. If this is a concern for lower-end/mobile GPUs with tight descriptor limits, let me know and I can look at making the bindings conditional on a specialization constant. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01Bd72UuZ4Q6pufJUGyvBcop --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_01Bd72UuZ4Q6pufJUGyvBcop)_

title: AdR-Gaussian: Accelerating Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Radius
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a recent explicit 3D representation that has achieved high-quality reconstruction and real-time rendering of complex scenes. However, the rasterization pipeline still suffers from unnecessary overhead resulting from avoidable serial Gaussian culling, and uneven load due to the distinct number of Gaussian to be rendered across pixels, which hinders wider promotion and application of 3DGS. In order to accelerate Gaussian splatting, we propose AdR-Gaussian, which moves part of serial culling in Render stage into the earlier Preprocess stage to enable parallel culling, employing adaptive radius to narrow the rendering pixel range for each Gaussian, and introduces a load balancing method to minimize thread waiting time during the pixel-parallel rendering. Our contributions are threefold, achieving a rendering speed of 310% while maintaining equivalent or even better quality than the state-of-the-art. Firstly, we propose to early cull Gaussian-Tile pairs of low splatting opacity based on an adaptive radius in the Gaussian-parallel Preprocess stage, which reduces the number of affected tile through the Gaussian bounding circle, thus reducing unnecessary overhead and achieving faster rendering speed. Secondly, we further propose early culling based on axis-aligned bounding box for Gaussian splatting, which achieves a more significant reduction in ineffective expenses by accurately calculating the Gaussian size in the 2D directions. Thirdly, we propose a balancing algorithm for pixel thread load, which compresses the information of heavy-load pixels to reduce thread waiting time, and enhance information of light-load pixels to hedge against rendering quality loss. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that our algorithm can significantly improve the Gaussian Splatting rendering speed.SIGGRAPH Asia 2024 Conference Papers (SA Conference Papers \u2724), December 03-06, 2024, Tokyo, Japa

cited.name: Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
ctx: A culling technique that uses an axis-aligned bounding box of the projected Gaussian ellipse to reduce ineffective rendering expenses, specifically addressing the inability of bounding circles to cull low-opacity pairs in the minor axis direction.
Substitute the coordinate relationships into the ellipse function to solve for the maximum coordinate values x{max} and y{max}.
Cull tiles based on the axis-aligned bounding box constructed by x{max} and y{max}, which correspond to the half-width w and half-height h of the bounding box.

cited.name: AdR-Gaussian
ctx: AdR-Gaussian is a rendering acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that optimizes the rasterization pipeline by moving serial culling operations to a parallel preprocessing stage and balancing computational loads across pixel threads.
It achieves significant speedups without reducing the total number of Gaussians, thereby avoiding the quality degradation associated with pruning-based acceleration methods.

AdR-Gaussian accelerates rendering by addressing two bottlenecks in the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline: the serial nature of culling in the Render stage and the uneven computational load across pixel threads.

It reduces training cost compared to multi-stage methods like BungeeNeRF by using a source image selection method and an attention-based feature fusion approach to extract and fuse the most relevant features of a target view from multi-height images.
Unlike BungeeNeRF, which requires manual splitting of training data by camera height and multi-stage training, AG-NeRF is fully differentiable and does not require a priori camera height knowledge.

cited.name: Perceptually-motivated variance metric
ctx: The perceptually-motivated variance metric quantifies the error between an 8-bit ambient occlusion (AO) approximation T and a high-fidelity ray-traced reference R.
It differs from raw pixel Mean Squared Error (MSE) by operating on log-transformed values and spatial gradients, thereby aligning with human visual sensitivity to radiance and its changes.
This metric is specifically designed for evaluating AO approximations where reflected ambient radiance is linear in accessibility.

cited.name: Ambient Occlusion Volume
ctx: It approximates the near-field ambient occlusion problem by computing an analytic shadow-volume-like enclosure around each polygon and applying a tunable occlusion function within that region.

It differs from disk-based methods (e.g., Bunnell, Hoberock/Jia) and Shopf et al.’s bounding cube method by using tight dynamic bounding volumes and partial coverage to avoid over-estimating occlusion and double-occlusion artifacts.
Typical value: 1m for human-scale scenes.

title: An accelerating splatting algorithm based on multi-texture mapping for volume rendering
abstract: Texture-mapping hardware has been successfully exploited for volume rendering. In this paper, we combine splatting method with 2D texture mapping efficiently and propose an algorithm for footprint algorithm based volume rendering accelerated by multi texture mapping. First of all, a regular data set is divided by some texture slices along the primary viewing direction. Then the segmented data are projected to the texture slices plane. Lastly, all these texture slices compose the final image by blending. With our algorithm, the scaled volume data set can be rendered effectively and fast but not degrade the quality of image remarkably.

cited.name: Splatting and Point-based Rendering
ctx: Splatting and Point-based Rendering is an object-order volume rendering method where 3D data voxels are projected onto the 2D screen (or an intermediate texture plane) and blended to form the final image.

It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large volumetric datasets by leveraging specialized texture hardware for fast composition, avoiding the need to project voxels directly to the screen plane in traditional immediate-mode splatting.

Unlike its sibling Ray-Driven Splatting, which uses ray-order accumulation for robust occlusion, this method relies on hardware-accelerated alpha blending of projected primitives, often using multi-texture mapping to accelerate the process.

cited.name: Multi-texture Mapping Splatting
ctx: Multi-texture Mapping Splatting is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that reduces the computational cost of depth sorting by segmenting the volume data into parallel texture slices along the primary viewing direction.

Unlike standard object-order splatting which sorts all voxels globally, this method projects voxels onto local texture planes and blends them using graphics hardware, trading increased memory usage for reduced sorting complexity.
It builds on Mueller's Splatting Approach by replacing 3D kernel evaluation with pre-computed 2D footprint lookups and leveraging texture mapping hardware for rasterization.

Unlike uniform rank decomposition, which applies the same rank to all blocks (leading to either quality loss or inefficient compression), this method assigns different ranks to different blocks based on their local complexity.

title: An extended triangulation to the Marching Cubes 33 algorithm
abstract: The Marching Cubes algorithm is arguably the most popular isosurface extraction algorithm. Since its inception, two problems have lingered, namely, triangle quality and topology correctness. Although there is an extensive literature to solve them, topology correctness is achieved in detriment of triangle quality and vice versa. In this paper, we present an extended version of the Marching Cubes 33 algorithm (a variation of the Marching Cubes algorithm which guarantees topological correctness), called Extended Marching Cubes 33. In the proposed algorithm, the grid vertex are labeled with “+,” “ −,” and “=,” according to the relationship between its scalar field value and the isovalue. The inclusion of the “=” grid vertex label naturally avoids degenerate triangles. As an application of our method, we use the proposed triangulation to improve the quality of the triangles in the generated mesh while preserving its topology as much as possible.

ctx: This method improves the aspect ratio of triangulations generated by Marching Cubes 33 by modifying scalar field values near isosurface intersections, while preventing topological errors using a verification step.

Unlike Raman and Wenger, this method correctly represents the topology of the trilinear interpolant even when \lambda=0, whereas Raman and Wenger cannot represent it correctly even at \lambda=0.

Unlike the Asymptotic Decider, which resolves ambiguity by analyzing the critical points of the trilinear interpolant, this method resolves ambiguity by tracking the connectivity of positive and negative regions via an interior test, and unlike the basic Marching Cubes 33, it explicitly handles the "=" (zero) label to…

title: Calculation of transfer functions for volume rendering of breast tomosynthesis imaging
abstract: Slice by slice visualization of Digital Breast Tomosynthesis (DBT) data is time consuming and can hamper the interpretation of lesions such as clusters of microcalcifications. With a visualization of the object through multiple angles, 3D volume rendering (VR) provides an intuitive understanding of the underlying data at once. 3D VR may play an important complementary role in breast cancer diagnosis. Transfer functions (TFs) are a critical parameter in VR and finding good TFs is a major challenge. The purpose of this work is to study a methodology to automatically generate TFs that result in appropriate and useful VR visualizations of DBT data. For intensity-based TFs, intensity histograms were used to study possible relationships between statistics and critical intensity values in DBT data. The mean of each histogram has proved to be a valid option to automatically calculate those critical values that define these functions. At this stage, eight visualizations were obtained by combining several opacity/color intensity-based functions. Considering the gradient, ten visualizations were obtained. Nine of the ten TFs were constructed considering the peaks of gradient magnitude histograms. The tenth function was a simple linear ramp. Finally, three intensity-based and three gradient-based functions were selected and simultaneously used. This resulted in nine final VR visualizations taking both information into account. The studied approach allowed an automatic generation of opacity/color TFs based on scalar intensity and gradient magnitude histograms. In this way, the preliminary results obtained with this methodology are very encouraging about creating an adequate visualization of DBT data by VR.

title: Compact, Fast and Robust Grids for Ray Tracing
abstract: The focus of research in acceleration structures for ray tracing recently shifted from render time to time to image, the sum of build time and render time, and also the memory footprint of acceleration structures now receives more attention. In this paper we revisit the grid acceleration structure in this setting. We present two efficient methods for representing and building a grid. The compact grid method consists of a static data structure for representing a grid with minimal memory requirements, more specifically exactly one index per grid cell and exactly one index per object reference, and an algorithm for building that data structure in linear time. The hashed grid method reduces memory requirements even further, by using perfect hashing based on row displacement compression. We show that these methods are more efficient in both time and space than traditional methods based on linked lists and dynamic arrays. We also present a more robust grid traversal algorithm. We show that, for applications where time to image or memory usage is important, such as interactive ray tracing and rendering large models, the grid acceleration structure is an attractive alternative.sponsorship: Ares Lagae is a Postdoctoral Fellow of the Research Foundation - Flanders (FWO).status: Publishe

Unlike dense voxel grids, they eliminate redundancy by using a perfect hash function to compress the spatial domain into a linear array, ensuring constant-time access to occupied cells while minimizing memory footprint.

This method is distinct from tree-based structures (like Octrees) which use explicit pointers or bitmasks for hierarchy, and from brick maps which group voxels into fixed-size blocks; Hash Grids rely on mathematical displacement to resolve spatial collisions deterministically.

title: Contouring Discrete Indicator Functions
abstract: Abstract We present a method for calculating the boundary of objects from Discrete Indicator Functions that store 2‐material volume fractions with a high degree of accuracy. Although Marching Cubes and its derivatives are effective methods for calculating contours of functions sampled over discrete grids, these methods perform poorly when contouring non‐smooth functions such as Discrete Indicator Functions. In particular, Marching Cubes will generate surfaces that exhibit aliasing and oscillations around the exact surface. We derive a simple solution to remove these problems by using a new function to calculate the positions of vertices along cell edges that is efficient, easy to implement, and does not require any optimization or iteration. Finally, we provide empirical evidence that the error introduced by our contouring method is significantly less than is introduced by Marching Cubes.

Unlike Marching Cubes, which assumes smoothness and uses linear interpolation, this method replaces the vertex position calculation with an area-matching interpolant that ensures the projected area inside the contour matches the occupancy values of the cells.

title: D-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scenes
abstract: Neural rendering techniques combining machine learning with geometric reasoning have arisen as one of the most promising approaches for synthesizing novel views of a scene from a sparse set of images. Among these, stands out the Neural radiance fields (NeRF) [31], which trains a deep network to map 5D input coordinates (representing spatial location and viewing direction) into a volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance. However, despite achieving an unprecedented level of photorealism on the generated images, NeRF is only applicable to static scenes, where the same spatial location can be queried from different images. In this paper we introduce D-NeRF, a method that extends neural radiance fields to a dynamic domain, allowing to reconstruct and render novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene. For this purpose we consider time as an additional input to the system, and split the learning process in two main stages: one that encodes the scene into a canonical space and another that maps this canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time. Both mappings are simultaneously learned using fully-connected networks. Once the networks are trained, D-NeRF can render novel images, controlling both the camera view and the time variable, and thus, the object movement. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on scenes with objects under rigid, articulated and non-rigid motions. Code, model weights and the dynamic scenes dataset will be available at [1].

cited.name: D-NeRF
ctx: D-NeRF is a method for synthesizing novel views at an arbitrary point in time of dynamic scenes with complex non-rigid geometries, optimized from a sparse set of input monocular views without ground-truth geometry or multi-view images.

It decomposes the learning process into two modules: a spatial mapping that encodes the scene into a canonical space, and a mapping that transforms this canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time.

Unlike naive extensions of NeRF that map (x, y, z, t) directly to density and radiance, D-NeRF effectively exploits temporal redundancy by enforcing a common canonical anchor (typically t=0), ensuring that the deformation displacement is zero at the canonical time.

title: D2VR: High-Quality Volume Rendering of Projection-based Volumetric Data
abstract: Volume rendering techniques are conventionally classified as either direct or indirect methods. Indirect methods require to transform the initial volumetric model into an intermediate geometrical model in order to efficiently visualize it. In contrast, direct volume rendering (DVR) methods can directly process the volumetric data. Modern CT scanners usually provide data as a set of samples on a rectilinear grid, which is computed from the measured projections by discrete tomographic reconstruction. Therefore the rectilinear grid can already be considered as an intermediate volume representation. In this paper we introduce direct direct volume rendering (D2VR). D2VR does not require a rectilinear grid, since it is based on an immediate processing of the measured projections. Arbitrary samples for ray casting are reconstructed from the projections by using the Filtered Back-Projection algorithm. Our method removes a lossy resampling step from the classical volume rendering pipeline. It provides much higher accuracy than traditional grid-based resampling techniques do. Furthermore we also present a novel high-quality gradient estimation scheme, which is also based on the Filtered Back-Projection algorithm.EUROVIS - Eurographics /IEEE VGTC Symposium on Visualizatio

It sets itself apart from grid-based Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by eliminating interpolation errors associated with voxel sampling, thereby producing higher visual quality for thin structures.
It applies the FBP reconstruction formula as a direct resampling scheme for arbitrary ray positions.

title: Deep Learning Based Super-Resolution for Medical Volume Visualization with Direct Volume Rendering
abstract: Modern-day display systems demand high-quality rendering. However, rendering at higher resolution requires a large number of data samples and is computationally expensive. Recent advances in deep learning-based image and video super-resolution techniques motivate us to investigate such networks for high-fidelity upscaling of frames rendered at a lower resolution to a higher resolution. While our work focuses on super-resolution of medical volume visualization performed with direct volume rendering, it is also applicable for volume visualization with other rendering techniques. We propose a learning-based technique where our proposed system uses color information along with other supplementary features gathered from our volume renderer to learn efficient upscaling of a low-resolution rendering to a higher-resolution space. Furthermore, to improve temporal stability, we also implement the temporal reprojection technique for accumulating history samples in volumetric rendering.

ctx: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) is a method for training implicit neural representations of 3D shape and texture using only 2D RGB image supervision, eliminating the need for 3D ground truth data.

ctx: DVR Training Losses constitute a multi-component objective function used to train the occupancy network f\theta and texture network t\theta in Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR).

The method solves the problem of optimizing implicit neural representations from 2D image supervision by distinguishing pixels into three disjoint sets (P0, P1, P2) based on object mask membership and predicted surface depth finiteness.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling photometric consistency, freespace regularization, and occupancy induction into separate loss terms applied to specific pixel subsets, rather than relying on a single global rendering loss.

title: DiffUS: Differentiable Ultrasound Rendering from Volumetric Imaging.
abstract: Intraoperative ultrasound imaging provides real-time guidance during numerous surgical procedures, but its interpretation is complicated by noise, artifacts, and poor alignment with high-resolution preoperative MRI/CT scans. To bridge the gap between preoperative planning and intraoperative guidance, we present DiffUS, a physics-based, differentiable ultrasound renderer that synthesizes realistic B-mode images from volumetric imaging. DiffUS first converts MRI 3D scans into acoustic impedance volumes using a machine learning approach. Next, we simulate ultrasound beam propagation using ray tracing with coupled reflection-transmission equations. DiffUS formulates wave propagation as a sparse linear system that captures multiple internal reflections. Finally, we reconstruct B-mode images via depth-resolved echo extraction across fan-shaped acquisition geometry, incorporating realistic artifacts including speckle noise and depth-dependent degradation. DiffUS is entirely implemented as differentiable tensor operations in PyTorch, enabling gradient-based optimization for downstream applications such as slice-to-volume registration and volumetric reconstruction. Evaluation on the ReMIND dataset demonstrates DiffUS's ability to generate anatomically accurate ultrasound images from brain MRI data. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/gduguey/DiffUS.

ctx: B-mode Image Reconstruction is a differentiable forward model for synthesizing ultrasound B-mode images from volumetric data, primarily used in differentiable ultrasound rendering.

It solves the inverse problem of reconstructing tissue properties by minimizing the discrepancy between simulated and measured echo signals, leveraging the differentiability of the wave propagation physics.

It distinguishes itself from standard ray-marching volume rendering by modeling coupled forward and backward wave amplitudes across voxel interfaces using a sparse linear system, rather than simple line integrals of density.

title: DiffusioNeRF: Regularizing Neural Radiance Fields with Denoising Diffusion Models
abstract: Under good conditions, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) have shown impressive results on novel view synthesis tasks. NeRFs learn a scene's color and density fields by minimizing the photometric discrepancy between training views and differentiable renderings of the scene. Once trained from a sufficient set of views, NeRFs can generate novel views from arbitrary camera positions. However, the scene geometry and color fields are severely under-constrained, which can lead to artifacts, especially when trained with few input views. To alleviate this problem we learn a prior over scene geometry and color, using a denoising diffusion model (DDM). Our DDM is trained on RGBD patches of the synthetic Hypersim dataset and can be used to predict the gradient of the logarithm of a joint probability distribution of color and depth patches. We show that, these gradients of logarithms of RGBD patch priors serve to regularize geom-etry and color of a scene. During NeRF training, random RGBD patches are rendered and the estimated gradient of the log-likelihood is backpropagated to the color and density fields. Evaluations on LLFF, the most relevant dataset, show that our learned prior achieves improved quality in the reconstructed geometry and improved generalization to novel views. Evaluations on DTU show improved Reconstruction quality among NeRF methods.

cited.name: Diffusion-Regularized NeRF Training
ctx: Diffusion-Regularized NeRF Training addresses the severe under-constraint problem in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), where limited input views lead to geometric artifacts such as "floaters" (semi-transparent material floating in mid-air) and implausible geometry.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods like RegNeRF by directly regularizing geometry via a Denoising Diffusion Model (DDM) trained on RGBD (color and depth) patches, whereas RegNeRF uses normalizing flows on RGB patches and Dreamfusion uses DDMs for text-guided generation rather than image-based regularization.

The method incorporates a learned prior over the joint distribution of color and depth, backpropagating the DDM's score function (gradient of the log-likelihood) to the NeRF's density and color fields during optimization.

title: DNGaussian: Optimizing Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Radiance Fields with Global-Local Depth Normalization
abstract: Radiance fields have demonstrated impressive performance in synthesizing novel views from sparse input views, yet prevailing methods suffer from high training costs and slow inference speed. This paper introduces DNGaussian, a depth-regularized framework based on 3D Gaussian radiance fields, offering real-time and high-quality few-shot novel view synthesis at low costs. Our motivation stems from the highly efficient representation and surprising quality of the recent 3D Gaussian Splatting, despite it will encounter a geometry degradation when input views decrease. In the Gaussian radiance fields, we find this degradation in scene geometry primarily lined to the positioning of Gaussian primitives and can be mitigated by depth constraint. Consequently, we propose a Hard and Soft Depth Regularization to restore accurate scene geometry under coarse monocular depth supervision while maintaining a fine-grained color appearance. To further refine detailed geometry reshaping, we introduce Global-Local Depth Normalization, enhancing the focus on small local depth changes. Extensive experiments on LLFF, DTU, and Blender datasets demonstrate that DNGaussian outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving comparable or better results with significantly reduced memory cost, a 25 × reduction in training time, and over 3000 × faster rendering speed. Code is available at: https://github.com/Fictionarry/DNGaussian.Full Tex

title: Draw the blocks: beveled chunk meshing, tier tiles, remesh budget (Phase 2c)
abstract: _Requested by **Austin** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01F18vwmDijamaDd8BJegwsp?thread=cmsg_01F18vwmDijamaDd8BJegwspELaPRpCRGhqjqhxFeLni7f)_ ## What Phase 2c: blocks are drawn. Every block is a beveled cube with its own panel, a dark groove where it meets its neighbors and ambient occlusion in the corners, in four material tiers (Scrap, Composite, Alloy, Energy-Infused) with smooth, detailed procedural tiles. Chunks re-mesh nearest the camera first inside a 3 ms budget. Nothing places a block yet (that is 2d), so two demo switches raise a structure before the first frame: `/?demo=outpost` and `/?demo=swatch`. Slabs, wedges and the lighting pass against references 04 and 05 are 2e. ![The demo outpost from the south, afternoon, Balanced](https://github.com/austinbryanprice-droid/Claude-Survivor-Builder/blob/claude/project-thread-o71hfu/docs/phase-2/blocks-outpost.jpg?raw=true) ![The four tiers side by side: Scrap, Composite, Alloy, Energy-Infused](https://github.com/austinbryanprice-droid/Claude-Survivor-Builder/blob/claude/project-thread-o71hfu/docs/phase-2/blocks-swatch.jpg?raw=true) ![A few steps from the Alloy wall: chamfers, grooves, ambient occlusion](https://github.com/austinbryanprice-droid/Claude-Survivor-Builder/blob/claude/project-thread-o71hfu/docs/phase-2/blocks-closeup.jpg?raw=true) ![The outpost gate at golden hour, the game's default light](https://github.com/austinbryanprice-droid/Claude-Survivor-Builder/blob/claude/project-thread-o71hfu/docs/phase-2/blocks-gate.jpg?raw=true) Headless Chromium on software GL at 1280 by 720, Balanced. Each reproduces from its URL (the table is in `docs/art-direction.md`), for example `/?demo=outpost&shot=outpost&quality=balanced&hud=0&stats=0&freeze=1`. ## What changed - **The mesher** (`src/world/voxels/mesher.ts`, pure, no three.js). A block is up to four kinds of piece: a panel per exposed face, a strip per exposed edge, a triangle per exposed corner, and a small cap where four blocks meet along an edge. Faces and chamfers a neighbor hides are dropped, so a wall is one closed surface with a groove between blocks. No greedy merging, as decided. The caps were found by the tests: without them four chamfered blocks around an edge leave a diamond shaft open. The tests weld the vertices of random worlds and check that every edge is used exactly twice in opposite directions, across chunk borders too. The hot path allocates nothing. - **Tier materials** (`src/engine/glsl/structure-bake.glsl.ts`, `texture-bake.ts`). The tiles are baked on the GPU, the first time a block is meshed, into array textures: per tier, four tile layouts of albedo with height, and gloss, metal and glow. Each face of each block picks a layout from its cell hash and turns it one of eight ways, so a wall never reads as one stamp repeated. A block's material id picks its tile, so a Phase 5 upgrade changes one number and the block re-meshes. No image files, nothing in `CREDITS.md`. - **The renderer** (`src/world/render/voxel-render.ts`, `structure-material.ts`, `src/world/voxels/remesh-queue.ts`). One material and one draw call per chunk that holds a block. The dirty chunks go into a `RemeshQueue`, nearest the camera first, and are meshed until 3 ms of the frame are spent, always at least one chunk. - **Plants give way to blocks.** Grass rooted inside or on top of a block, and a tree whose trunk a block stands in, are skipped when the vegetation is assembled (`rootBuried`, `trunkBlocked` in `scatter.ts`). It is redone when the camera moves a meter or `VoxelWorld.revision` says a block changed, so 2d only has to place blocks. - **`?demo=outpost` and `?demo=swatch`**, and four viewpoints for them (`outpost`, `gate`, `swatch`, `closeup`). Each demo places its blocks one at a time through `checkPlace`, so it also exercises the placement rules (the unit tests replay the edits and count no refusals). ## Worth a look - **Steel at golden hour.** The deep orange key turned Alloy tan, and a wall of it read as wooden crates in the game's default light. A metallic tile's diffuse term now takes the key only part of the way to its grey, and glints keep the full color. Composite still reads olive at golden hour. Whether that and the tile style suit references 04 and 05 is the 2e lighting pass. - **Frame budget.** The outpost is 4 chunks and 10 thousand triangles. The outpost view is 37 draws and 200k triangles on Low, 114 and 879k on Balanced, 153 and 1.87M on Ultra, against the valley's 111 and 855k on Balanced. A chunk is a draw in every pass, shadows included. There is no GPU in the sandbox, so the frame rate with blocks is unmeasured; `/?bench=1&demo=outpost` is the run to repeat on a real machine. - **Tile memory and the first block.** The baked tiles are 16 layers at 512 by 512 (256 on Low), two arrays with mipmaps: about 43 MB of video memory at Balanced and Ultra and 11 MB on Low. They are baked the first time a block is meshed (`Stage.structure`, `VoxelRenderer.warmUp`), so a world with no blocks pays nothing; baking them at start-up added 9 seconds to every page load under software rendering. On a real GPU the bake is a few milliseconds, but the first draw also compiles the shader, so 2d calls `warmUp` when the player enters Build Mode. - **Meshing is on the main thread.** A typical chunk takes 0.3 to 1.3 ms in the sandbox; a very dense one (a hollow room of 28 thousand triangles) takes about 7 ms, and one chunk is always meshed per frame, so it can cost a frame. The mesher is pure and can move to a Worker if Phase 6 needs it. - Decisions are in `docs/decisions.md` under "Phase 2c"; the budget table and known gaps are in `docs/art-direction.md`. ## Checks - `npm run check`: typecheck, ESLint with the layer rules, Prettier, 344 unit tests and the build all pass. New tests cover mesher geometry (closed surface, winding, ambient occlusion, hidden faces, tile layouts), the remesh queue order, the demo structures, hiding plants, and the new `?demo` switch. - `npx playwright test --workers=1` against the built site (the CI setting): 31 tests, about 7 minutes under software rendering, including five new ones: the outpost is meshed, drawn and free of shader errors; an unknown demo name builds nothing; a bare `?demo` raises the outpost; a placed block is meshed and a broken one is dropped; swapping the world rebuilds the demo without leaking meshes. They also check that a page with no blocks has not baked the tiles. --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_01AMEiVsYWT9F481mT7RMuPb)_

title: Efficient Encoding and Decoding of Voxelized Models for Machine Learning-Based Applications
abstract: Point clouds have become a popular training data for many practical applications of machine learning in the fields of environmental modeling and precision agriculture. In order to reduce high space requirements and the effect of noise in the data, point clouds are often transformed to a structured representation such as a voxel grid. Storing, transmitting and consuming voxelized geometry, however, remains a challenging problem for machine learning pipelines running on devices with limited amount of on-chip memory with low access latency. A viable solution is to store the data in a compact encoded format, and perform on-the-fly decoding when it is needed for processing. Such on-demand expansion must be fast in order to avoid introducing substantial additional delay to the pipeline. This can be achieved by parallel decoding, which is particularly suitable for massively parallel architecture of GPUs on which the majority of machine learning is currently executed. In this paper, we present such method for efficient and parallelizable encoding/decoding of voxelized geometry. The method employs multi-level context-aware prediction of voxel occupancy based on the extracted binary feature prediction table, and encodes the residual grid with a pointerless sparse voxel octree (PSVO). We particularly focused on encoding the datasets of voxelized trees, obtained from both synthetic tree models and LiDAR point clouds of real trees. The method achieved 15.6% and 12.8% reduction of storage size with respect to plain PSVO on synthetic and real dataset, respectively. We also tested the method on a general set of diverse voxelized objects, where an average 11% improvement of storage space was achieved.

title: Efficient NeRF Optimization -- Not All Samples Remain Equally Hard
abstract: We propose an application of online hard sample mining for efficient training of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). NeRF models produce state-of-the-art quality for many 3D reconstruction and rendering tasks but require substantial computational resources. The encoding of the scene information within the NeRF network parameters necessitates stochastic sampling. We observe that during the training, a major part of the compute time and memory usage is spent on processing already learnt samples, which no longer affect the model update significantly. We identify the backward pass on the stochastic samples as the computational bottleneck during the optimization. We thus perform the first forward pass in inference mode as a relatively low-cost search for hard samples. This is followed by building the computational graph and updating the NeRF network parameters using only the hard samples. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we apply our method to Instant-NGP, resulting in significant improvements of the view-synthesis quality over the baseline (1 dB improvement on average per training time, or 2x speedup to reach the same PSNR level) along with approx. 40% memory savings coming from using only the hard samples to build the computational graph. As our method only interfaces with the network module, we expect it to be widely applicable.

title: Embracing Raycasting for Virtual Reality
abstract: This paper proposes an acceleration method for direct volume rendering (DVR). Our approach works like a wrapper or braces surrounding raycasting implementations and requires very few changes to the existing code. Visualization systems can significantly improve their rendering performance in virtual reality setups and make DVR feasible in these environments. The first step—the opening brace—modifies the initial ray construction by adaptively reducing the ray density, hence feeding fewer rays to the raycaster. The second brace step is a composting computation after the ray traversal that re-samples the raycasting results across the screen to reconstruct the final image. The rendering resolution is adapted during run-time to the specifications of the VR hardware and the performance of the renderer to guarantee stable and high refresh rates necessary to avoid severe cyber-sickness symptoms. The presented method utilizes gaze-dependent resolution levels tailored towards the human visual system (HVS) and hardware characteristics found in state-of-the-art head-mounted displays (HMDs). The resolution, and therefore the number of processed fragments during ray traversal, is reduced in the peripheral vision, delivering unnoticeable losses in image quality while providing a significant gain in rendering performance

ctx: DCX Points-to-Voxels converts a set of 3D points (from PLY files or 3D Gaussian Splatting) into a sparse voxel grid by averaging point positions and colors within grid cells defined by a bounding box and resolution.
It differs from simple occupancy voxelization by storing averaged geometric and color data per voxel, and from dense voxelization by using hash maps or sparse arrays to store only occupied cells.
This method serves as the core voxelization step in pipelines converting point clouds to sparse voxel representations for downstream rendering or USD export.

It differs from its siblings by focusing on the visual representation of the voxel grid structure itself (solid cubes, wireframes, or colored points) rather than just the raw voxel occupancy data.
Input: A point cloud (typically pcl::PointXYZ), a voxel size parameter, a bounding box mode ("AABB" or "CUSTOM"), and a rendering mode ("A", "B", or "C").

title: EVER: Exact Volumetric Ellipsoid Rendering for Real-Time View Synthesis
abstract: We present Exact Volumetric Ellipsoid Rendering (EVER), a method for real-time differentiable emission-only volume rendering. Unlike recent rasterization based approach by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), our primitive based representation allows for exact volume rendering, rather than alpha compositing 3D Gaussian billboards. As such, unlike 3DGS our formulation does not suffer from popping artifacts and view dependent density, but still achieves frame rates of $\sim\!30$ FPS at 720p on an NVIDIA RTX4090. Since our approach is built upon ray tracing it enables effects such as defocus blur and camera distortion (e.g. such as from fisheye cameras), which are difficult to achieve by rasterization. We show that our method is more accurate with fewer blending issues than 3DGS and follow-up work on view-consistent rendering, especially on the challenging large-scale scenes from the Zip-NeRF dataset where it achieves sharpest results among real-time techniques.

cited.name: Ever Rendering
ctx: Ever Rendering is a real-time volumetric rendering method that represents a radiance field as a set of constant-density volumetric ellipsoids, avoiding the 2D billboard approximation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS).

Unlike its sibling Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive, it replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture volume density distributions for blending, enabling exact transmittance calculation without approximation errors.
A set of N 3D Gaussian ellipsoids, each defined by a center position \mathbf{t}k, a rotation matrix \mathbf{R}k, and a scaling vector \mathbf{s}k = [s{kx}, s{ky}, s{kz}]^T.

title: FaCT-GS: Fast and Scalable CT Reconstruction with Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Abstract Gaussian Splatting (GS) has emerged as a dominating technique for image rendering and has quickly been adapted for the X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction task. However, despite its growing popularity, the benefits of GS are typically not substantial enough to motivate a transition from well-established reconstruction algorithms. This paper addresses the most significant remaining limitations of the GS-based approach by introducing FaCT-GS, a framework for fast and flexible CT reconstruction. Enabled by an in-depth optimization of the voxelization and rasterization pipelines, our new method is significantly faster than its predecessors and scales well with projection and output volume size. Furthermore, the improved voxelization enables rapid fitting of Gaussians to pre-existing volumes, which can serve as a prior for warm-starting the reconstruction, or simply as an alternative, compressed representation. FaCT-GS is over 4 $$\times $$ × faster than the State of the Art GS CT reconstruction on standard $$512^2$$ 512 2 projections, and over 13 $$\times $$ × faster on 2k projections. Implementation and data available through: https://papieta.github.io/fact-gs/ .

cited.name: Training Pipeline
ctx: The training pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting is an iterative optimization process that minimizes a differentiable loss function between rendered images and ground-truth views by updating Gaussian parameters.

It distinguishes itself from standard neural field optimization by using a differentiable rasterizer to compute gradients directly on explicit geometric primitives (Gaussians) rather than implicit neural networks, allowing for adaptive control (pruning, cloning, splitting) of the scene representation during training.
Updated Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color, SH coefficients).

title: Fairy Lights in Femtoseconds: Aerial and Volumetric Graphics Rendered by Focused Femtosecond Laser Combined with Computational Holographic Fields
abstract: We present a method of rendering aerial and volumetric graphics using femtosecond lasers. A high-intensity laser excites a physical matter to emit light at an arbitrary 3D position. Popular applications can then be explored especially since plasma induced by a femtosecond laser is safer than that generated by a nanosecond laser. There are two methods of rendering graphics with a femtosecond laser in air: Producing holograms using spatial light modulation technology, and scanning of a laser beam by a galvano mirror. The holograms and workspace of the system proposed here occupy a volume of up to 1 cm^3; however, this size is scalable depending on the optical devices and their setup. This paper provides details of the principles, system setup, and experimental evaluation, and discussions on scalability, design space, and applications of this system. We tested two laser sources: an adjustable (30-100 fs) laser which projects up to 1,000 pulses per second at energy up to 7 mJ per pulse, and a 269-fs laser which projects up to 200,000 pulses per second at an energy up to 50 uJ per pulse. We confirmed that the spatiotemporal resolution of volumetric displays, implemented with these laser sources, is 4,000 and 200,000 dots per second. Although we focus on laser-induced plasma in air, the discussion presented here is also applicable to other rendering principles such as fluorescence and microbubble in solid/liquid materials.

cited.name: Grid Resolution Selection via Lambda
ctx: This variant assumes the size of an emission dot (voxel) is equal to the size of the laser focal point, which is an oval with two diameters.
The diameter perpendicular to the laser beam is the diffraction limit, determined by the original beam width a, focal length r, and wavelength \lambda as wf = \frac{2\lambda r}{a}.
The diameter along the laser beam is geometrically obtained from the relationship a: wf = r: wd/2, yielding wd = 4\lambda \left(\frac{r}{a}\right)^2.

title: Fast Cutting Operations on Three Dimensional Volume Datasets
abstract: This paper appeared in the conference and proceedings of Visualization in Scientific Computing, Rostock, May 30-June 1 1994. Abstract This paper is concerned with high quality volume visualisation with additional emphasis on real time cutting operations for displaying surface interiors. In many applications, it is necessary for a user to interactively perform cutting operations on a volume dataset in order to see different parts of the data. A method for implementing such operations, together with a direct surface rendering algorithm, has heen developed and results have demonstrated its efficiency in comparison with existing methods.

cited.name: Real Time Cutting Operations
ctx: Real Time Cutting Operations is a technique for clipping volume surfaces using cutting planes by maintaining near and far depth buffers per pixel, avoiding full re-rendering when planes change.

It differs from static cutting methods by maintaining the full volume dataset and using a halfspace check to dynamically filter voxels per frame, whereas static methods pre-filter and discard cut voxels.
For each pixel p, a surface point with depth d{surf} is displayed if and only if: D{near}(p) \le d{surf} \le D{far}(p) Points with depth in front of D{near}(p) or behind D{far}(p) are cut away.

cited.name: Direct Surface Rendering with Intersection Buffer
ctx: Direct Surface Rendering with Intersection Buffer is a volume rendering technique that generates an image-space representation of an isosurface defined by a threshold within a 3D volume, enabling interactive cutting operations without pre-computing a triangular mesh.
Unlike methods that extract polygonal meshes (e.g., Marching Cubes) or perform single-hit ray casting, this method stores all surface intersections for each ray in an intersection buffer.
This allows the user to define cutting planes interactively by comparing stored depths against near/far depth buffers, avoiding the need to retrace rays through the volume for every view change.

title: Fast Marching-Cubes-Style Volume Evaluation for Level Set Surfaces
abstract: We present an efficient and accurate volume evaluation method for grid-based level sets that computes the volume of the implicitly represented shape(s) in a manner consistent with Marching Cubes surface reconstruction. We utilize rotational symmetry to combine redundant Marching Cubes cases and avoid explicitly forming local triangulations using efficient volume computation formulae for pyramids and truncated prisms wherever possible, thereby achieving a fast and compact implementation. We demonstrate that our method is more efficient than previous approaches while generating results that converge with second-order accuracy and are perfectly consistent with volumes calculated directly from explicit Marching Cubes meshes. We provide a full C++17 reference implementation to foster adoption of the proposed method (https://github.com/tetsuya-takahashi/MC-style-vol-eval)

title: Fast parallel surface and solid voxelization on GPUs
abstract: This paper presents data-parallel algorithms for surface and solid voxelization on graphics hardware. First, a novel conservative surface voxelization technique, setting all voxels overlapped by a mesh's triangles, is introduced, which is up to one order of magnitude faster than previous solutions leveraging the standard rasterization pipeline. We then show how the involved new triangle/box overlap test can be adapted to yield a 6-separating surface voxelization, which is thinner but still connected and gap-free. Complementing these algorithms, both a triangle-parallel and a tile-based technique for solid voxelization are subsequently presented. Finally, addressing the high memory consumption of high-resolution voxel grids, we introduce a novel octree-based sparse solid voxelization approach, where only close to the solid's boundary finest-level voxels are stored, whereas uniform interior and exterior regions are represented by coarser-level voxels. This representation is created directly from a mesh without requiring a full intermediate solid voxelization, enabling GPU-based voxelizations of unprecedented size.</jats:p
