title: Fast Surface and Volume Rendering Based on Shear-Warp Factorization for a Surgical Simulator
abstract: Fast simultaneous visualization of 3D medical images and medical instruments is necessary for a surgical simulator. Because unconstrained motion of a medical instrument is more frequent than that of the patient, the visualization of medical instruments is performed in real time using surface rendering. However, volume rendering is usually used for realistic visualization of the 3D medical image. We have developed an algorithm to combine a volume-rendered image and a surface-rendered image using a Z-buffer for depth cueing, which is applied to a surgical simulator. Surface rendering is used for visualization of a medical instrument, whereas 3D medical images such as CT and MRI are usually visualized by volume rendering, because segmentation of the medical image is difficult. In this study, when the volume-rendered image is combined with the surface-rendered image, the amount of computation is reduced by early ray termination and instrument-region masking in the sheared image space. Using these methods, a fast combination of volume-rendered and surface-rendered images is performed with high image quality. The method is appropriate for real-time visualization of 3D medical images and medical instrument motion in the images, and can be applied to image-guided therapy and surgical simulators. © 2003 Wiley-Liss, Inc

cited.name: Shear-warp Factorization for Combined Surface/Volume Rendering
ctx: This method enables real-time visualization in surgical simulators by combining volume-rendered 3D medical images (organs) with surface-rendered medical instruments (e.g., needles) using shear-warp factorization.

It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering dynamic instruments against static volumetric data by leveraging the speed of surface rendering for instruments and the segmentation-free realism of volume rendering for organs.

Unlike standard shear-warp which renders only volume data, this approach integrates a Z-buffer comparison in the intermediate sheared space to correctly handle depth occlusion between the two modalities, using early ray termination and instrument-region masking to reduce computation.

cited.name: Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering with Masking and Early Ray Termination
ctx: This method accelerates the hybrid rendering of a volume-rendered organ and a surface-rendered instrument by combining early ray termination for the volume data with spatial masking in the sheared image space for the instrument.
It solves the performance bottleneck of real-time surgical simulators where a moving instrument must be composited over a large volume dataset.

Unlike standard early ray termination which only stops volume traversal, this method explicitly tracks the instrument's motion in 2D sheared space to limit recomputation to only the affected pixels, achieving speed-ups of up to 2.84x compared to full recomputation.

title: feat(render): voxels splatted to the pixels their footprints cover (ADR-0061)
abstract: ADR-0061 stage 3's raster, rebuilt: voxels are splatted to the pixels their footprints cover, instead of every pixel of a brick's rectangle walking the brick's cells. Stacked on #114 (stage 3). ## Why On `foliage_4k_production` stage 3's raster sent 14.9 M rays a frame through bricks, taking 59.7 M traversal steps and 15.2 M footprint tests for 1.78 M hits. At the first voxel levels a cell is about a pixel and a foliage footprint a fraction of its cell, so four in five voxels cover no pixel centre, and a brick's rectangle is mostly pixels no footprint covers. ## The splat (`vis_voxel_raster.comp`) - An invocation per voxel of the cluster. Its brick comes from a binary search over the bricks' first voxels, and its cell from the n-th set bit of the brick's mask. - Each voxel projects its footprint's box (a capsule's widened by its radius, within its cell) to the pixel centres it may cover: - the box's corners lie on the brick's grid of 32nds of a cell, so its centre and half-extents reach clip space as steps along that grid, the same for the whole cluster; - the projection lies within `(r_x + |x_c / w_c| r_w) / (w_c − r_w)` of the centre's in x, and likewise in y, widened by a 64th of a pixel; - a voxel wholly behind the near plane covers nothing; one reaching behind the camera's plane takes the whole target. - A subgroup pools its voxels' (voxel, pixel) pairs: an exclusive add, then a binary search per pair. The rays' tests fill the lanes whichever voxels cover pixels. - Each pair's ray is tested against that voxel alone (`vis_voxel_hit`). It takes the ray's span through the voxel's cell from the cell's own planes, then the footprint over that span. A hit takes the atomic max of `(1 / t, cluster, brick)`, so the nearest voxel wins. ## The search (`vis_voxel_find`) The voxel resolve and `gi update` find the pixel's voxel again in the brick the visibility buffer names: - first the cell holding the ray's point at the stored depth; - then the two cells along each axis whose centres lie nearest that point (which hold it whatever its rounding); - stopping at the first whose hit gives the stored depth again, bit for bit. A voxel's test depends only on the ray and the voxel, so every pass meets it at the same `t`. The DDA (`vis_voxel_trace`) is gone. The C twin's `nph_render_voxel_trace` is now the nearest of a brick's voxel hits, the lowest cell on a tie. ## New rules, checked A voxel cluster's bricks share one cell size, and their voxels follow one another in the bricks' order. The builder already makes them so. `nph_render_mesh_create` (`validate_voxel_cluster`) and the mesh loader (`views.c` `mesh_voxels`) refuse clusters that break either rule. ## The radiance cache's update, gated `gi_update.comp`'s voxel path was compiled into every frame's update. With the search in it, the driver spilled 2,816 B of shared memory a workgroup, and Bistro's update measured 0.011 ms slower than stage 3's. It is now specialised out (`k_voxels`) of the pipeline that frames without voxel meshes bind, as the meshlet cull's and the resolve's are. Specialised, the update is stage 2's binary exactly (42,240 B, 2,304 B shared) and takes Bistro's street 0.189 ms, its cost at Phase 13's start. Stage 3's update ran 0.010 ms faster on Bistro (0.179) only because the driver split that build's spills differently: 1,280 B shared plus 80 B local. That allocation is the driver's choice, not something our code controls, so the gate does not try to reproduce it. ADR-0061 records it. No test reached the update's voxel path before; only `render_perf`'s foliage did. A new test covers it (below). ## Tests - **`VoxelGpu.the_voxel_tests_match_their_cpu_twin`** (renamed): 16,384 rays through 256 random bricks, 2,609 hits. - 0 disagree on the hit, the voxel or the face; `t` is within 4.8e-6 of the brick (5.3e-6 on lavapipe). - The resolve's search from each hit's depth meets that hit again exactly: 0 misses. - **`Voxel.the_first_voxel_is_the_nearest_footprint_of_random_bricks`** (renamed): 25,600 rays, 3,965 hits, against a double-precision search of every footprint. 0 mismatches; worst `t` 1.9e-5 of the brick. - **`VoxelGpu.the_radiance_cache_holds_the_voxels_cells`** (new): at 30 m, 307 voxel pixels give 284 cells. - The cache holds every one of them and nothing else. - Planted bug, the triangle-only update bound in a voxel frame: 4 of 301 slots were expected cells. - **`VoxelGpu.malformed_voxel_clusters_are_refused`** (new), and the views fixture: mixed cell sizes and out-of-order voxels are refused. - **Unchanged from stage 3:** - the raster against the CPU's rays, pixel for pixel: 7 of 1,298, 0 of 476 and 0 of 105 pixels differ; - coverage against level 0: +7.1 / +3.7 / −4.8 / −4.9 %; - light against level 0: +10.0 / +9.7 / +7.2 % a pixel (lavapipe +9.6 at 40 m); - the voxel resolve against its C twin: ±0.04 %. - **Whole suites:** - RTX 3060 Ti: Development 97 of 97 (render 200 of 200), and Debug ASan 97 of 97 (render 200 of 200). - Lavapipe: 198 of 200 render tests, plus the two mesh-shader-only skips. Its subgroups of 8 run the splat's pooling as eight subgroups a workgroup. - glslang 14 sweep: 108 of 108 shaders. GCC 14, clang's CI warnings and clang-tidy 19 are clean on the changed C files. ## Cost RTX 3060 Ti, 240 frames, three interleaved rounds against stage 3 (#114), VS Code minimized. Final build (both commits): | scene | frame | passes | |---|---|---| | `foliage_4k_production` | 9.606 → 7.580 ms | voxel raster 4.640 + 0.808 → 2.795 + 0.577 ms; voxel resolve 0.094 → 0.069 ms | | `field_4k_production` | 3.993 → 3.981 ms | — | | `bistro_street_production` | 6.794 → 6.777 ms | `gi update` 0.179 → 0.189 ms | Before the gate (first commit alone), also three rounds: | scene | frame | passes | |---|---|---| | `lod_4k_production` | 3.703 → 3.698 ms | — | | `shadows_4k_production` | 4.200 → 4.202 ms | — | | `bistro_street_production` | 6.771 → 6.778 ms | `gi update` 0.178 → 0.190 ms | - Every other pipeline is stage 3's, byte for byte. With debug info stripped (`spirv-opt --strip-debug --strip-nonsemantic --compact-ids`), only `gi_update`, `vis_voxel_raster`, `vis_voxel_resolve(_rt)` and `vis_voxel_test` differ from stage 3's SPIR-V, and `render_perf`'s pipeline log agrees (binary sizes, registers, spills). - On the foliage scene, the other passes measure 0.5 to 2 % slower with unchanged pipelines. The frame is 2 ms shorter there; I have not isolated why they move. - **Against the stalled triangles:** `foliage_4k_triangles` still takes 5.6 ms. A voxel costs the raster about what a triangle does (~138 ps against ~146), but the first voxel levels hold about twice the triangles they replace. So the cooker's voxels stay opt-in (`--voxels`). - **The first voxel level's budget stays at 4× the triangles.** At 1× the frame is 5.84 ms. But the simplified triangle levels then drawn from 24 to 40 m cover 11.6–12.5 % fewer pixels than level 0, with 9 % less light a pixel, where the voxels cover 3.7–7.1 % more (ADR-0061 "Cost"). - **DRAM bytes:** - The declared footprint is unchanged: 39 MB read and 66 MB written for each voxel raster phase (the visibility buffer); 166 MB read and 33 MB written for the voxel resolve. - Undeclared reads through device addresses: - every drawn voxel's record, once by its lane: about 24 M × 16 B ≈ 390 MB a frame (stage 3's rays read one per footprint test, 15.2 M); - the bricks, 3.2 M × 32 B ≈ 100 MB, as before; - each pair's voxel again (a fifth of the voxels have pairs). - I did not measure DRAM traffic; that needs the elevated trace runner. ADR-0061's next work starts with testing each cell's rectangle before reading its voxel's record, which would skip the records of voxels whose cells cover no pixel centre. ## Docs `docs/render.md` "Voxels" (the test, the splat, the search, the numbers) and "Global illumination". ADR-0061: the raster section, "Cost", the budget finding, frames without voxels, the next work, and three rejected alternatives: - the DDA; - the search over all eight cells without the early stop: 0.104 ms against 0.068; - the register and queueing variants of the splat, none faster per cluster drawn. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: GL-NeRF: Gauss-Laguerre Quadrature Enables Training-Free NeRF Acceleration
abstract: Volume rendering in neural radiance fields is inherently time-consuming due to the large number of MLP calls on the points sampled per ray. Previous works would address this issue by introducing new neural networks or data structures. In this work, We propose GL-NeRF, a new perspective of computing volume rendering with the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature. GL-NeRF significantly reduces the number of MLP calls needed for volume rendering, introducing no additional data structures or neural networks. The simple formulation makes adopting GL-NeRF in any NeRF model possible. In the paper, we first justify the use of the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature and then demonstrate this plug-and-play attribute by implementing it in two different NeRF models. We show that with a minimal drop in performance, GL-NeRF can significantly reduce the number of MLP calls, showing the potential to speed up any NeRF model.NeurIPS 2024. Project page: https://silongyong.github.io/GL-NeRF_project_page

cited.name: VIRIM Architecture
ctx: VIRIM is a hardware architecture developed at the University of Mannheim that implements the Heidelberg ray tracing model for real-time volume visualization.
It addresses the performance bottleneck of conventional ray casting on moderate-sized datasets by using a warp array to rotate voxel planes and a ray array to pass rays through them.
The system supports shadow generation and perspective projections to achieve high image quality.

cited.name: GL-NeRF
ctx: GL-NeRF is a training-free acceleration method for volume rendering in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that reduces the number of neural network (MLP) calls per ray by replacing stochastic sampling with deterministic point selection based on Gauss-Laguerre quadrature.

Unlike sibling acceleration methods that introduce new data structures, depth oracles, or auxiliary neural networks, GL-NeRF modifies only the integration logic, requiring no additional representation or training.
GL-NeRF exploits the mathematical structure of the volume rendering integral.

cited.name: Volume Ray Casting
ctx: Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that constructs a 3D image by casting a ray from the camera through each pixel into the volumetric dataset, sampling the density along the ray, and compositing the results using front-to-back alpha blending.

Unlike slice-based methods (e.g., Shear-Warp or Slice Stack) which render 2D planes and suffer from edge-on gaps, Volume Ray Casting treats the volume as a solid object, providing full occlusion and transparency effects from any angle.
Volume Data: A 3D scalar field (density/intensity), typically stored in a sampler3D texture.

cited.name: VDB Volume Rendering with OpenVDB/NanoVDB
ctx: This method enables GPU volume rendering of large, sparse volumetric datasets by combining offline fixed-rate lossy compression on the CPU (using OpenVDB) with fast, low-overhead on-the-fly decompression and sampling on the GPU (using NanoVDB).

It solves the problem of rendering volumes that exceed single-GPU memory capacity by significantly reducing the memory footprint while maintaining random access patterns suitable for incoherent workloads like path tracing.

Unlike hierarchical space-skipping approaches which show diminishing returns with RGBA transfer functions, this method employs a uniform majorant grid for traversal acceleration to facilitate direct comparison with dense texture rendering.

title: GPU‐based Fast Ray Casting for a Large Number of Metaballs
abstract: Metaballs are implicit surfaces widely used to model curved objects, represented by the isosurface of a density field defined by a set of points. Recently, the results of particle-based simulations have been often visualized using a large number of metaballs, however, such visualizations have high rendering costs. In this paper we propose a fast technique for rendering metaballs on the GPU. Instead of using polygonization, the isosurface is directly evaluated in a per-pixel manner. For such evaluation, all metaballs contributing to the isosurface need to be extracted along each viewing ray, on the limited memory of GPUs. We handle this by keeping a list of metaballs contributing to the isosurface and efficiently update it. Our method neither requires expensive precomputation nor acceleration data structures often used in existing ray tracing techniques. With several optimizations, we can display a large number of moving metaballs quickly.Computer Graphics Forum27

title: GRAF: Generative Radiance Fields for 3D-Aware Image Synthesis
abstract: While 2D generative adversarial networks have enabled high-resolution image synthesis, they largely lack an understanding of the 3D world and the image formation process. Thus, they do not provide precise control over camera viewpoint or object pose. To address this problem, several recent approaches leverage intermediate voxel-based representations in combination with differentiable rendering. However, existing methods either produce low image resolution or fall short in disentangling camera and scene properties, e.g., the object identity may vary with the viewpoint. In this paper, we propose a generative model for radiance fields which have recently proven successful for novel view synthesis of a single scene. In contrast to voxel-based representations, radiance fields are not confined to a coarse discretization of the 3D space, yet allow for disentangling camera and scene properties while degrading gracefully in the presence of reconstruction ambiguity. By introducing a multi-scale patch-based discriminator, we demonstrate synthesis of high-resolution images while training our model from unposed 2D images alone. We systematically analyze our approach on several challenging synthetic and real-world datasets. Our experiments reveal that radiance fields are a powerful representation for generative image synthesis, leading to 3D consistent models that render with high fidelity.

ctx: GRAF is a generative model for 3D-aware image synthesis that learns a conditional radiance field from a collection of unposed 2D images using an adversarial framework.

Unlike voxel-based approaches (e.g., HoloGAN, PLATONIC GAN) which suffer from memory limitations and discretization artifacts, GRAF uses a continuous representation that scales well with image resolution and incorporates 3D consistency by design without learned projections.

title: GRF: Learning a General Radiance Field for 3D Representation and Rendering
abstract: We present a simple yet powerful neural network that implicitly represents and renders 3D objects and scenes only from 2D observations. The network models 3D geometries as a general radiance field, which takes a set of 2D images with camera poses and intrinsics as input, constructs an internal representation for each point of the 3D space, and then renders the corresponding appearance and geometry of that point viewed from an arbitrary position. The key to our approach is to learn local features for each pixel in 2D images and to then project these features to 3D points, thus yielding general and rich point representations. We additionally integrate an attention mechanism to aggregate pixel features from multiple 2D views, such that visual occlusions are implicitly taken into account. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can generate high-quality and realistic novel views for novel objects, unseen categories and challenging real-world scenes.

cited.name: Monte Carlo Volume Rendering
ctx: Monte Carlo Volume Rendering (MCS) is an image-order rendering technique that uses stochastic sampling to determine light transport paths within a volumetric dataset, rather than deterministic ray marching.
It solves the problem of high computational cost in dense volumes by skipping empty or transparent regions via exponential distance sampling and stochastic acceptance.

Unlike deterministic ray casting, MCS produces noisy but unbiased results that converge to the correct solution over multiple frames, making it suitable for real-time or interactive visualization where hardware acceleration is available and temporal accumulation is feasible.

cited.name: Hexahedron Projection for Curvilinear Grids
ctx: Hexahedron Projection is a cell projection method for direct volume rendering of curvilinear hexahedral grids that classifies the 2D projection of each hexahedron into specific topological cases and renders them as pre-defined triangle fans or strips.
It solves the problem of efficiently rendering non-planar faces in hardware by avoiding the computational geometry complexity of general line-sweep subdivision or full tetrahedral decomposition.

Unlike its siblings, which may rely on view-independent classification or full subdivision into tetrahedra, this method uses viewpoint-dependent case analysis to minimize vertex and fragment operations, offering a significant speedup over subdividing all cells into five tetrahedra.

ctx: Differentiable Sphere Tracing is a rendering technique that performs ray marching (sphere tracing) using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) decoded by a neural network, enabling gradient computation with respect to the SDF parameters, latent codes, or camera poses.

It builds on Sphere Tracing by wrapping the discrete marching steps in a differentiable computational graph (typically PyTorch), allowing backpropagation from the rendered image to the implicit shape representation.

Unlike Standard Constant Step Ray Marching which uses fixed steps, it uses the SDF value to determine step size, and unlike 3D Texture Distance Field for Implicit Surfaces which uses lookup tables, it evaluates a continuous neural function.

title: High-Quality Volume Rendering with Resampling in the Frequency Domain
abstract: This work introduces a volume rendering technique that is conceptually based on the shear-warp factorization. We propose to perform the shear transformation in the frequency domain. Unlike the standard shear-warp algorithm, we allow for arbitrary sampling distances along the viewing rays, independent from the view direction. The accurate scaling of the volume slices is achieved by using the zero padding interpolation property. Finally, a high quality gradient estimation scheme is presented which uses the derivative theorem of the Fourier transform. Experimental results show that the presented method outperforms established algorithms in the quality of the produced images. If the data is sampled above the Nyquist rate the presented method is capable of a perfect reconstruction of the original function.EUROVIS 2005: Eurographics / IEEE VGTC Symposium on Visualizatio

cited.name: Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering
ctx: Frequency Domain Shear-Warp Volume Rendering is a technique that performs the shear transformation of the shear-warp factorization in the frequency domain using the shifting theorem, allowing for arbitrary, view-independent sampling distances along viewing rays via zero-padding interpolation.

Unlike standard shear-warp algorithms where sampling distance is coarse and view-dependent, this method decouples sampling density from the viewing direction by resampling in the frequency domain, thereby avoiding the large spatial zero-padding required by spatial-domain shear methods.
The method builds on Frequency Domain Volume Rendering by replacing the spatial shear stage with frequency-domain operations.

cited.name: Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling
ctx: Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling is a direct volume ray casting technique that performs resampling (zooming and shearing) in the frequency domain using Fourier transforms to avoid blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors.

It exploits signal processing ideas such as the shifting theorem, the packing theorem, and the derivative theorem to achieve the best theoretical quality by using the ideal interpolation filter (sinc).

Unlike standard spatial domain filters (e.g., B-spline, Catmull-Rom) or methods that zoom the intermediate image, this method resamples every volume slice in object space before projection, ensuring perfect reconstruction if the sampling meets Nyquist criteria.

title: Implement GSDMC wind-speed isosurface extraction from 3D NetCDF wind-field data
abstract: Python implementation of Generalized Symmetric Dual Marching Cubes (GSDMC) for extracting constant-wind-speed isosurfaces from 3D NetCDF wind-field data (ERA5, WRF, generic layouts). ## Core algorithm (`gsdmc/core.py`) - Vectorised 8-bit case-index computation over all cells simultaneously - Per-active-cell QEF minimisation (`gsdmc/qef.py`) using edge intersection points and finite-difference gradient normals; Tikhonov-regularised toward the mass point for rank-deficient cases - Dual mesh assembly: `np.where` finds active primal edges; four adjacent-cell dual vertices form quads split to triangles with correct outward winding ## Supporting modules - **`reader.py`** – `read_wind_field()`: auto-detects U/V/W variable names for ERA5/WRF/generic layouts, collapses optional time dimension, returns `WindFieldData` with speed array + coordinate metadata / grid spacing - **`wind.py`** – `compute_wind_speed(u, v, w)` and `wind_speed_percentile()` - **`mesh.py`** – `Mesh` class with OBJ (save + load), ASCII PLY, and ASCII STL export - **`tables.py`** – cube vertex/edge topology and per-axis adjacent-cell offsets for dual-quad generation ## Usage ```python from gsdmc import read_wind_field, extract_isosurface, Mesh, wind_speed_percentile data = read_wind_field("era5_wind.nc") isovalue = wind_speed_percentile(data.speed, 90) # e.g. 90th-percentile speed vertices, triangles, normals = extract_isosurface( data.speed, isovalue=isovalue, spacing=data.spacing, origin=data.origin, ) Mesh(vertices, triangles, normals).save_obj("wind_iso.obj") ``` ## Tests 66 tests across `test_gsdmc.py`, `test_wind.py`, `test_reader.py`, `test_mesh.py` covering geometry correctness, edge cases (empty/trivial fields, tiny grids), QEF vs average-point mode, all three mesh I/O formats, and NetCDF reading variants. Original prompt > Python implementation of GSDMC for wind-speed isosurface extraction from 3D NetCDF wind-field data.

cited.name: Fast Neighbourhood Access via Delta Lookup Tables
ctx: A method to access immediate neighbours of a voxel in Morton-ordered memory without re-encoding coordinates, using precomputed offset tables that map a coordinate component to the memory stride required to reach its neighbour.

It solves the performance bottleneck of decoding a Morton index to (x,y,z), modifying coordinates, and re-encoding, by exploiting the property that the Morton index delta \Delta p for a single-axis step depends only on that axis's coordinate value.
This distinguishes it from full re-encoding methods and bitwise manipulation approaches (e.g., Fabian Giesen's method) by using static lookup tables for O(1) access.

title: Improving Neural Volume Rendering via Learning View-Dependent Integral Approximation
abstract: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) have achieved impressive view synthesis results by learning an implicit volumetric representation from multi-view images. To project the implicit representation into an image, NeRF employs volume rendering that approximates the continuous integrals of rays as an accumulation of the colors and densities of the sampled points. Although this approximation enables efficient rendering, it ignores the direction information in point intervals, resulting in ambiguous features and limited reconstruction quality. In this paper, we propose a learning method that utilizes learnable view-dependent features to improve scene representation and reconstruction. We model the volume rendering integral with a piecewise constant volume density and spherical harmonic-guided view-dependent features, facilitating ambiguity elimination while preserving the rendering efficiency. In addition, we introduce a regularization term that restricts the anisotropic representation effect to be local, with negligible effect on geometry representations, and that encourages recovering the correct geometry. Our method is flexible and can be plugged into NeRF-based frameworks. Extensive experiments show that the proposed representation can boost the rendering quality of various NeRFs and achieve state-of-the-art rendering performance on both synthetic and real-world scenes.

cited.name: Neural and primitive-based representations
ctx: Unlike dense grids, these methods avoid the need for large, uniform memory allocation, and unlike pure implicit fields, primitive-based variants often offer faster rendering speeds and easier integration with standard graphics pipelines.

Definition: A method that replaces the direct prediction of volume density and latent features with the prediction of Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients, allowing the scene geometry to be view-dependent (anisotropic) while keeping the MLP input isotropic (position only).

cited.name: Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning
ctx: Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning is a method that models volumetric density and latent features as view-dependent functions using spherical harmonics (SH) to eliminate directional ambiguity in neural rendering, replacing the isotropic point-sampled features of standard NeRF.

Unlike Mip-NeRF which samples cones to approximate pre-filtered representations, this method modifies the MLP to predict view-dependent SH coefficients directly, avoiding the need for shape-based sampling parameterization.
It is designed as a plug-and-play sub-model that can be integrated into various NeRF-based frameworks to improve reconstruction quality and reduce shape-radiance ambiguity.

title: Industrial Computed Tomography using Proximal Algorithm
abstract: In this thesis, we present ProxiSART, a flexible proximal framework for robust 3D cone beam tomographic reconstruction based on the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART). We derive the proximal operator for the SART algorithm and use it for minimizing the data term in a proximal algorithm. We show the flexibility of the framework by plugging in different powerful regularizers, and show its robustness in achieving better reconstruction results in the presence of noise and using fewer projections. We compare our framework to state-of-the-art methods and existing popular software tomography reconstruction packages, on both synthetic and real datasets, and show superior reconstruction quality, especially from noisy data and a small number of projections.

cited.name: ADMM Solver
ctx: The ADMM Solver is an optimization method for solving separable minimization problems of the form \minx f(x) + g(x), where f(x) is a data fidelity term and g(x) is a regularization prior.

It sets itself apart from direct solvers by decomposing complex objectives into simpler subproblems that can be solved via proximal operators, making it particularly suitable for volume reconstruction with total variation or L1 regularization.
Typical values are not specified in the sources.

title: Information Theory-Based Automatic Multimodal Transfer Function Design
abstract: In this paper, we present a new framework for multimodal volume visualization that combines several information-theoretic strategies to define both colors and opacities of the multimodal transfer function. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first fully automatic scheme to visualize multimodal data. To define the fused color, we set an information channel between two registered input datasets, and afterward, we compute the informativeness associated with the respective intensity bins. This informativeness is used to weight the color contribution from both initial 1-D transfer functions. To obtain the opacity, we apply an optimization process that minimizes the informational divergence between the visibility distribution captured by a set of viewpoints and a target distribution proposed by the user. This distribution is defined either from the dataset features, from manually set importances, or from both. Other problems related to the multimodal visualization, such as the computation of the fused gradient and the histogram binning, have also been solved using new information-theoretic strategies. The quality and performance of our approach are evaluated on different datasets.

cited.name: Information Theory-Based Multimodal Transfer Function Design
ctx: An automated method for designing multimodal transfer functions for two registered volume datasets X and Y, using mutual information decomposition to guide color fusion and opacity optimization.

It solves the problem of combining complementary information from different modalities (e.g., CT and MR) into a single coherent visualization where both inputs are represented at each voxel, rather than discarding one.

It sets itself apart from manual methods by automating the design and from single-modality optimization methods by defining an information channel between two input data sets and another between viewpoints and bins.

title: Inkjet printing-based volumetric display projecting multiple full-colour 2D patterns.
abstract: In this study, a method to construct a full-colour volumetric display is presented using a commercially available inkjet printer. Photoreactive luminescence materials are minutely and automatically printed as the volume elements, and volumetric displays are constructed with high resolution using easy-to-fabricate means that exploit inkjet printing technologies. The results experimentally demonstrate the first prototype of an inkjet printing-based volumetric display composed of multiple layers of transparent films that yield a full-colour three-dimensional (3D) image. Moreover, we propose a design algorithm with 3D structures that provide multiple different 2D full-colour patterns when viewed from different directions and experimentally demonstrates prototypes. It is considered that these types of 3D volumetric structures and their fabrication methods based on widely deployed existing printing technologies can be utilised as novel information display devices and systems, including digital signage, media art, entertainment and security.

cited.name: Inkjet Printing-Based Volumetric Display
ctx: This method constructs a physical volumetric display by printing photoreactive luminescent materials (fluorescent inks) onto stacked transparent films, which are then excited by external ultraviolet (UV) light to emit visible light.

It differs from Downing Three-Color Display by using a static, additive manufacturing approach (inkjet printing) to create discrete voxel layers, whereas Downing’s method typically relies on rotating or scanning mechanisms to synthesize volume.

The system solves the problem of creating full-color 3D images with motion parallax using commercially available printing hardware, supporting the projection of multiple distinct 2D patterns from different viewing angles.

title: Joint Optimization of Triangle Mesh, Material, and Light from Neural Fields with Neural Radiance Cache
abstract: Traditional inverse rendering techniques are based on textured meshes, which naturally adapts to modern graphics pipelines, but costly differentiable multi-bounce Monte Carlo (MC) ray tracing poses challenges for modeling global illumination. Recently, neural fields has demonstrated impressive reconstruction quality but falls short in modeling indirect illumination. In this paper, we introduce a simple yet efficient inverse rendering framework that combines the strengths of both methods. Specifically, given pre-trained neural field representing the scene, we can obtain an initial estimate of the signed distance field (SDF) and create a Neural Radiance Cache (NRC), an enhancement over the traditional radiance cache used in real-time rendering. By using the former to initialize differentiable marching tetrahedrons (DMTet) and the latter to model indirect illumination, we can compute the global illumination via single-bounce differentiable MC ray tracing and jointly optimize the geometry, material, and light through back propagation. Experiments demonstrate that, compared to previous methods, our approach effectively prevents indirect illumination effects from being baked into materials, thus obtaining the high-quality reconstruction of triangle mesh, Physically-Based (PBR) materials, and High Dynamic Range (HDR) light probe.

cited.name: Improved Perlin Noise (4D)
ctx: Improved Perlin Noise (4D) is a procedural noise function that generates smooth, coherent scalar values in four dimensions by interpolating dot products of gradient vectors at the corners of a 4D hypercube.
It extends the 3D Improved Perlin Noise method to support time-varying texture generation and volumetric animation by treating the fourth dimension as time or an additional spatial axis.

It is distinguished from its 3D sibling 3D Perlin-like Noise and Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) by its ability to produce seamless temporal evolution without spatial artifacts, and from Simplex Noise by its reliance on a regular hypercubic grid rather than a simplex lattice.

title: Kernel-Reflection Sequences
abstract: Complex geometries, like those of plants, rocks, terrain, or even clouds are challenging to model in a way that allows for real-time rendering but does not make concessions in terms of visible detail. In this paper we propose a procedural modeling approach, called KRS, or kernel-reflection sequences, inspired by iterated function systems. The model is composed of kernel geometries defined by signed distance functions, and reflection transformations that multiply them. We show that a global distance function can be evaluated over this structure without recursion, allowing for the implementation of real-time sphere tracing on parallel hardware. We also show how the algorithm readily delivers continuous level-of-detail and minification filtering. We propose several techniques to enhance modeling freedom and avoid conspicuous symmetries. Most importantly, we extend sphere tracing to conformally transformed geometries. We also propose a GPU load balancing scheme for best utilization of computing power. To prove that the model can be used to realize various natural phenomena in uncompromising detail and extents, without obvious clues of symmetry, we render aquatic and terrestrial surface formations and vegetation in real-time.

cited.name: Kernel-Reflection Sequences
ctx: Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) are a procedural modeling technique for generating complex, fractal-like geometries using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and reflection transformations.

Unlike standard Iterated Function Systems (IFS) that require recursive traversal, KRS evaluates a global distance function via a fixed, non-recursive algorithm, enabling efficient real-time sphere tracing on parallel hardware.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods by providing a closed-form iterative evaluation of reflected SDFs without recursion, allowing for continuous level-of-detail and automatic minification filtering.

cited.name: KRS Texturing
ctx: KRS Texturing is a shading technique for Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) that applies procedural or triplanar textures to kernel solids to eliminate observable repetitiveness.
It addresses the visual artifact where applying identical coordinates to all kernel instances produces an extremely repetitive pattern that undesirably emphasizes symmetries.
It sets itself apart from standard parametric texturing by handling complex or reflective kernels where simple u,v parametrization is not feasible.

title: Lagrangian Hashing for Compressed Neural Field Representations
abstract: We present Lagrangian Hashing, a representation for neural fields combining the characteristics of fast training NeRF methods that rely on Eulerian grids (i.e.~InstantNGP), with those that employ points equipped with features as a way to represent information (e.g. 3D Gaussian Splatting or PointNeRF). We achieve this by incorporating a point-based representation into the high-resolution layers of the hierarchical hash tables of an InstantNGP representation. As our points are equipped with a field of influence, our representation can be interpreted as a mixture of Gaussians stored within the hash table. We propose a loss that encourages the movement of our Gaussians towards regions that require more representation budget to be sufficiently well represented. Our main finding is that our representation allows the reconstruction of signals using a more compact representation without compromising quality.

cited.name: Lagrangian Hashing
ctx: Lagrangian Hashing is a hybrid neural field representation that combines the memory efficiency of Eulerian hierarchical hash grids (specifically InstantNGP) with the adaptive density control of Lagrangian point-based representations (such as 3D Gaussian Splatting).

It solves the problem of high-frequency detail reconstruction in neural rendering by allowing feature points to move freely in space within hash buckets, rather than being fixed to uniform grid vertices.

Unlike its sibling HashGrid Encoding, which uses static feature vectors per bucket, Lagrangian Hashing stores a mixture of Gaussians per bucket, enabling the representation to allocate its budget adaptively to regions requiring more detail.

cited.name: Lagrangian Per-Bucket Feature Representation
ctx: This method defines the feature retrieval mechanism for the deepest levels of a hierarchical hash grid in Lagrangian Hashing.
Instead of storing static feature vectors in hash buckets, it computes features as a weighted sum of isotropic Gaussians centered at learnable means.
This allows for continuous, position-dependent feature retrieval, distinguishing it from the static bucket lookups of InstantNGP.

title: Layers for Effective Volume Rendering
abstract: A multi-layer volume rendering framework is presented. The final image is obtained by compositing a number of renderings, each being represented as a separate layer. This layer-centric framework provides a rich set of 2D operators and interactions, allowing both greater freedom and a more intuitive 2D-based user interaction. We extend the concept of compositing which is traditionally thought of as pertaining to the Porter and Duff compositing operators to a more general and flexible set of functions. In addition to developing new functional compositing operators, the user can control each individual layers attributes, such as the opacity. They can also easily add or remove a layer from the composition set, change their order in the composition, and export and import the layers in a format readily utilized in a 2D paint package. This broad space of composition functions allows for a wide variety of effects and we present several in the context of volume rendering, including two-level volume rendering, masking, and magnification. We also discuss the integration of a 3D volume rendering engine with our 2.5D layer compositing engine.

cited.name: Specific Applications and Integrators

cited.name: Layer-Centric Volume Rendering Framework
ctx: The Layer-Centric Volume Rendering Framework is a system architecture that decomposes volume visualization into two distinct phases: rendering small regions of interest (ROIs) as separate layers, and compositing these layers using a rich set of 2D operators.

Unlike traditional single-pass ray casting, this method treats the final image as a composition of independent renderings, allowing for intuitive 2D-based user interactions and complex material manipulations.
It builds on Compositing and Blending by extending standard Porter-Duff operators to general functional compositing functions applied to layer textures.

title: Learning and Meshing From Deep Implicit Surface Networks Using an Efficient Implementation of Analytic Marching
abstract: Reconstruction of object or scene surfaces has tremendous applications in computer vision, computer graphics, and robotics. The topic attracts increased attention with the emerging pipeline of deep learning surface reconstruction, where implicit field functions constructed from deep networks (e.g., multi-layer perceptrons or MLPs) are proposed for generative shape modeling. In this paper, we study a fundamental problem in this context about recovering a surface mesh from an implicit field function whose zero-level set captures the underlying surface. To achieve the goal, existing methods rely on traditional meshing algorithms (e.g., the de-facto standard marching cubes); while promising, they suffer from loss of precision learned in the implicit surface networks, due to the use of discrete space sampling in marching cubes. Given that an MLP with activations of Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) partitions its input space into a number of linear regions, we are motivated to connect this local linearity with a same property owned by the desired result of polygon mesh. More specifically, we identify from the linear regions, partitioned by an MLP based implicit function, the analytic cells and analytic facesthat are associated with the function's zero-level isosurface. We prove that under mild conditions, the identified analytic faces are guaranteed to connect and form a closed, piecewise planar surface. Based on the theorem, we propose an algorithm of analytic marching, which marches among analytic cells to exactly recover the mesh captured by an implicit surface network. We also show that our theory and algorithm are equally applicable to advanced MLPs with shortcut connections and max pooling. Given the parallel nature of analytic marching, we contribute AnalyticMesh, a software package that supports efficient meshing of implicit surface networks via CUDA parallel computing, and mesh simplification for efficient downstream processing. We apply our method to different settings of generative shape modeling using implicit surface networks. Extensive experiments demonstrate our advantages over existing methods in terms of both meshing accuracy and efficiency. Codes are at https://github.com/Karbo123/AnalyticMesh.link_to_subscribed_fulltex

cited.name: Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing
ctx: A triggering strategy for Signed Distance Functions (SDF) that uses the Eikonal equation property to accelerate finding the zero-level set point x.
It initializes an arbitrary point x0 in the implicit field of SDF F and updates the point using the rule x{t+1} = xt - \eta F(xt) \nabla{xt} F, where \eta \le 1 is the step size.
This accelerates standard SGD when far from the surface and provides damping to prevent penetration when close.

cited.name: Residual Block with Shortcut (ReLU MLP Extension)
ctx: This method extends the analytic marching algorithm for implicit surface reconstruction to Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) constructed with residual blocks containing shortcut connections.
It enables the theoretical analysis and exact linear region partitioning of such architectures, allowing for efficient meshing via analytic marching.

It differs from the baseline MLP Neural Field by explicitly handling the additive shortcut path in the region-wise linear mapping, and from MLP with Input Skips by using a residual summation structure rather than concatenation or direct input reuse.

title: Level of Detail for Real-Time Volumetric Terrain Rendering
abstract: Terrain rendering is an important component of many GIS applications and simulators. Most methods rely on heightmap-based terrain which is simple to acquire and handle, but has limited capabilities for modeling features like caves, steep cliffs, or overhangs. In contrast, volumetric terrain models, e.g. based on isosurfaces can represent arbitrary topology. In this paper, we present a fast, practical and GPU-friendly level of detail algorithm for large scale volumetric terrain that is specifically designed for real-time rendering applications. Our algorithm is based on a longest edge bisection (LEB) scheme. The resulting tetrahedral cells are subdivided into four hexahedra, which form the domain for a subsequent isosurface extraction step. The algorithm can be used with arbitrary volumetric models such as signed distance fields, which can be generated from triangle meshes or discrete volume data sets. In contrast to previous methods our algorithm does not require any stitching between detail levels. It generates crack free surfaces with a good triangle quality. Furthermore, we efficiently extract the geometry at runtime and require no preprocessing, which allows us to render infinite procedural content with low memory consumption.Vision, Modeling & Visualizatio

Unlike octree decompositions which require complex stitching processes to handle discontinuities between cells of different resolutions, this method guarantees that neighboring cells share faces exactly, resulting in crack-free surfaces and well-shaped tetrahedra without degradation of element quality during…

It sets itself apart from bottom-up techniques by generating geometry on the fly, avoiding the massive memory and computation costs of full-resolution mesh generation during preprocessing.

title: Local Detail Enhancement for Volume Rendering under Global Illumination
abstract: We present a novel method for realistic perception enhanced volume rendering. Compared with traditional lighting systems, that either tend to eliminate important local shapes and details in volume data or cannot offer interactive global illumination, our method can enhance the edges and curvatures within a volume under global illumination through a user-friendly interface. We first propose an interactive volumetric lighting model to both simulate scattering and enhance the local detail information. In this model, users only need to determine a key light source. Next, we propose a new cue to intensify the shape perception by enhancing the local edges and details. The cue can be pre-computed and thus we can still keep the rendering process running real-time. Experiments on a variety of volume data demonstrate that the proposed method can generate more details, and hence more realistic rendering results.Pacific Graphics Short PapersShort Paper

cited.name: Noise Layer Evaluation
ctx: Noise Layer Evaluation is a procedural shading technique that computes a single layer of volumetric density or color by sampling a base noise function (such as Perlin, Simplex, or Worley) at a distorted position, applying non-linear power scaling, and optionally inverting the result.

It serves as a modular building block for complex volumetric effects, allowing artists to stack multiple layers with independent scales, powers, and noise types to create detailed textures like clouds, marble, or terrain.

Unlike single-function noise generators, this method encapsulates distortion, type selection, and post-processing into a unified evaluation step, distinguishing it from siblings like Worley Noise or Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) by adding configurable layer parameters and positional warping.

ctx: The Asymptotic Decider is a topological disambiguation test used in Marching Cubes to resolve face ambiguities where the sign pattern of a cell's vertices is insufficient to determine the unique connectivity of the isosurface intersection on that face.

title: Mega-NeRF: Scalable Construction of Large-Scale NeRFs for Virtual Fly- Throughs
abstract: We use neural radiance fields (NeRFs) to build interac-tive 3D environments from large-scale visual captures spanning buildings or even multiple city blocks collected pri-marily from drones. In contrast to single object scenes (on which NeRFs are traditionally evaluated), our scale poses multiple challenges including (1) the need to model thou-sands of images with varying lighting conditions, each of which capture only a small subset of the scene, (2) pro-hibitively large model capacities that make it infeasible to train on a single GPU, and (3) significant challenges for fast rendering that would enable interactive fly-throughs. To address these challenges, we begin by analyzing visi-bility statistics for large-scale scenes, motivating a sparse network structure where parameters are specialized to dif-ferent regions of the scene. We introduce a simple geomet-ric clustering algorithm for data parallelism that partitions training images (or rather pixels) into different NeRF sub-modules that can be trained in parallel. We evaluate our approach on existing datasets (Quad 6k and UrbanScene3D) as well as against our own drone footage, improving training speed by 3x and PSNR by 12%. We also evaluate re-cent NeRF fast renderers on top of Mega-NeRF and intro-duce a novel method that exploits temporal coherence. Our technique achieves a 40x speedup over conventional NeRF rendering while remaining within 0.8 db in PSNR quality, exceeding the fidelity of existing fast renderers.

cited.name: MegaNeRF

It differs from siblings like BlockNeRF and NeRFPlayer by using spatial partitioning primarily to enable data parallelism for scalable training, rather than just speeding up inference of a pre-trained single network.
It improves upon NeRF++ by replacing the unit sphere foreground with an altitude-constrained ellipsoid and partitioning training pixels by geometric visibility.

This approach specifically addresses the scalability limits of standard NeRF when applied to city-scale environments.

title: Multivariate Volume Data: Advances in Visualization and Analysis Techniques
abstract: Nanoscale imaging techniques employed at DOE’s modern X-ray facilities are important in guiding future experiments, enabling successful scientific discoveries, and bringing products to market. However, the increasing size and complexity of nanoscale imaging data have made the analysis process more difficult and, in some situations, infeasible. Nanoscale imaging techniques commonly produce multivariate volumetric data, which contains more than one channel per voxel and has become increasingly prevalent in important industries such as battery technology, manufacturing, and medical imaging. Due to its multidimensional nature, multivariate data is complex and usually requires substantial human effort to analyze. Often, each channel is visualized separately and individually. Such an approach, however, does not readily reveal the complex yet frequently important cross-channel interactions. Based upon RadVolViz [1], a novel research application for direct multivariate volume rendering and exploration, the open source prototype MultivariateView [2] was recently developed to enable intuitive and highly interactive exploration of multivariate volume datasets. MultivariateView utilizes the widely used open source frameworks trame [3] and VTK [4] in order to create a powerful, interactive web application. Fig. 1 provides an overview of the rendering and radial colormap features. We anticipate that the full integration of these features into the visualization library VTK will provide access to even more tools and filters within VTK’s ecosystem to greatly improve the power and capabilities of multivariate volume rendering. A lens feature within the prototype enables interactive exploration of different regions of the radial colormap, which translates to different phases/composites within the volume. As shown in Fig. 2, the four phases of the MIEC dataset [5] were successfully visualized by moving the lens around the radial colormap. This was also confirmed by the authors of the paper. Multimodal visualization and analysis techniques were successfully demonstrated through studying a medical dataset (a knee containing a sarcoma) containing four unique modalities per voxel: CT, PET, MRI-T1, and MRI-T2. Voxel similarity maps were likewise explored and were found to correctly separate voxels belonging to different phases, as demonstrated in Fig. 3. In particular, the t-SNE method appeared to be quite successful at separating voxels belonging to different phases within the MIEC dataset [5]. The t-SNE method was similarly able to segment out the sarcoma and other interesting features (such as the patient’s bone) within the medical dataset. A novel segmentation method in which SLIC superpixels [6] of the multivariate voxels are generated and subsequently merged through several steps of progressive agglomerative clustering was found to accurately segment multivariate phases/composites, as demonstrated in Fig. 4. Global consideration of similarity allows the algorithm to label similar disconnected regions of phases/composites as belonging to the same phase/composite. Many example datasets from several scientific disciplines have been successfully analyzed through the techniques discovered in this work. Future plans include integrating the newly discovered visualization and analysis techniques within the widely used open source visualization applications ParaView [7] and Tomviz [8]. All software produced for this research will be open source and freely available [9]. MultivariateView [2] overview, visualizing an MIEC dataset [5]. The radial multivariate transfer function editor on the left matches that described in the RadVolViz application [1], where voxels are mapped to the radial colormap according to the values of their channels (a voxel high in Ce, for instance, will appear close to the Ce node. A voxel high in Gd, will appear close to the Gd node. And a voxel that contains a mixture of each will appear in between). A subsampled distribution of voxels is plotted within the display to provide a general idea of the voxel distribution. Visualization of the four phases identified in the MIEC paper [5] by using the interactive lens exploration of MultivariateView [2]. The authors of the MIEC paper confirmed that the phases were correctly identified in these visualizations. t-SNE mapping of voxels demonstrated noticeable separation between the phases of the MIEC dataset [5]. In each of the above subfigures, the upper left region is a unitless 2D similarity plot of the voxels colored by k-means clustering, the upper right region is a rendering of the selected voxels using the same coloring from MultivariateView [2], and the bottom region shows parallel coordinates of the selected voxels (selected voxels are colored and unselected voxels are gray). The top-left and top-right subfigures show the CFO and CGO phases, respectively, as identified in the paper. The bottom left subfigure shows the two emergent phases. And the bottom right subfigure shows miasma (noise). It was a very interesting finding to see that the clustering separated out the noise into its own region. Segmentation by generating SLIC superpixels [6] followed by several iterations of merging. On the top left is the slice RGB-colored by RadVolViz [1]. The next image (top center) shows the initial SLIC segmentation. The other slices show the results obtained after progressive agglomerative clustering (merging) of the initial superpixels. Note that, due to global consideration of similarity, the merging algorithm has the ability to label similar disconnected regions of phases/composites as belonging to the same phase/composite.

title: NeRF++: Analyzing and Improving Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve impressive view synthesis results for a variety of capture settings, including 360 capture of bounded scenes and forward-facing capture of bounded and unbounded scenes. NeRF fits multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) representing view-invariant opacity and view-dependent color volumes to a set of training images, and samples novel views based on volume rendering techniques. In this technical report, we first remark on radiance fields and their potential ambiguities, namely the shape-radiance ambiguity, and analyze NeRF's success in avoiding such ambiguities. Second, we address a parametrization issue involved in applying NeRF to 360 captures of objects within large-scale, unbounded 3D scenes. Our method improves view synthesis fidelity in this challenging scenario. Code is available at https://github.com/Kai-46/nerfplusplus.

title: Neural RGB-D Surface Reconstruction
abstract: Obtaining high-quality 3D reconstructions of room-scale scenes is of paramount importance for upcoming applications in AR or VR. These range from mixed reality applications for teleconferencing, virtual measuring, virtual room planing, to robotic applications. While current volume-based view synthesis methods that use neural radiance fields (NeRFs) show promising results in reproducing the appearance of an object or scene, they do not reconstruct an actual surface. The volumetric representation of the surface based on densities leads to artifacts when a surface is extracted using Marching Cubes, since during optimization, densities are accumulated along the ray and are not used at a single sample point in isolation. Instead of this volumetric representation of the surface, we propose to represent the surface using an implicit function (truncated signed distance function). We show how to incorporate this representation in the NeRF framework, and extend it to use depth measurements from a commodity RGB-D sensor, such as a Kinect. In addition, we propose a pose and camera re-finement technique which improves the overall reconstruction quality. In contrast to concurrent work on integrating depth priors in NeRF which concentrates on novel view synthesis, our approach is able to reconstruct high-quality, metrical 3D reconstructions.

title: NeuVolEx: Implicit Neural Features for Volume Exploration
abstract: Direct volume rendering (DVR) aims to help users identify and examine regions of interest (ROIs) within volumetric data, and feature representations that support effective ROI classification and clustering play a fundamental role in volume exploration. Existing approaches typically rely on either explicit local feature representations or implicit convolutional feature representations learned from raw volumes. However, explicit local feature representations are limited in capturing broader geometric patterns and spatial correlations, while implicit convolutional feature representations do not necessarily ensure robust performance in practice, where user supervision is typically limited. Meanwhile, implicit neural representations (INRs) have recently shown strong promise in DVR for volume compression, owing to their ability to compactly parameterize continuous volumetric fields. In this work, we propose NeuVolEx, a neural volume exploration approach that extends the role of INRs beyond volume compression. Unlike prior compression methods that focus on INR outputs, NeuVolEx leverages feature representations learned during INR training as a robust basis for volume exploration. To better adapt these feature representations to exploration tasks, we augment a base INR with a structural encoder and a multi-task learning scheme that improve spatial coherence for ROI characterization. We validate NeuVolEx on two fundamental volume exploration tasks: image-based transfer function (TF) design and viewpoint recommendation. NeuVolEx enables accurate ROI classification under sparse user supervision for image-based TF design and supports unsupervised clustering to identify compact complementary viewpoints that reveal different ROI clusters. Experiments on diverse volume datasets with varying modalities and ROI complexities demonstrate NeuVolEx improves both effectiveness and usability over prior methods

title: Obscurance-based Volume Rendering Framework
abstract: Obscurances, from which ambient occlusion is a particular case, is a technology that produces natural-looking lighting effects in a faster way than global illumination. Its application in volume visualization is of special interest since it permits us to generate a high quality rendering at a low cost. In this paper, we propose an obscurancebased framework that allows us to obtain realistic and illustrative volume visualizations in an interactive manner. Obscurances can include color bleeding effects without additional cost. Moreover, we obtain a saliency map from the gradient of obscurances and we show its application to enhance volume visualization and to select the most salient views.publishedVersio

cited.name: Vicinity Shading
ctx: Vicinity shading is a pre-computed volumetric ambient occlusion technique that enhances volume visualization by calculating an "obscurance" value for each voxel, representing the occlusion information from its immediate neighborhood.

It differs from local volumetric shadowing methods (e.g., Hernell et al.) by explicitly testing visibility against the first occluder and ignoring the environment beyond it, rather than integrating attenuation over the entire ray distance.

This approach allows for interactive exploration and saliency map generation at a computational cost proportional to the number of voxels times the number of directions, significantly lower than the quadratic complexity of full volumetric shadowing.

title: Out-of-Core Compression and Decompression of Large n-Dimensional Scalar Fields
abstract: We present a simple method for compressing very large and regularly sampled scalar fields. Our method is particularly attractive when the entire data set does not fit in memory and when the sampling rate is high relative to the feature size of the scalar field in all dimensions. Although we report results for R{sup 3} and R{sup 4} data sets, the proposed approach may be applied to higher dimensions. The method is based on the new Lorenzo predictor, introduced here, which estimates the value of the scalar field at each sample from the values at processed neighbors. The predicted values are exact when the n-dimensional scalar field is an implicit polynomial of degree n-1. Surprisingly, when the residuals (differences between the actual and predicted values) are encoded using arithmetic coding, the proposed method often outperforms wavelet compression in an L{infinity} sense. The proposed approach may be used both for lossy and lossless compression and is well suited for out-of-core compression and decompression, because a trivial implementation, which sweeps through the data set reading it once, requires maintaining only a small buffer in core memory, whose size barely exceeds a single n-1 dimensional slice of the data.

cited.name: Lorenzo Predictor
ctx: The Lorenzo predictor is an isotropic predictive coding method for n-dimensional scalar fields that estimates a sample value from its 2^n - 1 immediate neighbors in a regular grid to generate residuals for compression.

It is distinguished from anisotropic scanline predictors by exploiting data coherence in all dimensions and is the simplest isotropic predictor capable of exactly reconstructing all polynomials of degree less than n.
For a dataset of size D^n, the footprint size is D^{n-1} + D^{n-2} + \dots + D + 1.

title: Parameter-space ReSTIR for Differentiable and Inverse Rendering
abstract: Differentiable rendering is frequently used in gradient descent-based inverse rendering pipelines to solve for scene parameters – such as reflectance or lighting properties – from target image inputs. Efficient computation of accurate, low variance gradients is critical for rapid convergence. While many methods employ variance reduction strategies, they operate independently on each gradient descent iteration, requiring large sample counts and computation. Gradients may however vary slowly between iterations, leading to unexplored potential benefits when reusing sample information to exploit this coherence. We develop an algorithm to reuse Monte Carlo gradient samples between gradient iterations, motivated by reservoir-based temporal importance resampling in forward rendering. Direct application of this method is not feasible, as we are computing many derivative estimates (i.e., one per optimization parameter) instead of a single pixel intensity estimate; moreover, each of these gradient estimates can affect multiple pixels, and gradients can take on negative values. We address these challenges by reformulating differential rendering integrals in parameter space, developing a new resampling estimator that treats negative functions, and combining these ideas into a reuse algorithm for inverse texture optimization. We significantly reduce gradient error compared to baselines, and demonstrate faster inverse rendering convergence in settings involving complex direct lighting and material textures.

cited.name: k-buffer
ctx: The k-buffer is a fixed-depth fragment sorting structure used in image-space volume rendering to manage visibility for non-convex grids.

It acts as a hardware-efficient alternative to the unbounded A-buffer by storing only a constant number k of fragments per pixel, combining incoming fragments with stored ones and discarding the farthest (for front-to-back) or closest (for back-to-front) to manage memory.

It is chosen when the fragment stream is approximately sorted (k-nearly sorted), allowing exact visibility sorting on the GPU with O(n) complexity, whereas the unbounded A-buffer requires potentially unbounded memory and the Z-buffer only handles single-layer visibility.

cited.name: Nearly-Sorted Object-Space Visibility Ordering
ctx: Nearly-Sorted Object-Space Visibility Ordering (k-NSS) is a relaxation of exact visibility sorting where primitives are ordered such that rasterized fragments are at most k positions out of order in the sorted sequence.

This allows for the use of faster, approximate object-space sorting algorithms (such as centroid sorting or coarse BSP traversal) while deferring the guarantee of correct compositing to an exact sorting step during fragment processing.

It differs from its parent Per-Pixel Sorting (General Variant) by performing the initial ordering in object space rather than per-pixel, and from siblings like Mammen's Technique by explicitly bounding the displacement error k to enable linear-time correction.

Unlike an SVO, which only encodes empty regions efficiently, the DAG additionally encodes identical regions of space by sharing pointers to identical subtrees.

title: PERF: Performant, Explicit Radiance Fields
abstract: We present a novel way of approaching image-based 3D reconstruction based on radiance fields. The problem of volumetric reconstruction is formulated as a non-linear least-squares problem and solved explicitly without the use of neural networks. This enables the use of solvers with a higher rate of convergence than what is typically used for neural networks, and fewer iterations are required until convergence. The volume is represented using a grid of voxels, with the scene surrounded by a hierarchy of environment maps. This makes it possible to get clean reconstructions of 360\ub0 scenes where the foreground and background is separated. A number of synthetic and real scenes from well-known benchmark-suites are successfully reconstructed with quality on par with state-of-the-art methods, but at significantly reduced reconstruction times

cited.name: NanoVDB Decompression
ctx: NanoVDB Decompression is a GPU volume rendering technique for large, sparse datasets that uses OpenVDB for offline, fixed-rate lossy compression on the CPU and NanoVDB for on-the-fly decompression and sampling on the GPU.
It enables random access sampling similar to dense 3D textures without complex cache management or synchronization, making it suitable for incoherent access patterns like path tracing.
Unlike block-based compression schemes (e.g., ZFP) that require complex control flow to amortize decompression costs, this method allows each GPU thread to decompress data independently.

cited.name: Explicit Radiance Fields
ctx: Explicit Radiance Fields (PERF) is a method for image-based 3D reconstruction that formulates volumetric reconstruction as a non-linear least-squares problem solved explicitly without neural networks.
It uses a voxel grid for the foreground and a hierarchy of environment maps for the background, optimizing color and opacity values directly via a Gauss-Newton solver.

Unlike Plenoxels which uses neural networks for view-dependent color, PERF assumes diffuse surfaces and achieves significantly faster convergence by leveraging analytical gradients and iterative linear solvers.

title: PeRFception: Perception using Radiance Fields
abstract: The recent progress in implicit 3D representation, i.e., Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), has made accurate and photorealistic 3D reconstruction possible in a differentiable manner. This new representation can effectively convey the information of hundreds of high-resolution images in one compact format and allows photorealistic synthesis of novel views. In this work, using the variant of NeRF called Plenoxels, we create the first large-scale implicit representation datasets for perception tasks, called the PeRFception, which consists of two parts that incorporate both object-centric and scene-centric scans for classification and segmentation. It shows a significant memory compression rate (96.4\%) from the original dataset, while containing both 2D and 3D information in a unified form. We construct the classification and segmentation models that directly take as input this implicit format and also propose a novel augmentation technique to avoid overfitting on backgrounds of images. The code and data are publicly available in https://postech-cvlab.github.io/PeRFception .

title: Point-NeRF: Point-based Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: Volumetric neural rendering methods like NeRF [34] generate high-quality view synthesis results but are optimized per-scene leading to prohibitive reconstruction time. On the other hand, deep multi-view stereo methods can quickly reconstruct scene geometry via direct network inference. Point-NeRF combines the advantages of these two approaches by using neural 3D point clouds, with associated neural features, to model a radiance field. Point-NeRF can be rendered efficiently by aggregating neural point features near scene surfaces, in a ray marching-based rendering pipeline. Moreover, Point-NeRF can be initialized via direct inference of a pre-trained deep network to produce a neural point cloud; this point cloud can be finetuned to surpass the visual quality of NeRF with 30× faster training time. Point-NeRF can be combined with other 3D re-construction methods and handles the errors and outliers in such methods via a novel pruning and growing mechanism.

title: Port B46: surface extractors batch
abstract: Closes #127 Ports the three remaining level-surface extractors: - `src/SurfaceExtractorCubes.ts` — cube-based extraction with the vertex-edge table and ear-clipping; the six face routines resolve the four-cut face ambiguity by the sign of `f00*f11 - f01*f10`, adding a branch point in the plus-sign (`det == 0`) case. - `src/SurfaceExtractorTetrahedra.ts` — 5-tetrahedra-per-cube extraction with linear interpolation, covering all 81 sign patterns including the zero-valued (degenerate) ones. - `src/SurfaceExtractorMC.ts` — Marching Cubes extraction over an `Image3`, built on the already-ported `MarchingCubes` 256-entry table. Port decisions (also recorded in the file headers): - `SurfaceExtractorCubes`/`SurfaceExtractorTetrahedra` derive from the ported `SurfaceExtractor` base (B20): the upstream pure virtual `Extract(level, vertices&, triangles&)` is `extractRational(level)`, which returns the two arrays. - Nested types are exported with the file-qualified names `SurfaceExtractorTetrahedraEdge` and `SurfaceExtractorMCMesh`; the cubes `VETable`/`TVertex` stay module-private. - `SurfaceExtractorMC` derives from `MarchingCubes`. The two upstream `Extract` overloads become `extractVoxel(level, perturb, F)` (returning `{ valid, mesh }`) and `extract(level, perturb)`, per the precedent that only the canonical query keeps the plain name. - The tetrahedra extractor replaces `std::map ` and `std::set `/`std::set ` with `Map`s keyed by canonical strings (rationals reduced to lowest terms). Vertex indices are assigned in insertion order, as upstream; edges and triangles are sorted at the end by the upstream `operator 0`, `det = (Real)0) { /* 1205 */ } else if (dx - dy + dz = (Real)0) { /* 6572 */ } else { /* 0752 */ } ``` `dx`, `dy`, `dz` are the fractional offsets within the voxel, so `dx + dy + dz >= 0` is unconditionally true. The `6572` corner tetrahedron therefore absorbs the central tetrahedron and the `0752` branch is unreachable. The plane through `(1,1,0)`, `(1,0,1)` and `(0,1,1)` that cuts off the corner `(1,1,1)` is `dx + dy + dz = 2`; the even-parity branch directly below uses the analogous cutting planes at 1 and is correct. **The port fixes this** (`dx + dy + dz >= 2`), because the wrong gradient corrupts `orientTriangles` results for every point of an odd-parity voxel that lies in the central tetrahedron. The fix is documented in a code comment at the site and is covered by the test `selects the correct tetrahedron in an odd-parity voxel`.

title: Pulsar: Efficient Sphere-based Neural Rendering
abstract: We propose Pulsar, an efficient sphere-based differentiable rendering module that is orders of magnitude faster than competing techniques, modular, and easy-to-use due to its tight integration with PyTorch. Differentiable rendering is the foundation for modern neural rendering approaches, since it enables end-to-end training of 3D scene representations from image observations. However, gradient-based optimization of neural mesh, voxel, or function representations suffers from multiple challenges, i.e., topological in-consistencies, high memory footprints, or slow rendering speeds. To alleviate these problems, Pulsar employs: 1) a sphere-based scene representation, 2) a modular, efficient differentiable projection operation, and 3) (optional) neural shading. Pulsar executes orders of magnitude faster than existing techniques and allows real-time rendering and optimization of representations with millions of spheres. Using spheres for the scene representation, unprecedented speed is obtained while avoiding topology problems. Pulsar is fully differentiable and thus enables a plethora of applications, ranging from 3D reconstruction to neural rendering.

Unlike its siblings, Pulsar parallelizes over pixels rather than spheres to avoid synchronization overhead, and it decouples geometry projection from appearance via a neural shading network, allowing unlimited spheres to contribute to color while restricting gradient propagation to the first few spheres to avoid…

It addresses the limitation of standard sphere-based rendering where color is often treated as a static attribute, failing to capture complex specularities or material variations that change with the viewing angle.

Unlike standard splatting which assigns a fixed color to each primitive, this method decouples geometry projection from appearance, allowing the network to predict the final color based on the underlying sphere features and the camera's viewing vector.

title: Radar Fields: An Extension of Radiance Fields to SAR
abstract: Radiance fields have been a major breakthrough in the field of inverse rendering, novel view synthesis and 3D modeling of complex scenes from multi-view image collections. Since their introduction, it was shown that they could be extended to other modalities such as LiDAR, radio frequencies, X-ray or ultrasound. In this paper, we show that, despite the important difference between optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image formation models, it is possible to extend radiance fields to radar images thus presenting the first "radar fields". This allows us to learn surface models using only collections of radar images, similar to how regular radiance fields are learned and with the same computational complexity on average. Thanks to similarities in how both fields are defined, this work also shows a potential for hybrid methods combining both optical and SAR images.
