title: A High-Performance SurfaceNets Discrete Isocontouring Algorithm
abstract: Isocontouring is one of the most widely used visualization techniques. However, many popular contouring algorithms were created prior to the advent of ubiquitous parallel approaches, such as multi-core, shared memory computing systems. With increasing data sizes and computational loads, it is essential to reimagine such algorithms to leverage the increased computing capabilities available today. To this end we have redesigned the SurfaceNets algorithm, a powerful technique which is often employed to isocontour non-continuous, discrete, volumetric scalar fields such as segmentation label maps. Label maps are ubiquitous to medical computing and biological analysis, used in applications ranging from anatomical atlas creation to brain connectomics. This novel Parallel SurfaceNets algorithm has been redesigned using concepts from the high-performance Flying Edges continuous isocontouring algorrithm. It consists of two basic steps, surface extraction followed by constrained smoothing, parallelized over volume edges and employing a double-buffering smoothing approach to guarantee determinism. The algorithm can extract and smooth multiple segmented objects in a single execution, producing a polygonal (triangular/quadrilateral) mesh with points and polygons fully shared between neighboring objects. Performance is typically one to two orders of magnitude faster than the current sequential algorithms for discrete isosurface extraction on small core-count commodity CPU hardware. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm on five different datasets including human torso and brain atlases, mouse brain segmentation, and electron microscopy connectomics. The software is currently available under a permissive, open source license in the VTK visualization system.

cited.name: Parallel SurfaceNets
ctx: Parallel SurfaceNets (PSN) is a high-performance, parallel discrete isocontouring algorithm that extracts a surface mesh from volumetric scalar fields, specifically segmented label maps.

It addresses the limitations of sequential algorithms like Marching Cubes (MC) and the memory bottlenecks of incremental allocation by using a four-pass parallel approach with computational edge trimming and pre-allocated output arrays.

Unlike MC, which produces duplicated polygons between adjacent labeled regions, PSN produces a mesh where boundaries between extracted objects are fully shared, and it extracts multiple segmented objects in a single execution rather than requiring separate passes per label.

title: A New Sampling Scheme for Slice Based Volume Rendering
abstract: In this paper we present a novel approach to generate proxy geometry for slice based volume rendering. The basic idea is derived from the behavior of a ray-caster and is a simple extension of the well known 2D object-aligned texture stack based technique. From this our novel scheme inherits the advantage that it enables hardware-based volume rendering for devices that do not support 3D textures. On these devices previous object-aligned 2D texture based approaches suffered from disturbing view angle dependent stack-switching artifacts which are avoided by our novel method. Our approach also shows benefits compared to the widely used view aligned slicing algorithm as it avoids jagged boundary artifacts and increases performance.IEEE/ EG Symposium on Volume Graphic

It approximates the uniform sampling pattern of ray casting more closely than spherical shell approaches while avoiding their large geometry overhead.

title: A novel interface for higher-dimensional classification of volume data
abstract: In the traditional volume visualization paradigm, the user specifies a transfer function that assigns each scalar value to a color and opacity by defining an opacity and a color map function. The transfer function has two limitations. First, the user must define curves based on histogram and value rather than seeing and working with the volume itself. Second, the transfer function is inflexible in classifying regions of interest, where values at a voxel such as intensity and gradient are used to differentiate material, not talking into account additional properties such as texture and position. We describe an intuitive user interface for specifying the classification functions that consists of the users painting directly on sample slices of the volume. These painted regions are used to automatically define high-dimensional classification functions that can be implemented in hardware for interactive rendering. The classification of the volume is iteratively improved as the user paints samples, allowing intuitive and efficient viewing of materials of interest.

Users paint sample points on slicing planes to indicate regions of interest, and a neural network learns to map voxel properties to an uncertainty value (0 to 1) representing membership in a material class.

cited.name: Region-growing Iso-surface Extraction
ctx: Region-growing Iso-surface Extraction is a method that generates high-quality, curvature-adaptive semi-regular meshes while preserving sharp features and extracting all disjoint components of an iso-surface.

It improves upon the original Marching Triangles algorithm by introducing a normal consistency constraint that ensures the intersection of the Delaunay sphere of a new triangle with the iso-surface is a topological disk, providing robustness for complex topologies.

Unlike Marching Cubes, which produces uniform grids, this method adapts triangle size to local curvature, and unlike standard Marching Triangles, it explicitly handles feature preservation and topological robustness via normal checks.

ctx: The Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Display (also known as the Optical Trap Display or OTD) is a free-space volumetric display that creates luminous image points in mid-air by trapping a microscopic particle using photophoretic forces and illuminating it with RGB lasers.

It solves the "clipping" limitation inherent in holographic and light-field displays, where image points are physically separated from the scattering surface, thereby restricting viewing angles and preventing geometries such as long-throw projections or wrap-around displays.

title: A Two-Step Surface Reconstruction Method Using Signed Marching Cubes
abstract: In this paper, we explore a new approach, a two-step surface reconstruction method to extract the target isosurface from a given implicit function efficiently. Our main contribution is that we improve the surface reconstruction process by accelerating the speed of evaluation using signed marching cubes. The basic strategy is to filter the invalid voxels that do not intersect with the target isosurface in a low-cost manner, and to evaluate the valid voxels that intersect with the target isosurface accurately. The improved signed marching cubes method consists of a rough evaluation step and an exact evaluation step. The coarse evaluation step evaluates the points of all voxels using the fast multipole method with a lower order. After the rough evaluation step, the voxels that intersect with the target isosurface are screened out. Then, the exact evaluation step evaluates the points of filtered voxels using the fast multipole method with a higher order. The experimental results show that, compared with the traditional marching cubes method, the improved reconstruction method reduces the amounts of calculation for invalid voxels that do not intersect with the target isosurfaces, which is useful to improve the efficiency of surface reconstruction.

cited.name: Two-Step Surface Reconstruction Method
ctx: By combining a low-cost rough evaluation using the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) with a lower expansion order to filter out non-boundary voxels, and a high-precision exact evaluation using a higher expansion order only for the remaining boundary voxels, the method significantly reduces computational cost while…

The implicit function s(x) is defined as: s(x) = \sum{j=1}^{N} \omegaj \Phi(x, xj) + p(x) where \Phi is the radial basis kernel (e.g., biharmonic or triharmonic spline) and p(x) is a first-degree polynomial satisfying \sum \omegai = \sum \omegai xi = \sum \omegai yi = \sum \omegai zi = 0.

The FMM approximates the kernel \Phi(x, y) using a finite series: \Phi(x, y) = \sum{n=1}^{p} \phin(x) \psin(y) + Rp(x, y) The approximate function value sp(x) is computed as: sp(x) = \sum{n=1}^{p} \Psin(y) \phin(x) + p(x) where \Psin(y) = \sum{j=1}^{N} \omegaj \psin(yj) are the precomputed moments.

cited.name: RLE Accelerated Sheet Buffer Splatting
ctx: RLE Accelerated Sheet Buffer Splatting is a volume rendering algorithm that accelerates object-order splatting by combining Run Length Encoding (RLE) with a sheet buffer approach, utilizing pre-classified and pre-shaded voxel data to skip transparent regions.

It solves the performance bottleneck of processing large volumes with high transparency by exploiting spatial coherence, allowing the renderer to traverse only non-transparent voxel scanlines while simultaneously updating the image plane.

Unlike standard splatting which processes every voxel, or Lacroute’s shear-warp method which uses a single RLE structure, this method maintains three sets of RLE structures for principal axes to ensure the sheet buffer remains parallel to the image plane, enabling flexible random access and avoiding alignment issues.

title: Accelerating Fourier volume rendering by polar coordinate data representation
abstract: Volume rendering is an important tool to visualize three-dimensional data in biomedicine by projecting the data to a two-dimensional plane. The projection is done by ray casting and its complexity is proportional to the number of three-dimensional data points. To reduce complexity, Fourier volume rendering (FVR) uses slice projection theorem to facilitate the integration of voxels along the ray casting path. In this paper, we proposed a new method for FVR that stored and processed the frequency domain data in polar coordinate. By exploiting three aspects of data processing which is previously impossible in rectilinear coordinate, our new method is much faster than the previous methods. The first aspect is data regularity. When data are stored in polar coordinate, extracting a slice involves accessing data stored in adjacent memory location. This regularity makes memory access more efficient. The second aspect is to utilize the high data density near the origin in polar coordinate. We can obtain two benefits from this aspect. The first allows us to extract a slice by nearest-neighbor interpolation instead of more complex interpolation but without sacrificing image quality. The second allows us to trade off between image quality and memory storage. The third aspect is to recognize that converting from rectilinear coordinate to polar coordinate is a one-time process. Therefore, we can use a better interpolation kernel with larger support in coordinate conversion. In turn, most of the computation is shifted to the preprocessing stage and interactive rendering can be made very fast. In the experiments, we show that the speed in interactive visualization for our new method is independent of the size of the interpolation kernel, therefore, achieving comparable image quality at a faster rate than previous methods.

cited.name: Polar Coordinate Fourier Volume Rendering
ctx: Polar Coordinate Fourier Volume Rendering (Polar FVR) is a volume rendering technique that stores and processes frequency domain data in polar coordinates to reduce computational complexity from O(n^2 \log n) to O(n^2) and improve memory access efficiency.

It sets itself apart from traditional Rectilinear FVR by exploiting data regularity and high sampling density near the origin, allowing slice extraction via nearest-neighbor or bilinear interpolation instead of trilinear interpolation, thereby shifting computational cost to preprocessing.
The layout ensures that data accessed during slice extraction are in adjacent memory locations.

cited.name: GPU Octree Volume Rasterization with Shadow Mapping
ctx: This method implements high-performance GPU volume rendering by decoupling the branch-intensive octree traversal from the raycasting loop, using a rasterization pass to identify active voxels and a shadow mapping pass for lighting.

It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional raycasting on sparse data by moving empty-space culling into a graphics pipeline stage, achieving 2 to 4 times faster rendering speeds than state-of-the-art algorithms on large out-of-core datasets.

Unlike sibling methods that rely on pure ray-tracing traversal or fixed-step DDA, this approach uses view-dependent proxy geometry rasterization to generate a per-pixel list of penetrated bricks, ensuring front-to-back processing and tighter ray segments.

title: Acceleration of direct volume rendering with texture slabs on programmable graphics hardware
abstract: This thesis proposes an efficient method to accelerate ray based volume rendering with texture slabs using programmable graphics hardware. In this method, empty space skipping and early ray termination are utilized without performing any preprocessing on CPU side. The acceleration structure is created on the fly by making use of depth buffer efficiently on Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) side. In the proposed method, texture slices are grouped together to form a texture slab. Rendering all the slabs from front to back viewing order in multiple rendering passes generates the resulting volume image. Slab silhouette maps (SSM) are created to identify and skip empty spaces along the ray direction at pixel level. These maps are created from the alpha component of the slab and stored in the depth buffer. In addition to the empty region information, SSM also contains information about the terminated rays. The method relies on hardware z-occlusion culling that is realized by means of SSMs to accelerate ray traversals. The cost of generating this acceleration data structure is very small compared to the total rendering time

The method relies on creating "Slab Silhouette Maps" (SSM) from texture slabs to identify empty spaces and terminated rays, storing this information in the depth buffer.

title: Adaptation of Dual Contouring and Marching Cubes Algorithms for 3D Reconstruction of the Human Lumbar Spine
abstract: The article deals with the problem of three-dimensional reconstruction of the human lumbar spine using the Marching Cubes and Dual Contouring surface triangulation algorithms for subsequent planning of a surgical intervention based on the analysis of digital computed tomography images. 3D reconstructions of the human lumbar spine are presented, as well as the results of a comparative analysis of the developed methods according to the following criteria: mesh generation speed; the number of generated cells; the absence of conflict situations (intersections of the surface). The optimal algorithm for solving the problem is determined on the basis of a comparative analysis.В статье рассматривается задача трехмерной реконструкции поясничного отдела позвоночника человека алгоритмами триангуляции поверхности Marching Cubes и Dual Contouring для последующего планирования хирургического вмешательства на основе анализа цифровых компьютерно-томографических изображений. cited.name: MPI Volume Rendering (3D Decomposition)
ctx: MPI Volume Rendering (3D Decomposition) is a distributed memory parallel volume rendering technique that partitions a 3D scalar volume dataset into a 3D grid of subdomains, assigning each subdomain to a distinct MPI process for independent ray casting.
It solves the scalability problem of rendering large volumetric datasets that exceed the memory or compute capacity of a single node by distributing both data and computation across a cluster.

It differs from Parallel Volume Rendering via k-d Tree Subdivision and Binary-Swap Compositing by using fixed-axis aligned subdomains rather than k-d tree based spatial subdivision, which avoids the overhead of tree construction but may lead to load imbalance if the volume density is non-uniform.

title: Add 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP notebook
abstract: ## Summary Adds `gauss_splat_mvp.ipynb` — a single, self-contained Jupyter notebook that implements the core of [3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., SIGGRAPH 2023)](https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/) in pure PyTorch, with no custom CUDA kernels. It is intended as a teaching / "grind on the math" reference rather than a production renderer. What's in it: - **Camera model**: pinhole `PinholeCamera` + `look_at` (OpenCV/COLMAP convention). - **Gaussian parameterization**: mean, scale (log-space), rotation (unit quaternion), per-Gaussian RGB color, opacity. Covariance built as `Σ = R S Sᵀ Rᵀ` so it's automatically symmetric PSD. - **Forward rasterizer**: - World→camera transform of means. - 3D covariance transformed into camera frame. - 2D screen-space covariance via the EWA / Zwicker-style projection Jacobian: `Σ_2d = J W Σ Wᵀ Jᵀ` plus a small isotropic dilation/blur for stability. - Depth sort and per-pixel front-to-back alpha compositing (same volume-rendering equation as NeRF, with anisotropic 2D Gaussian weights). - **Demo**: 5 hand-placed colored 3D Gaussians rendered from 4 training cameras + 1 held-out novel camera. We then init 40 random Gaussians and fit them to the training images by Adam on photometric L1 + MSE for 600 iterations. Final mean training loss is ~5e-4 and the held-out novel view matches the GT cleanly. - **Closing markdown**: explicit list of what's intentionally skipped vs. real 3DGS (tile-based CUDA rasterizer, spherical-harmonics view-dependent color, adaptive density control, real captures, SSIM losses). The notebook is committed with outputs already executed (loss curve + before/after grid embedded), so it renders nicely on GitHub without re-running. End-to-end run takes ~30 s on CPU on a 64×64 image. ## Review & Testing Checklist for Human - [ ] Open `gauss_splat_mvp.ipynb` and skim the math sections — sanity-check the projection-Jacobian formula and the alpha-compositing recurrence match what you expect. - [ ] Run all cells top to bottom in a fresh kernel and confirm the loss curve is monotonically decreasing and the final fit/novel-view grid roughly matches the embedded one. - [ ] Confirm the notebook fits how you want this kind of tutorial material organized in this repo (it's a standalone topic from the diffusion-world-model work). Happy to move it into a subfolder, add it to the README, or split it into multiple notebooks if you'd prefer. ### Notes - Dependencies are already in `requirements.txt` (`torch`, `numpy`, `matplotlib`). - `argsort` for the depth sort is non-differentiable across order changes — gradients flow through values given the ordering. This is also true of the production 3DGS rasterizer and is fine for a fit-from-scratch demo. - I deliberately kept the rasterizer as a `for i in range(N)` Python loop over Gaussians rather than vectorizing over all `(H, W, N)` at once — easier to read, and 40 Gaussians × 64×64 image is plenty fast on CPU. Easy to vectorize later if useful. - If you'd like the next step (e.g. add adaptive densification / pruning, swap to spherical-harmonics color, or scale up to a real COLMAP scene), just say the word and I'll layer it on top. Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/6b623c13251c4f10b5132c599e1ca55b

cited.name: 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP
ctx: 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP is a self-contained, pure-PyTorch implementation of the core 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering algorithm, designed as a teaching reference rather than a production renderer.

It solves the problem of understanding the mathematical pipeline of projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and rasterizing them via alpha compositing, without relying on custom CUDA kernels or optimized tile-based rasterization.
It differs from production implementations by using explicit Python loops for rasterization and omitting spherical harmonics, adaptive density control, and hardware-accelerated sorting.

title: Add `dual_contour` (DC+QEF) mesh extraction op
abstract: # Add `dual_contour` (DC + QEF) mesh extraction op ## Overview Adds `dual_contour`, a CUDA dual-contouring surface mesher that turns a narrow-band signed distance field on an OnIndex grid into a triangle mesh, alongside the existing `marching_cubes`. It composes directly with the `reinitialize_sdf` / `retopologize_sdf` ops, which produce exactly the kind of clean narrow-band SDF it consumes. The op is built on the NanoVDB VoxelBlockManager (VBM): the $3 \times 3 \times 3$ box stencil is decoded once per voxel and reused by every downstream stage. It returns `(vertices, faces, normals)` as three `JaggedTensor`s jagged over the grid batch — vertices and normals are `float32` of shape `[B, -1, 3]`, faces are `int64` of shape `[B, -1, 3]` with grid-local indices, and normals are the normalized SDF gradient at each vertex. ## Algorithm For each cube cell whose 8 corners are all active and straddle the isovalue, one vertex is placed by minimizing a quadratic error function (QEF) over the 12 edge zero-crossings $\mathbf{p}_i$ and their interpolated gradient normals $\mathbf{n}_i$: $$E(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i \big[\, \mathbf{n}_i \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}_i) \,\big]^2 .$$ Geometrically each term is the squared distance to the tangent plane at a crossing, so the minimizer best-fits all of them and snaps onto sharp features that a plain crossing-average would round off. Setting $\partial E / \partial \mathbf{x} = 0$ gives the $3 \times 3$ normal equations $$A\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}, \qquad A = \sum_i \mathbf{n}_i \mathbf{n}_i^{\top}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \sum_i \mathbf{n}_i \,(\mathbf{n}_i \cdot \mathbf{p}_i),$$ solved with a closed-form symmetric solve, re-centred on the crossing centroid and Tikhonov-regularized for stability in flat / underconstrained cells. Connectivity is the dual of marching cubes: for each sign-changing minimal grid edge, the 4 cells sharing that edge each contribute their vertex to one quad; quads are split into triangles and oriented outward by the SDF gradient. Triangle output is deterministic (per-cell count -> cumsum -> write), and unreferenced vertices are pruned. Optional cluster-collapse decimation: `reduce = F` collapses uniform $F \times F \times F$ index-space blocks of surface cells to a single QEF-solved vertex each ($\sim F^2$ fewer vertices); `adaptivity` keeps feature cells at full detail and only collapses "flat" coarse blocks (those whose cells' edge normals are well aligned). Connectivity merges for free, since quads referencing cells that collapsed to the same vertex become degenerate and are dropped. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["narrow-band SDF on OnIndex grid"] --> B["gatherFusedKernel: one VBM decode/voxel → neighbour table + gradient + surface flag + coord"] B --> C["compact surface cells"] C --> D{"decimate?"} D -- "reduce = 1, adaptivity = 0" --> E["QEF: one vertex per surface cell"] D -- "reduce / adaptivity" --> F["cluster cells → one merged QEF vertex per cluster"] E --> G["connectivity: quad per sign-changing minimal edge → triangles, oriented by the SDF gradient"] F --> G G --> H["prune unreferenced vertices + normalise normals"] H --> I["(vertices, faces, normals) JaggedTensors"] ``` ## Relationship to OpenVDB `VolumeToMesh` This follows the dual-contouring approach of OpenVDB's `tools/VolumeToMesh.h`, but is a leaner VBM-native reimplementation that diverges in two deliberate ways: it places vertices by a QEF least-squares solve (classic Dual Contouring) rather than by averaging the edge crossings (the "mass point" `VolumeToMesh` uses by default), and it decimates by simple cluster-collapse rather than `VolumeToMesh`'s seam-stitched octree region merge. It does not reproduce `VolumeToMesh`'s marching-cubes-style ambiguous-cell handling or its quad output (we always triangulate). For the watertight, smooth, isotropic narrow-band SDFs this op targets, these simplifications are reasonable. ## References (cited in the source) - T. Ju, F. Losasso, S. Schaefer, J. Warren, "Dual Contouring of Hermite Data", ACM TOG 21(3) / SIGGRAPH 2002 — the core method (QEF vertex placement on edge Hermite data, dual connectivity, octree adaptive simplification our decimation is a simplified form of). - M. Garland, P. Heckbert, "Surface Simplification Using Quadric Error Metrics", SIGGRAPH 1997 — the quadric error metric $A = \sum_i \mathbf{n}_i \mathbf{n}_i^{\top}$ that the vertex placement minimizes. - L. Kobbelt, M. Botsch, U. Schwanecke, H.-P. Seidel, "Feature Sensitive Surface Extraction from Volume Data", SIGGRAPH 2001 — placing the vertex at the intersection of the edge-crossing tangent planes. - W. Lorensen, H. Cline, "Marching Cubes: A High Resolution 3D Surface Construction Algorithm", SIGGRAPH 1987 — the sign-based isosurface extraction that dual contouring is the dual of. ## Shared VoxelBlockManager scaffolding Factors the NanoVDB VBM scaffolding shared by the VBM-based ops into a new header `src/fvdb/detail/utils/cuda/VoxelBlockManagerHelper.h`: the grid/buffer type aliases, the block width, the build-once `VBMHelper`, and the per-block decode helpers (`vbmDecodeBlock`, the `VbmFaceStencil` read, and the `vbmDecodeFaceStencil` preamble). `ReinitializeSdf` is refactored onto this header (its previous `VBM_FACES_BEGIN` macro is replaced by the shared, type-safe device helpers). The two ops still write their own per-voxel neighbour read — they differ in which neighbours they touch (6 faces vs the full 27-entry box stencil) — but the decode is now defined once. ## Public API and wiring - `Grid.dual_contour(field, iso=0.0, reduce=1, adaptivity=0.0)` and `GridBatch.dual_contour(...)`. - Functional entrypoints `fvdb.functional.dual_contour_single` / `dual_contour_batch`. - pybind binding `_fvdb_cpp.dual_contour` and the corresponding `.pyi` stub. - `src/fvdb/detail/ops/DualContour.{h,cu}`, added to the CUDA build in `src/CMakeLists.txt`. ## Tests `tests/unit/test_dc.py` covers both validity and analytic ground truth: - Valid closed genus-0 mesh on a sphere SDF: in-range non-degenerate triangles, no boundary or non-manifold edges, and Euler characteristic $V - E + F = 2$. - Analytic planar SDF reproduced exactly: interior vertices lie on the plane $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d + \mathrm{iso}$ and carry the plane normal $\mathbf{n}$ to float precision (QEF reproduces planes exactly). - Sphere radius / normals: every vertex within a sub-voxel band of the analytic radius, with radial normals. - Composition with `reinitialize_sdf` and `retopologize_sdf(pad=True)`. - Extent agreement with `marching_cubes` (cross-implementation sanity check). - Batch-vs-single parity on the non-decimated path. - Decimation bounds (`reduce=4` strictly fewer vertices; `adaptivity=0.5` non-empty, no more than full detail). - Empty-surface case returns correctly-shaped `(0, 3)` outputs. ## Assumptions and limitations - Field is cast to `float32` for the SDF; the QEF accumulators are `double` internally. - A `>= ~3-voxel` half-width band is required for a watertight result (e.g. from `retopologize_sdf(band=3)`). - Decimation (`reduce > 1` or `adaptivity > 0`) accumulates per-cluster QEFs with double `atomicAdd`, so decimated vertex positions are not bit-reproducible run to run; the decimation tests use count / validity / tolerance assertions rather than exact equality.

title: Add experimental micro voxel volume rendering with sparse brickmap
abstract: ## Summary Implements an experimental fullscreen voxel raymarching pass that renders a sparse brickmap volume between the main geometry pass and sky rendering. The system uses a two-level DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer) algorithm to efficiently traverse a coarse brick grid and fine-grained voxel data, with proper depth integration for compositing with rasterized geometry. ## Key Changes - **VoxelRaymarchPass**: New render pass that executes fullscreen voxel raymarching after MainRenderPass, writing hardware depth so voxels depth-test correctly against rasterized geometry and subsequent passes (sky, fog, bloom) - **Sparse Brickmap Structure**: - Coarse grid stores uint32 entries per 8³ brick cell: empty sentinel (0xFFFFFFFF), uniform-material sentinel (0x80000000 | material), or index into brick pool - Only mixed (surface) bricks occupy GPU memory; fully-buried terrain collapses to uniform entries - Significantly reduces memory footprint compared to dense voxel grids - **Procedural Demo Volume Generation** (`generateVoxelDemoVolume`): - Generates terrain heightfield using Perlin noise with FBM (fractional Brownian motion) - Carves caves below surface crust - Adds ore speckles and floating crystal spheres - Parallelized column fill using thread pool for performance - Compacts dense scratch grid into sparse brickmap on GPU - **Two-Level DDA Raymarching**: - Coarse pass traverses brick-sized cells - Fine pass descends into stored bricks for voxel-level detail - Uniform bricks hit immediately without fine traversal - Proper normal calculation for surface lighting - **Lighting & Shading**: - Sun shadow support via voxel raycast from hit point - Hemisphere ambient lighting (sky-tinted above, ground bounce below) - Per-voxel albedo variation using hash noise for readability - Integrates with atmosphere system for sun direction/color/intensity - **Render Graph Integration**: VelocityPass moved after VoxelRaymarchPass so motion vectors include voxel pixels; temporal denoisers read stale velocity (acceptable for low-frequency effects) - **ImGui Controls**: Added "Micro Voxels (Experimental)" panel with: - Enable/disable toggle - Volume origin and voxel size adjustment - Ray step count configuration - Grid size selection (128³, 256³, 512³) - Sun shadow and ambient intensity controls - Volume regeneration and shader hot-reload buttons - GPU/dense memory usage statistics - **Metal Shader** (`3d_voxel_raymarch.metal`): Fullscreen triangle pass implementing two-level DDA with proper AABB intersection, voxel traversal, and lighting calculations ## Implementation Details - Includes ` ` and ` ` headers for memory operations and parallelization - Lazy initialization: demo volume generated on first enable to avoid startup overhead - Graceful fallback: voxel pipeline creation wrapped in try-catch to allow shader compilation failures - Per-frame uniform buffers updated with camera/sun data each frame - Brick pool and index grid buffers recreated when grid dimensions change - Comprehensive statistics logging (solid voxel count, fill percentage, brick counts, GPU memory usage) https://claude.ai/code/session_01S3jx9NJjEtqcGPPkwebudm

cited.name: Sparse Brickmap Volume Rendering
ctx: Sparse Brickmap Volume Rendering is a voxel rendering technique that uses a two-level data structure (coarse brick grid and fine voxel bricks) to render sparse volumes efficiently, integrating hardware depth for correct compositing with rasterized geometry.
It builds on Sparse Page Table and Brick Pool by replacing the generic page-table indirection with a fixed 8^3 brick hierarchy optimized for two-level Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal.
Unlike dense voxel grids, it significantly reduces memory footprint by collapsing fully-buried terrain into uniform entries and storing only mixed (surface) bricks in a compact pool.

title: Add prbvolpath_sm: new unbiased differentiable volume integrator with sample matching
abstract: This PR adds `prbvolpath_sm`, a volumetric integrator that estimates extinction gradients with sample matching. > Ruihan Yu, Yu-Chen Wang, Jingwang Ling, Feng Xu, Shuang Zhao. > **Sample Matching for Joint Extinction Gradient Estimation in Differentiable > Volume Rendering.** ACM Transactions on Graphics 45(4), 2026. > [paper](https://auroraryan0301.github.io/samplematching/static/papers/sample_matching_paper.pdf) > · [supplementary](https://auroraryan0301.github.io/samplematching/static/papers/sample_matching_supplementary.pdf) > · [project page](https://auroraryan0301.github.io/samplematching/) > · [doi:10.1145/3811329](https://doi.org/10.1145/3811329) Denser media scatter more light toward the camera and also block more of the light passing through. These two terms of the extinction gradient have opposite signs. `prbvolpath` estimates them at unrelated points; `prbvolpath_sm` estimates both at the same points on each path segment, which cancels most of the variance. The primal image is the same as `prbvolpath`; all changes are in the adjoint pass. The adjoint pass runs as two kernels. The path replay loop writes one record per segment, and a second kernel reads the records and traces new rays for the gradient samples. `segment_slots` sets how many records a path may keep. Any number of slots is unbiased. By default it is `max_depth + 1`, so every segment gets a record. With one slot, a path keeps a single segment chosen by weighted reservoir sampling; this setting is also registered as `prbvolpath_sm_linear`, and the default as `prbvolpath_sm_quad`. Spectral variants and extinction that varies across channels are supported. Polarized variants and forward mode are not, same as `prbvolpath`. ## Testing Bunny cloud, one A40, 8000 iterations. PSNR is measured on the held-out view at 256 spp: | | `prbvolpath` | `prbvolpath_sm_linear` | `prbvolpath_sm_quad` (default) | |---|---|---|---| | gradient variance, same spp | 1 | 0.29 | 0.25 | | PSNR | 26.66 dB | 35.71 dB | 38.35 dB | | time | 41.6 h | 22.6 h | 26.3 h | ![extinction gradient mean and variance](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AuroraRyan0301/mitsuba3/pr-figures/fig_grad_z.png) Gradients agree with finite differences within 1% in RGB and spectral variants. The test suite passes on `cuda_ad_rgb`, `cuda_ad_spectral`, `llvm_ad_rgb` and `llvm_ad_spectral`. ## Checklist - [x] My code follows the [style guidelines](https://mitsuba.readthedocs.io/en/latest/src/developer_guide.html#coding-style) of this project - [x] My changes generate no new warnings - [x] My code also compiles for `cuda_*` and `llvm_*` variants. cited.name: Sample Matching for Extinction Gradients
ctx: Sample Matching for Extinction Gradients is a differentiable volumetric path tracing method that reduces the variance of extinction coefficient gradients by evaluating the positive scattering term and the negative transmittance term at shared spatial locations along each path segment.

Unlike the base Volumetric Path Tracing method, which estimates these two opposing terms at unrelated points, this technique exploits their negative correlation to cancel variance, while maintaining the same primal rendering output.
The method operates in two distinct phases: a primal pass identical to the base Volumetric Path Tracing integrator, and an adjoint pass that computes gradients via a two-kernel pipeline.

cited.name: Sample Matching
ctx: Sample Matching is a differentiable volume rendering estimator that implements sample matching to reduce variance in gradient estimation for volumetric path tracing.

It solves the high-variance gradient problem in differentiable volume rendering by estimating the transmittance and scattering terms of the Differentiable Radiative Transfer Equation (DRTE) at the same spatial points on each path segment, causing their opposite-sign contributions to cancel.
Unlike the base prbvolpath method which estimates these terms at unrelated points, Sample Matching confines all modifications to the adjoint pass while keeping the primal image rendering identical.

title: Add Rayleigh scattering phase function (importance-sampling compatible)
abstract: ## Summary Add a Rayleigh scattering phase function as a new material / phase function type for use in `Constant` volumes (fog/atmosphere). Must integrate with the existing `Pdf`-based importance sampling infrastructure — same path as Lambertian surfaces and the future volume NEE path. ## Phase function Rayleigh scattering derives from dipole radiation. The unpolarized (averaged) phase function is: ``` p(cosθ) = (3/4) × (1 + cos²θ) ``` Key properties: - **Two equal lobes**: forward (θ=0) and backward (θ=π) at 1.5× the isotropic average - **Null at 90°**: zero scattering at right angles - **Normalized**: ∫ p(θ) dΩ = 1 over the sphere ## Implementation plan ### 1. New `Pdf` variant: `RayleighSphere` **File:** `src/shading/pdf.rs` A `Pdf` variant that samples directions from the `(1 + cos²θ)` distribution and evaluates the corresponding probability density. **Sampling:** - The CDF is invertible in closed form - `cosθ` can be sampled by solving a cubic: `cos³θ + 3cosθ + 4(1-2ξ) = 0` for uniform random ξ ∈ [0,1] - Alternatively, rejection sampling from a bounding distribution (e.g., 1.5 × uniform) is simpler and efficient (75% acceptance rate) - φ sampled uniformly on [0, 2π] **Density:** ```rust fn density(&self, direction: Vector3) -> f64 { let cos_theta = self.w.dot(direction); // whichever axis is "forward" (3.0 / 4.0) * (1.0 + cos_theta * cos_theta) / (4.0 * PI) // normalized over sphere } ``` Wait — the `(1 + cos²θ)` distribution is normally defined with respect to the scattering angle θ between incident and scattered directions. For a `Pdf` variant, the reference direction should come from the incident ray direction, not a fixed axis. Actually: `Pdf` variants like `CosineHemisphere` use an `Onb` (orthonormal basis) oriented to the surface normal. For Rayleigh, the scattering is symmetric around the incident direction — the forward lobe points along the original ray direction, the backward lobe points opposite. The phase function only depends on `cosθ = ω_i · ω_o`. So the `Pdf` variant needs to encode the incident direction (or its reverse) to define the axis. A clean approach: `RayleighSphere { incident: Vector3 }` where `incident` is the direction the light came from. Then: - `density(dir)` = `(3/(16π)) × (1 + (incident.dot(dir))²)` — the full sphere normalization (divide by 4π since we're sampling over the sphere, not just `cosθ`) - `sample()` = generates `cosθ` from inverse CDF of `(1+cos²θ)`, φ uniformly, builds direction relative to `incident` ### 2. New material: `RayleighPhaseFunction` **File:** `src/shading/materials/rayleigh.rs` (new) Mirrors `Isotropic` structurally: ```rust pub struct Rayleigh { reflectance_texture: Arc , // albedo color emittance_texture: Arc , // always SolidColor::BLACK } impl Material for Rayleigh { fn scatter(&self, ray: Ray, ray_hit: &RayHit, hw: &HeroWavelengths) -> Option { Some(ScatterRecord::Pdf(Pdf::RayleighSphere { incident: (-ray.direction).unit_vector(), // incoming direction })) } fn brdf(&self, outgoing: Vector3, incident: Vector3, ...) -> ColorSpectrum { let albedo = self.reflectance_texture.value(u, v, p); let cos_theta = outgoing.dot(incident); albedo * (3.0 / 4.0) * (1.0 + cos_theta * cos_theta) / (4.0 * PI) } fn reflectance(&self, u: f64, v: f64, p: Point) -> ColorSpectrum { self.reflectance_texture.value(u, v, p) } } ``` ### 3. Wavelength-dependent scattering coefficient **File:** `src/geometry/volumes/constant.rs` (or a new volume type) Rayleigh's key feature is the λ⁻⁴ dependence. The scattering coefficient at each wavelength is: ``` σ_s(λ) = σ_s(λ₀) × (λ₀ / λ)⁴ ``` When used inside a `Constant` volume, the `intersect()` method currently uses a single `density` (σ_t) for distance sampling. For spectrally-varying density, you'd need: - Sample the distance using the **maximum** σ across all hero wavelengths (to avoid bias from different path lengths) - Apply per-wavelength transmittance weighting via MIS or track a spectral throughput vector This is a secondary concern — even without per-wavelength σ, Rayleigh still gives nice angular behavior. The λ⁻⁴ effect is the cherry on top. ### 4. `cos_theta` handling Same issue as #174 — volume scattering uses `∫ phase × L dΩ` (no cosine), so the `cos_theta` term in the Pdf path needs to be 1.0 for phase functions. The fix for #174 applies here identically. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] `Pdf::RayleighSphere` variant with correct sampling and density - [ ] `Rayleigh` material struct implementing `Material` trait, returning `Pdf(RayleighSphere)` from `scatter()` - [ ] `brdf()` returns `albedo × (3/(16π)) × (1 + cos²θ)` — the full phase function value including normalization - [ ] `brdf / pdf` ratio cancels correctly: `albedo × (3/16π)(1+cos²θ) / ((3/16π)(1+cos²θ))` = `albedo` - [ ] Works end-to-end with mixture PDF, MIS, and emissive importance sampling (same infrastructure as #174) - [ ] Usable from `Constant` volume construction (a `Constant::new_rayleigh()` constructor or a phase_function parameter) ## Out of scope - Per-wavelength scattering coefficient (λ⁻⁴ spectral variation) — deferred to a follow-up issue - Polarization tracking (Rayleigh is inherently polarized; unpolarized average is used) - Mie / Henyey-Greenstein phase functions (separate issue)

title: Add Spherical Beta view-dependent color for PLY gaussian splats
abstract: Exploratory draft: renders Spherical Beta (SB) view-dependent color for PLY gaussian splats. SB is the specular model from [Deformable Beta Splatting](https://rongliu-leo.github.io/beta-splatting/) (Liu et al., SIGGRAPH 2025). It adds a few explicit specular lobes on top of the SH color: 2 lobes are 12 floats per splat, against 45 for SH bands 1-3. Related: - playcanvas/supersplat#1036 adds the same lobes to SuperSplat (load, render, edit, export). - nerfstudio-project/gsplat#1056 trains and exports them. Its Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark has SH degree 0 + 2 lobes beating SH degree 3 by +0.15 to +0.30 dB PSNR, at about 45% of the PLY size. **Changes:** - PLY files with `sb_params_*` properties now render their lobes. Each lobe adds `pow(max(dot(dir, axis), 0), 4 * exp(beta)) * softplus(rgb)` to the SH / base color. Files without the properties are unaffected. - The lobes are converted once at load (axis from the spherical angles, sharpness, activated color) and stored as half floats, one 16-byte texel per lobe per splat. The shader is left with one `pow` per lobe. - Up to 4 lobes are rendered. The trainers default to 2. - The color the lobes are added to is clamped to zero first, matching the trainer. Many splats have a negative base color, which would otherwise absorb part of the highlight. - Works in the unified and non-unified paths, on WebGL2 and WebGPU. - Splats with lobes but no SH now re-evaluate their color as the camera moves. - Uncompressed PLY only for now. Compressed PLY, SOG and SPZ have no place for the lobe data. **Scope: lobes only, not the Beta kernel:** Deformable Beta Splatting has two parts: the Spherical Beta color lobes, and the Beta kernel, which replaces the Gaussian falloff with `opacity * (1 - r²)^beta` and a hard cutoff. This PR only adds the lobes. - The kernel would be much harder. It changes the splat shape, so it touches every renderer (quad, compute, shadow, picking), the quad extent and the bounds / culling math. It also needs another per-splat value, and SOG / splat-transform support. - It most likely brings less. The paper's ablation puts the kernel at +0.16 to +0.21 dB PSNR, against +0.07 to +0.22 dB plus a 55% smaller file for the lobes. - Only the paper's own code trains the kernel; gsplat#1056 keeps Gaussians. Files using the kernel, such as the paper's pretrained scenes on Hugging Face, won't render correctly with this PR. **Examples:** - `gaussian-splatting/viewer` sets `app.scene.gsplat.colorUpdateAngle = 0`. View-dependent color (SH or lobes) is then re-evaluated on every frame the camera moves, instead of in 10° steps, so highlights can be compared exactly. **Try it:** - Viewer: https://engine-ipzsitwwq-playcanvas.vercel.app/#/gaussian-splatting/viewer - Drag one of these sample PLYs into the viewer, then reload the page before dropping the other. Both are the same bonsai scene, trained separately by the author of the PRs above: - [SH0_SB2.ply](https://drive.google.com/file/d/100z7Dw6OdpDDnW5m2RCcuFPe_TbIZekh/view?usp=drive_link): SH degree 0 + 2 lobes (49 MB) - [SH3_SB0.ply](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1QHkVx2vRs8zslxCzpCmj25gLv6WsLBtA/view?usp=drive_link): SH degree 3, no lobes (111 MB) - The scenes are not axis aligned, so the orbit camera behaves strangely around them. **Specular comparison** (same view): SH degree 3 SH degree 0 + 2 lobes |

title: Add voxel-based ray tracing for GI and specular reflections
abstract: ## Summary Implements a new voxel-based ray tracing system using DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer) traversal through a 128³ block-occupancy grid. This provides an alternative global illumination method and a fallback for specular reflections when screen-space ray tracing misses. ## Key Changes - **New voxel_rt.glsl module**: Core DDA ray tracing implementation featuring: - `VoxelDDA()`: Efficient voxel grid traversal with axis-aligned hit detection - `SampleVoxelLighting()`: LPV-based lighting lookup at hit surfaces - `ApplyVoxelRT()`: Hemisphere GI sampling (drop-in replacement for SSRT) - `VoxelReflectionFallback()`: Specular reflection fallback when SSR coverage is incomplete - **Settings additions** (settings.glsl): - New `VOXEL_GI` indirect effect mode (option 6) - Configurable parameters: `VOXEL_GI_SAMPLES`, `VOXEL_GI_STEPS`, `VOXEL_REFL_STEPS` - Optional `VOXEL_RT_REFLECTIONS` feature flag for reflection fallback - **Integration points**: - composite1.fsh: Conditional inclusion and application of `ApplyVoxelRT()` when `VOXEL_GI` mode is active - specular.glsl: Optional voxel reflection fallback integrated after SSR with coverage-based blending - **Stability fixes** (composite6.fsh): - Added epsilon guards to prevent division by zero in `invTonemap()`, `FastCatmulRom()`, and TAA blending calculations ## Implementation Details - Requires LPV (Light Propagation Volumes) and `GL_ARB_shader_image_load_store` support - Uses feet-relative world-space coordinates consistent with existing camera systems - DDA traversal includes ray bias to avoid self-intersection and handles near-parallel rays gracefully - GI mode combines sky occlusion with LPV colour bleeding for realistic indirect lighting - Reflection fallback scales voxel lighting to match typical sky-reflection brightness ranges - Gracefully degrades to SSRT when voxel RT requirements aren't met https://claude.ai/code/session_01M5Hu8nctQxBQD7tn1sq9cN

cited.name: Voxel-based Ray Tracing for GI and Specular Reflections
ctx: A voxel-based ray tracing system that uses 3-D Digital Differential Analyzer (3D-DDA) traversal through a 128³ block-occupancy grid to provide global illumination (GI) and specular reflection fallbacks.
It serves as a drop-in replacement for Screen-Space Ray Tracing (SSRT) for GI and a fallback for Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) when coverage is incomplete.

Unlike Regular Grid Traversal which typically renders volumetric density, this method samples a pre-computed Light Propagation Volume (LPV) buffer at ray hit positions to compute indirect lighting and reflection color.

title: Add WebGPU ray tracing renderer with lighting and render tab
abstract: WebGPU-based ray tracing renderer as an alternative to the existing Three.js rasterizer, accessible via a dedicated Render tab in the header navigation. Includes directional lighting, shadow rays, and interactive controls. ### Core renderer (`webgpu-ray-tracer.ts`) - WGSL compute shader with DDA voxel grid traversal — each pixel casts a ray, steps through the 3D grid - Directional light source with diffuse (N·L) shading - Shadow rays via DDA traversal toward the sun for hard shadows on voxels and ground plane - Block colors from project palette via storage buffer - Ground plane with grid lines and shadow receiving - Subtle sky gradient background - Fullscreen triangle render pass to blit compute output to canvas - Exported pure functions (`packVoxelData`, `packPalette`, `buildUniformData`, `sunDirFromAngles`) for testability - `RenderSettings` interface with sensible defaults for all lighting parameters ### Render tab and UI - **Model/Render tab switcher** in the header nav bar — clicking Render switches the entire view mode - When in Render mode, modeling UI (block drawer, floating toolbar, objects panel) is hidden and replaced with a dedicated **Lighting sidebar**: - Sun Direction slider (0–360° azimuth) - Sun Elevation slider (5–90°) - Sun Intensity slider - Sun Color presets (Warm, White, Cool, Gold, Pink) - Ambient Light intensity slider - Shadow Strength slider - Reset to defaults button - Clicking Model switches back to the full modeling UI - Render tab gated on `WebGPURayTracer.isSupported()` ### Engine integration (`voxel-engine.ts`) - `setRayTracingEnabled(bool)` swaps between WebGL canvas and WebGPU canvas - Ray tracing auto-enables when entering the Render tab and auto-disables when switching back to Model - `setRenderSettings()` / `getRenderSettings()` for controlling lighting from the UI - Voxel data gathered from `ChunkManager.getVoxelAtWorldPos()` into flat buffer - Dirty tracking via store subscription — voxels and palette only re-uploaded on state change - Camera and lighting uniforms updated every frame (cheap write, always needed for orbit) - Existing orbit camera controls (right-click rotate, shift+click pan, scroll zoom) work on the ray traced view ```typescript // Toggle ray tracing on await engine.setRayTracingEnabled(true); // Update lighting engine.setRenderSettings({ sunAzimuth: 180, sunElevation: 45, sunIntensity: 1.5, ... }); ``` ### Tests - 21 unit tests covering voxel packing, palette packing, sun direction math, and uniform buffer layout (including lighting parameters) - All existing tests unaffected **Model tab:** ![Model tab](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b0d90d4c-f559-4cf4-aead-ad095c2cb3e3) **Render tab:** ![Render tab](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1922a245-a5c3-4a1b-ae2d-034a537e1671) Original prompt > could you give a web GPU based ray tracing renderer system a shot? --- 💡 You can make Copilot smarter by setting up custom instructions, customizing its development environment and configuring Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. title: AltNeRF: Learning Robust Neural Radiance Field via Alternating Depth-Pose Optimization
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have shown promise in generating realistic novel views from sparse scene images. However, existing NeRF approaches often encounter challenges due to the lack of explicit 3D supervision and imprecise camera poses, resulting in suboptimal outcomes. To tackle these issues, we propose AltNeRF---a novel framework designed to create resilient NeRF representations using self-supervised monocular depth estimation (SMDE) from monocular videos, without relying on known camera poses. SMDE in AltNeRF masterfully learns depth and pose priors to regulate NeRF training. The depth prior enriches NeRF's capacity for precise scene geometry depiction, while the pose prior provides a robust starting point for subsequent pose refinement. Moreover, we introduce an alternating algorithm that harmoniously melds NeRF outputs into SMDE through a consistence-driven mechanism, thus enhancing the integrity of depth priors. This alternation empowers AltNeRF to progressively refine NeRF representations, yielding the synthesis of realistic novel views. Extensive experiments showcase the compelling capabilities of AltNeRF in generating high-fidelity and robust novel views that closely resemble reality.

cited.name: AltNeRF
ctx: AltNeRF is a framework for creating resilient Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representations from monocular videos without relying on known camera poses.

It solves the problem of suboptimal reconstruction caused by the lack of explicit 3D supervision and imprecise initial camera poses by using an alternating algorithm to harmonize NeRF outputs with self-supervised monocular depth estimation (SMDE) priors.

Unlike methods that strictly align rendered depth with priors, AltNeRF uses error-tolerant regularization because the depth priors themselves are not precise, allowing it to progressively refine both the scene geometry and camera poses.

title: An Accelerating Texture-based Volume Rendering Algorithm with BVH
abstract: A method to accelerate 3D texture-based volume rendering is proposed based on hierarchical bounding volumes(BVH).First,a post-classification 3D texture volume rendering is realized using GPU fragment shaders.Then,the original volume data is divided based on space position layer by layer according to the height of BVH tree.In each layer,the volumes corresponding to BVH tree nodes are subdivided into eight sub-volumes along three orthogonal coordinate axes.The bounding volumes are established for sub-volumes and the correlative information is stored in the corresponding BVH tree nodes.Finally,when rendering the volume by traversing BVH tree,information of BVH tree nodes is read for judging whether the corresponding sub-volume should be rendered or jumped.The experimental results show that good accelerating effects can be obtained when combining this method with 3D texture volume rendering based on GPU.

title: An intuitive and semi-automated transfer function design for interactive region of interest-based direct volume rendering in mixed reality head mounted devices
abstract: Direct volume rendering (DVR) enables the visual exploration of regions of interest (ROI) in a volume in an interactive manner. Mixed reality head mounted devices (MR-HMDs) have the potential to expand the utility of DVR. MR-HMDs enable not only the high-quality and stereoscopic DVR but also its in-situ visualizations of complementary data to assist in the real-world tasks of users. The state-of-the-art MR-HMD works, however, mainly focus on investigating the feasibility and effectiveness of DVR to target MR applications. The interactive ROI-based exploration of DVR has been severely limited in prior research, and user optimization is still confined to the primitive image manipulation of pre-configured ROIs (e.g., view rotation). In this work, we propose an interactive and semi-automated exploration approach for ROI-based DVRs in MR-HMDs by introducing a new MR-HMD-based rendering parameters (i.e., transfer functions (TFs)) optimization and utilizing the built-in biometric interfaces. Using eye-gazing and hand gestures, users can select ROIs within an initial DVR visually and interactively. Our MR-TF approach (named hereafter) then automatically optimizes the corresponding TF toward ensuring the visibility of ROIs. Additionally, our MR-TF approach addresses a critical rendering issue in MR-HMDs, i.e., the color perception of ROIs should be consistent regardless of the variations of intermixing physical backgrounds. Our MR-TF approach quantifies the color perception and integrates to the TF optimization for enhanced ROIs. We achieve on-device implementation of our MR-TF approach on the commercial MR-HMD with low computing capability, Microsoft HoloLens 2. Our evaluations with different types of volumes demonstrate the capabilities and practicality of our MR-TF approach.

cited.name: MR-TF Approach
ctx: The MR-TF approach is an interactive method for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) in Mixed Reality Head-Mounted Displays (MR-HMDs) that combines biometric Region of Interest (ROI) selection with automatic Transfer Function (TF) optimization.

It solves the problem of manually tuning TFs for specific anatomical or material structures in complex volumes by allowing users to select a target region via eye-gaze and finger-pointing, then automatically optimizing TF parameters to maximize the visibility of that ROI while maintaining context.

It differs from general optimization methods by integrating real-time biometric input and optimizing for visibility tolerance weighted against physical background contrast, specifically tailored for low-spec MR hardware.

title: Are there other/better voxel meshing algorithm than Greedy Meshing
abstract: For the project I'm working, I have large voxel data I need to visualize within a mesh. While searching I rapidly find the Meshing in a Minecraft Game article article, written by mikolalysenko back in 2012, and according to my research seems to only source everyone is referring to answer this question. He describes three algorithm to solving this problem: the Stupid, the Culled and the Greedy. The two first are really non efficient, so I made a Python version of the code he provides for my project with two tweaks: I use Numba to speed up computations I directly compute the triangle vertices instead of quadrilaterals, to mach to our meshing function implementation @njit() def greedy_mesh(volume, dims): def f(i, j, k): return(volume[i + dims[0] * (j + dims[1] * k)]) points = [] # Sweep over 3-axes for d in range(3): u = (d + 1) % 3 v = (d + 2) % 3 x = [0, 0, 0] q = [0, 0, 0] mask = [0] * (dims[u] * dims[v]) q[d] = 1 x[d] = -1 while x[d] = 0 else False b = f(x[0] + q[0], x[1] + q[1], x[2] + q[2]) if x[d] < (dims[d] - 1) else False mask[n] = a != b n += 1 x[u] += 1 x[u] = 0 x[v] += 1 x[d] += 1 n = 0 # Generate mesh for mask using lexicographic ordering for j in range(0, dims[v]): i = 0 while i < dims[u]: if (n < len(mask)) and mask[n]: w = 1 # Compute width while (n + w < len(mask)) and (mask[n + w] and ((i + w) < dims[u])): w += 1 done = False h = 1 # Compute height (slighty awkward according to the autor) while (j + h) < dims[v]: for k in range(0, w): if not mask[n + k + h * dims[u]]: done = True break if done: break h += 1 # New quad x[u] = i; x[v] = j; du = [0, 0, 0] dv = [0, 0, 0] du[u] = w dv[v] = h # Triangles A = (x[0], x[1], x[2]) B = (x[0] + du[0], x[1] + du[1], x[2] + du[2]) C = (x[0] + du[0] + dv[0], x[1] + du[1] + dv[1], x[2] + du[2] + dv[2]) D = (x[0] + dv[0], x[1] + dv[1], x[2] + dv[2]) points.extend([A, B, C]) points.extend([A, C, D]) # Zero-out mask for l in range(0, h): for k in range(0, w): mask[n + k + l * dims[u]] = False i += w n += w else: i += 1 n += 1 # Unique set of points vertices = [i for i in set(points)] # Points indices = [] for p in points: indices.append(vertices.index(p)) return np.array(vertices), np.array(indices).reshape(-1, 3) I test out my code using the examples provides once again by mikolalysenko and it run perfectly fine. But then I tried to load bigger voxel data from our project (~ 300x300x300), and now the algorithm run for about 5s to process the data. Honestly I quite fast but not enough for usage, and we have much larger data sets. After a bit of profile, and without really any surprise, most of computation time is due to creation of the vertices and their indices at the end. Unfortunetly, this is the way the meshing function was created to work with and I'm not able to change this feature. That's finally leads my to my question: Is there today a voxel meshing algorithm better than Greedy Meshing that could helps me fulfill my requirements? Even if I believe there is no optimal solution for this kind of task (looks a bit like a P = NP problem), I cannot find alternative algorithms online even while looking for scientific papers. Do you have any suggestions or references regarding my problem?

cited.name: Greedy Meshing
ctx: Greedy meshing is a surface extraction algorithm that reduces the vertex and primitive count of a voxel mesh by merging adjacent, coplanar faces of identical material into maximal axis-aligned quads.

It solves the problem of excessive geometry in naive voxel rendering (where every exposed voxel face becomes a separate quad) by scanning the volume along each of the three principal axes and greedily expanding rectangles of identical visible faces.

Mask: A 2D boolean or integer array of size Du \times Dv (where u, v are the two axes perpendicular to the current sweep normal) used to track which cells in the current slice have been processed or to store the visibility/material state.

title: Art-directable multiple volumetric scattering

cited.name: Binary Greedy Meshing with Packed Quads
ctx: Binary Greedy Meshing (BGM) is a surface extraction algorithm that generates maximal axis-aligned quads from a binary voxel volume (solid/empty) by treating voxel slices as bitmasks and greedily expanding rectangles using bitwise operations.

Unlike Greedy Meshing, which typically processes individual faces or runs sequentially, BGM operates on packed binary planes (1 bit per voxel), allowing the entire greedy expansion to be performed with CPU-native bitwise instructions (trailing zeros, shifts, masks) rather than branching logic, significantly reducing…

The algorithm processes a voxel chunk by first generating face masks for all six directions, then grouping voxels by block type and ambient occlusion (AO) pattern into binary planes, and finally applying a bitwise greedy merge to each plane to emit quads.

title: Automatic size and variance determination for better surface splatting quality on close-up view
abstract: Surface splatting has been proven to be a viable alternative to traditional polygon rendering for highly detailed models. In terms of rendering performance, surface splatting has surpassed polygon rendering when it fully exploits today's graphics processing units (GPU). However, in terms of rendering quality, surface splatting could still be inferior to polygon rendering when the model is viewed close-up and when the size and variance of each splat is not computed properly. In this paper, we present a method that improves the image quality of surface splatting to the level comparable to polygonal rendering by automatically finding a suitable size and variance for each splat.

cited.name: Automatic Size and Variance Determination for Surface Splatting
ctx: This method improves the visual quality of surface splatting on close-up views by automatically computing the radius (ri) and variance (vi) for each splat to ensure hole-free rendering and smooth blending, comparable to polygon rendering.

Unlike methods that use global or fixed local variance and size, this approach calculates these parameters per-splat based on local point density, balancing blurriness and aliasing without manual user adjustment.

It builds on Splat Radius Adjustment Based on Normal Angle by providing the specific automatic formulas for size and variance that prevent the discontinuities and artifacts associated with improper parameter choices.

title: BC5 圧縮テクスチャ
abstract: # はじめに プログラムから, テクスチャ圧縮がしたいです. BC1, BC3, BC6h BC7についてはispc texture compressionを使おうと思っていましたが, BC5がないのです. https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/articles/fast-ispc-texture-compressor-update.html ガイドに仕様がちゃんと書いてあります. 簡単そうなので作ってしまいます. https://docs.microsoft.com/en-gb/windows/win32/direct3d10/d3d10-graphics-programming-guide-resources-block-compression#bc5 # ファイルフォーマット 4x4のブロックごとに圧縮するブロック圧縮です. BC4はRだけの1チャネル, BC5はRGの2チャネルを扱います. `4x4x2 = 32 bytes`を次の `tablex2 = 16 bytes`に圧縮します. BC5_UNORMとBC5_SNORMの2バリエーションです. 2つはシェーダでサンプルした場合, [0 1]の浮動小数点数になるか, [-1 1]の浮動小数点になるかが違います. テーブルは, 4x4の最小値と最大値が先頭に2バイト, 次に3bits x 16のテーブルへのインデックスが並びます. ```cpp /* MSB LSB | red_0 | 1 byte minimum color | red_1 | 1 byte maximum color | red_h | red_g | red_f | red_e | red_d | red_c | red_b | red_a | 3 bits x 8 | red_p | red_o | red_n | red_m | red_l | red_k | red_j | red_i | 3 bits x 8 */ ``` テーブルは明示的に持たず最大値, 最小値から計算します. UNORMとSNORMで１箇所異なりますが, 圧縮するだけならばどちらでも同じなので統一します. ```cpp static constexpr u32 Shift = 20; void createTable(s32 colors[8], s32 block[16]) { colors[0] = block[0]; colors[1] = block[0]; for(u32 i = 1; i < 16; ++i) { colors[0] = minimum(colors[0], block[i]); colors[1] = maximum(colors[1], block[i]); } colors[0] <<= Shift; colors[1] <<= Shift; if(colors[1] < colors[0]) { // 6 interpolated color values colors[2] = (6 * colors[0] + 1 * colors[1]) / 7; // bit code 010 colors[3] = (5 * colors[0] + 2 * colors[1]) / 7; // bit code 011 colors[4] = (4 * colors[0] + 3 * colors[1]) / 7; // bit code 100 colors[5] = (3 * colors[0] + 4 * colors[1]) / 7; // bit code 101 colors[6] = (2 * colors[0] + 5 * colors[1]) / 7; // bit code 110 colors[7] = (1 * colors[0] + 6 * colors[1]) / 7; // bit code 111 } else { // 4 interpolated color values colors[2] = (4 * colors[0] + 1 * colors[1]) / 5; // bit code 010 colors[3] = (3 * colors[0] + 2 * colors[1]) / 5; // bit code 011 colors[4] = (2 * colors[0] + 3 * colors[1]) / 5; // bit code 100 colors[5] = (1 * colors[0] + 4 * colors[1]) / 5; // bit code 101 colors[6] = 0; // bit code 110 colors[7] = 255<<Shift; // bit code 111 } } ``` ピクセル値に最も近いテーブルインデックスを検索して, 符号化します. ```cpp u64 findNearest(s32 colors[8], s32 x) { u32 index = 0; s32 mind = absolute(colors[0] - x); for(u32 i = 1; i < 8; ++i) { s32 d = absolute(colors[i] - x); if(d < mind) { mind = d; index = i; } } return index; } ``` # まとめ [GPUOpen Compressonator](https://gpuopen.com/compressonator/)と結果がことなるため, もっといい方法がありそうです.

cited.name: BC5 Compression
ctx: BC5 is a block compression format for 2-channel (RG) textures, compressing 4x4 blocks (32 bytes) into 16 bytes.
It supports two variants: BC5UNORM (outputs [0, 1] floats) and BC5SNORM (outputs [-1, 1] floats).
It is the 2-channel extension of BC4, which handles single-channel (R) data.

title: Beyond UV Mapping: Mesh Texture Compression via Surface-Aligned Texture Fields
abstract: Mesh texture compression typically relies on 2D UV atlases, whose chart discontinuities and mapping overhead can limit coding efficiency. To tackle this challenge, we introduce TexF, a surface-aligned texture field that organizes texture attributes in sparse voxels derived from the mesh surface. This representation supports high-resolution textures while preserving local 3D correlations for compression and enabling direct surface queries. For bitstream compression, TexF reuses established 3D attribute codecs, with voxel locations reconstructed from the decoded mesh without separate transmission. For GPU-resident compression, we develop 3DNTC, which combines quantized hash features with a lightweight decoder for random-access reconstruction at surface positions. Differentiable rendering enables image-space refinement of both voxel attributes and compressed neural fields. Experiments on the MPEG and AOM mesh compression benchmarks demonstrate improved average rate-distortion performance over representative UV-based methods for both bitstream and GPU-resident compression. 3DNTC also supports real-time rendering.

title: Bidirectional projective sampling for physics-based differentiable rendering
abstract: Background Physics-based differentiable rendering (PBDR) aims to propagate gradients from scene parameters to image pixels or vice versa. The physically correct gradients obtained can be used in various applications, including inverse rendering and machine learning. Currently, two categories of methods are prevalent in the PBDR community: reparameterization and boundary sampling methods. The state-of-the-art boundary sampling methods rely on a guiding structure to calculate the gradients efficiently. They utilize the rays generated in traditional path-tracing methods and project them onto the object silhouette boundary to initialize the guiding structure. Methods In this study, we propose an augmentation of previous projective-sampling-based boundary-sampling methods in a bidirectional manner. Specifically, we utilize the rays spawned from the sensors and also employ the rays emitted by the emitters to initialize the guiding structure. Results To demonstrate the benefits of our technique, we perform a comparative analysis of differentiable rendering and inverse rendering performance. We utilize a range of synthetic scene examples and evaluate our method against state-of-the-art projective-sampling-based differentiable rendering methods. Conclusions The experiments show that our method achieves lower variance gradients in the forward differentiable rendering process and better geometry reconstruction quality in the inverse-rendering results.

title: Bridge Sampling for Connections via Multiple Scattering Events
abstract: Abstract Explicit sampling of and connecting to light sources is often essential for reducing variance in Monte Carlo rendering. In dense, forward‐scattering participating media, its benefit declines, as significant transport happens over longer multiple‐scattering paths around the straight connection to the light. Sampling these paths is challenging, as their contribution is shaped by the product of reciprocal squared distance terms and the phase functions. Previous work demonstrates that sampling several of these terms jointly is crucial. However, these methods are tied to low‐order scattering or struggle with highly‐peaked phase functions. We present a method for sampling a bridge: a subpath of arbitrary vertex count connecting two vertices. Its probability density is proportional to all phase functions at inner vertices and reciprocal squared distance terms. To achieve this, we importance sample the phase functions first, and subsequently all distances at once. For the latter, we sample an independent, preliminary distance for each edge of the bridge, and afterwards scale the bridge such that it matches the connection distance. The scale factor can be marginalized out analytically to obtain the probability density of the bridge. This approach leads to a simple algorithm and can construct bridges of any vertex count. For the case of one or two inserted vertices, we also show an alternative without scaling or marginalization. For practical path sampling, we present a method to sample the number of bridge vertices whose distribution depends on the connection distance, the phase function, and the collision coefficient. While our importance sampling treats media as homogeneous we demonstrate its effectiveness on heterogeneous media.

cited.name: Bridge Sampling
ctx: Bridge Sampling is a method for sampling a subpath (bridge) of arbitrary vertex count connecting two vertices in a participating medium, where the probability density is proportional to all inner phase functions and reciprocal squared distance terms.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Equiangular Sampling and MVNEE by fixing the endpoint via rotation and uniform scaling of a preliminary path, which preserves angles and handles highly-peaked forward scattering more robustly.
Unlike Path Guiding, it does not use memory to store sampling densities or handle visibility explicitly during the sampling construction.

cited.name: GPU Instancing with Indirect Draw Calls
ctx: GPU Instancing with Indirect Draw Calls is a technique to render a large number of identical meshes (voxels) efficiently by using indirect draw calls.

Instead of issuing one draw call per instance, a single draw call is issued that reads instance counts and parameters from a GPU-accessible buffer, allowing the GPU to generate the draw commands itself.

It is distinguished from its siblings by decoupling the CPU-side draw call issuance from the GPU-side execution logic, enabling dynamic instance counts and reducing CPU-GPU synchronization overhead compared to standard hardware instancing.

ctx: Projected Tetrahedra (PT) is an object-order volume rendering technique that projects volumetric primitives, specifically tetrahedra, onto the 2D image plane to leverage hardware-accelerated rasterization.
It solves the problem of rendering unstructured tetrahedral grids by decomposing each 3D cell into a set of partially transparent 2D triangles, which are then composited in back-to-front order.
Unlike Tetrahedral Volume Rendering, which often relies on ray casting, PT uses explicit geometric projection and scan-conversion.

title: Closed Form Solution to the Volume Rendering Integral with Gaussian Transfer Functions
abstract: In direct volume rendering, transfer functions map data points to optical properties such as color and opacity. We have found transfer functions based on the Gaussian primitive to be particularly useful for multivariate volumes, because they are simple and rely on a limited number of free parameters. We show how this class of transfer function primitives can be analytically integrated over a line segment under the assumption that data values vary linearly between two sampled points. Analytically integrated segment can then be composited using standard techniques.

cited.name: Closed-Form Volume Rendering with Gaussian Transfer Functions
ctx: This method computes the emission-absorption volume rendering integral over a line segment in closed form by modeling the transfer function as a multivariate Gaussian primitive.
It assumes linear variation of data values between sampled points, allowing the density integral to be solved analytically using the error function.

This approach eliminates the sampling error inherent in numerical integration methods like those used in Emission-Absorption Volume Rendering, providing exact results for Gaussian-shaped transfer functions.

title: Colored Stochastic Shadow Mapping for Direct Volume Rendering
abstract: Creating direct volume renderings with shadows can lead to a better perception of the rendered images. Deep shadow maps is an effective and efficient approach to compute shadows at interactive rates. We propose an alternative approach based on colored stochastic shadow maps (CSSM), which can produce higher-quality colored shadows while using less texture memory. CSSM is based on a stochastic generation of the shadow map, which is queried multiple times for denoising during rendering.

cited.name: Colored Stochastic Shadow Mapping for Volume Rendering
ctx: Colored Stochastic Shadow Mapping (CSSM) is a two-step rendering technique for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) that generates physically plausible, colored shadows by adapting stochastic shadow mapping concepts to volumetric data.

Unlike traditional shadow maps that produce binary occlusion or deep shadow maps that require significant memory for piecewise linear approximations, CSSM stores a single stochastic depth sample per color channel, allowing translucent objects to cast partial, color-accurate shadows with minimal memory overhead.
CSSM operates in two distinct phases: CSSM Generation (building the shadow map) and DVR Rendering (compositing the volume with shadow factors).

title: Combining Silhouettes, Surface, and Volume Rendering for Surgery Education and Planning
abstract: We introduce a flexible combination of volume, surface, and line rendering. We employ object-based edge detection because this allows a flexible parametrization of the generated lines. Our techniques were developed mainly for medical applications using segmented patient-individual volume datasets. In addition, we present an evaluation of the generated visualizations with 8 medical professionals and 25 laypersons. Integration of lines in conventional rendering turned out to be appropriate. title: Compression and Interactive Visualization of Terabyte Scale Volumetric RGBA Data with Voxel-scale Details
abstract: We present a compressed volumetric data structure and traversal algorithm that interactively visualizes complete terabyte-scale scientific data. Previous methods rely on heavy approximation and do not provide individual sample-level representation when going beyond gigabytes. We develop an extensible pipeline that makes the data streamable on GPU using compact pointers and a compression algorithm based on wavelet transform. The resulting approach renders high-resolution captures under varying sampling characteristics in real-time.

cited.name: Compact pointer tree
ctx: The Compact Pointer Tree is a tree-based data structure and traversal algorithm designed for the interactive visualization of terabyte-scale RGBA volumetric data with voxel-level details.
It solves the problem of rendering massive, sparse volumes on GPUs by combining wavelet-based color compression with compact 8-bit relative pointers.

Unlike standard octrees that use fixed 8 children, this structure uses a variable branching factor N (2 \le N \le 6) to optimize memory usage, enabling real-time frame rates for 8K resolution volumes.

title: Constant-density participating media (fog)
abstract: _Requested by **Adrien** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01FDRReMmT65iKMpjZABM1ZS?thread=cmsg_01FDRReMmT65iKMpjZABM1ZSRkWbRhMJk8huNaHmWNhvgy)_ Before: light only interacted with surfaces, so scenes could not have haze, smoke or visible light beams. After: a scene can fill a sphere or box with fog of constant density (`medium`), or fill the whole scene (`fog`). A `volume` material sets its color and how much it scatters forward (Henyey-Greenstein `g`). `scenes/cornell_fog.scene` shows light shafts coming through a window into a hazy Cornell box (`renders/11-fog-shafts.png`). How: `constant_medium::hit` samples a free-flight distance `-ln(1-ξ)/density` inside the boundary and reports a scattering point if it comes before the exit or the next surface. `phase_material` samples and evaluates the phase function through the usual `pdf`/`eval` interface, so `ray_color` does NEE + MIS at scatter points without any changes. A shadow ray that scatters in the fog counts as blocked, which gives an unbiased estimate of transmittance. Transforms apply to the boundary, so density stays in world units. There's also a separate bug fix: `sample_light` sent shadow rays along the unnormalized vector to the light, so the 0.001 self-hit offset skipped about one scene unit. With a light outside a closed room, that made bright lines leak along every wall seam. The shadow direction is now normalized. Tests: the Henyey-Greenstein pdf integrates to 1 and matches its sampling for g in {0, 0.5, -0.7, 0.9}. A white medium (g = 0 and g = 0.7) disappears in the furnace test. The build has no warnings. --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_01YS38sopGE54uKQoBS12hhp)_
