title: constructive solid geometry / SDF based volume algorithm
abstract: # Description I got (re-)inspired to play around with a signed distance field based raymarch algorithm by a [gamedev video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=il-TXbn5iMA) on youtube. With that you can compose various 3D shapes with operations like union, difference/subtraction, intersection, xor as well as smooth variants of the former. You can also modify shapes, e.g. by applying rounding, bending or twisting. Here's a gear as an example: ```julia sdf_tree = CSG.diff( CSG.intersect( CSG.smooth_union( CSG.Cylinder(0.2, 0.7, color = :lightgray), CSG.union( map(1:4) do n CSG.Rect( Vec3f(0.1, 0.07, 0.2), color = :lightgray, translation = 0.8 * Vec3f(cos(n * pi/8 - pi/16), sin(n * pi/8 - pi/16), 0), rotation = qrotation(Vec3f(0, 0, 1), -n * pi/8 + pi/16), ) end..., mirror = (true, true, false) ), smooth = 0.02 ), CSG.Cylinder(0.1, 1, color = :orange) ), CSG.Cylinder(0.2, 0.4), ) csgplot(-1..1, -1..1, -1..1, sdf_tree) ``` The code is currently quite messy because it contains leftovers multiple prototypes. The first is an attempt to compute signed distance fields on the GPU directly, by encoding the operations on CPU and then decoding and processing them on the GPU. I got this to work, but it was very expensive on GPU. (I'd guess this is a combination of needing a lot of branching to determine what each operation is (e.g. `if (operation == op_translation) ...`) running for multiple operations that need to be evaluated multiple times as the raymarching gets evaluated.) This is currently still available as `sdfscatter()`. The second prototype moved the SDF generation to the CPU, evaluating distances once and storing them in a 3D array. That array is then passed to `volume` where the distances are used in ray marching. On the GPU side, this is should be faster and higher quality than the other volume algorithms. The conversion for this is currently disabled. The third and current prototype builds on the second. Loosely following the [gamedev video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=il-TXbn5iMA), I implemented a `Brickmap` to compress the signed distance data. This typically compresses the data by a factor of 10-100, which can then be used for more quality. From that point on, I added another compressing procedure for colors and tried optimizing the initial SDF generation. Some stats for the example above: - 32 operations total, evaluated in an effective 512^3 grid in a -1..1 box - dense array: - 512^3 * 2 byte for each distance: 256MB - 512^3 * 3 byte RGB color: 384MB (not implemented) - total 640MB - time: 19.3s (unoptimized) - Brickmap: (memory rounded) - 1.5MB brick indices (73^3 * 4 byte) - ~~7.6MB~~ 10MB distances in bricks (~~14716~~ 14716/19683 bricks ¹, each 8^3 * 1 byte, depends on the amount of surface area) - 0.06MB index remapping for colors (~~14716~~ 14716/16384 * 4 byte indices ¹, one per brick) - 4.0MB color (~~2312~~ 2312/2744 bricks ¹, each 8^3 * 3 byte, depends on the number of mixed color bricks) - ¹ these are dynamically resizing arrays with n_used / n_available elements - total: ~~13.2MB~~ 15.5MB - time: ~~2.2s~~ ~~0.77s~~ ~~0.60s~~ 0.28s (with optimizations to skip empty regions and locally irrelevant SDF nodes) TODO: - [x] localized edits (don't regenerate everything on change, just what's needed) - [x] extend `ShaderAbstractions.Sampler` update functions https://github.com/SimonDanisch/ShaderAbstractions.jl/pull/31 - [x] allow prefix operations in merge nodes (union, diff, etc) - more Optimizations... - [ ] consider always adding position data to shapes to reduce number of translation operations (is this actually worth it, or do translation happen at other points to allow other operations to acts on the centered shape?) - [x] consider eliminating unneeded SDF nodes based on a SDF sample ~~rather than~~ and bounding boxes - [x] broadcast each sdf operation over a brick instead of broadcasting the tree as whole (i.e. evaluate `if command.id == ...` once per brick instead of once per brick element) - [ ] consider reusing brick indices for coarse distance sampling - [ ] 2D shapes for extrusion (etc) - [ ] maybe add rotational symmetry operation - [ ] improve user interface - [x] add methods for each shape and merge command in clean module/namespace - [ ] clean up old prototypes/unused code - [x] delete sdfplot, volume extension (use different parent plot instead) and related code - [x] consider replacing operation enum with Symbols - [ ] documentation - [ ] tests Note that this pr requires https://github.com/JuliaGeometry/GeometryBasics.jl/pull/276, https://github.com/SimonDanisch/ShaderAbstractions.jl/pull/31 I should also note that [Inigo Quilez articles](https://iquilezles.org/articles/) are very helpful for this pr, especially the one on 3D signed distance functions. Almost all the operations and shape functions come from there. ## Type of change - [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) ## Checklist - [ ] Added an entry in CHANGELOG.md (for new features and breaking changes) - [ ] Added or changed relevant sections in the documentation - [ ] Added unit tests for new algorithms, conversion methods, etc. - [ ] Added reference image tests for new plotting functions, recipes, visual options, etc.

cited.name: Brickmap SDF Volume Rendering
ctx: Brickmap SDF Volume Rendering is a technique that represents 3D scenes as Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) trees of Signed Distance Function (SDF) primitives, evaluates the resulting distance field on the CPU, compresses it into a sparse Brickmap structure, and raymarches through it on the GPU.

It differs from direct GPU CSG evaluation by offloading the complex tree traversal and branching logic to the CPU, thereby avoiding high branching overhead on the GPU, and from dense volume rendering by using spatial compression to reduce memory footprint by 10-100x.
Inputs: A CSG tree defining primitive shapes (e.g., cylinders, boxes) and their transformations (translation, rotation, scaling) and operations (union, intersection, difference).

title: cvc::volslice: port VolumeRover2's view-aligned slice volume renderer
abstract: Ports volumerover2's `OpenGLVolumeRendering` "VolumeLibrary" (Thane/Bajaj, UT Austin 2002-2003, arand patches through 2012) — the classic back-to-front view-aligned-slice compositor — as **`cvc::volslice`**, the third volume-rendering path in the cvcGL scene graph beside `VolumeNode` (VTK's GPU raycaster) and `VolRenNode` (`cvc::volren`). Same design rules as the volren port: no globals/singletons, injected `cvc::app`, state tree as the source of truth, faithful sampling model with deviations opt-in and documented. [docs/VOLSLICE_API.md](../blob/feat/volslice/docs/VOLSLICE_API.md) is the contract. ## Shape - **`cvc::volslice` slicing engine** — pure geometry, no GL: the 256-case plane/cube clip table transcribed verbatim, the arand slice-count formula `N = 2·(10 + max_planes·q³)`, the 10·max_planes cap, near-plane peel, sub-cube crop. What the legacy read off the GL matrix stack is an explicit local→clip input. Runs in legacy ratio space and maps into the caller's box (uniform scale + translation preserve the algorithm), so slice counts match legacy for any box shape. 14 unit tests against independently derived values (270 default head-on planes, hexagon at the body diagonal, back-to-front ordering...). - **`state_settings`** under ` .volslice.*` — the volren binding pattern key-for-key (seed-suppressed ctor, all-or-nothing re-read, clamp-resources/reject-enums/raw-contract-values), with the shared `transfer_function.color/.opacity` CSV so one TF editor drives all three renderers. - **`cvc::gl::VolSliceNode`** — one volume per node (`VolumeNode`'s model; the scene composes multiples). Per tick: recompute slices from the live camera × node world transform, rewrite the mesh, sample a normalized R8 3D texture (the legacy UChar coercion — also what WebGL2 can LINEAR-filter) through a 256×1 RGBA LUT in a fragment replacement. Slice texcoords are computed in the vertex shader as an affine map of `vertexMC` — no tcoord array. - **`volslice_bunny`** demo (native + wasm gallery): the bunny SDF windowed around its zero level set, panel with the VolumeRover2 tunables. - Dropped, with reasons in the doc: the GL-extension impl zoo (only `FragmentProgramARBImpl` ever ran in practice), Cg-only shading, RGBA path, `blend_mode` (legacy shipped exactly one; additive was commented-out dead code and is inexpressible under the sequential pass — not a silent knob), out-of-core stubs. - One opt-in deviation: `opacity_correction` — spacing-corrected slice alpha so quality changes sharpness instead of density. Default OFF (faithful). ## Three findings worth reviewer attention **1. VTK 9's default translucent pass silently breaks slice compositing.** `vtkRenderer::UseOIT` (on by default) is order-independent weighted accumulation — measured `rgb=(ONE,ONE)` by reading GL blend state during the pass — under which a slice stack *averages* into an X-ray look. With `UseOITOff()`, VTK renders translucent geometry with **exactly the legacy blend state** (`SRC_ALPHA/ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, depth-write off). `addToRenderer()` flips the renderer and the header documents the scene-wide effect (other translucent actors then depth-sort as props, pre-VTK9 style). **2. `vertexMC` is not the true model coordinate.** The mapper's AUTO VBO shift-scale re-centers vertex data for boxes offset from the origin and compensates in `MCDCMatrix` — the demo bunny (box z∈[0,100]) rendered **zero pixels** while the origin-centered unit-test ball passed, because the texcoord map read a corner of the volume where density 0 → TF alpha 0. Fixed with `DISABLE_SHIFT_SCALE`; the render test now carries an off-origin-volume regression. Worth knowing for any future `vertexMC`-derived shader work. **3. GLES3 sampler precision is a wasm-only compile/precision hazard.** `sampler3D` has *no* default precision on GLES3 (unqualified = compile error on WebGL2) and `sampler2D` defaults to `lowp` — an 8-bit fraction that cannot address the LUT's 1/512-texel centers. Both samplers are declared `highp`; desktop GLSL takes the qualifiers as no-ops, so the native build catches neither. ## Verification - `volslice_test` (14) + `volslice_state_test` (6): unit + state binding. - `cvcgl_volslice_node`: offscreen render test, llvmpipe-friendly — silhouette radius 49.5px vs predicted ~50, plane counts 20/270 matching the formula end-to-end, transform tracking, near-plane dimming, opacity-correction band derived from the measured 8-bit accumulation limit, the OIT flip, and the off-origin regression. - Full suite: **3086/3086** locally. - Demo captured native (the gallery thumbnail is a real `--png` capture at 96³/q=0.7); wasm build exercised by the pages deploy on merge (`_wasm_demos` + `demos.json` + `DEMOS` wired). ## Follow-ups (documented in the API doc) Shaded path (on-the-fly gradients from the scene lights), RGBA volumes, and a volumetric-pass custom mapper to restore OIT coexistence.

title: DDNeRF: Depth Distribution Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: The field of implicit neural representation has made significant progress. Models such as neural radiance fields (NeRF) [12], which uses relatively small neural networks, can represent high-quality scenes and achieve state-of-the-art results for novel view synthesis. Training these types of networks, however, is still computationally expensive and the model struggles with real life 360° scenes. In this work, we propose the depth distribution neural radiance field (DDNeRF), a new method that significantly increases sampling efficiency along rays during training, while achieving superior results for a given sampling budget. DDNeRF achieves this performance by learning a more accurate representation of the density distribution along rays. More specifically, the proposed framework trains a coarse model to predict the internal distribution of the transparency of an input volume along each ray. This estimated distribution then guides the sampling procedure of the fine model. Our method allows using fewer samples during training while achieving better output quality with the same computational resources.

cited.name: DDNeRF
ctx: DDNeRF is a neural volume rendering method that improves sampling efficiency in hierarchical sampling by learning a continuous density distribution within each ray interval, rather than relying on a discrete piecewise-constant probability density function (PDF).

It sets itself apart from MipNeRF by using two separate networks for coarse and fine passes (like original NeRF) while modeling the coarse PDF as a mixture of truncated Gaussians, and from Hierarchical Sampling by replacing the discrete weight normalization with a parametric Gaussian distribution estimation.
For unbounded scenes, use a hybrid strategy: half samples uniformly below radius 1 from the origin, half using log-sampling (DONeRF) outside the sphere.

title: Design, Implementation and Characterization of a Quantum-Dot-Based Volumetric Display
abstract: In this study, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a volumetric display system based on quantum dots (QDs) embedded in a polymer substrate. Unlike conventional volumetric displays, our system does not require electrical wiring; thus, the heretofore unavoidable issue of occlusion is resolved because irradiation by external light supplies the energy to the light-emitting voxels formed by the QDs. By exploiting the intrinsic attributes of the QDs, the system offers ultrahigh definition and a wide range of colours for volumetric displays. In this paper, we discuss the design, implementation and characterization of the proposed volumetric display's first prototype. We developed an 8 × 8 × 8 display comprising two types of QDs. This display provides multicolour three-type two-dimensional patterns when viewed from different angles. The QD-based volumetric display provides a new way to represent images and could be applied in leisure and advertising industries, among others.

title: destruction: voxelize CSG mesh + render as voxels (Phase 1 of voxel destruction roadmap)
abstract: ## Context Phase 1 of the voxel destruction roadmap. No simulation yet — just visualize any CSG mesh or analytic primitive as a Minecraft-style voxel chunk pile. Lays the data structures everything else builds on. ## Goals 1. Voxelization algorithm: - For each "object" (analytic primitive or CSG mesh), determine its world-space AABB - Sample a 3D grid at user-specified voxel size (default 0.1 m) - For each voxel center, query SDF (use existing #97 SDF infrastructure where possible, or build a quick triangle-mesh-to-SDF helper for non-SDF sources) - Voxels with SDF ` — voxelize a specific object - Console command `voxelize_save ` — dump current voxel cache to disk ## File ownership - **NEW**: `src/destruction/Voxelizer.cpp/h`, `src/destruction/VoxelGrid.cpp/h`, `src/destruction/CMakeLists.txt` - **MODIFIED**: - top-level `CMakeLists.txt`, `src/CMakeLists.txt` — add subdirectory - `src/engine/Engine.cpp` — register cvars + commands + integration with primitive list. Surgical. - **Do NOT touch**: shaders/*, src/rhi_*, anything outside engine integration ## MVP discipline - NO simulation. The "voxelized" object just renders differently — no fracture, no rigid bodies. That's Phase 2. - Single voxel size per object. Adaptive resolution is Phase 3. - No GPU voxelization. CPU job system OK for now; SDF queries are cheap and voxelization is a one-time precompute. - No animation. Source object positions are read once at voxelization time; if the source moves, the voxel grid doesn't follow until re-voxelized. ## Acceptance criteria - `voxelize_object` + `r_voxelize_demo 1` renders the source object as a chunky-box pile in the path-traced scene - A 1m³ cube at 0.1m voxel size produces ~1000 voxel boxes that the path tracer renders correctly - Voxelization cache hits speed up repeated voxelization (timer logs delta) - `r_voxelize_demo 0` reverts to original mesh rendering — no regression ## Hard dependencies - This phase alone has no hard physics dependency (no simulation yet) - Phase 2 of THIS roadmap requires physics Phase 2 (rigid body) to be merged first ## What this WON'T do - Actually destroy anything (Phase 2) - Optimize chunk merging (Phase 3) - Fracture patterns (Phase 4) - VFX (Phase 5) - Variable voxel resolution (Phase 3 polish) - Real-time voxelization of moving objects (would need GPU sweep)

title: Differentiable Voxel-based X-ray Rendering Improves Sparse-View 3D CBCT Reconstruction
abstract: We present DiffVox, a self-supervised framework for Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) reconstruction by directly optimizing a voxelgrid representation using physics-based differentiable X-ray rendering. Further, we investigate how the different implementations of the X-ray image formation model in the renderer affect the quality of 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. When combined with our regularized voxel-based learning framework, we find that using an exact implementation of the discrete Beer-Lambert law for X-ray attenuation in the renderer outperforms both widely used iterative CBCT reconstruction algorithms and modern neural field approaches, particularly when given only a few input views. As a result, we reconstruct high-fidelity 3D CBCT volumes from fewer X-rays, potentially reducing ionizing radiation exposure and improving diagnostic utility. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/hossein-momeni/DiffVox.

title: Diffusion and multiple anisotropic scattering for global illumination in clouds
abstract: The diffusion method is a good approximation inside the dense core of a cloud, but not at the more tenuous boundary regions. We have also used this hardware volume rendering at key voxels in the low-density boundary regions to account for the multiple anisotropic scattering of the environment.

title: DOUBLE NERF: REPRESENTING DYNAMIC SCENES AS NEURAL RADIANCE FIELDS
abstract: Abstract. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) are non-convolutional neural models that learn 3D scene structure and color to produce novel images of a given scene from a new view point. NeRFs are closely related to such photogrammetric problems as camera pose estimation and bundle adjustment. NeRF takes a number of oriented cameras and photos as an input and learns a function that maps a 5D pose vector to an RGB color and volume destiny at point. The estimated function can be used to draw an image using a volume rendering pipeline. Still NeRF have a major limitation: they can not be used for dynamic scene synthesis. We propose a modified NeRF framework that can represent a dynamic scene as a superposition of two or more neural radiance fields. We consider a simple dynamic scene consisting of a static background scene and moving object with a static shape. We implemented our DoubleNeRF model using TensorFlow library. The results of evaluation are encouraging and demonstrate that our DoubleNeRF model achieves and surpasses the state of the art in the dynamic scene synthesis. Our framework includes two neural radiance fields for a background scene and dynamic objects. The evaluation of the model demonstrates that it can be effectively used for synthesis of photorealistic dynamic image sequence and videos.

title: DPPE: Dense Pose Estimation in a Plenoxels Environment using Gradient Approximation
abstract: We present DPPE, a dense pose estimation algorithm that functions over a Plenoxels environment. Recent advances in neural radiance field techniques have shown that it is a powerful tool for environment representation. More recent neural rendering algorithms have significantly improved both training duration and rendering speed. Plenoxels introduced a fully-differentiable radiance field technique that uses Plenoptic volume elements contained in voxels for rendering, offering reduced training times and better rendering accuracy, while also eliminating the neural net component. In this work, we introduce a 6-DoF monocular RGB-only pose estimation procedure for Plenoxels, which seeks to recover the ground truth camera pose after a perturbation. We employ a variation on classical template matching techniques, using stochastic gradient descent to optimize the pose by minimizing errors in re-rendering. In particular, we examine an approach that takes advantage of the rapid rendering speed of Plenoxels to numerically approximate part of the pose gradient, using a central differencing technique. We show that such methods are effective in pose estimation. Finally, we perform ablations over key components of the problem space, with a particular focus on image subsampling and Plenoxel grid resolution. title: DT-NeRF: A Diffusion and Transformer-Based Optimization Approach for Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Reconstruction
abstract: This paper proposes a Diffusion Model-Optimized Neural Radiance Field (DT-NeRF) method, aimed at enhancing detail recovery and multi-view consistency in 3D scene reconstruction. By combining diffusion models with Transformers, DT-NeRF effectively restores details under sparse viewpoints and maintains high accuracy in complex geometric scenes. Experimental results demonstrate that DT-NeRF significantly outperforms traditional NeRF and other state-of-the-art methods on the Matterport3D and ShapeNet datasets, particularly in metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, Chamfer Distance, and Fidelity. Ablation experiments further confirm the critical role of the diffusion and Transformer modules in the model's performance, with the removal of either module leading to a decline in performance. The design of DT-NeRF showcases the synergistic effect between modules, providing an efficient and accurate solution for 3D scene reconstruction. Future research may focus on further optimizing the model, exploring more advanced generative models and network architectures to enhance its performance in large-scale dynamic scenes, with the ultimate goal of enabling intelligent systems to perceive and reconstruct complex 3D environments autonomously.

title: DTIC ADA306215: Laser-Based 3-D Volumetric Display System (The Improved Second Generation).
abstract: NRaD, the RDT&E Division of the Naval Command, Control and Ocean Surveillance Center (NCCOSC), has developed and improved its second-generation device for displaying data, information, and scenes in a three-dimensional volume of image space. The device incorporates a 36-inch diameter double helix that spins at approximately 10 revolutions per second, providing a means to address a cylindrical volume. Under computer control, a laser beam is directed to illuminate certain discrete volume points (voxels) on the helix needed to create a scene. The laser light scatters from the surface of the helix, so, to the observer, each voxel appears to emanate from specific points in space. Each point has x-y coordinates determined by the position of the laser beam and a z coordinate determined by the height of the point on the helical surface. Any point within the cylindrical image volume can be computer-addressed to appropriately synchronize the laser beam, the Acousto-Optic (AO) Scanner, and the phase of the helix. Using a novel Acousto-Optic (AO) Random-Access Scanner, up to 40,000 laser-generated voxels refreshed at 20 Hz per color are projected onto the reflective surface of the rotating helix. (This is about 10 times more than the current state of the art.) The higher resolution allows improved color images, updated in real-time, for group viewing with the naked eye.

title: Efficient Multi-View Inverse Rendering Using a Hybrid Differentiable Rendering Method
abstract: Recovering the shape and appearance of real-world objects from natural 2D images is a long-standing and challenging inverse rendering problem. In this paper, we introduce a novel hybrid differentiable rendering method to efficiently reconstruct the 3D geometry and reflectance of a scene from multi-view images captured by conventional hand-held cameras. Our method follows an analysis-by-synthesis approach and consists of two phases. In the initialization phase, we use traditional SfM and MVS methods to reconstruct a virtual scene roughly matching the real scene. Then in the optimization phase, we adopt a hybrid approach to refine the geometry and reflectance, where the geometry is first optimized using an approximate differentiable rendering method, and the reflectance is optimized afterward using a physically-based differentiable rendering method. Our hybrid approach combines the efficiency of approximate methods with the high-quality results of physically-based methods. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that our method can produce reconstructions with similar or higher quality than state-of-the-art methods while being more efficient.

title: Efficient multiple scattering in hair using spherical harmonics
abstract: Previous research has shown that a global multiple scattering simulation is needed to achieve physically realistic renderings of hair, particularly light-colored hair with low absorption. However, previous methods have either sacrificed accuracy or have been too computationally expensive for practical use. In this paper we describe a physically based, volumetric rendering method that computes multiple scattering solutions, including directional effects, much faster than previous accurate methods. Our two-pass method first traces light paths through a volumetric representation of the hair, contributing power to a 3D grid of spherical harmonic coefficients that store the directional distribution of scattered radiance everywhere in the hair volume. Then, in a ray tracing pass, multiple scattering is computed by integrating the stored radiance against the scattering functions of visible fibers using an efficient matrix multiplication. Single scattering is computed using conventional direct illumination methods. In our comparisons the new method produces quality similar to that of the best previous methods, but computes multiple scattering more than 10 times faster.

title: EWA splatting
abstract: In this paper, we present a framework for high quality splatting based on elliptical Gaussian kernels. To avoid aliasing artifacts, we introduce the concept of a resampling filter, combining a reconstruction kernel with a low-pass filter. Because of the similarity to Heckbert's EWA (elliptical weighted average) filter for texture mapping, we call our technique EWA splatting. Our framework allows us to derive EWA splat primitives for volume data and for point-sampled surface data. It provides high image quality without aliasing artifacts or excessive blurring for volume data and, additionally, features anisotropic texture filtering for point-sampled surfaces. It also handles nonspherical volume kernels efficiently; hence, it is suitable for regular, rectilinear, and irregular volume datasets. Moreover, our framework introduces a novel approach to compute the footprint function, facilitating efficient perspective projection of arbitrary elliptical kernels at very little additional cost. Finally, we show that EWA volume reconstruction kernels can be reduced to surface reconstruction kernels. This makes our splat primitive universal in rendering surface and volume data.Engineering and Applied SciencesAccepted Manuscrip

cited.name: EWA Splatting
ctx: EWA Splatting is a high-quality volume rendering technique that eliminates aliasing artifacts by replacing the standard footprint function with a band-limited resampling filter.

It sets itself apart from basic splatting Splatting Without the Blur by combining an elliptical Gaussian reconstruction kernel with a Gaussian low-pass filter, and from Splat Radius Adjustment Based on Normal Angle by using a rigorous affine approximation of the projective mapping to derive an analytic 2D footprint.

Strengths: High-quality antialiasing without excessive blurring; handles arbitrary elliptical kernels; suitable for regular, rectilinear, and irregular volume datasets; universal splat primitive for surface and volume data.

title: EWA Volume Splatting
abstract: EWA Volume Splatting 1 Introduction Volume rendering is an important technique in visualizing acquired and simulated data sets in scientific and engineering applications. The ideal volume rendering algorithm reconstructs a continuous function in 3D, transforms this 3D function into screen space, and then evaluates opacity integrals along line-of-sights. In 1989, West-over [18, 19] introduced splatting for ...

cited.name: EWA Splatting
ctx: EWA Splatting is a high-quality volume rendering technique that eliminates aliasing artifacts by replacing the standard footprint function with a band-limited resampling filter.

It solves the problem of visual artifacts caused by incorrect visibility determination and sampling rate changes in perspective projections, which occur when reconstruction kernels overlap or when the sampling rate falls below the Nyquist frequency.

It sets itself apart from basic splatting Splatting Without the Blur by combining an elliptical Gaussian reconstruction kernel with a Gaussian low-pass filter, and from Splat Radius Adjustment Based on Normal Angle by using a rigorous affine approximation of the projective mapping to derive an analytic 2D footprint.

cited.name: Hierarchical DDA with Super-brick Skipping
ctx: This method accelerates ray tracing through sparse volumetric data by introducing a two-level occupancy hierarchy (super-bricks and bricks) to skip large empty regions, while maintaining pixel-identical output to the fine per-voxel DDA.

It solves the performance bottleneck of traversing empty space by verifying emptiness at a coarser granularity and using an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for early termination, ensuring exactness by only skipping verified empty blocks and terminating only when the ray definitively passes the occupied volume.
Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, volume header, brick masks, super-brick masks, and voxel data.

title: Extraction of isosurfaces from multi-material CT volumetric data of mechanical parts
abstract: We introduce a method for extracting boundary surfaces from volumetric models of mechanical parts by X-ray CT scanning. When the volumetric model is composed of two materials, one for the object and the other for the background (Air), these boundary surfaces can be extracted as isosurfaces using a contouring method such as Marching Cubes [Lorensen and Cline 1987]. For a volumetric model composed of more than two materials, we need to classify the voxel types into segments by material and use a generalized Marching Cubes algorithm that can deal with both CT values and material types. Here we propose a method for precisely classifying the volumetric model into its component materials using a modified and combined method of two well-known algorithms in image segmentation, region growing and Graph-cut. We then apply the generalized Marching Cubes algorithm to generate triangulated mesh surfaces. In addition, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by constructing high-quality triangular mesh models of the segmented parts.

cited.name: Vessel Voxelizer
ctx: Vessel Voxelizer is a CUDA-accelerated method that converts vascular structures, defined as line segments with associated radii, into a 3D "fuzzy" voxel volume where each voxel's value represents the fraction of its volume occupied by the vessels.

It differs from binary voxelization methods by outputting continuous occupancy values via supersampling, and from general mesh voxelization by operating directly on parametric tube primitives (line segments) rather than polygonal surfaces.

title: Fast Auto-Differentiable Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs for Solving Inverse Problems in Intraoperative Imaging.
abstract: The use of digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) to solve inverse problems such as slice-to-volume registration and 3D reconstruction is well studied in preoperative settings. In intraoperative imaging, the utility of DRRs is limited by the challenges of generating them in real time and supporting optimization procedures that rely on repeated DRR synthesis. Although immense progress has been made in accelerating the generation of DRRs through algorithmic refinements and GPU implementations, DRR-based optimization remains slow because most DRR generators do not offer a straightforward way to obtain gradients with respect to the imaging parameters. To make DRRs interoperable with gradient-based optimization and deep learning frameworks, we have reformulated Siddon's method, the most popular ray-tracing algorithm used in DRR generation, as a series of vectorized tensor operations. We implemented this vectorized version of Siddon's method in PyTorch, taking advantage of the library's strong automatic differentiation engine to make this DRR generator fully differentiable with respect to its parameters. Additionally, the use of GPU-accelerated tensor computation enables our vectorized implementation to achieve rendering speeds equivalent to state-of-the-art DRR generators implemented in CUDA and C++. We illustrate the resulting method in the context of slice-to-volume registration. Moreover, our simulations suggest that the loss landscapes for the slice-to-volume registration problem are convex in the neighborhood of the optimal solution, and gradient-based registration promises a much faster solution than prevailing gradient-free optimization strategies. The proposed DRR generator enables fast computer vision algorithms to support image guidance in minimally invasive procedures. Our implementation is publically available at https://github.com/eigenvivek/DiffDRR.

cited.name: Gradient Descent Registration via ZNCC
ctx: This method performs 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) slice-to-volume registration by minimizing the negative Zero-Normalized Cross-Correlation (ZNCC) between a fixed Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph (DRR) and a moving DRR using gradient descent.
It serves as the local refinement stage of the Hybrid 2D/3D Registration Optimization Pipeline, leveraging the locally convex loss landscape of ZNCC to converge quickly from random initializations.

Unlike the global network-based loss (LN) in its parent pipeline, this method relies on traditional gradient descent with momentum, requiring differentiable DRR generation to compute gradients with respect to pose parameters.

title: Fast Grid Traversal Algorithm integer based by Gemini 3.0 Pro (verified in Delphi/translated seems to work ! ;))
abstract: Fast, Exact, Stable algorithm ? Could be interesting (not yet sure if it will overflow, maybe not). I spent 5 minutes on verification. Perhaps in future I will investigate further until then you can beat me to it. This will be usefull for exact bullit hits instead of passing through on certain cases... ``` // Inputs: // startX, startY, startZ (Integer Grid Coordinates) // originX, originY, originZ (Ray Origin in world space) // vx, vy, vz (Ray direction vector, scaled to integers) // cellSize (Width of a voxel) // 1. Initialization Phase int X = startX; int Y = startY; int Z = startZ; int stepX = (vx >= 0) ? 1 : -1; int stepY = (vy >= 0) ? 1 : -1; int stepZ = (vz >= 0) ? 1 : -1; // Calculate distance to the first boundary in world units // If step is positive, boundary is (X+1)*CellSize. If negative, it is X*CellSize. int nextBoundaryX = (stepX > 0) ? (X + 1) * cellSize : X * cellSize; int nextBoundaryY = (stepY > 0) ? (Y + 1) * cellSize : Y * cellSize; int nextBoundaryZ = (stepZ > 0) ? (Z + 1) * cellSize : Z * cellSize; // Compute scale factors (Absolute values of cross-products) // Note: Use 'long long' to prevent overflow if the grid is large long long iDeltaX = cellSize * abs(vy * vz); long long iDeltaY = cellSize * abs(vx * vz); long long iDeltaZ = cellSize * abs(vx * vy); // Initialize iMax (Scaled t to next boundary) // Original logic: tMaxX = (nextBoundaryX - originX) / vx // Scaled logic: Multiply by S = |vx * vy * vz| // Result: (nextBoundaryX - originX) * vy * vz * sign_correction long long iMaxX = (nextBoundaryX - originX) * vy * vz; if (vx < 0) iMaxX = -iMaxX; // Correct for negative direction divisions if (vx == 0) iMaxX = LLONG_MAX; // Handle parallel rays long long iMaxY = (nextBoundaryY - originY) * vx * vz; if (vy < 0) iMaxY = -iMaxY; if (vy == 0) iMaxY = LLONG_MAX; long long iMaxZ = (nextBoundaryZ - originZ) * vx * vy; if (vz < 0) iMaxZ = -iMaxZ; if (vz == 0) iMaxZ = LLONG_MAX; // 2. Incremental Phase [cite: 76] // This loop mirrors the original paper's logic exactly // but uses integers instead of floats. Object* hit = NULL; do { if (iMaxX < iMaxY) { if (iMaxX < iMaxZ) { // X is the smallest, step in X X = X + stepX; if (X == justOutX) return NULL; // Outside grid [cite: 98] iMaxX = iMaxX + iDeltaX; // Integer Addition } else { // Z is the smallest, step in Z Z = Z + stepZ; if (Z == justOutZ) return NULL; iMaxZ = iMaxZ + iDeltaZ; // Integer Addition } } else { if (iMaxY < iMaxZ) { // Y is the smallest, step in Y Y = Y + stepY; if (Y == justOutY) return NULL; iMaxY = iMaxY + iDeltaY; // Integer Addition } else { // Z is the smallest, step in Z Z = Z + stepZ; if (Z == justOutZ) return NULL; iMaxZ = iMaxZ + iDeltaZ; // Integer Addition } } // Check voxel list [cite: 126] hit = CheckVoxelObjectList(X, Y, Z); } while (hit == NULL); return hit; ```

title: feat(ard): voxelization and rectangular decomposition (Phases 2 and 3)
abstract: The geometry pipeline that feeds the solver. Neither phase has a counterpart in the reference — it reads a pre-baked `.rec` box list produced by an offline MATLAB step (`Partition::readFromRecFile`) — so this is all new code rather than a port. **Stacked on #191**, which is stacked on #190. The diff here is the 7 Phase 2/3 files only. GitHub will retarget as each merges. ## What's here | File | Role | |---|---| | `voxelize.ts` | Rasterize surface triangles into a grid, then flood-fill the air region | | `voxelize-room.ts` | Thin `Room` adapter, kept out of the core | | `decompose.ts` | Greedy box growth + `validateDecomposition` | `decompose.spec.ts` carries the first **end-to-end test of Phases 2–5**: a shoebox and an L-shaped room go from triangles, through the voxelizer and decomposition, into real partitions with real interfaces, and a pulse driven in one partition reaches another through the seam. That's the sequence Phase 6's driver will run. 184 ARD tests pass (was 144); eslint clean; zero `tsc` errors. ## A claim in the plan that turned out to be wrong Phase 3 asserted that growing the longest run first "noticeably reduces the box count and therefore the interface area". **It doesn't.** Measured against a fixed x→y→z order: | shape | fixed | longest-first | |---|---|---| | corridor, L, cross, T, comb, staircase, pillared room, ball | — | **ties on all eight** | | 200 randomized air masks | mean **202.9** | mean 207.5 — *172 losses to 17 wins* | The stronger variant — try all six orders per seed, keep the largest box — also ties on every room-like shape and comes out slightly worse on random masks (205.2 vs 202.8), because greedily maximizing one box leaves worse leftovers. The reason is structural: the slab rule already extends maximally along each axis in turn, so for near-rectilinear geometry the result is order-independent. The option is kept but **defaulted off**, with a test pinning the negative result so the idea isn't rediscovered. Cutting the box count — and with it the interface area, where the error lives — needs a different lever: seed selection, or a merge pass. ## Other departures from the spec **No BVH in the voxelizer.** The spec called for a `three-mesh-bvh` box-vs-triangle query per candidate cell. Scattering each triangle into the cells its own bounding box covers is strictly better: work is proportional to the surface area in cells — the solid cells actually produced — rather than grid volume × `log(triangles)`, and it needs no acceleration structure. The overlap test is exact either way: full 13-axis SAT, because a conservative AABB test thickens oblique walls into a blob, changing the air volume and with it the modal frequencies. **Pure core, separate adapter.** `voxelize.ts` has no `three`, no stores, no DOM, so the geometry is testable on plain triangle lists. `voxelize-room.ts` is the thin adapter — the same split `radiance/patch.ts` already uses between `buildPatchesFromTriangles` and `buildPatchesFromRoom`. **Thin boxes are marked `fdtd`, not merged.** Merging was the spec's first suggestion, but the union of two boxes is only a box in special cases, so a merge pass would succeed rarely and silently leave the rest. Marking the kind always works and Phase 4 already implements the partition — which is exactly why the reference keeps an FDTD partition around. **Leaks reported, not thrown.** `voxelize` sets `leaked` and a warning; `decompose` is what refuses. A caller may still want the grid in order to find which surface is open. ## Design notes worth a look - **Leak detection.** The grid is padded a cell on every side, so the exterior always touches the rim. If the fill reaches it, either the seed was outside or the surfaces don't close — and a gap of one cell drains the interior, making the "air region" the whole bounding box. Silently decomposing that would produce large, quiet nonsense. - **Sealed voids are excluded.** The fill is 6-connected from a seed, so a closet nobody opened stays solid — it isn't part of the room's acoustic volume. - **`validateDecomposition`** checks the cover is a true partition: every air cell in exactly one box, no box touching solid, `assignment` agreeing with the boxes. Cheap next to a simulation and worth running before Phase 6 spends minutes on a bad cover. ## Mutation-checked | injected bug | tests failed | |---|---| | slab test only examines the seed row (boxes would overlap) | 7 | | flood fill ignores walls | 5 | | thin-box detection disabled | 1 | | conservative AABB instead of exact SAT | 1 | ## Known limits - **Staircasing.** Non-axis-aligned surfaces become stair steps. Intrinsic to grid methods, not a choice here, and part of why the plan keeps ARD to the low-frequency band. - **Corner attribution.** Where two surfaces meet, the shared cell is attributed to whichever triangle reached it first. Phase 6 may want an area-weighted rule for per-band absorption at corners. - Same 4 pre-existing failures in `dir-angle-conversions.spec.ts` / `temperature-air-absorption.spec.ts`, unchanged and unrelated. ## Next Phases 1–5 are now done and tested together. What remains is **Phase 6 onward** — the simulation driver and worker, the solver class, the UI wiring — plus §5's cost envelope, which is the open question the numerics can't answer. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01HUuVL5ALKyoGFhUnacVsjA --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_01HUuVL5ALKyoGFhUnacVsjA)_

cited.name: Voxelization via Triangle Scattering
ctx: Voxelization via Triangle Scattering converts a triangle mesh into a 3D grid of voxels to identify the air region for acoustic simulation.
It rasterizes surface triangles into the grid using an exact overlap test and isolates the connected air volume via flood fill, avoiding acceleration structures like BVHs.

It differs from its parent CPU Mesh Voxelization by scattering triangles into cells rather than iterating cells against triangles, and from Inner Loop Optimizations for CPU Mesh Voxelization by prioritizing exact geometric overlap over conservative bounding box approximations.

title: feat(export): dual contouring for sharp-feature mesh export (roadmap S9, #391)
abstract: ## What **S9 — dual contouring**, the sharp-feature mesher (3D-Rendering-Roadmap §S9, Refs #391 #389). Marching Cubes puts surface vertices on grid edges, so a hard crease (a Mandelbox facet edge, a KIFS corner) is rounded into a chamfer at grid resolution. Dual contouring places **one vertex per cell**, positioned by a QEF over the cell's Hermite data, so the vertex snaps onto the intersection of the tangent planes — onto the crease. > Stacked on #444 → #443 → #442 → #441 (needs the shared writers incl. 3MF, colour, onReport). Retarget to `main` as the stack merges. ## How - **`DualContourMesher`** (pure): samples the DE on the grid, gathers Hermite data (crossing point + DE gradient normal) on sign-changing edges, solves a **regularised QEF** per active cell — normal equations `(ATA + λI)p = ATb + λc` biased toward the cell mass point and clamped to the cell, robust against rank-deficient planar/edge cases **with no SVD dependency** — then joins the four cells around each sign-changing grid edge into a quad. Smooth per-vertex normals like the MC path. Interior mesher (closed when the shape is inside the cube; a DC boundary cap is a follow-up). - **`UserBulbMeshExporter.ExportDualContouring`** (+ `IDistanceEstimator` overload): same extension dispatch (OBJ/STL/PLY/glTF/3MF), per-vertex colour and print-readiness callback as the MC path. ## Tests `DualContouringTests`: - `Sphere_Dc_Is_Closed_Manifold_Outward_Solid` — closed, 2-manifold, outward, ~4/3·π volume (topology + winding sound). - `Box_Dc_Puts_A_Vertex_Nearer_The_Sharp_Corner_Than_Mc` — on an L∞ box, DC lands a vertex on the true 3D corner far tighter than MC, while staying a valid closed solid (the point of DC). - `Dc_Carries_Color_And_Reports_Print_Ready` — colour + print-readiness ride the shared writers. Suite **1645/1645**. ## Follow-ups - UI mode selector (Marching Cubes / Dual contouring) on the export panel. - DC boundary cap (the analog of #422 for the DC path). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

cited.name: Dual Contouring
ctx: It solves the topological ambiguities and sharp-feature rounding inherent in Marching Cubes by utilizing Hermite data (intersection points and surface normals) to optimize vertex placement via Quadratic Error Function (QEF) minimization.

Unlike its sibling Surface Nets, which places vertices at the centroid of edge intersections, Dual Contouring positions vertices to best fit the local surface geometry, allowing it to snap to creases and sharp features.

Regularization: To handle collinear normals (where Ac is singular), add a regularization term \lambda I to Ac and a bias term \lambda c{cell} to bc, where c{cell} is the cell center and \lambda is a small constant (e.g., 10^{-6}).

cited.name: AMR Volume Ray-Casting
ctx: AMR Volume Ray-Casting is a volume rendering technique that ray-marches Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) octrees directly without resampling to a uniform grid, avoiding the (2^{l{max}})^3 memory blow-up.

It solves the problem of efficiently visualizing sparse, multi-resolution simulation data by storing each leaf once in a per-level hash and stepping by the local cell size, ensuring computational cost scales with the actual simulation data rather than the bounding box.
Each leaf is stored exactly once.

title: feat(render): the light in the air: sun shafts and the glow round lamps, in their shadows (r_volumetric)
abstract: Roadmap item 18 (Wave D): volumetric light. A half-resolution ray-march pass, the approach Frostbite and UE4 used before froxels, built on the shadow maps the fork already has. ## What it does `r_realtimeLighting 2` only. A post pass at ¼ × ¼ of the view runs after the MSAA resolve and before bloom and the tone map. It marches the ray from the eye to the depth buffer and adds the light the air scatters toward the eye: - **Sun:** 16 steps, each sampled in the finest of the four cascades that holds it, so shafts through windows and doors and between trees carry the cascades' shadows. The march stops at `r_volumetricRange` (3000 units). - **Every lamp lit this frame:** - Only the segment of the ray inside the lamp's reach is marched (ray-sphere test). - 4 steps, spread by the angle at the lamp (equi-angular sampling, Kulla & Fajardo 2012), so the 1/d² falloff cancels against the sampling density. - The same shade, cone and fade terms `RtLightParticle` uses, plus one tap of the lamp's cube shadow. - Lamps whose upper-bound contribution (π/h of the lamp for a ray passing h away) is under the visible threshold are skipped. - **Scattering and noise:** Henyey-Greenstein forward scattering (g 0.5). Per-pixel interleaved-gradient jitter, evened out by the existing depth-aware blur. ## Cvars - `r_volumetric`: default 1, latched. - Live (density 0 skips the pass): - `r_volumetricDensity` 1 - `r_volumetricAnisotropy` 0.5 - `r_volumetricSun` 1 - `r_volumetricLamps` 1 - `r_volumetricRange` 3000 - New GPU timer: `volume`. ## Measured GTX 1080, 2560×1440, rtl 2, MSAA 4×: | Scene | `volume` | |---|---| | m3l2 house room (sun through windows and door) | 0.91 ms (sun and blur 0.41) | | Tech demo lamp hall (48 coloured lamps) | 0.93 ms (sun and blur 0.44) | The path to that: | Version | `volume` | |---|---| | Half size, 8 uniform steps, 4-tap shadows, loose cull | 4.4 ms | | Real cull, 1-tap shadows | 3.6 ms | | Equi-angular, 4 steps | 2.3 ms | | Quarter size | 0.9 ms | ## Look - **m3l2:** sun shafts from the windows and the open door fall to the floor. Outdoors there is a light warm haze that doesn't wash the scene out. - **Tech demo hall:** each coloured lamp lights the air around and below it. ## Not done - Froxel or temporal accumulation (would allow more steps). - Linking the density to a map's fog. - Extinction (the scene isn't dimmed by the haze). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01DR3T9M7Erwj1bUnuQrqKZ4

cited.name: Light Injection Pass
ctx: The Light Injection Pass is a post-processing technique that adds volumetric light scattering (such as sun shafts and lamp glow) to a rendered scene by marching rays from the camera through the volume to sample light sources and their occlusion.
It solves the problem of visualizing light interacting with participating media (air/fog) in real-time without full path tracing, relying on pre-existing shadow maps for occlusion.

Unlike Shadow Volume Rendering which uses geometric volumes, or Volume Shadow Calculation via Light Strength Buffer which may use different accumulation buffers, this method specifically targets direct illumination scattering using a ray-marching approach over a depth buffer, executed as a distinct post-process step.

cited.name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced)
ctx: A display-only rendering pipeline for trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes that projects 3D Gaussian distributions into 2D screen-space quads, sorts them by camera-space depth on the CPU, and renders them using hardware instancing with standard alpha blending.

It solves the problem of correct transparency compositing in 3DGS without requiring GPU compute shaders or writable GPU buffers (SSBO), which are often unavailable in constrained environments like WebGL or specific engine versions (e.g., Filament 1.71.5).

Unlike the official tile-based CUDA rasterizer, this method relies on a CPU-side back-to-front sort and generic instanced drawing, trading raw performance for broad compatibility and implementation simplicity.

title: feat(tools): voxel_isosurface — marching-cubes isosurface extraction from a 3D voxel field (ArcGIS Export Voxel Isosurface)
abstract: ## Summary `voxel_isosurface` — Extract a triangulated isosurface at one or more threshold values from a 3D voxel field (a multidimensional raster), via marching cubes. **ArcGIS counterpart:** [Export Voxel Isosurface](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/latest/tool-reference/multidimension/export-voxel-isosurface.htm) ## Motivation GeoLibre can now *build* 3D fields — `idw_3d` (#488) interpolates volumetric point observations onto a grid, `interpolate_from_spatiotemporal_points` (#463) writes multidimensional rasters, and the bundled kriging tools produce 3D-capable output. There is no way to turn any of them into geometry you can look at. The entire contouring suite (`contours_from_raster`, `contour_with_barriers`, `percentile_contours`, `volume_percentile_contours`) is 2D: it extracts *lines* from a *plane*. Extracting *surfaces* from a *volume* is the 3D analogue and is absent from both registries — nothing in either matches marching cubes, isosurface, or voxel. This is the recommendation with the most upside for the repo's identity. It is pure computational geometry with no dependencies, it completes the round-14/15 3D push by giving that suite a renderable output, and it lands directly in the repo's web-delivery lane: an isosurface mesh is exactly what a browser viewer consumes. It's also the natural pairing for `minimum_bounding_volume` (#484) and `inside_3d` — one builds containers by hand, this one derives them from data. Typical uses: plume and contamination envelopes from `idw_3d` output, ore-grade shells, cloud/aerosol layers from atmospheric stacks, and geological unit boundaries. ## Proposed behavior - `input` — multidimensional/3D raster, or a stack of aligned bands treated as Z slices (required) - `values` — one or more threshold values, comma-separated; one surface per value - `output` — triangle mesh geometry, one feature per threshold, with the threshold as an attribute - `format` (optional) — `multipatch` (default, consistent with the existing 3D tools) or `obj`/`gltf` for direct web use - `z_spacing` (optional) — vertical spacing between slices when the source carries no dimension metadata; defaults to `1` - `close_boundaries` (optional, default `true`) — cap surfaces where they meet the volume edge, so the result bounds a closed solid rather than leaking; this is what makes the output usable by `inside_3d` - `smooth` (optional) — Laplacian smoothing iterations over the extracted mesh, default `0` - `decimate` (optional) — target triangle-reduction fraction, since raw marching-cubes output is dense ## Implementation sketch Pure Rust, no external crates: 1. **Marching cubes.** Walk every 2×2×2 cell of the voxel grid. Classify the eight corners against the threshold into an 8-bit index, look the index up in the standard 256-entry edge table, and emit triangles with vertices placed by **linear interpolation** along each crossed edge (not at edge midpoints — midpoint placement is what makes isosurfaces look blocky). The edge/triangle tables are static const data and should be committed as such, with the table's provenance noted in a comment. 2. **Ambiguity.** The classic marching-cubes ambiguous cases produce holes in the surface. Resolve with the asymptotic decider on ambiguous face configurations; a test that extracts a sphere and asserts the mesh is **closed** (every edge shared by exactly two triangles) is the right way to catch a regression here, and is worth writing first. 3. **Vertex welding.** Adjacent cells generate duplicate vertices on shared edges. Weld by hashing quantised edge identity — keying on the edge's grid indices rather than the float coordinates, which avoids the float-equality trap entirely. 4. **Boundary capping.** With `close_boundaries`, treat the volume's outer faces as a threshold-exceeding wall so surfaces reaching the edge are sealed. 5. **Smoothing / decimation.** Optional Laplacian smoothing over the welded mesh, then quadric-error-metric decimation to the requested fraction. Both operate on the welded topology from step 3. 6. **Output.** Multipatch through the same geometry path `minimum_bounding_volume` (#484) uses; `gltf`/`obj` as plain buffer writes for browser consumption. Thresholds are independent, and within one threshold the cell sweep is embarrassingly parallel — `dispatch_worker` over Z slabs (native threads, serial WASM fallback), merging at the weld step. Fully deterministic: no RNG, no `Date::now`. Wiring follows the standard 3-file pattern: a new module in `crates/geolibre-tools/src/voxel_isosurface.rs` implementing `wbcore::Tool`, three lines in `lib.rs` (`mod` + `Box::new` in `geolibre_tools()` + a `geolibre_param_schemas` match arm, enforced by a unit test), and a README table row. **Estimated effort:** medium

title: feat(viz): hierarchical brick-map DDA for /spike.html
abstract: ## Summary PR #2 of the WebGPU raymarcher direction. Replaces the dense voxel buffer used by the Step 0 spike (PR #66 / `1e837af`) with a sparse brick-map representation that the marcher walks hierarchically — empty top-level cells stride 8 voxels at a time, occupied bricks are descended into for fine DDA. Drone airspace is overwhelmingly empty (>99% sky), so this is the storage shape later PRs will need (sensor primitive in PR #3, terrain streaming in PR #4+). For the heightmap stand-in, brick count is roughly `top²` (~256 bricks at N=128) instead of the worst-case `top³` (4096) — the memory win grows with sparsity. Zero impact on the production viz: still hidden behind `/spike.html`, not built into production output. ## Files added - `client/webgpu/brickmap.ts` — host-side brick map allocation (`createBrickMap`) and one-shot build dispatch (`buildBrickMap`) - `client/webgpu/shaders/build_brickmap.wgsl` — compute pass that scans each top-level cell, atomically allocates a pool slot, and copies the brick's voxels in ## Files modified - `client/webgpu/shaders/march.wgsl` — hierarchical DDA. Top-level walk strides `BRICK` voxels at a time; descent re-derives `fv` from the actual ray position in the occupied brick; ascent recomputes `c_tmax` for the new top cell. Reuses the AABB clip + safe-rd primitives from PR #1 (so axis-aligned and outside-grid rays still work correctly). `Grid` struct's reserved word becomes `top_size`. - `client/spikeMain.ts` — wires `createBrickMap` + `buildBrickMap`, binds `top_grid` + `brick_pool` instead of the dense voxel buffer, fills the new `top_size` slot of the `Grid` uniform. ## Test plan - [x] `npm run typecheck` passes - [x] `npm run build` passes - [x] `dotnet build -c Release` passes (pre-push hook validation) - [ ] Visit `/spike.html` via `npm run dev` in a WebGPU-capable browser; confirm the heightmap renders identically to PR #1's Step 0 output (same camera orbit, same surface) - [ ] Toggle camera viewing angles to verify the hierarchical DDA handles boundary-crossing transitions cleanly (no popping or missing voxels at brick edges) - [ ] Optional: bump `N` to 256 in `spikeMain.ts` and confirm it still renders smoothly — the brick map's stride wins should become more visible at larger grid sizes ## Why this matters for ResQ Viz This is the same storage structure the eventual mesh-link line-of-sight sensor query (PR #4) will use: same compute kernel, just dispatched from a different ray source. PR #3 will introduce that ray-batch API on top of this DDA. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Refactor** * Optimized voxel storage architecture by transitioning from dense buffer representation to sparse brick-map structure, reducing memory footprint and improving ray traversal efficiency by enabling hierarchical skipping of empty regions.

ctx: Hierarchical Brick-Map DDA is a ray traversal technique that replaces a dense voxel buffer with a sparse hierarchical structure (brick-map) to skip empty regions.

title: feat: solid voxelization of normalized meshes (issue 0010)
abstract: ## Summary Implements [issue 0010](docs/issues/0010-solid-voxelization.md) (child of the M1 tracking issue 0001): convert a normalized `MeshData` (watertight assumed) into the solid voxel target that `growAssembly` consumes. Method was fixed in advance by the [issue 0008 spike](docs/issues/0008-spike-voxelization-method.md); no design decisions were open. ``` MeshData (mm / Z-up / grounded) → 6-direction majority vote (±X/±Y/±Z odd-even ray parity) → { voxels: Map , seed } // voxel centers at (i,j,k)·voxelMm — grow.ts convention ``` ## Changes - `src/domain/voxelize.ts` — `voxelizeSolid(mesh, voxelMm, colorId)`. Hand-rolled Möller–Trumbore ray-triangle intersection accelerated by per-axis uniform triangle grids (3 shared grids vs the spike's 6 — cheaper index construction). Majority threshold `votes >= 3` (ties inside) — **verified identical to the spike's measured baseline** (`Math.ceil(6/2)`). Zero three.js dependency; `colorId` is a parameter so the domain layer stays palette-free (this deviates from the issue's originally drafted signature; the issue doc is updated accordingly). - `src/domain/voxelize.test.ts` — 6 tests with analytic ground truth. - Issue doc updated: contract signature + per-criterion evidence, marked done. ## Acceptance criteria (measured) - [x] Error rate ≤ 2% vs analytic solution — sphere **1.44%** (r=20mm, 1280 faces), box **0.0047%** - [x] Interior is filled (solid, not shell) — central 3×3×3 block fully filled (sphere placed off-origin to avoid the axis-aligned ray degeneracy known from the spike) - [x] Seed = filled voxel on lowest-k layer nearest the (i,j) bbox center (same policy as `generator.cellsToVoxels`) - [x] 40³-equivalent timing logged — **~75ms** (20480-face icosphere, 32764 voxels; spike measured 85–103ms) ## Review notes (orchestrated delegation) Implemented by a sonnet implementer subagent; reviewed with all four checks re-run independently (lint / format:check / **109 tests** / build — green). The majority-vote threshold claim ("follows the spike baseline") was cross-checked against the spike source before approval. Zero review round-trips needed. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

cited.name: Solid Voxelization via 6-Direction Odd-Even Ray Parity
ctx: This method converts a normalized, watertight mesh into a solid voxel target by determining the inside/outside status of each voxel center using the parity of ray intersections along six axis-aligned directions.

It differs from its parent Stochastic Ray-Casting Voxelization by using deterministic, axis-aligned rays and a majority vote on parity rather than random rays and intersection counts, providing a robust, non-stochastic solution for solid interior filling.
mesh: A watertight mesh defined by vertex positions and triangle indices.

title: Feature-Driven Ambient Occlusion for Direct Volume Rendering
abstract: Ambient occlusion techniques were introduced to improve data comprehension by bringing soft fading shadows. They consist in attenuating light by considering the occlusion resulting from the presence of neighboring structures. Recently introduced in volume rendering, we show that the straightforward application of ambient occlusion in direct volume rendering has its limits as rendering a multi-layer volume results in overdarkening the internal layers of the volume. This paper proposes to address the overdarkening issue by computing ambient occlusion according to the features present in the dataset. This allows us to neglect inter-occlusions between features without losing the auto-occlusions that give cues on the shape of the considered features. We use a GPU-based approach with bricking to speed up the computations of our ambient occlusion method. Results show that our approach not only improves the visual quality of images compared to classical ambient occlusion, but it is also less parametersensitive, thus furthermore improving usability for every-day users.

cited.name: Feature-Driven Ambient Occlusion
ctx: Feature-Driven Ambient Occlusion is a shading technique for direct volume rendering (DVR) that computes ambient occlusion separately for identified features (layers) to prevent the overdarkening of internal layers caused by inter-occlusions from neighboring features, while preserving auto-occlusions.

Unlike classical ambient occlusion, which darkens internal layers in multi-layer volumes due to inter-occlusions, this method neglects inter-occlusions between features to prevent overdarkening while keeping auto-occlusions.

Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V, a transfer function mapping scalar values to opacity \alpha and color, a set of identified features k \in [1, nf] where nf is the number of features, and parameters L (number of rays), M (samples per ray), R\Omega (occlusion sphere radius), and a (initial offset).

title: Feature/center instancing
abstract: Option B from `discussion.md` §3B. Written up in full as its new §7. `buildBlock()` now returns the occupancy walk's own output instead of a baked mesh — a flat grid index, a six-bit surviving-face mask and an orbit byte per occupied cell, plus the axis centre table. Six bytes a voxel where six baked quads were over a kilobyte. `src/scene/instancing.js` draws that from a shared 24-vertex cube template, resolving position, the gamut ramp, the orbit hue ramp and face occlusion in a patched stock material's vertex shader. ### No behaviour change `Core.meshArrays()` still returns exactly what it always did — it is now `expandInstances(instanceArrays(...))`, so the occlusion rules have one implementation, the OBJ exporters still get real triangles, and **every `pos`/`idx` hash in `golden.json` is unchanged**. All four render modes became four indexings of the same instance attributes, so the derived wire/points/centres geometries and their byte accounting are gone, and switching modes now allocates nothing on the GPU. `lattice/recipe.js` no longer imports THREE at all. Hidden faces are sent outside the clip volume rather than simply drawn, so culling survives the translucent fade-in — otherwise every specimen would show its own interior on the way up. ### Measured (vs. the pre-branch core) | | before | after | |---|---|---| | geometry build | — | **1.9–4.6×** faster | | whole build | — | 1.3–1.8× faster | | specimen at R=64 | 42.0 MB | **649 KB** | | worker message at R=64 | 42.3 MB | 457 KB (92×) | | resident, 294 on-screen specimens | 27.8 MB | **0.66 MB** | This answers §3C: at R=64 baked geometry exhausted `CACHE_BYTES` after **six** specimens; it now does so after about **394**. Nothing in `config.js` changed. ### The one regression Instancing submits whole cubes and discards hidden faces in the vertex shader. For every shipped preset that is exactly 1.00× (none of them culls a face). For a zero-gap layout it is 2.0× (`3:0.5,5:0.0`) to 3.3× (4·4·4 inner 0) the triangles — vertex work only, no fragments. Skipping them needs either six draw calls a specimen or a per-frame buffer rebuild, both of which cost more than they save. ### Verification - `npm test` — 19 tests. New `test/instancing.test.js` pins the record itself and runs a CPU model of the vertex shader that reproduces the baked mesh vertex for vertex and colour for colour, plus a bound on how far the GPU's f32 arithmetic can drift (<1e-7 of the unit box — under half a step of an 8-bit channel). - `npm run test:browser` — 7 tests, now serial (~2 min; two headless Chromes on software WebGL contend badly). New `test/browser/render-modes.test.js` drives all twelve render × colour combinations and asserts on pixels, because a failed shader compile does not throw: three logs it and draws nothing. - Additionally, `main` and this branch were screenshotted side by side across all twelve combinations, eight frames averaged: worst channel difference **0.93 of 255**, no shader errors. ### Also answers 5.4 The 3³ LOD proxy now removes 22% of submitted triangles for 0.033 ms a frame and 20 KB, having previously also saved a 40 MB buffer and its upload. Most of its value is gone — your instinct was right — but the GPU side is not measurable under software rendering, so nothing was removed. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

cited.name: Procedural Instancing for Voxel Blocks
ctx: Procedural Instancing for Voxel Blocks is a rendering technique that replaces baked mesh geometry with a compact instance record per voxel, resolving position, color, and occlusion in the vertex shader using a shared cube template.

It differs from standard instancing by computing transformations, visibility culling, and texture selection procedurally within the shader based on a dense, bit-packed instance buffer, allowing for significant memory reduction and cache efficiency compared to pre-baked geometries.
If hidden, move the vertex corners outside the clip volume (e.g., set clip distance to -1.0 or push vertices to infinity).
