title: Fix sawtooth edges and depth of iso_categorical labels rendering
abstract: # References and relevant issues None that I could find. # Description Fixes sawtooth edges when rendering labels in 3D. A staircase seen at a grazing angle, while moving the camera. main: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8de8058f-87d1-45ab-9de5-0602adcfdcde this PR: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/38fd0886-9868-49cf-8da8-b609f0c40e15 Longer recording, switching between old and new, fast and smooth shaders: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2b92c6b1-3794-4244-99fd-b00781b2f75a ## The issue In 3D, labels layers are rendered with the `iso_categorical` method (or `translucent_categorical` when `rendering='translucent'`). Both march along each view ray in fixed steps (`relative_step_size`, 0.8 voxel by default) and only test the voxel at each sample. A ray that only clips the corner of a voxel, between two samples, misses it. Whether that happens depends on where the samples fall, which drifts from pixel to pixel, so straight edges seen at grazing angles render as a sawtooth that shifts as the camera moves. A smaller step makes the teeth finer but never removes them. ## The fix At the first unclipped sample, the shader now walks through every voxel the ray passes through, in order (Amanatides & Woo), and stops at the first one with a non-transparent label. No voxel can be skipped, so in volume depiction the result no longer depends on `relative_step_size`. Clipping planes are evaluated where the ray enters and leaves each voxel, so cut surfaces stay where they were. The ray is shortened by a tiny margin at both ends, as otherwise rounding reads the neighbouring voxels when a plane starts exactly on a voxel boundary. Both categorical methods share the new snippet, and the `fast` and `smooth` gradient modes only change how the hit voxel is shaded, so all combinations are fixed. ## Also fixed by this **Depth across scales.** The new code sets each pixel's depth to the point where the ray enters the hit voxel, in data coordinates. On main, the depth (`frag_depth_point = iloc * u_shape`) was shifted by half a voxel along each axis, in the layer's own voxels. Layers with different `scale` are shifted by different amounts, so where two surfaces are close, the one behind can be drawn in front. As the shift is along every axis, how much it matters depends on the viewing direction; the figure uses the direction where it is largest: **Plane depiction.** With `depiction='plane'`, main's sub-stepping read the voxels just before the plane instead of those at it, so a plane at z = 5 showed the data at z = 4. The traversal reads the voxels within the plane's thickness: ## Performance The traversal visits every voxel along the ray. Each visit costs more than a sample of the old loop, and at oblique angles a ray crosses more voxels than it took samples. Frame times on an M1 Max (canvas about 2000 × 1800 px, `iso_categorical`, default step 0.8), main → this PR: | data | axis-aligned view | oblique view | |---|---|---| | empty, 256³ (worst case) | 3.6 → 4.3 ms (1.2×) | 3.7 → 6.3 ms (1.7×) | | 300 nuclei, 256³ | 3.1 → 3.4 ms (1.1×) | 3.7 → 4.6 ms (1.3×) | | 1500 nuclei, 512³ | 6.7 → 7.2 ms (1.1×) | 8.1 → 9.8 ms (1.2×) | `translucent_categorical` is similar (1.1× to 1.8×). The old cost grows with 1/step while the new one does not depend on it: compared with main at step 0.4 (which still has the artifacts, only finer), this PR is as fast or faster in all of these cases (0.66× to 1.0×). Dense labels, where rays stop almost immediately, render in under 1 ms either way. What remains is the cost of reading every voxel along the ray. I have a prototype for a follow-up PR that skips empty space using a coarse map of which 8 × 8 × 8 blocks contain labels. In the same benchmark it renders identically and is faster than main everywhere (0.5× to 0.93×), but it needs a second texture and has to be kept up to date when the data changes or is painted, so I'd rather keep it separate from this fix. ## Tests Two tests in `src/napari/_vispy/_tests/test_vispy_labels_layer.py`, both failing on main: - `test_labels_iso_categorical_independent_of_step_size`: a staircase at a grazing angle renders identically with step sizes 0.8 and 0.1. - `test_labels_iso_categorical_depth_across_scales`: of two overlapping layers with different scales, the one in front is drawn in front. ## Not in this PR vispy's own `iso`, `mip` and `minip` methods, used for image layers, compute the depth in the same way and have the same half-voxel offset. Fixing that belongs in vispy.

cited.name: iso_categorical
ctx: isocategorical is a volume rendering method designed for categorical label datasets (e.g., segmented anatomical structures) that replaces fixed-step sampling with exact voxel traversal to eliminate sawtooth artifacts at grazing angles.
Unlike standard isosurface methods that rely on scalar field thresholds, this method tests discrete integer labels, stopping at the first non-transparent voxel encountered along the ray.

It sets itself apart from its siblings by ensuring that every voxel the ray physically intersects is visited, making the result independent of the sampling step size and preventing rays from skipping thin voxel corners.

title: fix(fluoro): backward pass ignores post-render normalisation and inversion, so pose gradients are wrong and the documented 2D/3D registration workflow anti-converges
abstract: ## What's wrong `SlangDiffDRRFunction` stitches together derivatives of two different functions. The forward pass hands PyTorch a normalised, inverted image, computed in numpy outside the autograd graph, while the backward pass applies PyTorch's upstream gradient verbatim to the Slang autodiff of the raw Beer-Lambert intensity. The Jacobian of the post-processing is never applied. With the package defaults (`normalize=True, invert=True`) the returned pose gradient is not merely inaccurate, it is directionally wrong, and the gradient-based 2D/3D registration workflow that the README advertises ("Compute exact gradients for 2D/3D registration", fluoro-simulator/README.md:12) and that the module's own docstrings demonstrate (renderer lines 654 to 665 and 800 to 814) does the opposite of registering. Adam faithfully ascends the loss surface. On a real chest CT the pose error grows from 19.0 mm and 12.4 degrees to 137.6 mm and 118.1 degrees within 200 iterations, while the identical renderer with the post-processing kept inside the graph converges to 0.0005 mm and 0.0009 degrees. In the cleanest sub-case (`invert=True, normalize=False`) the returned gradient is the exact negative of the true one, component for component, to the last bit. ## Where the boundary breaks (all references are to commit `945948d`, which is what head is at th time of writing) The forward pass of the autograd function (`fluorosim/rendering/diffdrr_slang_renderer.py`:570-598) calls `renderer.render()`, which dispatches the Slang forward kernel and then, on the CPU and outside any graph, applies per-frame min-max normalisation (lines 382 to 385) and inversion to the clinical convention (lines 388 to 389). That post-processed array is what `torch.from_numpy` returns to autograd as the graph output (line 598). The backward pass (lines 600 to 630) takes `grad_output`, which PyTorch computed with respect to that post-processed image, and passes it unmodified to `render_with_gradients` (lines 620 to 625). There it is uploaded as `gradOutput` and consumed by `renderDRR_backward` (`diffdrr_slang.slang`, line 362) as the upstream gradient of `computePixelIntensity`, whose output is the raw intensity `I = i0 * exp(-integral)` (shader line 297). The `[Differentiable]` region ends at the raw intensity; the graph output does not. Three aggravating observations: 1. Both `normalize` and `invert` default to `True` (`SlangDiffDRRConfig`, renderer lines 133 to 134, mirrored in `XrayPhysics`, `config.py` lines 141 to 142), so every user following the documented examples hits this. 2. `render_with_gradients` has the same inconsistency as a standalone API: it returns the normalised, inverted image (lines 504 to 517) alongside gradients of the raw one (lines 495 to 502), and its own docstring example (lines 426 to 435) computes $\mathtt{grad\_output}=2(\mathtt{synthetic}-\mathtt{target})$ from precisely that returned image. 3. The shader ships a `normalizeImage` kernel (shader lines 391 to 408) that is never dispatched, let alone differentiated. The Python-side numpy normalisation is the one that runs. ## The missing Jacobian Let $r$ be the raw image, let $\Delta = \max(r) - \min(r)$ and let $\varepsilon$ be the stability constant. Under the defaults the graph output is $$ f(r) = 1 - \frac{r - \min(r)}{\Delta + \varepsilon}. $$ Let $J_r = \frac{\partial r}{\partial \theta}$ be the Jacobian of the raw renderer with respect to pose and let $g = \partial L / \partial f$ be the upstream gradient. The backward pass returns $J_r^{\mathsf T}g$. The correct gradient is $$ \nabla_\theta L = J_r^{\mathsf T}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right)^{\mathsf T}g = -\frac{1}{\Delta + \varepsilon}J_r^{\mathsf T}g + \text{terms through }\min(r)\text{ and }\max(r). $$ The omitted leading factor is negative: the sign flips. The magnitude error, $1/(\Delta + \varepsilon)$, is largely laundered by Adam's per-parameter preconditioning, which is why the failure presents as clean anti-convergence rather than mere sluggishness. The trailing terms arise because $\min(r)$ and $\max(r)$ are themselves pose-dependent, which also means a constant rescaling of the returned gradient would not fix the defaults case. With `invert` alone the relationship is exact: $\frac{\partial f}{\partial r} = -I$, so the returned gradient is precisely the negative of the true one. The reproduction below confirms this bitwise. ## How to reproduce Reproducer is too big for an issue, so it's [here](https://gist.github.com/chrisvoncsefalvay/084c206a1e289aee9c2f2f9bbe1c86d4). It downloads the 3D Slicer CTChest sample volume (SHA256-pinned), resamples it to 2.5 mm isotropic and maps HU to μ with the package's own `VolumePreprocessor`. The ground truth pose is rotation $\theta^\star=(7,-5,9)^\circ$ and translation $t^\star=(14,-10,8)\,\mathrm{mm}$, a clearly visible misalignment of 12.4 degrees and 19.0 mm; the optimisation starts from zero. The loss is MSE on the rendered images, per the module's own registration example, with Adam at identical hyperparameters for both arms and 200 iterations. Because the defect lives in the Python-side composition rather than in the kernel, the script isolates it with a line-faithful PyTorch transcription of `computePixelIntensity` (shader line numbers cited throughout the source), replicating both autograd boundary conditions exactly: the current one, labelled current@945948d in the figures (post-processing outside the graph, upstream gradient applied to the raw-intensity VJP, exactly as the repository computes it at that commit) and the corrected one (identical renderer, post-processing inside the graph). This makes the reproduction runnable on any machine. I've included a `--parity` mode that checks the transcription against the live Slang renderer on a CUDA host -- i've put this into a separate flag so it can be de-CId. Gom8ry follows the package defaults for source-to-detector and source-to-isocentre distances; the march step is 2.5 mm and the detector 128 px, both purely for CPU runtime. I've included two presentations. The volume is oriented so the identity-pose march axis is the anatomical anteroposterior axis, giving a posteroanterior projection rather than a vertex view along the slice stack, and the pixel pitch is 6.0 mm, since the default 512 px at 0.5 mm is a 256 mm plate and hence, at the default magnification of 2, a 128 mm field at the isocentre that crops a thorax to a mediastinal keyhole. Neither choice touches the gradient path, both merely make the evidence legible. Identical renderer, identical optimiser, identical target and seed. The only difference between the arms is whether the post-processing Jacobian participates in the chain rule. The first arm is labelled current@945948d, the gradient path exactly as the repository computes it at that commit, so the label stays auditable once a fix lands. | | current@945948d gradient path | corrected gradient path | |---|---|---| | final loss (from 2.82e-2) | 3.14e-1 | 1.3e-8 | | rotation error (from 12.45 deg) | 118.1 deg, having peaked at 120.2 | 0.0009 deg | | translation error (from 18.97 mm) | 137.6 mm, increasing monotonically | 0.0005 mm | | recovered pose | (-91.5, 29.4, -46.3) deg, (5.8, -70.0, -115.6) mm | (6.999, -5.000, 9.000) deg, (14.000, -10.000, 8.000) mm | The image evidence. The current@945948d path has rolled the patient a quarter turn onto their side and differentiated them straight out of the frame in 200 iters: In the invert-only configuration the current@945948d gradient is the exact negative of the corrected one (`np.array_equal(g_current, -g_corrected)` evals `True`), with cosine similarity to finite differences of -0.991 against +0.991 and sign agreement on 0 of 6 pose components against 6 of 6. Under the full defaults the story is barely different: with the whole thorax and background air in frame the extremal pixels are stable, the min-max Jacobian is dominated by its constant $-1/(\Delta + \varepsilon)$ factor, and the current gradient comes out anti-aligned with the truth at cosine -0.988, against +0.985 for the corrected one, with sign agreement 0 of 6 against 5 of 6, robust across finite-difference step sizes (-0.99 against +0.99 at a 2.5 times coarser step). In narrower fields, where the identity of the extremal pixels switches with pose, the pose-dependent min and max terms add a decorrelating component on top of the sign flip. Either way the returned direction is unusable. ## How to fix it The best fix for the existing API is to apply the missing vector-Jacobian product at the shared renderer boundary. `render_with_gradients()` already has both quantities required for that calculation: the raw image from its forward dispatch and the upstream gradient with respect to the processed image. It should map that gradient back to raw-intensity space before uploading it to the Slang backward kernel: ```python # after the fwd dispatch raw_image = self._output_texture.to_numpy().reshape(height, width) if raw: image = raw_image else: image = _postprocess_image(raw_image, cfg) grad_output = _postprocess_vjp(raw_image, grad_output, cfg) # upload grad_output, now dL/d(raw_image), and dispatch Slang bwd ``` The normalisation VJP must include both the direct $1/(\max(r)-\min(r)+\varepsilon)$ term and the terms through $\min(r)$ and $\max(r)$. Gradients at tied extrema should be shared across the tied pixels, matching `torch.amin` and `torch.amax`. Inversion is the simpler first step: negate the incoming gradient before applying the normalisation VJP. This placement preserves the current outputs of `render()`, `render_with_gradients()`, the exported `SlangDiffDRRFunction` and `TorchSlangDiffDRR`, while fixing both the standalone NumPy API and the Torch path. A keyword-only `raw=True` option can make the alternative contract explicit: return raw Beer-Lambert intensity and interpret `grad_output` with respect to that raw image. Moving the display transform into `TorchSlangDiffDRR` is attractive in isolation, but it would make the exported and documented `SlangDiffDRRFunction.apply()` return a different quantity and would still leave the standalone `render_with_gradients()` boundary to repair separately. Applying the VJP at the shared boundary fixes every affected entry point without changing their default observable behaviour. Two adjacent notes while I'm in the neighbourhood. First, for the differentiable path specifically, per-frame min-max normalisation is a questionable companion to gradient-based registration even once differentiated, both because the switching extremal pixels noted above make the objective only piecewise smooth in pose and for radiometric consistency between frames. a fixed windowing, or a normalisation-invariant loss such as NCC, would serve registration better. I've made this point in my other issue. Second, `backward` currently re-renders the forward pass inside `render_with_gradients`, which doubles the cost of every optimisation step. Caching the forward result in `ctx` would neatly halve it. Happy to file separate issues as this has been bloated enough as is. Gradient audit, for good measure -- really nicely shows the inversion:

cited.name: Differentiable DRR with Post-Processing Normalization and Inversion
ctx: This method corrects the gradient computation in differentiable Digital Radiograph Reconstruction (DRR) pipelines where post-rendering normalization and inversion are applied outside the automatic differentiation graph.

It solves the problem of anti-convergence in 2D/3D registration caused by omitted Jacobians for min-max normalization and clinical inversion, which flip gradient signs and scale magnitudes incorrectly.

It sets itself apart from standard differentiable volume rendering by explicitly handling the non-linear, pose-dependent boundary conditions introduced by global image statistics (\min and \max) at the Python/CUDA interface.

title: fix(fluoro): bwd pass is almost an order of magnitude of fwd
abstract: ## What's broken `render_with_gradients` is vastly slower than the forward render. On an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, `render_with_gradients` at a 256 px detector, 1.0 mm step and a $128^3$ volume measures 2.365 ms against 0.263 ms for the raw forward render, and a full optimisation step through `SlangDiffDRRFunction` measures 2.954 ms. Netting out the re-rendered forward, the readbacks and the launch overhead, roughly 1.8 ms is `bwd_diff` execution alone, about seven times the marching kernel it differentiates. The reason behind this is that the reverse-mode transform of the `[MaxIters(2048)]` march loop must store or recompute per-iteration state, and the package pays that price on every pixel of every backward pass. It does not, actually, need to. The adjoint of a Beer-Lambert line integral is, as we all remember, a single forward-like march: accumulate the optical depth and its six-component pose derivative in one pass, multiply at the end. A hand-written adjoint kernel should cost roughly one forward, bounding the whole optimisation step near 1.0 to 1.1 ms at this configuration, an end-to-end speedup of about 2.7x. ## Where we lose time (all references are to commit 945948d, which is what head is at the time of writing) The backward kernel (`diffdrr_slang.slang` lines 341 to 386) calls `bwd_diff(computePixelIntensity)` per pixel (lines 373 to 381). The march inside `computePixelIntensity` iterates up to `MAX_STEPS = 2048` with trilinear fetches per step; reverse-mode through that loop synthesises per-iteration state handling that the forward never pays. Measured decomposition at 256 px, 1.0 mm, $128^3$ volume (medians over 30 repetitions) on the Blackwell: | component | ms | |---|---| | raw forward render (kernel + readback + launch) | 0.263 | | marching kernel alone (slope of the $1/\Delta t$ regression) | 0.16 | | fixed launch and Python glue (both sweep intercepts) | 0.10 to 0.15 | | CPU post-processing | 0.024 | | host upload of the returned image | 0.021 | | `render_with_gradients` (re-rendered forward + bwd_diff + readbacks) | 2.365 | | full autograd step, current@945948d | 2.954 | The residual attributable to `bwd_diff` execution is about 1.8 ms, roughly 7x the marching kernel. This may be quantitatively different because `pretending to support sm_6_0` suggests a codegen issue, but codegen goes either way, the ratio ought to be the same. ## Maths time Per pixel, with samples $x_i = s(\theta) + t_i(\theta)\,d(\theta)$ and weights $\Delta t$, $$I = i_0 \ e^{-A} \qquad A = \sum_i \mu(x_i)\ \Delta t, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = - \frac{\partial L}{\partial I}\ I \frac{\partial A}{\partial \theta}.$$ The pose derivative of the optical depth is one march: $$\frac{\partial A}{\partial \theta} \=\ \sum_i \nabla\mu(x_i)\cdot\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial \theta}\ \Delta t \+\ \sum_i \mu(x_i) \ \frac{\partial \Delta t}{\partial \theta} $$ where $\partial x_i/\partial\theta = \partial s/\partial\theta + t_i\,\partial d/\partial\theta + d\,\partial t_i/\partial\theta$. Every per-ray Jacobian ($\partial s$, $\partial d$, $\partial t_\mathrm{near}$, $\partial t_\mathrm{far}$ with respect to the six pose parameters) is closed form and computed once per pixel: three Euler derivative matrices applied to constant vectors + the slab-face formulas for the intersection derivatives. Since the eight corner values already fetched determine it exactly, the trilinear gradient $\nabla\mu$ is free at each sample. So the adjoint is a single march accumulating $A$ and the six-vector $\partial A/\partial\theta$ together, followed by one multiplication. The cost of that is the forward's fetches + a modicum of extra arithmetic, say 1-1.5x the forward march, giving us a 5.5x save. As a bonus the forward intensity never needs re-rendering. ## Reproduction The big shared ablator [here](https://gist.github.com/chrisvoncsefalvay/39e3431eeb4211e1d6c565b66ae34b2c) has it. ``` pip install numpy slangpy matplotlib torch # CUDA build python throughput_ablation.py --repo /path/to/i4h-sensor-simulation/fluoro-simulator --out report_perf ``` With the adjoint in place, the optimisation step is bounded by one forward march, one adjoint march, the gradient reduction and the fixed overheads That empirically gives around 1.0-1.1 ms vs the measured 2.954 ms, near 2.7x, without even addressing residency or batching. Free perfomance is good.

cited.name: Adjoint Beer-Lambert Marching
ctx: Adjoint Beer-Lambert Marching computes the gradient of the Beer-Lambert line integral with respect to pose parameters in a single forward-like pass, avoiding the storage or recomputation of per-iteration state required by naive reverse-mode differentiation of the marching loop.

It differs from the naive reverse-mode transform of the marching loop, which synthesizes per-iteration state handling, by costing roughly one forward march (1-1.5x forward cost) instead of ~7x, providing a significant speedup and eliminating the need to re-render the forward intensity.

Inputs: Pose parameters \theta (6 degrees of freedom: 3 translation, 3 rotation), volume density field \mu(x), ray origin s(\theta), ray direction d(\theta), near/far intersection distances t{near}, t{far}, incident intensity i0, and loss gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial I}.

cited.name: Flat blocking multi-resolution volume rendering
ctx: Flat blocking multi-resolution volume rendering is a strategy for loading and rendering large volume datasets by dividing the volume into sub-blocks of equal physical size but assigning each block a different resolution (Level of Detail, LOD) based on its internal data variation.
It solves the problem of memory bandwidth and rendering time for large volumes by avoiding uniform high-resolution storage.
Unlike hierarchical structures that change spatial extent, this method keeps block dimensions constant while varying the voxel count within them.

cited.name: Regular Grid
ctx: A Regular Grid is a spatial acceleration structure that divides a scene's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) into a fixed-size, uniform 3D grid of cells (voxels).
It accelerates ray tracing by allowing rays to skip empty cells, thereby reducing the number of primitive intersection tests.

An optimized approach (as in) iterates primitives first, calculates their bounding voxel range, and inserts them only into those specific cells, reducing complexity to O(P \cdot \text{avg\voxels\per\prim}).

cited.name: Voxel Polygon Rendering
ctx: Voxel Polygon Rendering is a hybrid real-time rendering technique that projects a 2D voxel height map onto the screen as vertical bars, solving the problem of rendering high-detail terrain at constant speed without traditional 6DOF polygon operations.

It sets itself apart from its sibling Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by introducing "voxel polygons" to vary local detail and an s-buffer (vertical c-buffer) to handle floating geometry, whereas the sibling relies on a simpler per-column depth buffer for stacking.
Input: A voxel map (array of height and color per location), camera parameters (limited to Y-axis rotation and small X-axis tilt), and a set of "voxel polygons" defining local geometry variations.

title: Floaters No More: Radiance Field Gradient Scaling for Improved Near-Camera Training
abstract: NeRF acquisition typically requires careful choice of near planes for the different cameras or suffers from background collapse, creating floating artifacts on the edges of the captured scene. The key insight of this work is that background collapse is caused by a higher density of samples in regions near cameras. As a result of this sampling imbalance, near-camera volumes receive significantly more gradients, leading to incorrect density buildup. We propose a gradient scaling approach to counter-balance this sampling imbalance, removing the need for near planes, while preventing background collapse. Our method can be implemented in a few lines, does not induce any significant overhead, and is compatible with most NeRF implementations.

cited.name: Gradient Scaling for Near-Camera Training
ctx: Gradient scaling is a technique for differentiable volume rendering optimization that prevents background collapse and near-camera floaters by counter-balancing the sampling density imbalance close to cameras.

It sets itself apart from alternatives like near-plane clipping or occlusion losses by addressing the root cause (gradient magnitude imbalance) directly during backpropagation, rather than imposing priors on density distribution or restricting ray origins.
If the scene scale differs significantly, \sigma should be estimated from camera calibration.

title: Fourier Volume Rendering
abstract: By using the Fourier Slice Theorem, projections of volume data of size N 3 can be generated in O(N 2 log N) time. An image for any viewing direction can be obtained by taking a 2D slice from a 3D spectrum at the appropriate direction and then inverse Fourier transforming it. In this paper, we have implemented this idea, and the resulting image can be generated faster than conventional volume rendering. 2D IFFT: Perform a 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) on the 2D slice I(u, v) to obtain the spatial domain projection image.

title: Fourier Volume Rendering final version
abstract: In this report a direct volume rendering technique called Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) is explored in depth. FVR computes projection of a three dimensional dataset. Conventional volume rendering methods have a complexity of O�N 3 �. FVR has a complexity of O�N 2 logN � and thus can be computed much faster. The mathematical theory behind FVR is explained first. Then FVR itself is discussed, and an example is given. The reason why the Hartley transform was chosen instead of the Fourier transform is explained. Finally a possible real time implemention in hardware is discussed. The last chapter handles about a completely different subject. It is about coronary artery extraction out of a three dimensional dataset of the heart obtained by MRI. Images computed using FVR look like X-ray pictures. FVR is a fast method for computing projections. A hardware implementation mainly concerns a resampling chip that can resample a plane out of a three dimensional dataset in 150 ns. This chip should use a resampling filter of size 5 � 5 � 5, which needs 64 voxels to compute one sample point.

title: Froxel volumetric fog with path-traced volumetric shadows
abstract: Implements a frustum-aligned volumetric fog grid (froxels) in the Caustica path tracer, lit entirely by path tracing rather than a shadow map. ## What it does - **`froxel.rgen`** (world raygen idx 2): each frustum voxel reconstructs its world position, computes height-falloff density, and casts the same `visibility()` NEE shadow ray the surfaces use, accumulating real per-channel Beer–Lambert transmittance through tinted glass/ice/water/entity dielectrics — so a magenta pane scatters magenta fog. In-scatter = `σₛ · HG(phase) · illuminance · toLight` plus an isotropic sky-ambient fill; stores `float4(inscatter, density)`. - **`froxel.comp`**: per-pixel screen raymarch over the grid with analytic segment Beer–Lambert integration, stopped at the reversed-Z surface depth, composited as `scene·T + fog·preExposure` (same exposure seam as the path tracer). - **Java**: `RtFroxel` compute pipeline, `RtContext.createStorageImage3D`, `RtPipeline` `WORLD_FROXEL` binding + `traceVolume` 3D dispatch, `RtComposite` frame-graph wiring (light pass → barrier → raymarch → barrier before DLSS-RR), `WorldPush froxel0/1/2`, `nearPlaneDistance()`. - **Config**: `CausticaConfig.Rt.Fog` — enabled/density/strength/phase-g/ambient/far/height-falloff, live-tunable via `-Dcaustica.*` or TOML. ## Constraints honored - No shadow map — the grid's light is path-traced via the existing NEE ray, inheriting real color transmission through glass. - Reuses the pathtracer's ACEScg basis, `dominantCelestialLight`, and `preExposure` seam. ## CI Relies on the GitHub Actions gradlew build to compile the new Slang shaders and verify generated `WorldPushData`/`RtBindings`. Default fog density/falloff are plausible starting values pending runtime tuning.

cited.name: Froxel Volumetric Fog with Path-Traced Shadows
ctx: Froxel Volumetric Fog with Path-Traced Shadows is a real-time rendering technique that simulates light scattering in participating media by dividing the camera view frustum into a 3D grid of voxels ("froxels") and computing their illumination via path-traced Next Event Estimation (NEE) shadow rays.

Unlike sibling methods that rely on shadow maps or precomputed lighting passes, this approach inherits real color transmission through tinted dielectrics (e.g., magenta glass scattering magenta fog) and dynamic sky-dome lighting, distinguishing it from Froxel Volumetric Fog with Precomputed Lighting which uses…
It solves the problem of flat, uniform screen-space fog by providing spatially varying, shadowed, and spectrally accurate volumetric lighting.

title: Froxel-based volumetric fog and light shafts
abstract: ## Summary Implements Wronski/Frostbite-style **frustum-aligned volumetric fog** (froxels) that composites over the path-traced radiance and feeds DLSS-RR, giving Minecraft-RTX-like atmospheric fog and **dynamic sun/moon god rays / light shafts**. The volume is a frustum-aligned grid: XY is a screen tile footprint and Z is an exponential depth distribution. Lighting work is done **once per froxel** (amortized ray-queried occlusion) instead of per-pixel per step, which is the spatial-accumulation savings a froxel grid exists to deliver; per-pixel fog cost collapses to a fixed march in the integrate pass. ## Files - **`shaders/pipelines/froxel/froxel_common.slang`** — `FroxelPush` ABI (near/far, tile size, slices, density/phase/albedo, device addresses, packed dims), frustum-ray reconstruction identical to `world.primary.rgen`, exponential slice distribution, smooth value-noise fog field, normalized Henyey-Greenstein phase. - **`shaders/pipelines/froxel/lighting.comp.slang`** — one thread per froxel fills the volume (`rgb = in-scatter, w = extinction`). Samples the fog density, casts 4 jittered ray-query occlusion rays toward the **dominant sun/moon** derived from the *same* sky module + transmittance LUT the path tracer uses (so fog, terrain light and the drawn disc can't disagree). Submerged cameras get an 8× density boost for underwater murk. Only froxels with non-negligible density cast shadow rays. - **`shaders/pipelines/froxel/integrate.comp.slang`** — one thread per pixel; reconstructs the view ray + surface distance from the reversed-Z guide depth, marches the froxel column with the exact constant-extinction integral, emits `fogInScatter + transmittance * surfaceRadiance`. 1:1 copy when disabled so the frame graph always has a valid image. - **`RtFroxel.java`** — two compute pipelines (lighting: set0=TLAS/set1=LUT; integrate: set1 storage images), a 4-slot TLAS descriptor ring mirroring the existing `AccelStructureSet` pattern, resize-aware volume/history buffers, per-frame push constants, and a temporal EMA gated on a still camera (with a `historyReady` guard so the first frame / post-resize never reads uninitialized device memory). - **`RtComposite.java`** — creates `RtFroxel` lazily, allocates a render-res `foggedOutput`, records lighting → integrate after the trace, and feeds the fogged image to DLSS-RR (or the fallback blit) via a `rrSceneImage()` helper. - **`CausticaConfig.Rt.Froxel`** — tunable density, height falloff, phase-g, scatter albedo, noise intensity/scale, intensity, temporal blend, tile size, depth slices, far. - **`layout_probe.slang` + `GenerateShaderRecords.groovy`** — probe/register `FroxelPushData` codegen. ## Notes / caveats - **No local toolchain was available** (`java`/`gradle`/`slangc` all absent), so nothing was compiled or SPIR-V validated. All code is correctness-by-inspection against the existing `RtSkyLut`, `RtOverlayPipelines`, and world shader ABI. When you next build, the two most likely things to confirm are: 1. `RayQuery` in a **compute** stage compiles (the repo currently only uses it in a fragment shader — `block_outline`). If not, the fix is localized (drop `RAY_FLAG_FORCE_OPAQUE` or route occlusion through the existing shadow SBT). 2. Slang's reflected push-constant size for `FroxelPush` stays within `maxPushConstantsSize`. - The occlusion ray uses `RAY_FLAG_FORCE_OPAQUE` (matching `block_outline`): god rays appear through canopy **gaps** and around solid geometry. Cutout-foliage/window transmission via the shadow any-hit SBT is a follow-up refinement. - Temporal accumulation reduces flicker/stabilizes a still view; per-frame `SHADOW_SAMPLES` reduction relying on history is a possible next optimization. ## Verification - Default config: `ENABLED=true`, `TILE_SIZE=8`, `DEPTH_SLICES=48`, `FAR=192`, `DENSITY=0.02`, `HEIGHT_FALLOFF=0.06`, `PHASE_G=0.60`, `SCATTER_ALBEDO=0.95`, `NOISE_INTENSITY=0.15`, `NOISE_SCALE=6.0`, `INTENSITY=1.0`, `TEMPORAL=true`, `TEMPORAL_BLEND=0.80`.

It solves the high computational cost of per-pixel ray marching by collapsing per-pixel fog cost to a fixed march in an integrate pass, delivering spatial-accumulation savings.

Inputs: Camera frustum parameters (near/far planes), tile size, depth slice count, fog density parameters, phase function parameters, albedo, noise parameters, and scene geometry (via TLAS for ray queries).

title: Full Monte-Carlo Volumetric Scattering
abstract: I would like to add full monte-carlo volumetric scattering to my path tracer, but I'm having a hard time researching how to do it. Let me explain what I would like to do: A ray enters a material, and we apply the BTDF, then after some distance, a volumetric scattering event happens, after which (in the isotropic case), the ray scatters in any direction in the sphere. This repeats until the ray exits the material with another BTDF. My questions are as follows: How do I choose the distance between scatter events? Intuition tells me there should be some kind of scatter pdf, which gives the probability to scatter after a certain distance? Would this be correct? Would the pdf be a linear function for isotropic materials? Does this function have a name or something I can Google? Would Beer-Lambert still apply between scatter events? I would think not. Since Beer-Lambert is a simplification of actual scattering calculations. Then again, perhaps Beer-Lambert is a calculation at the micro scale, and path tracing is on a macro scale. What is the volumetric equivalent to a BSDF? It looks like I can use a phase function such as Henyey-Greenstein to determine the new direction, but what do I use for attenuation? Lastly, what are some better Google phrases for Monte-Carlo volumetric scattering? Searching volumetric scattering, or SSS, ends up giving papers, methods, and blog posts about the simplfications of full Monte-Carlo simulation (Dipole, in-scattering, out-scattering, diffusion, etc.)

abstract: Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering Level-of-detail decomposition of a Gabor Field: frequency- and orientation-selectivity lets us mask particle collections at render time for continuous LOD, faster rendering, and a controllable bias-variance trade-off when sample cost matters. cited.name: Gabor Fields
ctx: Gabor Fields are a continuous volumetric representation that decomposes a signal into a low-pass Gaussian base and a residual of anisotropic Gabor kernels, enabling orientation-selective level-of-detail and accelerated rendering via control variates.

Unlike standard Gaussian-based representations, Gabor Fields achieve approximately 2 dB higher PSNR at equal primitive counts and render up to 1.4× faster at equal variance by concentrating spectral energy in specific frequency bands and orientations.

In the Fourier domain, each Gabor kernel consists of two symmetric lobes at \pm \boldsymbol{\omega}j, concentrating the spectrum in a specific frequency band and orientation, unlike a plain Gaussian which spills across all frequencies.

title: GANeRF: Leveraging Discriminators to Optimize Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have shown impressive novel view synthesis results; nonetheless, even thorough recordings yield imperfections in reconstructions, for instance due to poorly observed areas or minor lighting changes. Our goal is to mitigate these imperfections from various sources with a joint solution: we take advantage of the ability of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to produce realistic images and use them to enhance realism in 3D scene reconstruction with NeRFs. To this end, we learn the patch distribution of a scene using an adversarial discriminator, which provides feedback to the radiance field reconstruction, thus improving realism in a 3D-consistent fashion. Thereby, rendering artifacts are repaired directly in the underlying 3D representation by imposing multi-view path rendering constraints. In addition, we condition a generator with multi-resolution NeRF renderings which is adversarially trained to further improve rendering quality. We demonstrate that our approach significantly improves rendering quality, e.g., nearly halving LPIPS scores compared to Nerfacto while at the same time improving PSNR by 1.4dB on the advanced indoor scenes of Tanks and Temples.

cited.name: GANeRF

Unlike NeRFLiX [Zhou et al. 2023], which uses a non-adversarial network trained on multiple scenes with a hand-crafted noise simulation model, GANeRF uses direct backpropagation from a discriminator to a full-resolution NeRF for view-consistent synthesis.
Input: A set of posed input images capturing a static 3D scene, a 3D radiance field representation (e.g., Nerfacto [Tancik et al. 2023]), and a 2D patch discriminator.

title: Gaussian Splatting: An Introduction
abstract: Gaussian Splatting has emerged as a powerful technique for signal representation, especially in 3D. This paper introduces Gaussian Splatting and demonstrates its application across 1D, 2D, and 3D cases. We also discuss Gaussian Splatting in relation to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), highlighting the computational trade-offs and performance benefits. Through this work, we aim to bridge the gap between foundational concepts in view synthesis and advanced research, making Gaussian Splatting a more approachable and widely understood technique in the field of signal processing and computer vision. We provide code examples and detailed explanations to make the topic accessible to a broader audience, enabling readers to dive into more advanced technical papers with ease. **This is an MLBriefs article, the source code has not been reviewed!** **The original source codes are available here: [[2D Gaussian Splatting|https://github.com/OutofAi/2D-Gaussian-Splatting]] and [[Gaussian Splatting|https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/gsplat]] (last checked 2025/06/17).**

It differs fundamentally from Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs): while GMMs use Gaussians to model the distribution of data points, 1D Gaussian Splatting uses them to approximate the value of the signal itself.

title: GigaVoxels, Real-time Voxel-based Library to Render Large and Detailed Objects
abstract: International audienceWe present an implementation of the GigaVoxels rendering engine used to render large scenes and detailed objects in real-time. Implemented in CUDA, it leverages the performance and features of massively parallel graphics processors. It is based on a volumetric pre-filtered geometry representation and an associated voxel-based approximate cone tracing that allows a high performance rendering with high quality filtering. The underlying data structure exploits the fact that in CG scenes, details are often concentrated on their interface and shows that volumetric models might become a valuable alternative as a rendering primitive for real-time applications. Our solution is based on an adaptive hierarchical data representation depending on the current view, coupled to a ray-casting rendering algorithm. The core system, a GPU cache mechanism, provides a paging of data in video memory and is coupled with a data production pipeline able to dynamically load or produce voxel data on the GPU. Data production and caching in video memory is based on data requests and usage information emitted during rendering. We illustrate our approach with several applications. We present features provided by the library trough examples taking from our SDK, and show a survey of our programming paradigm

ctx: Ray marching with single scattering is a real-time technique for rendering volumetric clouds using OpenGL/WebGL ray marching, procedural noise or 3D textures for density, and physically-based single scattering illumination.

It solves the problem of rendering translucent, animated volumetric media efficiently by approximating light transport with a single scattering event per sample, balancing visual fidelity against computational cost.

It differs from SDF Cloud Rendering by generating density via procedural noise or texture lookups rather than signed distance fields, and from Atmospheric Ray Marching by targeting localized cloud volumes with explicit bounding or spherical boundaries and wind animation rather than global atmospheric scattering.

title: GNeRF: GAN-based Neural Radiance Field without Posed Camera
abstract: We introduce GNeRF, a framework to marry Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) with Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) reconstruction for the complex scenarios with unknown and even randomly initialized camera poses. Recent NeRF-based advances have gained popularity for remarkable realistic novel view synthesis. However, most of them heavily rely on accurate camera poses estimation, while few recent methods can only optimize the unknown camera poses in roughly forward-facing scenes with relatively short camera trajectories and require rough camera poses initialization. Differently, our GNeRF only utilizes randomly initialized poses for complex outside-in scenarios. We propose a novel two-phases end-to-end framework. The first phase takes the use of GANs into the new realm for optimizing coarse camera poses and radiance fields jointly, while the second phase refines them with additional photometric loss. We overcome local minima using a hybrid and iterative optimization scheme. Extensive experiments on a variety of synthetic and natural scenes demonstrate the effectiveness of GNeRF. More impressively, our approach outperforms the baselines favorably in those scenes with repeated patterns or even low textures that are regarded as extremely challenging before.

cited.name: GNeRF
ctx: GNeRF is a two-phase, end-to-end trainable framework that jointly optimizes coarse camera poses and neural radiance fields using adversarial training, then refines them with photometric loss, enabling novel view synthesis from randomly initialized poses in complex scenes.

Unlike methods that require short trajectories or rough initialization (e.g., iNeRF, NeRF++), GNeRF handles complex outside-in scenarios and scenes with low texture or repeated patterns where traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) fails.

It builds on Radiance-field optimization by introducing a GAN-based generator-discriminator pair and an inversion network to decouple pose estimation from direct photometric gradient propagation, which is prone to local minima.

title: Greedy Meshing Algorithm
abstract: The below is lightly edited, but mostly generated. Requires more review and consideration. ------- Summary ------- The current voxel-to-mesh pipeline converts each visible face of every block into triangles and merges block geometry into a per-chunk mesh (`VoxelChunk::from_grid`). This produces correct geometry but can create many small quads/triangles, increasing vertex/index counts and GPU upload bandwidth. The repository contains a TODO in `engine_core/src/scene_builders.rs`: "Implement proper greedy meshing before re-enabling smoothing" which remains outstanding. Why it matters --------------- - Greedy meshing (merging adjacent coplanar faces with identical attributes into larger quads) greatly reduces vertex and index counts for voxel terrains, reducing CPU work, GPU upload time, and draw cost. - This is especially important for large worlds and streaming many chunks. Current state ------------- - Face culling is implemented: hidden faces are removed at block level (`VoxelGrid::should_render_face`, `VoxelChunk::extract_visible_faces`). - However, there is no greedy meshing / rectangle merging pass. `VoxelChunk::from_grid` appends extracted block faces directly; `grid_to_chunks` simply collects chunk meshes without merging. Goal (what to implement) ----------------------- Implement a greedy meshing pass that operates per-chunk (intra-chunk) to combine adjacent coplanar faces that share the same merge key (material, double-sided flag, UV mapping, transparency). The pass should be conservative about attributes that affect final shading (normals, UV transforms, AO) to avoid visual artifacts. Requirements / Acceptance criteria --------------------------------- 1. Correctness - Visual parity: small test cases (islands, plateaus, cliffs) must render without incorrect seams or shading artifacts. - Transparent materials must not be merged with opaque neighbors; transparency must be part of the merge key. 2. Performance - Achieve a significant vertex/index reduction (typical target: 4×–10× reduction on natural terrain). Measure on representative chunks and report before/after counts. 3. Tests - Unit tests for rectangle packing (maximal rectangle detection) on synthetic 2D masks. - Integration test: For a small heightmap, compare indices/vertices before/after; assert reduction and expected values for a golden fixture. 4. Non-regression - Keep pipeline deterministic and add regression test(s) that validate packed geometry for a known input. Design notes and implementation plan (incremental) ------------------------------------------------ Stage 0 — Prep (refactor) - Introduce a `mesh_builder` module (or `voxel::mesher`) with a `MeshBuilder` trait and two implementations: `NaiveMeshBuilder` (current) and `GreedyMeshBuilder` (new). This lets you toggle behavior for testing. Stage 1 — Face extraction (already present) - Use `VoxelGrid::get_visible_faces` and the existing per-face extraction to produce a sliceable representation per-block. Optionally convert these into a `Face` struct (axis, dir, x,y,z, material_id, flags, uv_index). Stage 2 — Greedy meshing pass (single-chunk) - For each axis (X, Y, Z): - For each slice perpendicular to that axis, build a 2D mask / grid where each cell holds an optional `face_key` or `None`. - Run maximal-rectangle detection in the 2D mask to find contiguous runs of identical keys (the "greedy" step). - Emit `MergedFace` entries for each rectangle (origin, size, axis, dir, key). Stage 3 — Finalize geometry - Convert `MergedFace` entries into vertices/indices (triangulate quads), compute UVs, and generate per-vertex normals. - Optionally compute simple ambient occlusion per-vertex (corner-occlusion approximation) if desired. Stage 4 — Tests and measurement - Add unit tests for the rectangle finder with edge cases (holes, L-shapes, single cells). - Measure vertex/index counts and time for representative chunks before/after. Edge cases & cautions --------------------- - UV mapping: If a material uses non-uniform UV transforms per-block, include UV transform index in the merge key. Merging faces with different UV transforms will produce incorrect texturing. - Smoothing/normals: If smoothing changes per-vertex normals, compute normals after merging (i.e., mesh then smooth) rather than attempting to merge based on smoothed normals. - Chunk boundary merging: Implement only intra-chunk merging at first. Cross-chunk merging can be added later (requires coordination and streaming-aware updates). Follow-ups ---------- - Add a benchmark harness that builds a few representative chunks and prints vertex/index counts and generation time. - Investigate optional cross-chunk merging once intra-chunk is validated? References & resources ---------------------- - Original greedy meshing article / implementation (Mikola Lysenko): https://0fps.net/2012/07/07/meshing-in-a-minecraft-game/ - Example implementations in Rust (search public repos) for reference algorithms. - Use C++ algorithms and convert as a backup?

title: HAME-NeRF: High Accuracy Mesh Extraction Leveraging Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) have transformed image-based 3D reconstruction through differentiable volumetric rendering, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis. However, their implicit volumetric nature is incompatible with the polygonal meshes needed for real-time graphics and simulation applications. The proposed model defines the volume density function as the Secant Hyperbolic Function applied to a signed distance function (SDF) representation. To enable accurate surface representation, the sharpness of the density transition is modulated by a spatially-varying parameter β(x) , which is learned through a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Experimental results on the NeRF-Synthetic and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets demonstrate improved surface reconstruction accuracy and visual quality compared to NeRF2Mesh, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed enhancements for efficient and high-fidelity real-time scene reconstruction.

cited.name: HAME-NeRF
ctx: HAME-NeRF is a two-stage framework for extracting high-fidelity, textured surface meshes from RGB images by defining volume density as a Secant Hyperbolic Function applied to a Signed Distance Function (SDF).

It builds on NeuS by introducing a spatially-varying sharpness parameter \beta(\mathbf{x}) learned via an MLP, which enhances flexibility for complex surfaces compared to methods using fixed \beta values.

Unlike NeuS which focuses on differentiable volume rendering for surface representation, HAME-NeRF explicitly optimizes a mesh through differentiable rendering and iterative refinement, achieving superior geometric accuracy and visual quality on synthetic benchmarks compared to NeRF2Mesh.

title: HexPlane: A Fast Representation for Dynamic Scenes
abstract: Modeling and re-rendering dynamic 3D scenes is a challenging task in 3D vision. Prior approaches build on NeRF and rely on implicit representations. This is slow since it requires many MLP evaluations, constraining real-world applications. We show that dynamic 3D scenes can be explicitly represented by six planes of learned features, leading to an elegant solution we call HexPlane. A HexPlane computes features for points in spacetime by fusing vectors extracted from each plane, which is highly efficient. Pairing a HexPlane with a tiny MLP to regress output colors and training via volume rendering gives impressive results for novel view synthesis on dynamic scenes, matching the image quality of prior work but reducing training time by more than 100×. Extensive ablations confirm our HexPlane design and show that it is robust to different feature fusion mechanisms, coordinate systems, and decoding mechanisms. HexPlane is a simple and effective solution for representing 4D volumes, and we hope they can broadly contribute to modeling spacetime for dynamic 3D scenes.11Project page: https://caoang327.github.io/HexPlane.

title: How is Signed Distance Field Ray Marching implemented for a dynamic world?
abstract: I think I understand the basics of Signed Distance Field Ray Marching. You model your scene with a bunch of distance fields (such as these: http://iquilezles.org/www/articles/distfunctions/distfunctions.htm ), then for each pixel you cast a ray, start from the start of the ray, find the distance to the nearest object at that point, and increment the point by the nearest distance, until you hit something. I managed to do a simple renderer, and that is where most descriptions of the technique stop. This leaves me with some questions on how SDF Ray Marching can be used in a real world scenario: Question 1: In a real game, the scene is usually complex and loaded on the CPU, with many dynamic objects. I understand basic occlusion culling (such as octrees), and with polygonal rendering, I would create a list (on the CPU) of items in the view frustrum to render. So, imagine I have a very complex scene with many characters and dynamic objects moving on the screen, controlled by the CPU. How would I stream the objects I want to render to the GPU each frame? Every example has the scene hardcoded in GLSL. Can someone share an example of the level being streamed to the shader dynamically? Question 2: How can objects have multiple colours? The distance functions only return a distance, but how do implementations commonly pass the colour back? (e.g. you hit a red sphere and not a blue cube.) If this were a CPU implementation, I could call a global function inside of the distance function when it's a hit to terminate the ray marcher, and that could also pass the hit object's texture/colour. But, how would you return the item's colour or texture in GLSL? Thank you.

title: HyperNeRFGAN: Hypernetwork approach to 3D NeRF GAN
abstract: The recent surge in popularity of deep generative models for 3D objects has highlighted the need for more efficient training methods, particularly given the difficulties associated with training with conventional 3D representations, such as voxels or point clouds. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), which provide the current benchmark in terms of quality for the generation of novel views of complex 3D scenes from a limited set of 2D images, represent a promising solution to this challenge. However, the training of these models requires the knowledge of the respective camera positions from which the images were viewed. In this paper, we overcome this limitation by introducing HyperNeRFGAN, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture employing a hypernetwork paradigm to transform a Gaussian noise into the weights of a NeRF architecture that does not utilize viewing directions in its training phase. Consequently, as evidenced by the findings of our experimental study, the proposed model, despite its notable simplicity in comparison to existing state-of-the-art alternatives, demonstrates superior performance on a diverse range of image datasets where camera position estimation is challenging, particularly in the context of medical data.

cited.name: HyperNeRFGAN
ctx: HyperNeRFGAN is a generative model that uses a hypernetwork to produce the weights of a simplified NeRF target network, trained using the StyleGAN2 objective to generate 3D representations from a Gaussian noise distribution.

It solves the problem of 3D-aware image generation when camera positions are unavailable or unreliable by removing viewing directions from the NeRF input and using a hypernetwork to implicitly encode 3D structure.

Unlike siblings such as Latent-NeRF which optimize latent codes for specific instances, HyperNeRFGAN generates the network parameters themselves, allowing for the synthesis of novel 3D objects from noise.

title: I/O-Conscious Volume Rendering
abstract: Most existing volume rendering algorithms assume that data sets are memory-resident and thus ignore the performance overhead of disk I/O. While this assumption may be true for high-performance graphics machines, it does not hold for most desktop personal workstations. To minimize the end-to-end volume rendering time, this work re-examines implementation strategies of the ray casting algorithm, taking into account both computation and I/O overheads. Specifically, we developed a data-driven execution model for ray casting that achieves the maximum overlap between rendering computation and disk I/O. Together with other performance optimizations, on a 300-MHz Pentium-II machine, without directional shading, our implementation is able to render a 128x128 greyscale image from a 128x128x128 data set with an average end-to-end delay of 1 second, which is very close to the memory-resident rendering time. With a little modification, this work can also be extended to do out-of-core visualization as well.

cited.name: I/O-Conscious Volume Rendering
ctx: I/O-Conscious Volume Rendering is an out-of-core rendering technique that minimizes end-to-end rendering time by overlapping disk I/O with rendering computation using a data-driven execution model where data blocks are accessed as indivisible units.

It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Out-of-core brick-based volume rendering, by tightly integrating algorithm-specific prefetching with the ray casting traversal to ensure data is available exactly when needed, rather than relying on general-purpose disk prefetching or fixed memory budgets.
Unlike program-driven approaches where the renderer controls the I/O, this method uses a dedicated prefetch thread that mirrors the ray caster's traversal logic to hide latency.

title: IBGS: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently emerged as a fast, high-quality method for novel view synthesis (NVS). However, its use of low-degree spherical harmonics limits its ability to capture spatially varying color and view-dependent effects such as specular highlights. Existing works augment Gaussians with either a global texture map, which struggles with complex scenes, or per-Gaussian texture maps, which introduces high storage overhead. We propose Image-Based Gaussian Splatting, an efficient alternative that leverages high-resolution source images for fine details and view-specific color modeling. Specifically, we model each pixel color as a combination of a base color from standard 3DGS rendering and a learned residual inferred from neighboring training images. This promotes accurate surface alignment and enables rendering images of high-frequency details and accurate view-dependent effects. Experiments on standard NVS benchmarks show that our method significantly outperforms prior Gaussian Splatting approaches in rendering quality, without increasing the storage footprint.

title: Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching: Curvature-Bounded Contraction and Fixed-Point Projection for Real-Time Implicit Surface Rendering
abstract: Rendering implicit surfaces, neural signed distance fields (SDFs), and level sets on resource-constrained mobile and XR platforms is fundamentally hindered by the computational stall of sphere tracing near grazing angles and silhouette edges. In standard sphere tracing, the spatial advance is conservatively bounded by the radial distance φ(r(t)), which approaches zero near surface horizons even when the ray intersects geometry far along its directional path. This induces severe iteration inflation (40–60+ steps per ray) and tail-latency spikes. In this paper, we formulate ray-surface intersection as a curvature-accelerated contraction operator Phit on the Eikonal distance field. By evaluating directional first- and second-order derivatives along the one-dimensional ray trajectory, Phit constructs a rational Halley contraction bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints. To balance arithmetic throughput against query evaluation complexity, we introduce an Adaptive Hybrid Marcher that executes single-query Lipschitz advances in open space and selectively activates second-order Halley contraction only within grazing silhouette horizons. Upon entering the root neighborhood, the operator achieves terminal orthogonal projection with fixed-point invariance (||Phit2 - Phit|| ≤ 10−15). We implement the engine in C++20 with AVX2 acceleration, thread-safe re-entrant context encapsulation, and zero dynamic heap allocation during traversal. Empirical benchmarks across constructive solid geometry (CSG) manifolds and authentic 3D biological cortical meshes demonstrate throughput of 27.0–33.3 MRays/s on multi-threaded CPUs. While classical sphere tracing retains higher raw throughput on simple analytical primitives due to single-query simplicity, our adaptive hybrid formulation truncates the grazing stall tail by up to 4× on silhouette rays (reducing traversal from 55 to 14 steps) with a 20% reduction in full-frame mean iterations (14.6 to 11.6 steps), providing deterministic frame pacing for latency-critical applications.

cited.name: Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching
ctx: Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching is a ray-surface intersection method that formulates intersection as a curvature-accelerated contraction operator on the Eikonal distance field to solve the computational stall of sphere tracing near grazing angles and silhouette edges.

It sets itself apart from its parent, Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints, by selectively activating second-order Halley contraction only within grazing silhouette horizons while maintaining single-query Lipschitz advances in open space, thereby truncating the grazing stall tail by up to 4×.

cited.name: SfMNeRF
ctx: SfMNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis and 3D-scene geometry reconstruction that improves Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) under sparse input conditions by integrating Structure-from-Motion (SfM) constraints and depth prediction into the training loop.

It explicitly constrains the 3D-scene geometry using matched feature positions, epipolar geometry, and multi-view photometric consistency, thereby reducing geometric ambiguity and preventing the model from getting stuck in local minima.

Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on implicit volume rendering, SfMNeRF adds auxiliary geometric loss terms to enforce that identical features share world coordinates and that corresponding points lie on epipolar lines.

title: Information-based Transfer Functions for Multimodal Visualization
abstract: Transfer functions are an essential part of volume visualization. In multimodal visualization at least two values exist at every sample point. Additionally, other parameters, such as gradient magnitude, are often retrieved for each sample point. To find a good transfer function for this high number of parameters is challenging because of the complexity of this task. In this paper we present a general information-based approach for transfer function design in multimodal visualization which is independent of the used modality types. Based on information theory, the complex multi-dimensional transfer function space is fused to allow utilization of a well-known 2D transfer function with a single value and gradient magnitude as parameters. Additionally, a quantity is introduced which enables better separation of regions with complementary information. The benefit of the new method in contrast to other techniques is a transfer function space which is easy to understand and which provides a better separation of different tissues. The usability of the new approach is shown on examples of different modalities.Eurographics Workshop on Visual Computing for Biomedicin

title: Integrating Real-Time Fluid Simulation with a Voxel Engine
abstract: We present a method of adding sophisticated physical simulations to voxel-based games such as the hugely popular Minecraft (2012. http://minecraft.gamepedia.com/Liquid ), thus providing a dynamic and realistic fluid simulation in a voxel environment. An assessment of existing simulators and voxel engines is investigated, and an efficient real-time method to integrate optimized fluid simulations with voxel-based rasterisation on graphics hardware is demonstrated. We compare graphics processing unit (GPU) computer processing for a well-known incompressible fluid advection method with recent results on geometry shader-based voxel rendering. The rendering of visibility-culled voxels from fluid simulation results stored intermediately in CPU memory is compared with a novel, entirely GPU-resident algorithm.

ctx: Isosurface extraction converts a discretized scalar field into a polygonal mesh (typically triangles) representing the locus of points where the field equals a specific threshold (isovalue).
Unlike Blocky meshing, which produces voxel-aligned "cuberille" meshes, isosurface methods generate smooth, curved approximations by interpolating within cells.
It is a general approach covering a whole family of algorithms, some of which are adaptive, supplemented with sharp feature detection, or capable of preserving the topology of non-manifold surfaces.

title: Interactive explanation of marching cubes and dual contouring
abstract: Interactive explanation of marching cubes and dual contouring https://ift.tt/jyuagrN This is Words and Buttons Online — a collection of interactive #tutorials , #demos , and #quizzes about #mathematics , #algorithms and #programming . Interactive explanation of marching cubes and dual contouring Marching cubes and dual contouring are mostly known as 3D mesh generating algorithms, but since it's hard to explain 3D things using 2D display, we will concentrate on planar analog. We will do contours. What is contouring ? Let's say we have a function. x 2 + y 2 = 4 This function represents a circle. Now let's say we don't want a perfect circle, but its contour — a set of line segments that represent the circle within some tolerable error. With the contour, we can do things that would be tricky to do with the circle itself. Like intersecting it with some other arbitrary curve or storing it in the same array with lines, triangles, and all the other contours regardless of their original nature. Conceptually, contouring is simple. Let's rewrite our function: F(x, y) = x 2 + y 2 - 4 Now we cover the plane with a grid. For every two adjacent cells, its shared border becomes a piece of the contour if the function F(x,y) changes sign between these two cell's centers. And that's it. This simple rule is enough for simple contouring. Well, technically, it does represent the original curve. And the error is predictable. It never exceeds half of the cell's diagonal. But this contour has way too many corners for a circle. We need something better. Marching cubes What if we add line segments that go across the cells? We can measure function signs in every corner for each square, and add line segments accordingly. For now, let's connect the sign-changing edges from middle to middle. There are 4 squares, 2 signs; there are only 16 combinations of sign change possible. Since pairs of signs for each shared edge change synchronously for both cells, the line segments connect automatically into a continuous contour. It's a little better than before, but it is still far from the shape we want. What if we don't put our line segments ends in the middle of edges, but try to find a better place for them? We have not only the function's signs but also the values so why don't we exploit that? One way to find a better place to put line segments' ends will be by using linear interpolation. This is not flawless. Since our target function is not necessarily linear, we can't expect linear interpolation to approximate it perfectly well. Ideally, we should have been looking for an actual point where the curve intersects an edge and not an interpolative prediction. But linear interpolation still works well enough most of the time, and it's super cheap to compute. Here, you can try it out yourself. Just click and drag anywhere on the canvas. The ironic drawback of marching cubes is that they don't work very well with real cubes. It gets better with a finer grid, sure, but conceptually this is the weak spot. For this problem, we need something different. Intermezzo Marching cubes is not a single algorithm. It's a general approach covering a whole family of algorithms. Some are adaptive. Some are supplemented with sharp feature detection. Some can preserve the topology of non-manifold surfaces. Some work faster than others. Some have better memory consumption. Just as that, dual contouring is not a single dual method. There are plenty. From primitive surface nets to the most sophisticated adaptive methods. We will not look into them. I believe, the most important lesson we can take from dual methods is the idea of duality. The very concept, not the specific algorithm. We will look into this right now. Dual contouring With marching cubes we did the following: If a function changes its sign in a cube , we add a line segment from edge to edge . The exact ends of each segment are being placed anywhere on the edges to minimize the difference between an isoline and a contour. Conceptually, dual contouring goes like this: If a function changes its sign on the edge , we add a line segment from cube to cube . The exact ends of each segment are being placed anywhere in the cubes to minimize the difference between an isoline and a contour. Noticed anything? Exactly! This is the same algorithm. Only cubes now play as edges and edges as cubes. That's the duality . And now, since we get to place a segment end anywhere in the cube, we can also choose it to be on the corner. Here, try it yourself. Click and drag. Duality is a fascinating concept. The way you get new properties from an algorithm by merely swapping planes and points is, in a way, a mathematical miracle. Conclusion In practice, marching cubes and dual contouring tend to be complicated because we want more than just a contour or a triangle mesh out of them. We want them to work with sharp features, textures, open surfaces, non-manifold models, and all in a reasonable time, too. But conceptually, they are both rather simple. I hope this explanation shows it well. via Words and buttons online October 8, 2022 at 05:21PM
