title: Ref-DVGO: Reflection-Aware Direct Voxel Grid Optimization for an Improved Quality-Efficiency Trade-Off in Reflective Scene Reconstruction
abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) have revolutionized the field of novel view synthesis, demonstrating remarkable performance. However, the modeling and rendering of reflective objects remain challenging problems. Recent methods have shown significant improvements over the baselines in handling reflective scenes, albeit at the expense of efficiency. In this work, we aim to strike a balance between efficiency and quality. To this end, we investigate an implicit-explicit approach based on conventional volume rendering to enhance the reconstruction quality and accelerate the training and rendering processes. We adopt an efficient density-based grid representation and reparameterize the reflected radiance in our pipeline. Our proposed reflection-aware approach achieves a competitive quality efficiency trade-off compared to competing methods. Based on our experimental results, we propose and discuss hypotheses regarding the factors influencing the results of density-based methods for reconstructing reflective objects. The source code is available at https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo.

cited.name: Ref-DVGO
ctx: Ref-DVGO is a reflection-aware neural rendering method that combines the fast hybrid implicit-explicit representation of Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) with the reflection direction reparameterization of Ref-NeRF to achieve high-quality photorealistic novel view synthesis of reflective scenes with reduced…

It replaces the large spatial Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) of Ref-NeRF with six distinct voxel grids, significantly reducing GPU memory requirements and training duration while maintaining competitive quality for shiny objects.
Hyperparameters: number of progressive scaling steps (default 10), directional MLP size (default 8 layers, 256 units), and loss weights.

title: Refactor volumes, add Rayleigh phase function, fix some bugs
abstract: Rework of volume rendering, including: - Remove `RayTracer::march` method and treat volume scattering events in an uniform way with the other types of bounces. - Remove the possibility of several distance samples per ray. It was used to provide a way to reduce sampling variance for scenes with fog while making each ray more computationally heavy. This was removed in favor of tracing more rays as it is more efficient for complex scenes and fits to the fashion of modern path tracers like appleseed, as well as to drastically simplify the lighting code. Equiangular sampling still remains as an example of usage of the new volume API and for reducing the noise for single-scattering homogeneous media. However, it is now set as disabled by default, since it is less efficient for small enclosed volumes (Multiple scattering is the main option to move further and if we want to enhance it for fog rendering, we have to look for more advanced importance sampling methods) - Remove `MaterialSampler` as it is not needed anymore. Add BSDF wrapper for phase functions. - FINALLY completely removed chromatic fireflies for multiple scattering. =) Additionally: - Rayleigh phase function was added for media with small particles (as more physically accurate version of isotropic scattering) - Volumes can now be rendered even if the camera is enclosed inside them (solve #2057) - Solve #2287 - Solves bug when the glass absorption is not fully accounted when there are lights behind glass: Before: ![before](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10550749/50840966-f5eab300-1363-11e9-962e-7c97cd43081f.png) After: ![after](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10550749/50840938-ea978780-1363-11e9-951a-adb2de7015fb.png) No absorption: ![no_absorption](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10550749/50840974-faaf6700-1363-11e9-95b5-641b7dfa71e0.png) Scene (compare with no nee): [incorrect_glass_transmittance_light_behind.zip](https://github.com/appleseedhq/appleseed/files/2737420/incorrect_glass_transmittance_light_behind.zip)

cited.name: Rayleigh Phase Function
ctx: The Rayleigh phase function models the angular distribution of light scattered by media containing small particles.
Unlike the isotropic phase function, it introduces anisotropy, and unlike the Henyey-Greenstein function, it is derived from physical dipole radiation principles rather than empirical fitting.
Limitations: Only valid for particles much smaller than the wavelength of light, and uses an unpolarized average that does not track polarization states.

title: Regarding spectral tracking code wrong (eval_spectral_tracking)
abstract: I suspect that the implementation of spectral tracking is wrong. I have a smoke medium with 20% scattering and 80% absorption. With delta tracking, I get this result. ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1354859/127605620-8327e496-f687-4e78-bc49-028341001c2e.png) but spectral tracking gives me this result which is clearly wrong as I should get similar result as delta tracking. ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1354859/127605669-fecf7328-93e9-4d3c-8921-d7db727a0273.png) I have managed to fix it. Following is my code which is as per the original spectral decomposition paper. ``` std::pair eval_spectral_tracking(vsdf& vsdf, float max_distance, rng_state& rng, const ray3f& ray) { auto object = vsdf.object; auto density_vol = object->density_vol; auto emission_vol = object->emission_vol; auto max_density = density_vol->max_voxel * object->density_mult; auto majorant_density = max_density; auto imax_density = 1.0f / max_density; auto path_length = 0.0f; auto tr = vec3f(1); auto f = vec3f(1); auto sigma_s = vsdf.scatter * max_density; auto Ps = sigma_s * imax_density; while (true) { path_length -= log(1 - rand1f(rng)) * imax_density; if (path_length >= max_distance) break; auto current_pos = ray.o + path_length * ray.d; auto sigma_t = vec3f(eval_vpt_density(vsdf, current_pos)); auto sigma_n = majorant_density - sigma_t; auto sigma_a = sigma_t - sigma_s; auto Pt = sigma_t * imax_density; auto Pn = sigma_n * imax_density; auto Pa = 1.0 - Ps - Pn; auto contrib = zero3f; tr *= exp(-sigma_t*path_length); if (max(Pa) > rand1f(rng)) { //ABSORPTION contrib = sigma_a / (majorant_density * Pa); contrib /= max(contrib); vsdf.event = EVENT_ABSORB; vsdf.density = sigma_t; return { path_length, tr * contrib }; } else if (max(Pt) > rand1f(rng)) { // SCATTER contrib = sigma_s / (majorant_density * Ps); contrib /= max(contrib); vsdf.event = EVENT_SCATTER; vsdf.density = sigma_t; return { path_length, tr * contrib }; } contrib = sigma_n; contrib /= max(contrib); f *= contrib; } return { max_distance, f }; } ``` Following is the correct output. ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1354859/127605912-bef1db53-07ef-4593-98a4-64a6d68a32df.png)

ctx: Spectral tracking is a volume rendering technique that efficiently handles per-wavelength optical properties by decomposing the medium's scattering and absorption coefficients into spectral components, using a single majorant density to drive the sampling process for all wavelengths simultaneously.
In the implementation, this is often combined with the path length update: pathlength -= \log(1 - \text{rand1f}(rng)) \times \text{imax\density}.
Termination Check: If pathlength >= maxdistance, break the loop and return {maxdistance, f}.

title: Regularised marching tetrahedra: improved iso-surface extraction
abstract: Marching cubes is a simple and popular method for extracting iso-surfaces from implicit functions or discrete three-dimensional (3-D) data. However, it does not guarantee the surface to be topologically consistent with the data, and it creates triangulations which contain many triangles of poor aspect ratio. Marching tetrahedra is a variation of marching cubes, which overcomes this topological problem. Improvement in triangle aspect ratio has generally been achieved by mesh simplification, a group of algorithms designed to reduce the large number of triangles. Vertex clustering is one of the simplest of these algorithms, but does not in general maintain the topology of the original mesh. We present a new algorithm, regularised marching tetrahedra, which combines marching tetrahedra and vertex clustering to generate iso-surfaces which are topologically consistent with the data and contain a number of triangles appropriate to the sampling resolution (typically 70 % fewer than marching tetrahedra) with significantly improved aspect ratios. This improvement in aspect ratio greatly enhances the display of the surface, particularly when it is rendered using simple interpolated shading. cited.name: Regularised Marching Tetrahedra
ctx: Regularised Marching Tetrahedra (RMT) is an iso-surface extraction algorithm that combines the topological consistency of the Marching Tetrahedra Algorithm with vertex clustering to generate simplified surfaces with improved triangle aspect ratios.

Unlike standard Marching Tetrahedra, which can produce thin, degenerate triangles that degrade interpolated shading, RMT reduces the triangle count by approximately 70% while preserving the original topology by basing clustering on the tetrahedral lattice.
Ensure that the decomposition is consistent across shared faces and edges of the original grid cells to prevent topological holes or overlaps.

title: Removing excess topology from isosurfaces
abstract: Many high-resolution surfaces are created through isosurface extraction from volumetric representations, obtained by 3D photography, CT, or MRI. Noise inherent in the acquisition process can lead to geometrical and topological errors. Reducing geometrical errors during reconstruction is well studied. However, isosurfaces often contain many topological errors in the form of tiny handles. These nearly invisible artifacts hinder subsequent operations like mesh simplification, remeshing, and parametrization. In this article we present a practical method for removing handles in an isosurface. Our algorithm makes an axis-aligned sweep through the volume to locate handles, compute their sizes, and selectively remove them. The algorithm is designed to facilitate out-of-core execution. It finds the handles by incrementally constructing and analyzing a Reeb graph. The size of a handle is measured by a short nonseparating cycle. Handles are removed robustly by modifying the volume rather than attempting "mesh surgery." Finally, the volumetric modifications are spatially localized to preserve geometrical detail. We demonstrate topology simplification on several complex models, and show its benefits for subsequent surface processing.

title: Render the MRMS volume through a sparse page table and brick pool
abstract: ## Summary Implements the two OpenVDB/NanoVDB ideas that apply to the web raymarcher, without the library: 1. **Empty-space skipping.** The shader fetches a page-table entry for the ray position each step. An empty page is jumped to its exit face in one loop iteration (one-level DDA) and the ray lands back on its jittered sample lattice so cadence does not change at page entries. 2. **Leaf bricks with a page table.** `build_volume_texture` now emits a page table (one RG8 entry per 8³-texel page: pool slot + 1, or 0 for no echo) and a pool of resident bricks, each the 8³ core wrapped in a one-texel apron copied from neighboring logical texels (clamped at the grid edge) so trilinear filtering never leaves the brick. The dense logical grid is never materialized. ### Effects - **Full source resolution at 120 NM.** The dense grid capped each axis at 256 cells, so a ~440-cell request was coarsened 2× horizontally. The sparse grid allows a 2048-cell logical axis; `coarsenX/Z = 1` in the common case. - **Bounded uploads.** Resident bricks are capped at `MAX_VOLUME_BRICKS = 8192` (a 16.4 MB pool at 2 KB per brick). Past that the grid coarsens by the next whole footprint multiple after a count-only pass, so the pool is bounded without failing on widespread rain. - **Terrain occlusion survives skipping.** `buildGroundPageMax` records the highest ground under each page column (one-column halo for the linearly filtered heightfield). An empty page is jumped only when it lies wholly above that value; otherwise it is stepped with the per-sample ground test and no volume fetch. - **Phase bleed on every stored copy.** Empty texels bordering echo adopt the neighbor's phase in cores and aprons alike, so brick faces do not tint toward rain. - **Debug panel.** New `Volume Bricks` row: resident bricks, filled logical texels, cell size, coarsening multiple. ### Extinction recalibration (follow-up commit) Andy reported light precipitation reading as nearly invisible on the preview. Root cause: the old dense grid max-pooled 0.5 NM source cells into 1 NM texels, which filled the gaps of scattered light echo (a region 50% filled at source resolution read ~94% filled) and so gave light precipitation about twice its true optical path. The cubic extinction ramp had been tuned against that. Old-vs-new headless renders of the same live payloads measured the new grid 17–28% dimmer in lit-pixel energy, concentrated in light and moderate echo: | Scene | Old | Cubic at source res | 2.75 power | |---|---|---|---| | KATL wide | 6.11M | 5.08M (−17%) | 6.12M (0%) | | KATL close | 4.57M | 3.65M (−20%) | 4.75M (+4%) | | KSEA stratiform | 270k | 193k (−28%) | 259k (−4%) | Doubling extinction (+24–41%) and a 2.5 power (+20–33%) overshot because the pooling barely inflated solid heavy echo. The ramp is now `pow(t, 2.75)`; cores, which saturate, are unchanged. Documented in the shader, `docs/rendering-weather-volume.md`, and the decision note. ### GPU smoke test (`npm run test:smoke:volume`) `scripts/volume-smoke/` bundles the real `NexradVolumeRaymarch` over the shipped WASM decoder, renders it in headless Chromium on SwiftShader WebGL2 against a committed KMIA AVMR fixture (or `--live , `), and fails on any console error (shader compile failures land there), on budget coarsening, on a page-table/pool layout mismatch, or on a broken occlusion invariant (60,000 ft flat ground must render zero pixels; a camera under the ground must render zero pixels). The browser is driven over the DevTools Protocol with Node's built-in WebSocket, since master dropped Playwright. Not part of CI; screenshots land in `.tmp/volume-smoke/`. ### Not changed - `MAX_RAY_STEPS` stays at 384, so this change only reduces per-pixel work. - The native iOS/macOS renderer still consumes `build_render_volume` flat columns for its instanced boxes. ## Validation - `cargo test -p approach-viz-core`: 119 passed; `cargo check --workspace` clean; wasm32 and ios feature builds clean. - `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`, `npm run format:check`, `npm test`: clean on the merged tree. - `npm run build:sw && npx next build`: succeeds. - `npm run test:smoke:volume`: passes on the fixture and on live KATL weather (456 × 385 × 96 logical texels at 1×, 2,158 bricks, 5.0 MB pool). - WASM rebuilt with wasm-pack 0.15 and binaryen 117. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_017f8QAd1T7ks8XW5JV2RdJQ

cited.name: Sparse Page Table and Brick Pool
ctx: Sparse Page Table and Brick Pool is a sparse volume representation that avoids materializing a dense 3D grid by using a two-level structure: a page table mapping logical 8^3-texel regions to resident bricks, and a pool of apron-padded bricks.
It allows full source resolution (up to 2048 cells per axis) while bounding memory usage and enabling empty-space skipping.
It is implemented in Unreal Engine as "Heterogeneous Volumes" and "Sparse Volume Textures" (SVT), and in web-based raymarchers as a replacement for dense coarsened grids.

title: Render: scatter local lights in the volumetric fog volume
abstract: Part of #357. Local lights now scatter in the volumetric fog volume. ## Change **Inject shader (`fog_scattering.comp.glsl`).** At each froxel midpoint, the shader runs the same `select_lights` cluster lookup that surfaces use and loops the selected lights. It skips: - the sun index, which is already added; - lights without `LIGHT_VOLUMETRIC`; - lights whose `sample_light` radiance is zero. Each remaining light adds `albedo × HG(dot(ray, light_dir), fog_anisotropy) × radiance × visibility`. Visibility is one zero-normal `shadow_visibility` sample when `light_casts_shadow`, and 1 otherwise. Directional lights other than the sun are included. **`Light.volumetric`.** - A positive bool. The `directional`, `point` and `spot` constructors set it to true, following the `ViewDesc.share_shadows` precedent. - A bare `Light{}` does not scatter, as the docstring, `materials.md` and `sky.md` state. - It maps to the new `LIGHT_VOLUMETRIC` bit (`abi/c3d.abi`, regenerated). `LightGpu` keeps its size. - The light inspector gains a checkbox. **Serialization.** - `Light` moves to serial version 2, following the `FootIk`/`LodGroup` convention. The old layout is kept as a private `LightV1` with the old fingerprint, read by `read_light_v1` with `volumetric = true`, and `text_default_versions = {1}`. - Checked end to end with throwaway programs. A v1 payload written by main reads back identical with `volumetric` true, in both binary and text. A v2 round trip keeps `volumetric = false`. **Example.** `sky` gains: - `--local-lights N`: lamps along the path ahead of the eye-level presets. The first 8 cast shadows; the atlas grows to 32 layers at 1024 when lamps exist. - `--lamp-range` and `--lamps-in-fog on|off`, added for the reproducible cost and opt-out rows below. - A "Lamps in fog" checkbox. **Docs.** `sky.md` describes the rule, the cost lever (froxels × lights per cluster), the opt-out and the cluster-grid fallback share; `materials.md`, `serialization.md` and `benchmarking.md` cover the field, version 2 and the new flags. No measurements. ## Behaviour change This is intended and default on: scenes with fog and local lights change. The following are byte-identical to main (1280×720, 8 frames, validation on): | Scene | Main view | Mirror | | --- | --- | --- | | no lamps, noon | `92c01c8c…` | `c1d95e8d…` | | no lamps, pan | `61c8e483…` | `7508efcc…` | | no lamps, valley | `e0e1d21a…` | `0e648e91…` | | no lamps, twilight | `4a72dde3…` | `8c5e27a4…` | | 6 lamps opted out, twilight | `77e57119…` | same as main with 6 lamps | | 6 lamps opted out, pan | `87e3f430…` | same as main with 6 lamps | ## Screenshots (lavapipe) Twilight, 6 lamps. **Before (main):** ![before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fesoliveira014/c3d.c3l/screenshots/issue-357/pr2-before-twilight.png) **After:** ![after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fesoliveira014/c3d.c3l/screenshots/issue-357/pr2-after-twilight.png) **Difference ×8:** ![diff](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fesoliveira014/c3d.c3l/screenshots/issue-357/pr2-diff-x8-twilight.png) ## Cost (lavapipe, environment only; the reviewer measures at 1440p on the 4090) FOG_SCATTERING at noon, 1280×720, MEDIUM, O3. Each figure is the median of three per-run medians, in ms. In layout A, `--lamp-range 400` puts every lamp in every cell. | Layout | Lights per cell | Main view | Mirror | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | main, no lamps | 0 | 2.80 | 1.59 | | PR, no lamps | 0 | 2.89 | 1.59 | | A, 4 lamps | 4 | 6.13 | 2.56 | | A, 16 lamps | 16 | 10.87 | 3.99 | | A, 64 lamps (the cluster maximum) | 64 | 19.56 | 6.15 | | A, 64 lamps opted out | 64 | 9.89 | 3.21 | | range 14, 64 lamps | 3-5, plus flat fallback | 8.54 | 3.08 | | range 14, 64 lamps, `far_distance` 200 (throwaway build) | 3-5 | 5.31 | 2.48 | **Opt-out still walks the list.** Opting a light out saves its radiance and its shadow sample, but not the per-light read. `sky.md` says so. **Flat-list fallback.** Froxels past the cluster grid fall back to the flat light list. The share was computed on the CPU from the slice and cluster depth mappings, assuming a 60° vertical FOV, near 0.1 and `far_distance` 100. It is the same for every quality: | `max_distance` | Share of froxels past the grid | | --- | --- | | 50 | 0% | | 100 | 0% | | 200 (default) | 22.6% | | 500 | 51.0% | | 1000 | 65.4% | Another 2.2% fall in front of the near plane at 200. title: Rendering discrete participating media using geometrical optics approximation
abstract: We consider the scattering of light in participating media composed of sparsely and randomly distributed discrete particles. The particle size is expected to range from the scale of the wavelength to several orders of magnitude greater, resulting in an appearance with distinct graininess as opposed to the smooth appearance of continuous media. One fundamental issue in the physically-based synthesis of such appearance is to determine the necessary optical properties in every local region. Since these properties vary spatially, we resort to geometrical optics approximation (GOA), a highly efficient alternative to rigorous Lorenz—Mie theory, to quantitatively represent the scattering of a single particle. This enables us to quickly compute bulk optical properties for any particle size distribution. We then use a practical Monte Carlo rendering solution to solve energy transfer in the discrete participating media. Our proposed framework is the first to simulate a wide range of discrete participating media with different levels of graininess, converging to the continuous media case as the particle concentration increases.

title: Rendering Point Clouds with Compute Shaders and Vertex Order Optimization
abstract: While commodity GPUs provide a continuously growing range of features and sophisticated methods for accelerating compute jobs, many state-of-the-art solutions for point cloud rendering still rely on the provided point primitives (GL_POINTS, POINTLIST, ...) of graphics APIs for image synthesis. In this paper, we present several compute-based point cloud rendering approaches that outperform the hardware pipeline by up to an order of magnitude and achieve significantly better frame times than previous compute-based methods. Beyond basic closest-point rendering, we also introduce a fast, high-quality variant to reduce aliasing. We present and evaluate several variants of our proposed methods with different flavors of optimization, in order to ensure their applicability and achieve optimal performance on a range of platforms and architectures with varying support for novel GPU hardware features. During our experiments, the observed peak performance was reached rendering 796 million points (12.7GB) at rates of 62 to 64 frames per second (50 billion points per second, 802GB/s) on an RTX 3090 without the use of level-of-detail structures. We further introduce an optimized vertex order for point clouds to boost the efficiency of GL_POINTS by a factor of 5x in cases where hardware rendering is compulsory. We compare different orderings and show that Morton sorted buffers are faster for some viewpoints, while shuffled vertex buffers are faster in others. In contrast, combining both approaches by first sorting according to Morton-code and shuffling the resulting sequence in batches of 128 points leads to a vertex buffer layout with high rendering performance and low sensitivity to viewpoint changes.

cited.name: Marching Tetrahedra
ctx: Marching Tetrahedra is an isosurface extraction algorithm that decomposes each cubic voxel into tetrahedra to resolve the topological ambiguities inherent in Marching Cubes.
By processing each tetrahedron independently, it guarantees a unique, unambiguous intersection for every configuration, producing a crack-free mesh without the need for special case handling.

title: Robust Material Graphs for Volume Rendering
abstract: A good transfer function in volume rendering requires careful consideration of the materials present in a volume. In this work we propose a graph based method that considerably reduces manual effort required in designing a transfer function and provides an easy interface for interaction with the volume. Our novel contribution is in proposing an algorithm for robust deduction of a material graph from a set of disconnected edges. Since we compute material topology of the objects, an enhanced rendering is possible with our method. This also allows us to selectively render objects and depict adjacent materials in a volume.Pacific Graphics Short PapersVisualization and GP

cited.name: Robust Material Graph Deduction
ctx: Robust Material Graph Deduction automatically discovers material interiors and their spatial interconnectivity to generate transfer functions, solving the problem of manual TF creation by ensuring materials are mapped beyond just their boundaries.

It differs from sibling methods like Feature Graph by explicitly modeling the topology of adjacent materials as a graph G(M, I) and optimizing for separation energy to merge similar materials, whereas siblings may focus on static feature clustering or distance metrics without topological graph reconstruction.
Compute Initial Edge Set \hat{I}: For each edge pixel in the volume, perform a bidirectional traversal along the local gradient to search for a low value L and a high value H in a small neighborhood.

title: Robust Watertight Manifold Surface Generation Method for ShapeNet Models
abstract: In this paper, we describe a robust algorithm for 2-Manifold generation of various kinds of ShapeNet Models. The input of our pipeline is a triangle mesh, with a set of vertices and triangular faces. The output of our pipeline is a 2-Manifold with vertices roughly uniformly distributed on the geometry surface. Our algorithm uses an octree to represent the original mesh, and construct the surface by isosurface extraction. Finally, we project the vertices to the original mesh to achieve high precision. As a result, our method can be adopted efficiently to all ShapeNet models with the guarantee of correct 2-Manifold topology.

cited.name: Robust Watertight Manifold Surface Generation
ctx: This method converts an input triangle mesh into a watertight 2-manifold surface with roughly uniformly distributed vertices using an octree-based signed distance field (SDF) representation and isosurface extraction.
It differs from uniform grid marching cubes by adaptively refining only the volume near the surface, reducing storage and computation linearly with the final mesh size.

Unlike sibling methods that fit explicit surface primitives (e.g., QEF) or use complex occlusion handling, this pipeline guarantees topological correctness by defining "positive" space via boundary-connected BFS and resolving non-manifold ambiguities through vertex/edge splitting.

title: RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel-view synthesis but remains limited on GPUs at high resolutions. Through a stage-wise Roofline characterization, we identify two distinct hardware bottlenecks: global memory traffic dominates the front end, whereas instruction throughput limits rasterization. Guided by this analysis, we develop RoofGS, a rendering framework that applies bottleneck-specific optimizations rather than generic kernel acceleration. For the memory-bound front end, we design a resolution-adaptive quantized depth sorting key that compresses each key to 32 bits. For the compute-bound rasterizer, we introduce a range-aware bit-level fast exponential approximation tailored to the bounded exponent range after opacity culling, with a derived per-pixel error bound. These two core techniques are complemented by additional optimizations (kernel fusion, compact attribute storage, culling, dual-pixel evaluation) that additionally reduce memory traffic and improve instruction-level parallelism. Experiments show that RoofGS achieves a 10.1$\times$ end-to-end speedup over 3DGS at 4K on an RTX 4090, increasing throughput from 61 to 616 FPS, with only a 0.028 dB PSNR loss.

cited.name: MPI Volume Rendering (1D/2D Decomposition)
ctx: MPI Volume Rendering (1D/2D Decomposition) is a distributed-memory parallel volume rendering technique that partitions a 3D scalar dataset spatially along the X and/or Y axes (1D or 2D decomposition) to distribute the rendering workload across multiple MPI processes.
Each process independently ray casts its assigned subdomain using front-to-back compositing and early ray termination, then sends the resulting sub-image to a root process for assembly.

It differs from Scalable Distributed Volume Rendering (SDVR) by using a static spatial decomposition of the data volume rather than a dynamic object-space or pixel-based distribution, and from Round-Robin Data Distribution by assigning contiguous spatial blocks to processes rather than interleaved slices.

title: rupMC: a ray-unit parallel marching cubes algorithm on CPU/GPU heterogeneous architectures
abstract: ABSTRACT The marching cubes (MC) algorithm is widely used for extracting isosurfaces from volume data and 3D visualizations because of its effectiveness and robustness but require extensive memory and computing time for large-scale applications. Additionally, MC isosurfaces lack topologic information, making them difficult to use in some geologic applications. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes an enhanced MC using CPU/GPU heterogeneous architecture called the ray-unit parallel MC (rupMC) algorithm. First, ray units form the basic voxel to determine how the surface intersects to reduce repeated computations and enhance efficiency. Then, rupMC uses multiple computing processes and threads on a CPU/GPU heterogeneous architecture to process points concurrently. Finally, the unique surface intersection indices are preserved to compose the surface triangles, and the topological surface information is directly embedded in the triangle compositions. Experiments on five stratum datasets of varying sizes demonstrated that, rupMC achieved approximately dozens of times faster than other serial MC and 4 times faster than a parallel DMC. rupMC demonstrated high scalability and adaptability to various CPUs/GPUs and datasets of various sizes. rupMC has remarkable capabilities for efficiently and feasibly extracting precise surface intersections and triangles, making it well-suited for large-scale and high-density applications.

cited.name: Ray-Unit Parallel Marching Cubes
ctx: Ray-Unit Parallel Marching Cubes (rupMC) is an enhanced Marching Cubes algorithm designed for CPU/GPU heterogeneous architectures that reduces redundant edge intersection computations and preserves topological information of the isosurface.

It replaces the standard cubic voxel with a ray unit to ensure each edge intersection is calculated and stored exactly once, while parallelizing I/O via OpenMPI and computation via CUDA to handle large-scale datasets efficiently.

Unlike standard MC, which suffers from repeated calculations on shared edges and lacks explicit topological connectivity, rupMC embeds topological relationships directly into the triangle composition using unique intersection indices.

title: Single Scattering Effects for Computer Games
abstract: Abstract — This paper addresses the rendering of single scattering effects such as glows and shafts of light, along with volumetric shadows induced by shadow casters in the participating media in real-time. Our method is easy to integrate in a video game graphics engine using the shadow volume technique since it requires only a little additional texture memory and is implemented with simple shaders. Realistic images can be produced in real-time for usual graphic scenes and at a high level framerate for complex scenes, allowing changes in the properties of participating medium, animations of objects and even light sources movements.

cited.name: Single Scattering Illumination
ctx: Single Scattering Illumination is a volumetric lighting model that computes the radiance contribution of light undergoing exactly one scattering event within a participating medium.

It solves the problem of realistic volumetric lighting by distinguishing between light scattered along the view ray (Direct Single Scattering, DSS) and light scattered along illumination rays from scene points (Indirect Single Scattering, ISS).

Unlike basic volume rendering which often ignores volumetric shadows or uses approximations, this method provides an analytic formulation for both direct and indirect contributions, including occlusion handling via shadow volumes, enabling real-time hardware rendering of complex volumetric lighting effects.

title: Sparse chunk (brick) storage: decouple resolution from memory
abstract: Proposal: replace each layer's dense box with a sparse map of fixed-size chunks. ```rust enum Chunk { Solid(u8), // one palette index, whole chunk Dense(Box ), // 16³ of them } // absent from the map = Empty struct VoxelGrid { chunks: HashMap } ``` with the invariants ```text an all-empty Dense chunk → removed an all-one-colour Dense chunk → Solid(colour) ``` One level of adaptivity rather than an octree. Addressing stays arithmetic — `chunk = p >> 4`, `local = p & 15` — so nothing has to traverse a tree to read a voxel, and brush / flood / plane / mirror / `set_voxel` keep the shape they have. ## Why this and not an octree An octree splits and merges on every brush stroke that crosses a node boundary, and every read is a traversal. A chunk map keeps the dense-array code that already exists and confines the cleverness to one type. Most of the compression an octree would give on voxel models comes from large uniform interiors, and `Solid` captures exactly that. ## What it buys, in this codebase specifically Two of these are present-day problems, not projections. - **Sparsity *inside* a layer.** `Bounds` made layers cost their bounding box rather than the scene, which was the big win. But a hollow shell still allocates its whole box: a 128³ shell layer is 2 MB of mostly air. Chunks would hold the shell and nothing else — and this is the property the roadmap's own observation depends on, that detail concentrates on surfaces. - **Meshing.** `mesh::extract` walks every filled cell of every visible layer and asks `owner_at` per cell, which is O(layers) each. That is the cost that grows with resolution, and chunk-level dirty tracking is the actual fix: rebuild the edited chunk and its six neighbours, skip Empty, and drop a Solid chunk's interior faces outright. Greedy meshing then becomes per-chunk, which is where it wanted to be anyway. - **Bulk fills.** `tools::box_cells` materialises `Vec ` of every cell in the box — no cap. At today's 256³ ceiling that is 16.7 M entries, 200 MB, and survivable. On a larger canvas it is fatal. A chunk-aware `fill_box` writes `Solid` for interior chunks and only materialises the boundary ones, which is most of the octree's benefit for none of its complexity. (`apply_edits` already caps at 2 097 152 candidate cells for the same reason; that cap could relax.) - **Resolution stops being a number you pick up front.** `--size` and the scene range become a work area rather than an allocation. - **It composes with objects (#14).** `Object { grid: SparseChunkGrid, transform }` is a clean end state, and a chunk-aligned translation is a rekey of the map rather than a copy. Worth being honest that a *non-aligned* translation still touches every chunk — object moves get cheap only on multiples of 16. ## What it costs, honestly - **It touches the hot path everywhere.** `get`/`set` are what the raycaster, the region flood, the mesh extractor and every tool are written against. This is a bigger change than layer bounds was. - **It makes the common case slower.** A hash lookup plus a branch, against a bounds test plus an array index. The default scene is 32³ and a character is 16³ — at that size the current design is strictly better, and this pays off at a scale voxeler does not reach yet. - **The `Solid` invariant is a second representation of one fact**, which is the class of thing this codebase has been deliberate about removing (the composite cache was deleted for being scene-sized; `in_ball` exists so one radius rule is not written twice). A stale `Solid` reads as the wrong colour everywhere at once. It needs to live in exactly one place, with the promotion and demotion tested in both directions. - **`.vxm` would want a version.** VXM3 stores filled voxels at four bytes each, so a `Solid` chunk costs 16 KB on disk to say "red". A chunk-aware VXM4 would encode runs — with VXM3/2/1 still loading, as they do now. - **`.vox` caps at 256 anyway.** An unbounded canvas diverges from the interop ceiling, and export would have to say so. - **The scene range is load-bearing in the UI.** `raycast` clips to it, the work plane spans it, `frame_volume` frames it, `Bounds` clamps to it. Making it optional is a UX change as much as a storage one. ## Details worth keeping from the proposal - **16³, agreed.** 8³ multiplies map overhead; 32³ means one voxel edit materialises 32 KB. 16³ is 4 KB per dense chunk, which is cache-friendly and cheap to promote. - **Index 0 = empty first; occupancy bitset only if needed.** It is simpler, and index 0 is *already* reserved as air by the `.vox` convention this project follows — so the 256th colour may never be wanted, and the bitset may never be needed. ## Suggested staging Not one change. In this order, each landing on its own: 1. **Chunk-aware bulk writes**, behind the existing API. `fill_box` and friends stop materialising a cell list. Fixes a real limit today, no storage change. 2. **Chunk-level dirty tracking for meshing**, still over dense layers. Fixes the cost that actually grows. 3. **The storage swap itself**, layer by layer, with `get`/`set`/`iter_filled` unchanged at the boundary so the raycaster and region code do not move. 4. **Unbounded canvas**, once storage no longer depends on the scene range. ## Sequencing against the other issues #13 (selection and transform) does not depend on storage and is the biggest user-facing gap — worth doing first regardless. Between this and #14 (objects), this should come first if both are wanted: objects built on dense layers would be rebuilt underneath when chunks land, whereas objects on a chunk grid get cheap aligned transforms for free. From the roadmap discussion. Related: #14, #17.

title: Sparse Volumes for Large Scale 3D Modelling
abstract: Modern emergence of automation in the industry and everyday life is leveraged by extensive research in mobile robotics. Novel 3D sensors such as laser scanners or cameras enable cars to drive autonomously, UAVs to observe critical environments, or an underwater robot to construct pipelines. However, 3D sensor samples do not provide the intrinsic information a robot needs to operate on. Voxel based shape modelling has been identified as a fruitful solution. However, its application is limited to small areas since processing and visualization of large environments is very challenging. Dense voxel grids allow fast data access but suffer from a large memory overhead. Modelling an area of 100x100x100m with a resolution of 1cm would result in a 3.7TB memory requirement. cited.name: Hashed-Octree
ctx: The Hashed-Octree is a sparse voxel representation that combines octrees with hash tables to provide constant-time data access complexity for huge 3D environments, addressing the O(d) access time of standard Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs).

Unlike its siblings which may rely on Morton codes or pointer trees, this method uses a direct hash of coordinate-aligned root keys for top-level access, reducing data access complexity from O(d) to O(db) where db is the depth of internal octrees (typically d=1).
Uses a dense hash map (e.g., google::densehashmap) to store octree root nodes.

title: Storing voxels for a voxel Engine in C++
abstract: I am trying to write a little voxel engine because it's fun, but struggle to find the best way to store the actual voxels. I'm aware I will need chunks of some sort so I don't need to have the entire world in memory, and I'm am aware I need render them with reasonable performance. I read about octrees and from what I understand it starts with 1 cube, and in that cube can be 8 more cubes, and in all those 8 cubes can be another 8 cubes etc. But I don't think this fits my voxel engine because my voxel cubes/items will all be the exact same size. So another option is to just create an array of 16*16*16 size and have that be one chunk, and you fill it with items. And parts where there aren't any items will have 0 as value (0 = air). But I'm afraid this is going to waste a lot of memory and won't be very fast. Then another option is a vector for each chunk, and fill it with cubes. And the cube holds its position in the chunk. This saves memory (no air blocks), but makes looking for a cube at a specific location a lot slower. So I can't really find a good solution, and I'm hoping someone can help me with that. So what would you use and why? But another problem is rendering. Just reading each chunk and sending it to the GPU using OpenGL is easy, but very slow. Generating one mesh per chunk would be better, but that means every time I break one block, I have to rebuild the entire chunk which could take a bit of time causing a minor but noticeable hiccup, which I obviously don't want either. So that would be harder. So how would I render the cubes? Just create all the cubes in one vertex buffer per chunk and render that and maybe try to put that in another thread, or is there another way? Thanks!

It differs from flat arrays by trading O(1) direct access for logarithmic traversal time to save space, and differs from instancing by allowing the culling of hidden faces and merging of coplanar geometry rather than rendering all cubes regardless of occlusion.

cited.name: Surf²f Training and Rendering Pipeline
ctx: Surf²f is a hybrid neural representation that simultaneously learns an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF) and an explicit surrogate surface mesh, unified by a shared neural shader for both volume and surface rendering.
It solves the synchronization and efficiency issues inherent in separate implicit and explicit surface representations by maintaining a parallel dual-stream architecture.

Unlike methods that rely solely on SDF volume rendering or static mesh extraction, Surf²f enables real-time interactive rendering of the extracted mesh while leveraging volume rendering for training stability, outperforming NDS, UNISURF, and NeuS in both geometric accuracy and rendering speed.

title: SurfelNeRF: Neural Surfel Radiance Fields for Online Photorealistic Reconstruction of Indoor Scenes
abstract: Online reconstructing and rendering of large-scale indoor scenes is a long-standing challenge. SLAM-based methods can reconstruct 3D scene geometry progressively in real time but can not render photorealistic results. While NeRF-based methods produce promising novel view synthesis results, their long offline optimization time and lack of geometric constraints pose challenges to efficiently handling online input. Inspired by the complementary advantages of classical 3D reconstruction and NeRF, we thus investigate marrying explicit geometric representation with NeRF rendering to achieve efficient online reconstruction and high-quality rendering. We introduce SurfelNeRF, a variant of neural radiance field which employs a flexible and scalable neural surfel representation to store geometric attributes and extracted appearance features from input images. We further extend the conventional surfel-based fusion scheme to progressively integrate incoming input frames into the reconstructed global neural scene representation. In addition, we propose a highly-efficient differentiable rasterization scheme for rendering neural surfel radiance fields, which helps SurfelNeRF achieve 10× speedups in training and inference time, respectively. Experimental results show that our method achieves the state-of-the-art 23.82 PSNR and 29.58 PSNR on ScanNet in feedforward inference and perscene optimization settings, respectively.11Project website: https://gymat.github.io/SurfelNeRF-web

cited.name: Neural Surfel Radiance Fields
ctx: Neural Surfel Radiance Fields (SurfelNeRF) is an online photorealistic reconstruction method that represents a scene as a dynamic collection of neural surfels, combining explicit geometric attributes with neural appearance features.

Unlike standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) which rely on offline optimization and volumetric sampling, SurfelNeRF progressively integrates incoming image streams into a global model using a differentiable rasterization-based rendering scheme, achieving significant speedups in both training and inference.

It solves the problem of real-time, large-scale indoor scene reconstruction by replacing expensive volume integration with a hybrid rasterization-ray tracing approach that evaluates density and radiance only at surfel intersections.

title: Terrain: binary greedy meshing + packed quads for blocky voxel terrain (#727)
abstract: A second voxel mesher alongside marching cubes, selected per volume via `TerrainComponent::m_VoxelMesher`. Marching cubes stays the right tool for organic isosurfaces and is functionally untouched; this one treats the SDF as solid/empty and merges co-planar visible faces into maximal axis-aligned quads with bitwise operations, drawn instanced from an 8-byte packed record. ## The two deliberate divergences from the reference Ported from `D:\repos\VoxelEngine` (MIT, same stack). Two things are done differently on purpose, each fixing a limitation of the original — both are documented at the code and pinned by tests: 1. **Extents are stored biased-by-one.** The reference masks width/height with `0x1F` unbiased, which is why it documents *"the 2-byte quad encoding cannot express 32³ chunks"*. `VoxelChunk::CHUNK_SIZE` here **is** 32, so the quads that would silently vanish are exactly the largest ones greedy meshing exists to produce (a flat chunk face is the best case). Biasing costs nothing and removes the limitation. Pinned by `VoxelQuadEncoding.FullSpanExtentSurvivesTheRoundTrip`. 2. **Padding is uniform on all three axes** — u64 columns over a 34-bit padded span — instead of padding X/Z in the array dimensions and special-casing ±Y against the neighbour chunk's edge bit (the reference has to, because a u32 column has no room for the two Y padding bits). All six directions then run identical code, which is why the chunk-boundary cases are not a separate bug surface. Pinned by `VoxelGreedyMesherBoundary.EveryAxisCullsAgainstItsNeighbour`. ## Encoding decision 32-bit geometry word, 28 bits used: `x/y/z` 5 bits each, `width-1`/`height-1` 5 bits each, face direction 3 bits, 4 reserved. Material is a **separate** u32 (8 bits used) rather than stuffed into the spare 4 bits — 16 materials is not enough for a terrain palette and the instance stride is 8 bytes either way once the pair is aligned. The bit layout is *derived* from `CHUNK_SIZE`, with a `static_assert` that turns a future chunk-size increase into a loud compile error instead of silent truncation. The chunk origin and voxel size ride the model matrix, which is what keeps the per-quad record at 32 bits. ## Acceptance criteria **1 — substantially fewer triangles at identical silhouette.** Measured, same volume, both meshers: | Terrain | Greedy | Marching cubes | Triangles | Geometry bytes | |---|---|---|---|---| | Rugged noise | 8,469 quads / 16,938 tris / 67,752 B | 31,869 tris / 2,676,996 B | **1.88×** | **39.5×** | | Terraced | 5,342 quads / 10,684 tris / 42,736 B | 27,726 tris / 2,328,984 B | **2.60×** | **54.5×** | Both figures are reported because they behave differently. The **triangle** ratio is entirely terrain-dependent: a high-frequency noise field at coarse voxels gives almost every column its own height, so top faces cannot merge and the mesh is dominated by one-voxel-wide cliff strips — close to the worst case. The **byte** ratio is not terrain-dependent, and it is what the packed-quad encoding actually claims. Silhouette overlap against marching cubes is **0.77 IoU**, measured on the entity-ID attachment. I originally asserted `>4×` on triangles by guesswork and it failed at 1.88×. Rather than tune the threshold to pass, I added the byte measurement and a terraced measurement (the shape a cubic world really has), and set floors well *below* the measured values so the test cannot lie in either direction. **2 — no seams or double-drawn faces at chunk boundaries.** Verified from four angles including one sitting exactly on the `x = 64` chunk-border plane looking straight down it, and one from underneath (−Y faces exist nowhere else in a heightfield volume). Screenshots committed under `OloEditor/assets/tests/visual/VoxelGreedy_*.png`. Also verified live in the editor over MCP against the new sandbox scene, with `olo_shader_errors` returning 0. **3 — meshing runs on the task system.** `VoxelGreedyMeshBuilder` snapshots a padded neighbourhood on the game thread and dispatches the merge to a worker (`Tasks::Launch`, `BackgroundNormal`); the game thread only uploads finished buffers. The snapshot is the thread-safety seam — everything downstream is a pure function of an immutable blob, so a concurrent `CarveSphere` cannot race the mesher. ## Two behaviours gated on the cubic mesher Both are load-bearing and worth arguing with if you disagree: - The voxel volume is **seeded from the height field**. Marching cubes deliberately leaves it sparse (it is a carve-only override there), but a cubic world's voxels *are* the terrain, so there has to be a way to fill the extent. Only an auto-seeded volume is dropped when the mesher switches back; a user-carved one is never touched. - The heightmap surface **stops drawing**, gated on cubic geometry actually existing (not merely on the mesher being selected — the streaming branch never creates `m_TerrainData`, so selection alone would hide the tiles and draw nothing). ## Review guide **Where I'd look hardest** 1. `OloEditor/assets/shaders/include/VoxelQuadUnpack.glsl` ↔ `Terrain/Voxel/VoxelQuad.h` — the same contract (bit layout, face numbering, per-face U/V basis) written twice with nothing linking them. A mismatch compiles, passes every CPU test, and silently transposes/offsets/inside-outs the quads. `VoxelFaceBasisContract.*` pins the C++ half only. 2. `Terrain/Voxel/VoxelGreedyMesher.cpp` `MeshDirection` — the `kWidthIsInnerExtent` table is **not** uniform across the six faces (it follows from the U/V ordering). Getting it wrong does not lose a quad, it transposes one: a 1×8 strip renders as 8×1, which still merges and still draws. 3. `Scene.cpp` — the two gated behaviours above, and `VoxelGreedyMeshBuilder::DispatchDirty`'s neighbour ring (editing one chunk invalidates the six that touch it; rebuilding rather than dirtying them is what stops a cascade). **What I verified, and how** - 28 CPU contract tests. The load-bearing one expands every merged quad back into unit faces and compares that **multiset** against an independently written per-voxel mesher, in both directions plus per-key counts, over 7 volume shapes. A size-only comparison passes on exactly the bug it exists to catch (one face emitted twice, another dropped), and `MeshNaive` shares no code with `Mesh` so a face-culling bug cannot hide behind common code. - Full suite: **6,001 passed / 1 failed / 45 skipped**. The failure is `AssetContentValidity.SandboxAssetRegistryDeserialisesAndPathsResolve`, pre-existing and environmental: it wants generated `Assets/cache/embedded/*.png` files, that path is **gitignored** (0 tracked files), `AssetRegistry.oar` is unmodified by this branch, and the untouched base repo on `master` has the same 0 files, so it fails there identically. - Live editor over MCP on `Scenes/VoxelGreedyMeshTest.olo`: scene opens, 0 shader errors, four poses shot including down a chunk border. **Least confident about** The **Vulkan** path. The three greedy shaders declare the two-stream vertex pull (bindings 57/63) exactly like `Foliage_Instance.glsl`, and the block name at 63 is `OloInstancePull` rather than `OloBonePull` (the backend matches on the binding *number*, not the name — but I have not run it). Vulkan's deferred editor frame is separately known-frozen (#823), so I verified on GL only. If the Vulkan nightly goes red here, that is the first thing to check. **Deliberately not tested** - Deferred/G-Buffer path — the G-Buffer variant compiles and mirrors the forward one, but every screenshot is from the forward path. - Shadow casting from packed quads — `Terrain_VoxelGreedyDepth.glsl` unpacks through the same shared include as the lit shader (which is the point: a divergent depth stage is how peter-panning happens), but I have no shot that isolates a voxel shadow. - Non-32 chunk sizes — the `static_assert` makes that a compile error rather than a silent truncation, which is the intended behaviour, not a tested one. ## Notes for the reviewer - **A pre-existing bug I did not fix:** `Terrain_Voxel.glsl` and `Terrain_Voxel_GBuffer.glsl` (the marching-cubes voxel shaders) decode the triplanar normal map *before* checking whether the array is bound, so an unbound array yields a unit-length `(-1,-1,-1)` that rotates the normal ~55° off true. The greedy shaders had the same defect inherited by copy — it rendered the whole terrain black — and are fixed here; the MC ones are left alone to avoid moving goldens in an unrelated path. Worth a follow-up. - The MCP registry emits `VoxelMesher` as a **clamping** ranged field while both loaders **reject**. An out-of-range MCP write becomes `GreedyCubic` rather than the default. That is generator behaviour driven by `OLO_SERIALIZE(Reject, Min, Max)`; I left it because an MCP write is an interactive editor action with visible feedback, not untrusted disk data. Closes #727 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added Greedy Cubic voxel meshing alongside Marching Cubes. * Added inspector mesher selection with live remeshing and performance statistics. * Added procedural voxel terrain with Stone, Dirt, and Grass materials. * Added optimized instanced rendering and shadow support for voxel meshes. * Added a voxel greedy-meshing test scene. * **Save Games** * Terrain meshing preferences are preserved, with safe defaults for older or invalid saves. * **Documentation & Tests** * Added meshing guidance and automated coverage for geometry, materials, serialization, and visual output.

cited.name: Binary Greedy Meshing with Packed Quads
ctx: Binary Greedy Meshing (BGM) is a surface extraction algorithm that generates maximal axis-aligned quads from a binary voxel volume (solid/empty) by treating voxel slices as bitmasks and greedily expanding rectangles using bitwise operations.

It solves the problem of excessive triangle counts in blocky voxel terrain by merging adjacent visible faces into the largest possible quads, reducing geometry by 1.88×–2.60× in triangle count and up to 54.5× in memory compared to Marching Cubes, while maintaining a blocky aesthetic.
Input: A voxel chunk of size N \times N \times N (typically N=16 or N=32) with block types and a Signed Distance Field (SDF) or height field determining solidity.

ctx: Projected Tetrahedra (PT) is an object-order volume rendering technique that projects volumetric primitives, specifically tetrahedra, onto the 2D image plane to leverage hardware-accelerated rasterization.
It solves the problem of rendering unstructured tetrahedral grids by decomposing each 3D cell into a set of partially transparent 2D triangles, which are then composited in back-to-front order.
Unlike Tetrahedral Volume Rendering, which often relies on ray casting, PT uses explicit geometric projection and scan-conversion.

title: Textured-GS: Gaussian Splatting with Spatially Defined Color and Opacity
abstract: In this paper, we introduce Textured-GS, an innovative method for improving the rendering quality of 3D Gaussian splatting that incorporates spatially defined color and opacity variations using Spherical Harmonics (SH). This approach enables each Gaussian to exhibit a richer representation by accommodating varying colors and opacities across its surface, significantly enhancing rendering quality compared to traditional methods. To demonstrate the merits of our approach, we adapted the Mini-Splatting architecture to integrate textured Gaussians without increasing the number of Gaussians. Our experiments across multiple real-world datasets show that Textured-GS consistently outperforms both the baseline Mini-Splatting and standard 3DGS in terms of visual fidelity. These results highlight the potential of Textured-GS to advance Gaussian-based rendering technologies, promising more efficient and high-quality scene reconstructions. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ZhentaoHuang/Textured-GS.

title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of a Fast Algorithm for Extracting Polygons from Signed Distance Bounds
abstract: Recently there has been renewed interest in signed distance bound representations due to their unique properties for 3D shape modelling. This is especially the case for deep learning-based bounds. However, it is beneficial to work with polygons in most computer-graphics applications. Thus, in this paper we introduce and investigate an asymptotically fast method for transforming signed distance bounds into polygon meshes. This is achieved by combining the principles of sphere tracing (or ray marching) with traditional polygonization techniques, such as Marching Cubes. We provide theoretical and experimental evidence that this approach is of the $O(N^2\log N)$ computational complexity for a polygonization grid with $N^3$ cells. The algorithm is tested on both a set of primitive shapes as well as signed distance bounds generated from point clouds by machine learning (and represented as neural networks). Given its speed, implementation simplicity and portability, we argue that it could prove useful during the modelling stage as well as in shape compression for storage. The code is available here: https://github.com/nenadmarkus/gridhoppin

cited.name: Gridhopping
ctx: Gridhopping is an algorithm for transforming a Signed Distance Bound (SDB) into a polygon mesh by combining sphere tracing (ray marching) with traditional polygonization techniques like Marching Cubes.
It efficiently isolates the O(N^2) cells containing the surface of a shape within an N^3 grid, achieving O(N^2 \log N) complexity.
Unlike standard enumeration which checks every cell, gridhopping uses rays to "hop" over empty space, making it asymptotically faster for large N.

title: Topology, Accuracy, and Quality of Isosurface Meshes Using Dynamic Particles
abstract: This paper describes a method for constructing isosurface triangulations of sampled, volumetric, three-dimensional scalar fields. The resulting meshes consist of triangles that are of consistently high quality, making them well suited for accurate interpolation of scalar and vector-valued quantities, as required for numerous applications in visualization and numerical simulation. The proposed method does not rely on a local construction or adjustment of triangles as is done, for instance, in advancing wavefront or adaptive refinement methods. Instead, a system of dynamic particles optimally samples an implicit function such that the particles' relative positions can produce a topologically correct Delaunay triangulation. Thus, the proposed method relies on a global placement of triangle vertices. The main contributions of the paper are the integration of dynamic particles systems with surface sampling theory and PDE-based methods for controlling the local variability of particle densities, as well as detailing a practical method that accommodates Delaunay sampling requirements to generate sparse sets of points for the production of high-quality tessellations.

cited.name: Dynamic Particle Distribution
ctx: Dynamic Particle Distribution is a particle-based sampling method for isosurface mesh generation that uses inter-particle forces to drive particles to local energy minima, controlling density via a sizing field h and correcting for Euclidean distance approximation artifacts using a contraction factor g.

It builds on Point Engine for Scalar Fields by taking the initial vertex positions and refining them into a uniformly distributed point cloud suitable for high-quality triangulation, rather than outputting a mesh directly.
Unlike Marching Cubes variants which produce fixed topological structures, this method adapts particle density to the local curvature and feature size of the implicit surface.

title: Topology-Caching for Dynamic Particle Volume Raycasting
abstract: In this paper we present a volume rendering technique for the ad-hoc visualization of interactive particle systems. We focus on methods for an efficient spatial caching (topology caching) of particles when applying a raycasting approach. Thus, we get a fast reconstruction of the scalar field which is defined by the particles' entities. The node-cache allows for efficient caching and pre-fetching of a subset of the octree nodes. The influence-cache provides fast access to all particles which contribute to a specific node including level-of-detail particles. Finally, the introduced slab-cache allows for efficient volume rendering and gradient computation. Our algorithms are completely built and managed on the GPU and interactive frame rates for up to several 105 particles are achieved.

cited.name: Topology-Caching for Dynamic Particle Volume Raycasting
ctx: Topology-Caching is a GPU-based volume rendering technique for the interactive visualization of dynamic particle systems (e.g., SPH) that reconstructs a scalar field via raycasting without preprocessing.

It solves the performance bottleneck of gathering particle contributions for field reconstruction by using three GPU-managed caches: a node-cache for accelerated tree traversal, an influence-cache for fast particle access, and a slab-cache for intermediate compositing.

Unlike scattering approaches that cause memory collisions or splatting techniques that require sorting, this method uses a gathering principle with coherent ray packets and stackless traversal to achieve interactive frame rates for hundreds of thousands of particles.

title: Trilinear rendering - diffdrr
abstract: Trilinear rendering - diffdrr Trilinear interpolation Rendering the same view with trilinear interpolation is much faster. The main hyperparameter to control is n_points, which is the number of points to sample per ray. The rendering cost of trilinear interpolation is the same as Siddon's method when n_points is about 2,000 points.

cited.name: Interpolation and Sampling Techniques
ctx: Interpolation and Sampling Techniques constitute the family of methods responsible for retrieving scalar values from discrete voxel grids at arbitrary query positions along viewing rays, thereby reconstructing a continuous scalar field to mitigate discretization artifacts such as aliasing and blockiness.
The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring).
Trilinear interpolation, often referred to as Trilinear rendering, is a widely used technique in volume rendering, particularly for generating Digital Radiographic Reconstructions (DRR).

abstract: A DL architecture aiming to convert voxel model into high resolution SDF representation.

cited.name: Vox2SDF
ctx: Vox2SDF is a neural network pipeline that converts a discrete 3D voxel grid into a continuous Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation.

It solves implicit surface reconstruction from discrete inputs by encoding the voxel structure into a latent vector and decoding it via a position-conditional MLP to predict SDF values at arbitrary 3D points.
Unlike DeepSDF Neural Network, which relies on a global latent code independent of input geometry, Vox2SDF derives its latent code directly from the input voxel grid using a 3D CNN encoder.

title: Twinklebear/webgpu-volume-pathtracer

cited.name: Volume Path Tracing with Delta/Ratio Tracking
ctx: A path tracing method for volumetric rendering implemented in WGSL that uses delta tracking (Woodcock tracking) to sample scattering events and ratio tracking for transmittance estimation.
It renders a 3D volume texture using ray-box intersection and Monte Carlo integration.

It differs from standard path tracing by explicitly separating the sampling of scattering events (via rejection sampling in delta tracking) from the estimation of transmittance (via ratio tracking), allowing for distinct handling of emission and absorption in heterogeneous media.

cited.name: IsoOctree
ctx: IsoOctree is an unconstrained isosurface extraction method that operates on arbitrary octrees by computing the Euclidean Distance Transform (EDT) of an input mesh and adapting the octree to sample this transform.
It solves the problem of generating simplified, adaptive polygonal representations of meshes by refining the octree resolution near the surface and in high-curvature regions.

It sets itself apart from constrained octree methods by allowing arbitrary octree structures (non-conforming) and by operating on the distance field rather than raw scalar voxel data, enabling direct mesh simplification.

title: Unfolding 3D Gaussian Splatting via Iterative Gaussian Synopsis.
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a state-of-the-art framework for real-time, high-fidelity novel view synthesis. However, its substantial storage requirements and inherently unstructured representation pose challenges for deployment in streaming and resource-constrained environments. Existing Level-of-Detail (LOD) strategies, particularly those based on bottom-up construction, often introduce redundancy or lead to fidelity degradation. To overcome these limitations, we propose Iterative Gaussian Synopsis, a novel framework for compact and progressive rendering through a top-down "unfolding" scheme. Our approach begins with a full-resolution 3DGS model and iteratively derives coarser LODs using an adaptive, learnable mask-based pruning mechanism. This process constructs a multi-level hierarchy that preserves visual quality while improving efficiency. We integrate hierarchical spatial grids, which capture the global scene structure, with a shared Anchor Codebook that models localized details. This combination produces a compact yet expressive feature representation, designed to minimize redundancy and support efficient, level-specific adaptation. The unfolding mechanism promotes inter-layer reusability and requires only minimal data overhead for progressive refinement. Experiments show that our method maintains high rendering quality across all LODs while achieving substantial storage reduction. These results demonstrate the practicality and scalability of our approach for real-time 3DGS rendering in bandwidth- and memory-constrained scenarios.

cited.name: Iterative Gaussian Synopsis
ctx: It begins with a full-fidelity model and progressively derives coarser levels through adaptive, learnable pruning of anchors and downsampling of hierarchical grids, ensuring coherent simplification without the error accumulation inherent in bottom-up training.
Unlike bottom-up approaches (e.g., LapisGS) that build coarse layers first and add enhancements, this method derives coarser levels from the full-fidelity model, ensuring inter-layer consistency.
It differs from independent per-resolution models (e.g., Scaffold-GS) by sharing a foundational codebook and grids, extracting all LODs from a single optimization.

title: UNISURF: Unifying Neural Implicit Surfaces and Radiance Fields for Multi-View Reconstruction
abstract: Neural implicit 3D representations have emerged as a powerful paradigm for reconstructing surfaces from multi-view images and synthesizing novel views. Unfortunately, existing methods such as DVR or IDR require accurate per-pixel object masks as supervision. At the same time, neural radiance fields have revolutionized novel view synthesis. However, NeRF’s estimated volume density does not admit accurate surface reconstruction. Our key insight is that implicit surface models and radiance fields can be formulated in a unified way, enabling both surface and volume rendering using the same model. This unified perspective enables novel, more efficient sampling procedures and the ability to reconstruct accurate surfaces without input masks. We compare our method on the DTU, BlendedMVS, and a synthetic indoor dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that we outperform NeRF in terms of reconstruction quality while performing on par with IDR without requiring masks.

cited.name: Unified Neural Implicit Surface and Radiance Field Rendering
ctx: UNISURF is a unified framework for 3D reconstruction that combines the geometric precision of implicit surface rendering with the structural learning capabilities of volume rendering, enabling accurate surface reconstruction from multi-view RGB images without requiring per-pixel object masks.

Unlike standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) which rely on hierarchical two-stage sampling to resolve ambiguities, UNISURF eliminates this need by parameterizing occupancy directly via a continuous field and using a decaying sampling interval around the estimated surface.
This allows the model to render both through the volume (for coarse structure) and directly on the surface (for geometric precision).

title: Unityでボクセルデータからメッシュを生成する方法(Marching Cubes)
abstract: # はじめに ![img.jpg](https://qiita-image-store.s3.ap-northeast-1.amazonaws.com/0/2606983/fce41c6a-a1db-09f5-cd85-5f6c640c97a3.jpeg) [前回の記事](https://qiita.com/GossiperLoturot/items/671ae90dfa0dc8ebacfa)の中でNaiveSurfaceNetsとMarchingCubesとの比較について書きましたが、MarchingCubesの詳細を記述していなかったので、本記事では、前回の記事で使用したMarchingCubesの実装とその説明を書きたいと思います。 # 環境 - OS: Windows11 - CPU: Ryzen 5 3600 3.6GHz 6core - Unity 2023.1 alpha (.net starndard 2.1) # 実装 前回に引き続きボクセルデータのポリゴン化を行います。はじめに書いた通りMarchingCubesと呼ばれる手法でUnity上に実装をします。そして様々なボクセルデータに対する処理時間や頂点数を調べたいと思います。 ## Marching Cubes MarchingCubesはボクセルデータをポリゴン化する手法です。Wikipediaでは[マーチングキューブ法](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/マーチングキューブ法)として詳細まで説明されるなど、NaiveSurfaceNetsと比べて有名な手法であることが分かります。本記事では、[Paul Bourke氏によるMarchingCubesのC言語実装](http://paulbourke.net/geometry/polygonise/)をもとに進めていきたいと思います ### ボクセルデータ ボクセルデータはボクセルの値が実数であるものを使います。負の数が内側、正の数が外側として解釈します。 ### 頂点と面の配置 下図のように立方体上の8つのボクセルの状態(全256通り)に対して、それぞれ頂点と面の配置を定義することでポリゴン化を行います。これは点の配置の回転と状態の反転をもとに下図のような15パターンに単純化されます。 ![figure1.png](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/MarchingCubes.svg/640px-MarchingCubes.svg.png) By Jmtrivial - Own work, GPL, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=1282165 ### 頂点の補間 頂点の位置はボクセルの値をもとに表面を滑らかにするよう位置を補間します。上のように頂点の配置を定めると、頂点は異なる側同士のボクセルからなる辺上に存在します。そして下図のように、その辺上で正負が反転する位置を線形補間によって求め、頂点の位置とします。 ![figure2.jpg](https://qiita-image-store.s3.ap-northeast-1.amazonaws.com/0/2606983/9018838e-ef22-3ca9-2e1a-db30a49b85c9.jpeg) ## ソースコード ```cs // using UnityEngine; // using Unity.Collections; // using System.Text; // using System.Linq; public void Execute(float[] voxel, int size, out NativeArray vertices, out NativeArray triangles) { // 頂点と三角面の配列 余分に確保 var vertexBuf = new NativeArray (size * size * size * 12, Allocator.Temp, NativeArrayOptions.UninitializedMemory); var triangleBuf = new NativeArray (size * size * size * 18, Allocator.Temp, NativeArrayOptions.UninitializedMemory); var vertexCount = 0; var triangleCount = 0; for (var x = 0; x voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 0, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 1, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 2, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 3, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 4, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 5, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 6, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 7, size)]) kind |= 1 ## 結果 実装したプログラムを処理時間と頂点数、三角面数で比較します。処理時間はUnityEditor上でプログラムを10回実行したときの中央値です。 ### ケース1 ボクセルデータのサイズを$32 \times 32 \times 32$、値を$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 − 15^2$としたとき |処理時間|頂点数|三角面数| |-|-|-| |3.2ms|25k|8,360| ### ケース2 ボクセルデータのサイズを$16 \times 16 \times 16$、値を$-1 \le x \le 1$の範囲の乱数としたとき (サイズ$32 \times 32 \times 32$の場合、頂点数がUInt16の範囲を超えます) |処理時間|頂点数|三角面数| |-|-|-| |2.7ms|31k|10k| ### ケース3 ボクセルデータのサイズを$16 \times 16 \times 16$、値を$x + y + z$が$2$の倍数の場合$1$、そうでない場合$-1$としたとき (サイズ$32 \times 32 \times 32$の場合、頂点数がUInt16の範囲を超えます) |処理時間|頂点数|三角面数| |-|-|-| |3.3ms|40k|13k| # 参考 https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/マーチングキューブ法 http://paulbourke.net/geometry/polygonise/

title: Unityでボクセルデータをもとにメッシュを生成する方法(Naive Surface Nets)
abstract: # はじめに ![image.jpg](https://qiita-image-store.s3.ap-northeast-1.amazonaws.com/0/2606983/13447a64-cf75-256f-c988-2fc52b9c2629.jpeg) UnityでAstroneerのような立体的な地形編集を実装しようと思い、ボクセルデータのポリゴン化について調べていたのですが、関連する日本語記事があまり見つからなかったので、私が行った実装と説明を書きたいと思います。 # 環境 - OS: Windows11 - CPU: Ryzen 5 3600 3.6GHz 6core - Unity 2023.1 alpha (.net starndard 2.1) # 実装 実装するにおいてMarchingCubesやMarchingTetrahedraなど様々な手法があります。できるだけ簡単な手法を...と行きたいところですが、それぞれ計算負荷や生成される頂点数などが異なり利点と欠点があります。ゲームに実装すると考えるとできるだけ計算負荷と頂点数が小さくなるものを選びたいです。ということで本記事ではNaiveSurfaceNetsと呼ばれる手法で実装を行いたいと思います。 ## Naive Surface Nets 私はNaiveSurfaceNetsと呼ばれる手法は[mikolalysenko氏のブログ](https://0fps.net/2012/07/12/smooth-voxel-terrain-part-2/)で知ったのですが、仕組みには[元となる論文](https://www.merl.com/publications/docs/TR99-24.pdf)があるそうです。しかし、[mikolalysenko氏のNaiveSurfaceNetsの実装](https://github.com/mikolalysenko/mikolalysenko.github.com/blob/master/Isosurface/js/surfacenets.js)と元となった論文を見ると、かなり異なることがわかります。どうやらmikolalysenko氏によると、もとの論文をそのまま実装すると計算負荷が高くなってしまうようです。本記事ではmikolalysenko氏のNaiveSurfaceNetsの実装をもとに進めていきたいと思います。 ### ボクセルデータ ボクセルデータをもとにポリゴン化を行うわけですが、この時に使うボクセルデータはボクセルの値が実数のものを使用します。そして、ある(整数座標上の)点においてボクセルの値が負の値の場合はその点は面の内側、正の値の場合は面の外側と解釈します。なぜボクセルの値を2値にせずにこのようなことを行うかというと、表面を滑らかにするために頂点を生成する位置を補間できるようにしたいからです。 ### 頂点の生成 下図のように8つの点を含む立方体につき一つの頂点を生成していきます。8つの点がすべて内側またはすべて外側に存在する場合、立方体は面を生成する領域にいないとして頂点を生成することを諦めます。逆に一つでも異なる側の頂点が存在する場合、頂点を生成することとします。 ![figure1.jpg](https://qiita-image-store.s3.ap-northeast-1.amazonaws.com/0/2606983/50d76136-6769-f40d-101e-93d671575848.jpeg) ### 頂点の位置 表面を滑らかにするために、頂点の位置はボクセルデータの実数値をもとに補間したものを使用します。まず、立方体の辺において、下図のように異なる側同士の点でつながっているすべての辺に対して、両端の点の値をもとに正負が反転する位置を線形補間によって求めます。最後に、それらすべての位置の中心を最終的な頂点の位置とすることで頂点の補間が完了します。 ![figure2.jpg](https://qiita-image-store.s3.ap-northeast-1.amazonaws.com/0/2606983/9018838e-ef22-3ca9-2e1a-db30a49b85c9.jpeg) ### 面の追加 下図のように頂点につき最大3つの面を生成していきます。両端が異なる側同士の辺がある場合、その辺と交わるような面を追加できると判定して、面が外側を向くように追加していきます。 ![figure3.jpg](https://qiita-image-store.s3.ap-northeast-1.amazonaws.com/0/2606983/0b201c80-d4c4-0f5e-e9aa-6ae09ecafb53.jpeg) ## ソースコード ```cs // using UnityEngine; // using Unity.Collections; // 使用方法 // var size = 32; // var voxel = new float[size * size * size]; // Execute(voxel, size, out var vertices, out var triangles); // mesh.SetVertices(vertices); // mesh.SetIndices(triangles, MeshTopology.Triangles, 0); // vertices.Dispose(); // triangles.Dispose(); public void Execute(float[] voxel, int size, out NativeArray vertices, out NativeArray triangles) { // 頂点位置->頂点番号を記憶する配列 var idxBuf = new NativeArray (size * size * size, Allocator.Temp, NativeArrayOptions.UninitializedMemory); // 頂点・三角面の配列とその総数。サイズを余分に確保し、最後に不要な部分を切り落とす。 var vertexBuf = new NativeArray (size * size * size, Allocator.Temp, NativeArrayOptions.UninitializedMemory); var triangleBuf = new NativeArray (size * size * size * 18, Allocator.Temp, NativeArrayOptions.UninitializedMemory); var vertexCount = 0; var triangleCount = 0; for (var x = 0; x voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 0, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 1, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 2, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 3, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 4, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 5, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 6, size)]) kind |= 1 voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, 7, size)]) kind |= 1 > p0 & 1) == (kind >> p1 & 1)) continue; // 両端の点のボクセルデータ上の値を取り出す var val0 = voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, p0, size)]; var val1 = voxel[ToIdx(x, y, z, p1, size)]; // 線形補間によって値が0となる辺上の位置を算出して加算 vertex += Vector3.Lerp(ToVec(x, y, z, p0), ToVec(x, y, z, p1), (0 - val0) / (val1 - val0)); crossCount++; } vertex /= crossCount; vertexBuf[vertexCount] = vertex; idxBuf[ToIdx(x, y, z, 0, size)] = vertexCount; vertexCount++; // 面の追加は0 > 1 & 1) != 0 != outside) triangleCount = MakeFace(triangleBuf, triangleCount, v0, v3, v7, v4, outside); // ビットマスクから4ビット目(3の位置の点の状態)を取り出す if ((kind >> 3 & 1) != 0 != outside) triangleCount = MakeFace(triangleBuf, triangleCount, v0, v4, v5, v1, outside); // ビットマスクから5ビット目(4の位置の点の状態)を取り出す if ((kind >> 4 & 1) != 0 != outside) triangleCount = MakeFace(triangleBuf, triangleCount, v0, v1, v2, v3, outside); } idxBuf.Dispose(); vertices = vertexBuf.GetSubArray(0, vertexCount); triangles = triangleBuf.GetSubArray(0, triangleCount); } // v0, v1, v2, v3から構築される面を追加する static int MakeFace(NativeArray triangleBuf, int triangleCount, int v0, int v1, int v2, int v3, bool outside) { if (outside) { triangleBuf[triangleCount ] = v0; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 1] = v3; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 2] = v2; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 3] = v2; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 4] = v1; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 5] = v0; } else { triangleBuf[triangleCount ] = v0; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 1] = v1; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 2] = v2; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 3] = v2; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 4] = v3; triangleBuf[triangleCount + 5] = v0; } return triangleCount + 6; } // 整数座標から配列に入るときの順序を取得 // +X+Y+Z方向に広がる立方体上のi番目の頂点として順序を取得 static int ToIdx(int x, int y, int z, int i, int size) { x += neighborTable[i][0]; y += neighborTable[i][1]; z += neighborTable[i][2]; return x + y * size + z * size * size; } // 整数座標から配列に入るときの順序を取得 // -X-Y-Z方向に広がる立方体上のi番目の頂点として順序を取得 static int ToIdxNeg(int x, int y, int z, int i, int size) { x -= neighborTable[i][0]; y -= neighborTable[i][1]; z -= neighborTable[i][2]; return x + y * size + z * size * size; } // 整数座標から実数座標を取得 // +X+Y+Z方向に広がる立方体上のi番目の頂点として実数座標を取得 static Vector3 ToVec(int i, int j, int k, int neighbor) { i += neighborTable[neighbor][0]; j += neighborTable[neighbor][1]; k += neighborTable[neighbor][2]; return new Vector3(i, j, k); } // 立方体上の頂点の番号の決め方 static readonly int[][] neighborTable = new int[][] { new int[] { 0, 0, 0 }, new int[] { 1, 0, 0 }, new int[] { 1, 0, 1 }, new int[] { 0, 0, 1 }, new int[] { 0, 1, 0 }, new int[] { 1, 1, 0 }, new int[] { 1, 1, 1 }, new int[] { 0, 1, 1 }, }; // 辺のつながり方 static readonly int[][] edgeTable = new int[][] { new int[] { 0, 1 }, new int[] { 1, 2 }, new int[] { 2, 3 }, new int[] { 3, 0 }, new int[] { 4, 5 }, new int[] { 5, 6 }, new int[] { 6, 7 }, new int[] { 7, 4 }, new int[] { 0, 4 }, new int[] { 1, 5 }, new int[] { 2, 6 }, new int[] { 3, 7 }, }; ``` ## 結果 実装したNaiveSurfaceNetsと比較対象として[MarchingCubes](https://qiita.com/GossiperLoturot/items/15750b9c452cdf0fcd73)を処理時間と頂点数、三角面数で比較します。処理時間はUnityEditor上でプログラムを10回実行したときの中央値です。 ### ケース1 ボクセルデータのサイズを$32 \times 32 \times 32$、値を$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 15^2$としたとき ||MarchingCubes|NaiveSurfaceNets| |---|---|---| |処理時間|3.2ms|3.3ms| |頂点数|25k|4,184| |三角面数|8,360|8,364| ### ケース2 ボクセルデータのサイズを$32 \times 32 \times 32$、値を$sinx + siny + sinz + (x^2 + y^2 + z^2) / 8^2$としたとき ||MarchingCubes|NaiveSurfaceNets| |---|---|---| |処理時間|3.2ms|3.6ms| |頂点数|25k|4,295| |三角面数|8,412|8,532| ### ケース3 ボクセルデータのサイズを$16 \times 16 \times 16$、値を$-1 \le x \le 1$の範囲の乱数としたとき (サイズ$32 \times 32 \times 32$の場合MarchingCubesの頂点数がUInt16の範囲を超えます) ||MarchingCubes|NaiveSurfaceNets| |---|---|---| |処理時間|2.7ms|2.2ms| |頂点数|31k|3,338| |三角面数|10k|8,164| # おわりに NaiveSurfaceNetsはMarchingCubesに比べて、処理時間があまり変わらないのにもかかわらず、かなりの頂点数を削減できたことに驚きました。今回のプログラムはC#で記述しましたが、C/C++やRustで記述すれば処理時間もかなり小さくすることが可能かと思います。 # 参考
